Decision:
Adopt option 1: extend the court-case-service domain to include nomsNumber and propagate it through prepare-a-case to the custody endpoint. nomsNumber will be an optional field on the case/defendant identity, populated during the existing person-matching flow and persisted for reuse. We will perform a one-time enrichment when a case/defendant is first matched (using existing identifiers to resolve nomsNumber via authoritative sources) and store it to avoid per-request lookups. Prepare-a-case will pass the persisted nomsNumber when calling prison-api custody endpoints.

To mitigate data gaps and drift:
- If nomsNumber is absent at call time, perform a best-effort on-demand enrichment once, persist the result, and retry the custody call.
- Provide an administrative/background re-enrichment process to backfill existing records and periodically reconcile in cases of identifier merge/split events or known changes.
- Implement a verification path: if prison-api returns not found for a known nomsNumber, trigger a refresh of the mapping before surfacing an error.
- Track provenance and last-verified timestamp to support auditing and targeted revalidation.

This decision minimizes latency and external coupling at request time, reduces failure blast radius from community lookups, and provides consistent identity for downstream custody operations. It accepts a controlled increase to our data model and introduces enrichment/backfill jobs instead of introducing a new runtime dependency on community-api for every custody request.

We will separate concerns by adopting single-responsibility service functions with a transactional outbox.

- The command-handling service function will:
  - Validate and transform the command.
  - Persist the data to Firebase.
  - Append a domain-event record to an Outbox collection/document in the same write operation (transaction or batched write), but will not publish to the messaging topic directly.

- A dedicated broadcaster service function will:
  - Consume new Outbox records.
  - Publish the corresponding messages to the target topic.
  - Mark Outbox records as published (idempotently) to prevent duplicates.

- Each service function will have only one external side effect to test:
  - Command handler: Firebase write (including outbox append).
  - Broadcaster: Messaging publish (and outbox status update).

- Idempotency keys will be included in outbox records to ensure safe retries.
- Failure handling and retries are isolated in the broadcaster, providing at-least-once delivery while avoiding dual-mocking in unit tests.

This decision reduces test complexity, improves reliability of write-then-publish via the outbox, and enforces clear ownership and composition of responsibilities.

Adopt a containerized, code-defined development environment that mirrors production using Docker and Docker Compose, complemented by Dev Containers for IDE parity, and backed by Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform) for consistent service configuration across environments. All application services, dependencies (e.g., databases, message brokers, caches), and supporting cloud services are defined as version-controlled Compose files (with profiles for dev/test) derived from the same Dockerfiles used in production to ensure image parity. Cloud integrations are emulated locally via LocalStack (AWS) and MinIO (S3), with Testcontainers used in automated tests for reproducible integration scenarios. Configuration is centralized through a .env file with sane defaults and developer overrides, and pinned image/tags to guarantee reproducibility.

A devcontainer.json (and containerized toolchain) standardizes local runtime, language versions, linters, and CLIs, enabling one-click onboarding in supported IDEs. Make/NPM scripts (or Taskfile) provide uniform commands (bootstrap, up, seed, test, down, clean). Seed data, migrations, and fixtures are part of the codebase and run deterministically at startup.

Terraform (with per-environment workspaces) defines cloud resources; a dev module mirrors production settings where feasible and aligns names/config with local emulations. CI validates the environment by building images, bringing up the full stack, running migrations, and executing tests to enforce drift detection and prevent configuration rot.

## Decision
Adopt an event-driven CQRS architecture with a denormalized, materialized projection of tides and per-task statuses to power a near real-time, pipeline-like UI.

- Source of truth: Tide and Task lifecycle changes are emitted as domain events (e.g., TideCreated, TaskQueued, TaskStarted, TaskSucceeded/Failed/Cancelled, TaskRetryScheduled).
- Transport: Events are published to a durable message broker (e.g., Kafka/NATS) with keys partitioned by Tide ID to preserve per-tide ordering.
- Projection service: A stateless projector consumes events and maintains:
  - A current-state read model for fast UI queries (per tide, ordered tasks with status, timestamps, attempt count, owner, dependencies, logs pointers).
  - An append-only task status history for drill-down and auditing.
- Storage: PostgreSQL is the primary read store:
  - tides_read (one row per tide incl. aggregate status and progress).
  - tasks_read (one row per task per tide; JSONB for task-specific metadata).
  - task_status_history (timeseries of state transitions).
  - Proper indexes on (tide_id), (tide_id, task_order), (tide_id, task_id, updated_at desc).
- Real-time delivery: A push layer broadcasts incremental updates via WebSockets or SSE. The projector publishes lightweight change notifications to a pub/sub channel; UI clients subscribe by tide_id to receive diffs.
- Consistency and latency: Eventual consistency with target end-to-end latency under 500 ms. Exactly-once effect in projections achieved via idempotent upserts and consumer offset tracking per partition. Out-of-order handling within a tide is mitigated by partitioning; projector also guards with monotonic sequence numbers if present.
- Recoverability: Projections are fully rebuildable by replaying events. Blue/green rebuild supported by swapping read model tables or schemas. Dead-letter and retry policies handle transient failures.
- API: Read model exposed via REST/GraphQL optimized for:
  - Get tide pipeline (ordered tasks, statuses, summaries).
  - Stream updates for a tide (server push).
  - Fetch task status history and latest logs pointers.
- Observability: Metrics for projection lag, update latency, and websocket delivery success; structured logs with tide_id/task_id correlation.

This decision prioritizes fast, scalable reads and real-time UX while keeping writes append-only and projections deterministic and rebuildable.

Adopt CommonJS as the standard module system for all HapiJS plugins and package entry points. Specifically:
- Export plugins using module.exports = { name, version, register }.
- Import internal and external plugins with require(...) rather than ES module default imports.
- Configure package.json with "type": "commonjs" (or omit "type") and point "main" to the CommonJS build output.
- Ensure the TypeScript build targets CommonJS (compilerOptions.module = "commonjs") and emits .js compatible with Node’s require.
- Avoid export default for plugin modules; if ES module interop is needed elsewhere (e.g., utility libraries), use named exports or separate ESM-only files that are not used as Hapi plugins.
- Update documentation and examples to use CommonJS require/module.exports consistently.
- Add lint/build checks to prevent accidental default exports in plugin entry points.
- For consumers in ESM projects, document interop via createRequire or dynamic import with .default fallback, but do not publish an ESM plugin entry to avoid ambiguity.

This decision removes ambiguity between CommonJS and ES modules, aligns with Hapi’s CommonJS expectations, and provides a single, predictable consumption model across all packages.

We will standardize on the ECS-Optimized Amazon Linux 2 (AL2) AMI for all ECS clusters and adopt the Docker overlay2 storage driver. All new capacity will be provisioned with the AL2 ECS-Optimized AMI; legacy ECS-Optimized (devicemapper) hosts are deprecated and will be drained and retired.

Given the single 30GB root volume on AL2:
- The root disk will be reserved for the OS, container images/layers, and logs only.
- Application writable data will be externalized to dedicated storage: per-service EBS volumes (gp3) or instance store (where available) mounted to /var/lib/docker/volumes/<service> or bind mounts, defined via ECS task definitions.
- For workloads with high image churn or large layers, we will increase the root EBS volume size at launch (default 60–100GB) and enforce docker system prune and log rotation.
- We will not rely on loop-lvm/devicemapper options; all host/user-data and configuration scripts will be updated to overlay2 conventions and AL2 paths.

Operationally:
- AMI pipeline, autoscaling launch templates, and golden images will be updated to AL2.
- Monitoring/alerts will track root volume utilization, Docker layer growth, and container log sizes.
- Rollout will be done per cluster with blue/green capacity to avoid disruption; tasks will be drained before host retirement.

Adopt a trait-based composition model in the DSL to define ops from reusable, explicit “facets” instead of inheritance. Each facet (e.g., Transform1In, Pairwise2In, HasAxesArg, HasEpsilonArg) declares inputs/arity, argument schema, constraints, semantic contracts, and doc fragments. Ops declare a set of facets to compose their full interface and behavior; multiple facets are allowed.

Composition rules:
- Additive merge by default; conflicts require explicit override in the op.
- Facet fields are addressable via namespaced bindings and are accessible directly in op definitions and templates.
- Constraints from all facets must hold; ops can strengthen but not weaken constraints without an explicit override.

Documentation and code generation:
- Docs are assembled from facet doc fragments plus op-specific notes; no copy & paste in op docs.
- Code signatures, validators, and client bindings are generated from the composed schema.
- Relationships become explicit: the op’s facet list is emitted into metadata and visualized as a graph.

Governance and migration:
- Deprecate existing base-op inheritance; keep a compatibility adaptor that converts single-inheritance bases into equivalent facets for one release cycle.
- Introduce schemas for facet and op definitions, with CI linting for conflicts, missing docs, and constraint violations.
- Provide a facet library for common patterns (transform, pairwise, reduction, broadcasting, dtype/policy, shape semantics).

This decision reduces repetition, makes relationships explicit, enables multiple “inheritance” via composition, and provides direct access to shared fields.

We will implement export of search results as downloadable files to enable offline use and sharing. Exports will be initiated from the search UI and reflect the user’s current query, filters, and sort order. We will support two formats: CSV (RFC 4180, UTF‑8, with header row) for spreadsheet use and JSON (newline-delimited JSON for streaming) for programmatic use. Initial column/field sets mirror visible columns, with admin-configurable mappings; sensitive fields are excluded by default and only included when explicitly permitted.

Exports run asynchronously via a background job to ensure responsiveness and scalability. Users receive in-app notification and an email (optional) with a time-limited, single-use, pre-signed URL to download. To manage large result sets, we will page through results server-side at export time and enforce a configurable row cap (default 100k rows), with automatic chunking into multiple files and ZIP packaging when necessary. All exports contain a manifest (JSON) describing query parameters, generation time, record count, and schema version for reproducibility.

Security and compliance: exports respect row- and field-level authorization; operations are audited (who, when, what query, counts); rate limits and per-user concurrency limits apply; files are retained for 7 days (configurable) then purged. Data consistency is ensured by using a point-in-time snapshot or versioned read where supported; otherwise we record the time window in the manifest. An API endpoint mirrors this functionality for automation, with the same limits and controls.

Adopt a two-tier kata model for each language feature: an Intro kata for breadth and an Expert kata for depth. 
- Scope: Intro katas prioritize core mental models and typical usage (approx. 80/20 coverage); Expert katas aim for spec-conformant completeness, including edge cases, coercion rules, errors, and interop. 
- Size/time: Intro: 15–30 minutes, 3–6 focused tasks; Expert: 60–120 minutes, multi-stage tasks with increasing rigor. 
- Accuracy policy: No knowingly false statements in any kata. Intro may omit complexities but must not contradict the spec; Expert must reference and align with the latest spec sections. 
- Naming and discoverability: “<Feature> — Intro” and “<Feature> — Expert”, with cross-links and a short “When to choose this” blurb. 
- Content standards: 
  - Intro: minimal API surface, canonical examples, common pitfalls called out at a high level, a single coherent narrative. 
  - Expert: exhaustive behavior matrix, edge cases, error conditions, iterator/protocol interactions, invariants; includes citations and, where feasible, conformance-style tests. 
- Authoring workflow: Start with Intro to validate pedagogy; create Expert once Intro is stable. Refactor existing oversized katas into the two tiers. 
- Review: Intro review emphasizes pedagogical clarity and correctness; Expert review includes spec citation checks and adversarial test coverage. 
- Maintenance: On spec changes, update Expert first, then sync Intro; track with versioned metadata and changelogs. 
- Community feedback: Collect difficulty/clarity signals separately for Intro vs. Expert to inform iteration.

All application services and supporting components will be packaged and deployed as OCI-compliant containers, in line with Hackney’s API Playbook guidance. We will standardize on Dockerfiles with multi-stage builds, minimal/base-hardened images (e.g., distroless or Alpine where appropriate), non-root users, explicit healthchecks, and deterministic, pinned versions. Images will be built and signed in CI, scanned for vulnerabilities, and pushed to a central registry; only passing, signed images are promoted.

Runtime will target the organisation’s container orchestration platform (e.g., Kubernetes/EKS/ECS per environment), with deployment via Infrastructure as Code. Services will be 12-factor compliant: configuration via environment variables, secrets sourced from the approved secret manager, and stateless processes with persistent state held in managed services. Resource requests/limits, liveness/readiness probes, network policies, and autoscaling will be defined per service. Observability will be standardised through container-native logging, metrics, and tracing.

Local development will use containers (Docker/Compose or dev containers) to mirror production. Shared build patterns (base images, builder cache, common entrypoints) and a single CI pipeline template will enforce consistency, reproducibility, and security controls across all services.

Only in exceptional, justified cases (e.g., vendor constraints) may a component run outside containers; such exceptions require explicit approval, documented risk controls, and an integration plan. This decision ensures portability, operational consistency, and compliance with Hackney’s preference for containers across digital services.

## Decision
We will establish a single, authoritative Design Guideline as the source of truth for UX, UI, accessibility, content, and front-end implementation standards, and mandate adherence for all team members and deliverables. The guideline will be versioned, documented, and maintained in a centralized repository with clear ownership by the Design System Guild (cross-functional representatives from Design, Frontend, QA, and Product).

Compliance is required for:
- Visual design (components, spacing, typography, color, motion)
- Interaction patterns and accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA minimum)
- Content style and terminology
- Front-end implementation (design tokens, component library usage, code conventions)

Enforcement will be automated and procedural:
- Design tokens and component libraries are the only approved implementation for UI; custom components require an approved exception.
- Linters, style checkers, and UI snapshot tests in CI/CD will enforce naming, accessibility, and token usage; non-compliance will block merges.
- Design reviews and code reviews will include a guideline compliance checklist; release gates will require sign-off.

Change management:
- Proposals use a lightweight RFC process; the Guild reviews and approves changes.
- Guidelines are semantically versioned; deprecations include migration guides and timelines.
- Breaking changes require communicated upgrade paths and tracked adoption.

Support and accountability:
- Onboarding, playbooks, and examples will be provided.
- Metrics (adoption, exceptions, defect rates) will be tracked; repeated non-compliance escalates to engineering management.
- Temporary exceptions require written justification, scope, and expiry.

Adopt a mature, well-supported DDD library providing standardized building blocks (Entity, ValueObject, AggregateRoot, DomainEvent, Specification, Result/Either, Guard/Validation) and deprecate our custom implementations. We will:

- Select the library via a short evaluation spike (API stability, ecosystem health, documentation, extensibility, performance, license), then pin to a specific version and manage upgrades via dependabot and scheduled maintenance.
- Replace custom base classes and utilities with the library’s equivalents, preserving existing public APIs through thin adapter/wrapper layers where necessary to avoid breaking changes.
- Keep domain logic unchanged; only infrastructural DDD primitives are swapped. Persistence and messaging integrations remain intact, with adapters bridging any differences in ID, equality, and event dispatch semantics.
- Enforce usage via code standards, templates, and linting/architecture rules; block new custom DDD primitives. Extension points must use composition or documented subclassing from the library, avoiding forks.
- Migrate incrementally by bounded context, starting with ValueObjects and Result types, then Entities/Aggregates, then DomainEvents/Specifications. Each step includes contract tests to ensure behavioral parity.
- Provide a compatibility package that maps old types to new ones and mark custom classes as deprecated with a defined removal window.
- Establish a small internal guidance guide and examples, and incorporate library training into onboarding.

Non-goals: reinterpreting domain models, altering business behavior, or introducing cross-context coupling. Success is measured by reduced bespoke code, fewer DDD inconsistencies, and lower maintenance overhead.

Adopt Terraform as the standard Infrastructure as Code tool for the Data Submission Service across all environments and cloud providers. Use Terraform’s provider ecosystem to abstract vendor differences, enabling portability, consistency, and repeatability while avoiding provider-specific templates (e.g., CloudFormation, ARM) and ad‑hoc scripting.

Implementation details:
- Organize configurations using a modular structure (root modules per environment; reusable child modules per component).
- Pin Terraform and provider versions; enforce code formatting and validation (fmt, validate) and static analysis (tflint).
- Manage state remotely with a locked backend (e.g., Terraform Cloud/Enterprise or cloud-native remote state with locking) and per-environment workspaces.
- Store code in a dedicated repository with change control via pull requests, code owners, and CI checks.
- Integrate with CI/CD to run plan on pull requests and apply on protected branches with manual approval gates.
- Use policy-as-code (e.g., Sentinel or OPA/Conftest) to enforce guardrails (tagging, encryption, network rules, cost limits).
- Manage secrets via the cloud provider’s secret manager and Terraform data sources; avoid storing secrets in state where possible.
- Maintain environment parity via variables and module composition; segregate prod and non-prod state and credentials.
- Document modules and usage; provide examples and test with terratest where applicable.

This decision replaces manual scripting and provider-specific IaC for this service.

## Decision
We will incorporate iterative qualitative usability testing as a mandatory part of our UI design and implementation process for the frontend.

- Scope: All new or significantly modified user-facing workflows must undergo at least one round of moderated qualitative usability testing before final approval. High-risk or high-traffic workflows may require multiple rounds.
- Participants: 5–8 representative users per round, reflecting target personas and contexts (including low-bandwidth and constrained devices). Continue testing until issue saturation is reached.
- Method: Moderated remote sessions using realistic tasks and data via interactive prototypes or staging builds. Sessions are recorded (with consent) and time-boxed (30–60 minutes).
- Artifacts: Each study will produce a test plan (goals, tasks, success criteria), facilitator guide, consent script, anonymized notes, and a findings report with severity ratings and recommended changes.
- Outcome criteria: Issues observed in 3+ participants, or rated high/critical severity, must be logged and prioritized before release. Minor issues are tracked for future iterations. Task completion and observed friction guide priority; we do not rely on quantitative scores for go/no-go decisions.
- Integration: Usability testing is part of the Definition of Done for UI-impacting RFCs and PRs. Findings and decisions are linked in the RFC PR (https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-rfc-frontend/pull/15) and stored alongside design artifacts.
- Roles: A facilitator (not the primary implementer) conducts sessions; a note-taker documents observations. Product/design leads triage and prioritize outcomes.
- Ethics & privacy: Obtain informed consent, anonymize data, and store recordings securely with limited access.
- Cadence: Run studies early (prototype), before merge (staging), and post-release as needed for regression and continuous improvement.

Decision
Adopt PEtab as the primary external input and interchange format for Maud, replacing the custom TOML over a staged transition. Maud will introduce an internal canonical model representation; PEtab will be the preferred on-disk interface, with TOML supported temporarily via import/export tools.

- Implement a PEtab reader/writer that maps Maud concepts to PEtab:
  - Model structure via SBML (or PEtab’s model reference).
  - Parameters, bounds, and transformations via PEtab parameter table.
  - Measurements/observables and conditions via PEtab measurement/observable/condition tables.
  - Priors via PEtab’s prior specifications; where gaps exist, use a namespaced PEtab extension column set documented by Maud and upstreamed to PEtab where feasible.

- Provide a lossless TOML→PEtab→internal conversion path and a best-effort PEtab→TOML exporter for backward compatibility.

- Introduce schema validation in CI for PEtab inputs and deprecate TOML as follows:
  - Phase 1 (immediate): Dual support with converters and documentation.
  - Phase 2 (after two minor releases): Warn on TOML usage; PEtab examples become canonical.
  - Phase 3 (after four minor releases or when automation pipeline is ready): Remove TOML support.

- Ensure interoperability with automated data generation pipelines: ingest model structure from SBML/3D-GEM sources, experimental data from measurement outputs, and priors from preliminary analyses into PEtab-compliant tables.

- Document the mapping, extensions, and versioning policy; pin supported PEtab versions and provide migration scripts when PEtab evolves.

Success is defined by: reduced input complexity and file length, easier onboarding through a standard format, compatibility with existing PEtab tooling, and a clear path to fully automated input generation with minimal manual trimming.

Adopt an event-driven, serverless data processing pipeline on AWS to eliminate VM provisioning and idle cost. Use S3 as the ingestion point; S3 ObjectCreated events will trigger processing. Implement processing stages as AWS Lambda functions (packaged as container images if needed) and orchestrate them with AWS Step Functions for clear control flow, retries, and observability. Persist intermediate work items in SQS to decouple bursts and enable horizontal scaling. Index results into Amazon OpenSearch Service (managed Elasticsearch-compatible) using VPC access where required.

Operational guarantees:
- Automatic scale-to-zero when idle; scales up on new data arrival.
- Built-in retries, exponential backoff, and DLQ via SQS for poison messages.
- Idempotent processing using object versioning and content hashes to prevent duplicate indexing.
- Concurrency limits and batch sizing tuned to OpenSearch index throughput to avoid overload.
- End-to-end tracing and metrics via CloudWatch and X-Ray.

Constraints and fallbacks:
- If a processing step exceeds Lambda limits (memory/runtime), run that step on ECS Fargate, invoked from Step Functions, while keeping the rest in Lambda.
- Use infrastructure as code (e.g., CDK/Terraform) to define S3 notifications, IAM roles, VPC networking, Step Functions state machines, and alarms.
- Employ least-privilege IAM and encryption at rest/in transit for S3 and OpenSearch.

This decision prioritizes minimal operational overhead, cost efficiency for periodic workloads, and straightforward integrations limited to S3 and OpenSearch without managing servers.

Implement layered brute-force mitigation for the specified endpoints (Actor Login, One Time Passcode, Viewer Code) using edge and application-level controls:

- Edge (WAF/CDN/API Gateway):
  - Path-scoped IP rate limiting and burst control for the targeted endpoints.
  - Automated temporary IP blocking on anomaly spikes; support for deny/allow lists (e.g., office IPs, monitoring).
  - Optional bot/automation heuristic where available; no CAPTCHA at edge.

- Application:
  - Redis-backed atomic counters (sliding window + token bucket) keyed by:
    - Actor Login: per-username/email, per-IP, and combined (username+IP).
    - One Time Passcode: per-session/reference and per-IP.
    - Viewer Code: per-viewer-code and per-IP.
  - Thresholds and actions (configurable via env/feature flags):
    - Soft threshold: introduce exponential backoff (e.g., +1s, +2s, up to 30s) and require additional friction (e.g., secondary challenge) where UX allows.
    - Hard threshold: temporary block (e.g., 15 minutes) on the identifier and/or IP; escalate lock duration on repeated cycles (e.g., 15m → 1h → 24h).
    - Global IP hard cap to catch distributed attempts per IP across identifiers.
  - Responses:
    - Use generic error messages to avoid account/code enumeration.
    - During backoff: 401/403 with delayed response.
    - During hard block: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After.
  - Resets:
    - Successful authentication/validation resets counters for that identifier.
    - Counters expire via TTL (e.g., 30–60 minutes).
  - Observability and operations:
    - Structured audit logs of failed attempts, blocks, and resets (without sensitive data).
    - Metrics and alerts for threshold breaches and block rates.
    - Admin override endpoint to unblock identifiers/IPs with audit trail.

This decision prioritizes per-identifier protection to limit credential stuffing efficacy, per-IP controls to curb abuse, preserves UX for legitimate users, and remains configurable without code changes.

Adopt UITestablePage as the single standardized interface for defining and exposing accessibility identifiers across the app. All new UI screens, components, and flows must implement UITestablePage for their test IDs. Existing mechanisms (e.g., hardcoded identifiers, ad hoc extensions, legacy AccessibilityIdProvider) are deprecated and must be replaced during ongoing feature work or when touching affected code.

Scope and enforcement:
- Mandatory for all feature teams on new or modified UI code.
- Introduce a lint/checkstyle rule and CI guard to flag non-compliant identifier definitions.
- Update code review checklists to require UITestablePage adoption.

Migration:
- Phase 1 (immediate): Add UITestablePage to shared UI module, provide base helpers and mapping utilities; document naming conventions and patterns.
- Phase 2 (rolling): Replace legacy identifiers opportunistically per feature and during refactors; add shim adapters to bridge old identifiers to UITestablePage where necessary to keep tests green.
- Phase 3 (cleanup): Remove deprecated providers and unused identifiers after adoption reaches ≥90%; delete shims.

Naming and conventions:
- Define a canonical, stable naming scheme within UITestablePage to ensure deterministic, platform-agnostic test IDs.
- Prohibit dynamic or content-derived identifiers except when explicitly supported by the interface.

Backward compatibility and risk:
- Maintain a temporary compatibility layer to avoid breaking existing automated tests.
- Any exceptional cases require an approved ADR variance with a deprecation plan.

Definition of Done:
- All relevant components implement UITestablePage.
- Lint passes with no violations.
- Automated tests updated to consume UITestablePage identifiers.
- Documentation and examples published in the developer guide.

Adopt and enforce inclusive, human-centered terminology across all project artifacts. We will replace terms with historical, racial, gendered, ableist, or violent connotations and avoid idioms that may exclude or harm. This applies to source code identifiers, APIs, database schema, infrastructure, UI text, logs, metrics, alerts, docs, commit messages, and release notes.

Preferred replacements (non-exhaustive):
- whitelist/blacklist → allowlist/denylist
- master/slave → primary/replica or leader/follower (context-dependent)
- master branch → main
- kill/terminate → stop/end
- sanity check → quick check/smoke check
- dummy → sample/example
- grandfathered → legacy exception
- native (when ambiguous) → built-in/first-class

Implementation and governance:
- Establish a project terminology guide with approved alternatives and rationale; maintain it in-repo.
- Enable linters/CI checks and code review templates to flag discouraged terms in code and documentation.
- Provide language-agnostic utilities (e.g., spellcheck dictionaries) and editor configurations to assist contributors.
- Require inclusive terminology compliance for new and modified code (“on-touch” updates). Avoid mass renames unless risk is low and automated.
- Rename the default branch to main and update automation, CI, and documentation accordingly.

Backward compatibility:
- For public APIs and schemas, introduce inclusive aliases, mark old terms as deprecated, and provide migration guides.
- Use non-breaking database migrations (views/synonyms) where feasible; schedule breaking changes for major versions with clear timelines.
- Wrap or document third-party dependencies that use excluded terms; prefer inclusive alternatives when selecting new vendors.

Support and exceptions:
- Offer contributor guidance and training resources; encourage questions in reviews.
- Define a lightweight exception process for unavoidable uses (e.g., quoting standards), requiring justification and documentation tags.

This decision is effective immediately and will be revisited periodically to expand the glossary and refine enforcement.

We will retire the overloaded term “environment” from CNP infrastructure and Jenkins library APIs and replace it with a canonical, explicit vocabulary and types. All public functions in the Jenkins shared library will accept and propagate clearly named fields instead of a single env/environment argument.

Adopted canonical concepts and names:
- deploymentEnvironment: Logical stage of software lifecycle (e.g., dev, test, staging, prod).
- subscriptionId: Azure subscription GUID.
- tenantId: Azure AD tenant GUID (when relevant).
- region: Azure region (e.g., uksouth).
- platformTarget: Concrete platform location for workloads (e.g., aksCluster + namespace, or appServicePlan).
- resourceGroup: Azure resource group name (when relevant).
- application: Logical application/service identifier (e.g., serviceName).
- version: Build/deploy artifact version or tag.

Library API change:
- Introduce a typed/context map named deploymentContext with the above keys. No function may accept a parameter named environment/env.
- Validate deploymentContext at boundaries (missing/unknown keys fail fast).
- Existing APIs will gain new overloads using deploymentContext and mark old environment/env parameters as deprecated with deprecation warnings.

Migration plan:
- Phase 1: Add deploymentContext and dual-path compatibility shims; document mapping from legacy environment to explicit fields.
- Phase 2: Update pipelines and templates to pass deploymentContext; introduce linting to forbid new uses of environment/env.
- Phase 3: Remove deprecated parameters and shims after one release cycle.

Governance:
- Publish a glossary and examples in the library docs; require code review to enforce the canonical names.
- Provide helper builders (e.g., ctxFromAzure(subscriptionId, region, platformTarget, ...)) to reduce boilerplate.

Outcome:
- Eliminates semantic ambiguity, reduces bugs, and enables multiple deploymentEnvironments per subscription (and vice versa).
- Improves readability, testability, and flexibility for future targets without overloading a single “environment” variable.

Use upstream Yocto layers as pinned Git submodules and isolate project-specific changes in a dedicated meta-company overlay layer.

- Add third-party layers as Git submodules under a /layers directory, pinning each to an explicit commit (not branches) to ensure reproducibility.
- Maintain a lockfile-like manifest (e.g., .gitmodules plus a layers.yaml) that records exact revisions and layer priorities, consumed by CI to assemble the build environment deterministically.
- Create and own a meta-company layer for all customizations via .bbappend, configuration fragments, and recipes that depend on upstream layers without modifying them.
- Establish an update policy: periodically fast-forward submodules to upstream stable tags or LTS branches after CI validation; urgent security updates may advance only the affected layer.
- Avoid forking third-party layers by default. Fork only when upstream is unmaintained or a required change cannot be reasonably carried as a .bbappend/.cfg; any fork must track upstream remotes and carry a minimal patch delta with a merge-back plan.
- Enforce CI gates: consistency checks (layer compatibility, Yocto release), license scans, and reproducible builds on the pinned revisions.
- Document layer versions and compatibility in release notes; changes to submodule SHAs are treated as dependency updates and follow change control.

We will replace the monolithic frontend/get_translations with a parameterized translation API that supports selective retrieval by area and domain, and we will correct the modeling of integration titles to reduce payload size.

- Introduce frontend/translations(languages, areas, domains, include_config_flow=false)
  - areas: subset of {title, config, options, device_automation, state}
  - domains: explicit list of domains to fetch; when empty, only core/UI strings are returned
  - include_config_flow: when true, automatically include all integrations that expose a config flow for the requested areas (typically config/options); when false, only currently loaded integrations are considered
- Define a new area “title”; move localized titles from config.title into title. Titles that do not require translation must be omitted from strings and sourced from manifest.json. Only products with localized branding retain a title in strings.
- Keep platform-specific state translations (e.g., strings.sensor.json merged into sensor) but return them only when area includes state and the relevant domain is requested.
- Default client behavior: request only what is needed for the current view (e.g., title + config for a single integration’s config flow; state only for domains displayed with textual states).
- Backward compatibility: retain frontend/get_translations for one deprecation cycle, mapping to the new API with areas={title,config,options,device_automation,state}, include_config_flow=true, domains=loaded+config-flow. Mark as deprecated and remove after two stable releases.
- Performance and caching:
  - Support ETag/If-None-Match keyed by (language, area set, domain set, include_config_flow) to enable incremental caching per client.
  - Enable gzip/brotli compression on responses.
  - Version translation bundles per integration to allow clients to cache per-domain/area shards.
- Tooling and validation:
  - Add CI lint to forbid non-localized titles in strings and require manifest title usage instead.
  - Add migration script to move config.title to title where translations are retained; strip titles where manifest suffices.

This decision reduces average payload size by scoping requests to needed areas/domains, removes unnecessary titles from translation files, and aligns titles with their proper source of truth while preserving compatibility during the transition.

## Decision
Define service boundaries using Domain-Driven Design with bounded contexts as the primary decomposition unit. Establish domains and subdomains via collaborative Event Storming and capability mapping, then align each service to a single bounded context with clear ownership of aggregates, data, and domain events. Prioritize high cohesion and low coupling, with contracts derived from business capabilities and ubiquitous language.

Adopt a “start larger, evolve smaller” approach: initially implement a modular monolith or a small set of macroservices per bounded context; split only when driven by evidence (e.g., independent scaling needs, divergent change cadence, cross-team contention, or persistent coupling friction). Avoid premature fine-grained decomposition.

Codify service sizing and split/merge criteria:
- One bounded context per service or tightly-related capabilities; no cross-context data ownership.
- Stable, business-relevant event boundaries; minimize cross-context synchronous calls.
- Independent deployability and operability (observability, on-call).
- Team alignment (Conway’s Law) and manageable cognitive load.

Standardize event contracts and governance:
- Contract-first events with versioning, schema registry, idempotency, and backward compatibility.
- Event catalog documenting producers, consumers, and ownership.
- Naming conventions and clear semantic rules for domain vs. integration events.

Define transactional boundaries via aggregates and sagas; prefer asynchronous choreography across contexts, with orchestration only where business invariants require it. Protect boundaries with anti-corruption layers at integrations.

Introduce architectural fitness functions and telemetry to guide evolution (e.g., change frequency, dependency analysis, runtime coupling, lead time). Review decomposition quarterly and at major domain shifts.

This decision reduces over-/under-splitting risk by anchoring boundaries in domain models, delaying irreversible fragmentation, and using measurable signals and governance to safely evolve service granularity in an event-driven architecture.

Standardize health signaling across all services by implementing two mandatory, lightweight health interfaces and wiring them to the orchestrator’s probes:

- Liveness: Expose an endpoint that returns success if the process is running and the service’s internal event loop is responsive (e.g., HTTP GET /health/live, or gRPC Health Checking Protocol “SERVING”). It must not depend on external systems to avoid cascading restarts. Failures here allow the orchestrator to restart the container.

- Readiness: Expose an endpoint that returns success only when the service can accept traffic (e.g., HTTP GET /health/ready, or gRPC “SERVING” for specific service names). It may include critical dependency checks (e.g., DB connectivity) and configuration validation. Failures here remove the pod from load balancers without restarting it.

Implementation requirements:
- Provide libraries/templates in each supported language to ensure consistent semantics and responses (HTTP 200/503, minimal payload with service name, version, build SHA, and timestamp).
- Configure probe policies per service with sensible defaults: initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, successThreshold, failureThreshold.
- Keep handlers fast (<50 ms) and resource-light; no I/O in liveness; bounded, cached checks in readiness.
- For non-HTTP services, use the gRPC Health Checking Protocol; for other protocols, provide an exec/TCP alternative.
- Container images must declare probes; CI enforces presence and correct wiring.
- Optional /health/startup may be used for long inits; prefer Kubernetes startupProbe when applicable.

We will standardize on hapi as the default Node.js web framework for new backend services and major service rewrites. Hapi’s plugin-based architecture and convention-rich approach provide better modularity, clearer ownership boundaries (per plugin/route set), and reduced risk of route and middleware conflicts across larger teams compared to express.

Actions:
- Adopt @hapi/hapi as the service framework and @hapi/joi (or successor) for request/response validation.
- Provide a company boilerplate and shared plugins for auth, logging, metrics, configuration, error handling, and health checks to ensure consistency and accelerate delivery.
- Define routing, validation, auth, and error-handling standards using hapi plugins and server extensions, avoiding ad-hoc per-route middleware patterns.
- Establish testing patterns using integration-first tests against the hapi server instance.
- Update developer onboarding and documentation to reflect hapi conventions and shared modules.
- Create CI templates that include linting, security scanning, and contract testing tailored for hapi services.

Migration and exceptions:
- Existing express services may be maintained; migrate opportunistically during significant feature work or refactors when cost-effective.
- Any new service choosing a different framework requires an explicit architecture review and approval, with documented justification (e.g., hard real-time constraints or specialized runtime needs).

This decision aims to improve team scalability, service consistency, and operational reliability through standardized, modular service construction.

## Decision
Establish a CCS Common Security Control Baseline (CSCB) as the mandatory, reusable set of security controls for all CCS-delivered services, aligned to the HMG Security Policy Framework (SPF) and underpinned by NCSC’s Cyber Assessment Framework (GovAssure) and the NCSC Cloud Security Principles. The CSCB will:

- Define a minimum, policy-compliant baseline for services at OFFICIAL (and overlays for OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE and above as required).
- Provide standard overlays for contextual risks (e.g., citizen data, payment processing, critical national infrastructure interfacing), enabling risk-based tailoring without divergence from SPF.
- Include authoritative mappings to departmental and supplier-specific security profiles to demonstrate equivalence, reducing duplication and bespoke assurance burden.
- Recognize shared responsibility and inherited controls from underlying platforms and SaaS, with clear inheritance guidance and evidence requirements.
- Mandate common assurance artifacts (e.g., SoA, risk register, DPIA, supply chain assurance, vulnerability and configuration management, incident response, business continuity), with evidence structured for reuse across procurements.
- Adopt a standardized control catalog format and interoperable data model (e.g., OSCAL) to enable automated assurance, continuous compliance monitoring, and evidence portability.
- Require independent assessment aligned to GovAssure where applicable, with continuous control monitoring for high-criticality services.
- Be governed centrally by CCS with versioning, change control, and a published deprecation/transition policy; departments retain the right to request overlays for specific threats/regulatory obligations.
- Be a contractual requirement in CCS procurements and framework agreements, with compliance attestation and remediation timelines.

This decision creates a single, SPF-aligned security control language and assurance pathway that can be uniformly applied across HMG, while allowing controlled, risk-based extensions to meet department-specific needs without recreating bespoke profiles.

Adopt a repository-scoped documentation model with a centralized website for cross-cutting content.

- Scope and placement:
  - Each product/tool maintains its own docs in its GitHub repo under /docs (e.g., sdk/docs, hub/docs, lotion/docs). These include guides, API/reference, tutorials, upgrade notes, and changelogs specific to that repo.
  - The website hosts non-repo-specific content: FAQs, whitepapers, conceptual overviews, Cosmos background, product comparisons, and ecosystem-wide guides.
  - The website “Docs Portal” will serve as a navigation hub that deep-links to repo docs; no duplication of repo docs on the website.

- Versioning:
  - Docs versioned per repo release tags; latest is default, with a version switcher where supported.
  - Breaking changes and migration guides live alongside versioned docs in each repo.

- Ownership and governance:
  - Each repo’s CODEOWNERS own its docs. PRs to code and docs follow the same review policy.
  - A shared docs style guide and templates (Getting Started, Concepts, How-to, Reference) enforced across repos.

- Tooling and CI:
  - Standardize on a common docs toolchain per repo (e.g., Markdown + static site generator) with CI for link checking, linting, and preview builds.
  - Central search on the website indexes repo docs for unified discovery.

- Cross-linking:
  - Use canonical URLs and relative links within repos; cross-repo links use permanent URLs to versioned pages.
  - Website provides curated entry points and topic maps that route users to the correct repo docs.

- Migration and deprecation:
  - Audit existing SDK documentation; relocate non-SDK materials to the website and product-specific content to its respective repo.
  - Implement URL redirects for moved pages to preserve external links.

- Success criteria:
  - Clear separation of concerns, reduced maintenance overhead, cohesive navigation from the website, reliable versioning, and measurable improvements in discoverability and contributor workflow.

We will containerize all application services with Docker and treat images as immutable, versioned artifacts. Images will be built via multi-stage Dockerfiles to produce small, secure runtimes (rootless where possible) and pushed to a private container registry with semantic version tags and a moving latest tag for non-production only. Configuration and secrets will be injected at runtime via environment variables and/or mounted secrets, keeping images environment-agnostic; persistent data will reside on managed volumes.

Deployments will be orchestrated (Kubernetes preferred; Docker Compose for local) using declarative manifests/Helm charts. Updates will follow rolling or blue-green strategies to achieve zero/near-zero downtime, gated by readiness/liveness probes. Image pull policies and tag pinning will ensure controlled rollouts; production will reference immutable version tags, with progressive delivery (canary) used when appropriate.

The CI/CD pipeline will build, scan, sign (SBOM + sigstore/cosign), and push images; it will then apply environment-specific manifests, performing health-checked rollouts with automated rollback on failure. Automated update agents (e.g., Renovate) will open PRs for base image and dependency refreshes; we will not auto-update running containers outside the orchestrator.

Security hardening (minimal base images, non-root user, read-only filesystem, restricted capabilities) and runtime resource limits will be enforced. Observability (structured logs, metrics, traces) will be standardized to monitor deployments and update outcomes.

Adopt TOML (v1.0) as the canonical configuration format for stentor.

We will standardize on a single file named stentor.toml located at the project root by default, with optional overrides via a CLI flag and environment variables. TOML is purpose-built for configuration, offers stricter and more predictable parsing and typing out of the box, and avoids YAML’s implicit type coercions and punctuation/indentation pitfalls. TOML’s nested tables and arrays provide sufficient expressiveness for our expected hierarchical structures while remaining readable and easy to review in code. Its deterministic syntax simplifies validation, error reporting, and diffing in CI.

Implementation details:
- Parse using a well-maintained TOML 1.0 library.
- Enforce a defined schema with explicit typing and required/optional fields; fail fast on unknown keys and type mismatches.
- Support comments in config while keeping the parser strict (no implicit conversions).
- Provide clear, minimal examples and a template stentor.toml.
- Allow environment variable overrides with explicit mapping rules and precedence (env > CLI > file > defaults).
- Optionally provide a one-time migration/convert command for users with existing YAML, but do not support YAML at runtime.

This decision prioritizes predictability, safety, and maintainability while preserving human-friendly editing and sufficient nesting capabilities.

We will implement the frontend in TypeScript (strict mode) targeting modern browsers, transpiling to JavaScript via a standard build pipeline. TypeScript is selected to improve correctness, maintainability, and developer velocity through static typing, superior IDE support, and safer refactoring, while remaining fully interoperable with the JavaScript ecosystem.

Scope:
- All new frontend code will be authored in TypeScript (.ts/.tsx).
- UI framework choice remains decoupled; this decision supports React/Vue/Svelte/vanilla.
- Shared frontend types may be generated from backend schemas (e.g., OpenAPI/GraphQL) to enforce end-to-end type safety.

Standards and tooling:
- ECMAScript modules, target ES2020 (or as required by supported browsers).
- tsconfig with strict type checks (noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, noUncheckedIndexedAccess).
- Vite (or equivalent) for dev/build; ESLint + TypeScript ESLint + Prettier for lint/format.
- Path aliases for modularity; incremental builds + source maps for DX.
- Typed testing (Vitest/Jest) and Storybook with TS support.

Interoperability and migration:
- Existing JavaScript modules may be incrementally migrated; .d.ts shims for untyped libs.
- NPM/Yarn/PNPM allowed; Node LTS required.

Non-goals:
- This decision does not mandate a specific UI framework or CSS solution.

Risks and mitigations:
- Learning curve: provide starter templates and lint rules.
- Type churn: adopt pragmatic typing guidelines and shared utilities.

Review:
- Reassess annually or upon major ecosystem shifts.

We will use Rails ActiveStorage for image upload, processing, storage, and delivery for the link_platform logo feature.

- Scope: Handle user-uploaded logos (PNG, JPG, SVG with safeguards), generate constrained variants (thumbnail, medium), store in S3 in production (local in dev/test), support direct-from-browser uploads, and serve via CDN.

- Rationale: ActiveStorage is the Rails-standard, well-maintained, and tightly integrated with ActiveRecord (our chosen ORM). It provides minimal setup, built-in direct uploads, variant processing, backgrounding, and first-class support for S3/GCS/DO Spaces. It reduces custom code and maintenance risk compared to rolling our own or adopting a more customizable but heavier abstraction.

- Implementation decisions:
  - Services: S3 (prod/staging) with private buckets and signed URLs; local disk (dev/test).
  - Processing: image_processing gem with libvips for fast, safe variants; disallow rasterization of SVGs (store as-is, validate content type/size).
  - Uploads: Direct uploads via ActiveStorage’s JS or UJS, with background variant generation through ActiveJob.
  - Validation: Use active_storage_validations (content type, size) plus server-side verification to prevent spoofing; virus scanning via ClamAV or provider-integrated scanning if required.
  - Delivery: Use CDN in front of S3; cache-control headers for variants; purge on detach.
  - Query performance: Use includes/preload on attachments to avoid N+1; limit number of variants and attachments per record.

- Trade-offs: Accepts extra join/queries compared to table-per-attachment approaches; mitigated with eager loading. Ties us to ActiveRecord, which is aligned with our stack.

- Revisit criteria: If we require advanced resumable/parallel multipart uploads, cross-ORM support, or complex multi-store routing, evaluate Shrine.

Adopt Clean Architecture with strict separation of concerns and dependency inversion:

- Structure the system into four layers: Domain (entities, value objects, domain services, domain events), Application (use cases/interactors, input/output ports, orchestrating business rules), Infrastructure (frameworks, databases, external services, repositories, adapters), and Presentation (UI, MVVM/MVC/MVI depending on platform).
- Invert dependencies toward the Domain and Application layers using interfaces; Infrastructure provides implementations (e.g., Repository, Gateway, MessageBus adapters).
- Define stable contracts:
  - Domain models are persistence-agnostic and immutable where feasible.
  - Application layer exposes use case APIs returning DTOs/Result types; no UI or persistence types leak across boundaries.
  - Presentation consumes use cases via an injected façade; state/view-models map DTOs to UI models.
- Enforce module boundaries at build time (separate packages/modules) and via code ownership. No cross-layer imports except inward.
- Use a DI container to wire interfaces to implementations, enable testing with fakes, and support environment-specific Infrastructure.
- Data mapping is explicit: mappers/assemblers convert between domain entities, DTOs, and UI models; avoid anemic domain by keeping invariants in entities/value objects.
- Handle errors via typed results or exceptions mapped at boundaries; propagate domain errors as meaningful codes/messages to UI.
- Organize features as vertical slices within the layers (feature modules) to localize changes and scale teams.
- Testing strategy: Domain and Application are unit-tested heavily; Presentation uses component tests; Infrastructure relies on integration/contract tests.
- Coding standards: pure functions where possible, side effects isolated to Infrastructure, eventing for cross-cutting concerns, and logs/metrics at boundaries.

Adopt a strict no-modification-on-access policy for KeySet: all structural mutations (including hash rebuilds) must occur during explicit mutation phases (e.g., kdbGet, kdbSet, ksAppend) and never during read-only operations (e.g., ksLookup, iteration). kdbGet must return a complete, lookup-stable KeySet with all keys and auxiliary structures (hashes) fully built, ensuring deterministic, side-effect-free access thereafter. No lazy or on-demand default value calculation is permitted during access; defaults must be fully resolved by plugins during kdbGet or via explicit pre-processing steps, such that lookups never trigger key creation, metadata alteration, or rehashing. If a requested key is absent post-kdbGet, accessors return “not found” without attempting fallback computation. This decision guarantees predictable performance, thread-safety for read phases, reproducible behavior, and simpler reasoning about system state. It also imposes requirements on plugin authors: any enrichment (e.g., defaults, cascading merges) must be completed by the end of kdbGet, and plugins must not perform hidden mutations during read APIs. Failure to meet these constraints is treated as a contract violation.

- Automate ingestion of nightly Syndication and POMI ETL outputs into profiles-db via a CI/CD pipeline triggered on ETL completion (or nightly schedule fallback).
- Introduce a two-phase load with a staging schema: load and validate into staging, then atomically promote (schema swap or view switch) to production on success to avoid downtime.
- Implement a data validation gate comprising schema/contract checks, referential integrity, uniqueness, required fields, domain/value ranges, incremental diff checks, record counts, and anomaly detection thresholds; block promotion and alert on failure.
- Use idempotent, transactional upserts with checksums/watermarks to support partial retries and ensure consistency.
- Version each dataset load (timestamp + ETL run ID), persist lineage/metadata, and expose current version via an endpoint/metric for observability and rollback.
- Provide automated rollback to last known good dataset by reverting the schema/view pointer if validation or post-promotion smoke tests fail.
- Decouple data refresh from application redeploys: profiles-db runtime remains static; only data changes via the pipeline/migration jobs.
- Publish and enforce a machine-readable data contract (eg, JSON Schema/Avro) with producers; validate artifacts before load and fail fast on breaking changes.
- Add monitoring and alerting (load status, validation results, row deltas, latency, error rates) and dashboards; notify on-call via standard incident channels.
- Implement access controls and secrets management for pipeline-to-DB connectivity; audit all loads and promotions.
- Provide a manual approval step for exceptional cases and the ability to run ad-hoc replays/backfills with the same validation gates.
- Document runbooks and codify the pipeline as code (eg, GitHub Actions/Argo Workflows/Terraform) to ensure repeatability and traceability.

Implement a cluster-wide TaskManager backed by shared coordination and persistence to provide homogeneous task orchestration across nodes.

- Introduce a distributed TaskRegistry persisted in a shared data store (e.g., Cassandra/SQL) as the single source of truth for task definitions, status, history, and metrics. All task state transitions are recorded centrally.
- Use a distributed work queue (e.g., RabbitMQ/Kafka/SQS) as the submission and dispatch mechanism. All nodes publish tasks to the queue; worker executors on each node consume from the queue.
- Assign globally unique TaskIds at submission time. Enforce ownership leasing with heartbeats to prevent concurrent execution and to enable failover (lease expiration triggers reassignment).
- Standardize task lifecycle: submitted -> scheduled -> running -> completed/failed/cancelled with explicit retry policy and backoff. Support at-least-once execution; require idempotent task handlers.
- Provide cluster-wide APIs/CLI to submit, list, inspect, cancel, and rerun tasks regardless of the originating node. All reads query the shared registry; writes go through the queue and registry transactionally where applicable.
- Implement execution isolation and fairness via configurable worker pools, priorities, and per-task-type concurrency limits. Support node-level capacity advertisement and dynamic scaling.
- Ensure observability with centralized logs, progress updates, per-task metrics, and audit trail in the registry; emit events on state changes.
- Handle node failures with lease-based recovery, in-flight task requeueing, and deduplication tokens. Support graceful shutdown/drain to minimize disruption.
- Maintain backward compatibility: node-local scheduling APIs delegate to the distributed manager. Provide a migration path to move existing tasks into the shared registry.
- Secure the system with authenticated API access, per-tenant scoping where applicable, and encryption-in-transit for queue/registry traffic.

We will standardize on using the language-native dependency manager for each codebase (e.g., npm/pnpm/yarn for Node.js, Maven/Gradle for Java, pip/Poetry for Python, Cargo for Rust, Go modules for Go, etc.) and require reproducible builds via pinned versions and committed lock files. All projects must:

- Use the canonical tool for their language and commit the lockfile to version control.
- Pin direct dependencies and constrain transitive updates via lockfile updates only.
- Route all dependency resolution through a centralized repository manager (e.g., Nexus/Artifactory/GitHub Packages) that proxies public registries, caches artifacts, enforces license policies, and enables offline builds.
- Integrate automated dependency update tooling (e.g., Renovate or Dependabot) to propose version bumps with CI validation.
- Enforce security and compliance: enable vulnerability scanning on dependency graphs, configure blocklists/allowlists, and require human review for high-risk updates.
- Produce a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) during CI for every build and sign artifacts where supported.
- Cache dependencies in CI to accelerate builds, with deterministic cache keys based on lockfiles.
- Document and version any overrides, mirrors, or vendored dependencies; vendoring is permitted only with explicit approval and rationale.
- Define update cadence: patch updates auto-merged after green CI; minor updates reviewed weekly; major updates planned and tracked.
- Apply reproducibility checks in CI (e.g., checksum/lockfile drift detection) and fail builds on unmanaged changes.

This decision centralizes dependency management, improves security and compliance, and ensures consistent, repeatable builds across environments while minimizing manual effort.

Adopt a first-class, CI-agnostic “Release” construct in sfpowerscripts to standardize how artifacts are assembled, versioned, promoted, and deployed across all CI/CD platforms.

Key elements:
- Introduce a release definition (release.yaml) describing artifacts (packages, dependencies), environments, sequencing, pre/post hooks, approvals, and changelog scope.
- Provide new CLI surface: sfp release create (assemble artifacts via fetch and stamp manifest), sfp release changelog (generate notes from last successful release), sfp release promote (move release across environments), and sfp release deploy (execute deployment plan).
- Standardize a release bundle format containing: manifest.json (version, commit SHA, source branch, timestamps, environment matrix), artifact references with integrity hashes, dependency graph, and changelog.
- Use semantic versioning (with optional build metadata) and annotate VCS with signed release tags for traceability.
- Persist release bundles in pluggable artifact stores (e.g., Azure Artifacts, GitHub Packages, S3, Nexus) via an abstracted publisher interface; store minimal release index locally and remotely for discovery.
- Ensure idempotent, resumable deployments with dry-run, policy gates, and rollback hooks; approvals and gates integrate via CI but are orchestrated by the release plan.
- Maintain backward compatibility: keep existing fetch/deploy/changelog commands; internally route through the Release orchestration path and deprecate direct usage on a published timeline.
- Provide cross-platform execution via the CLI and Node API without reliance on CI-native “release” features; emit machine-readable logs/annotations and optional telemetry.
- Include supply-chain safeguards: checksums, optional signing, and provenance metadata embedded in the manifest.

We will support reading streams within the same transaction that calls loadStream() by introducing a transaction-scoped stream handle (TransactionalStream) that is bound to the transaction context.

- loadStream() returns a TransactionalStream whose lifecycle is tied to the transaction; it cannot escape the transaction boundary and is automatically closed on commit/rollback and on retry aborts.
- Reads are only permitted while the transaction is active; attempting to read after commit/rollback throws an error.
- The stream observes a consistent snapshot for the duration of the transaction; deletions or changes outside the transaction trigger a read conflict that aborts the transaction, ensuring atomicity when writes depend on read data.
- Retries re-acquire the stream transparently; all previously created stream handles are closed during retry to prevent resource leaks.
- Resource and latency controls: enforce maximum read time per transaction, backpressure-aware chunked reads, and configurable limits on total bytes read to keep transactions bounded.
- API contracts and static/runtime guards prevent passing the stream outside the transaction scope.
- Observability hooks will record stream open/close events and bytes read per transaction for leak detection and tuning.

This decision ensures retry safety, resource hygiene, and transactional consistency for stream-based workloads.

Decision: Consolidate CI/CD into programme clusters and retire the separate tools cluster. Deploy Concourse inside each programme cluster and use it for both CI and CD. Eliminate Flux-based deployment (and our fork) by implementing the same git-commit signature verification via existing Concourse resources. Concourse will integrate with Kubernetes authentication; each Concourse Team maps 1:1 with a Kubernetes Namespace, inheriting RBAC for least-privilege access. Concourse workers and pipelines run in-cluster using namespace-scoped service accounts; no external credentials or shared kubeconfigs will have cluster-modifying permissions.

Pipeline and cluster configuration lives in Git per team/namespace, with Concourse watching branches and applying state to the cluster. Concourse UI becomes the primary source of deployment visibility and audit. Where required, supporting components (e.g., image scanning, Notary, registry cache/proxy) will be deployed per programme cluster or consumed as managed/shared services without requiring cross-cluster credentials.

Security and multi-tenancy will be enforced via Kubernetes RBAC, NetworkPolicies, ResourceQuotas/LimitRanges, Pod Security controls, and worker isolation (e.g., dedicated worker pools, node selectors/taints). Observability will be standardized with cluster-native logging/metrics/tracing for Concourse and pipelines.

Implementation will proceed per cluster: deploy Concourse, bootstrap teams/namespaces, migrate pipelines from Flux, validate signature verification, and cut over. Upon successful adoption, decommission Flux (including our fork) and the separate CI tools cluster components. Success is measured by improved deployment visibility, reduced cross-cluster configuration, removal of external write credentials, and simplified operations with a single control plane per programme cluster.

Adopt PostgreSQL (v15+) as the primary database and use its native full‑text search augmented with Hunspell-based Czech support. We will:

- Install Czech Hunspell dictionaries (czech.aff, czech.dic) on all database nodes and create an ispell dictionary and a custom Czech text search configuration (tsconfig) wired to those dictionaries.
- Use language-aware FTS per record: persist a language code and maintain a generated tsvector column per text field using the corresponding tsconfig (Czech, English, etc.). For languages without a custom dictionary, use appropriate Snowball stemmers or simple dictionaries.
- Create GIN indexes on the tsvector columns for fast search; use GIST/pg_trgm indexes on raw text for fuzzy matching and typo tolerance where needed.
- Normalize input with unaccent and ICU collations for proper tokenization and sorting; ensure consistent ICU locale settings across environments.
- Expose query patterns via to_tsquery/plainto_tsquery for exact/stemmed search and pg_trgm-based similarity for suggestions/autocomplete. Prefer websearch_to_tsquery for user-entered queries.
- Handle mixed-language content by either selecting tsconfig per field from stored language metadata or building composite tsvector columns (weighted) when content spans multiple languages.
- Validate dictionary coverage and stemming quality for Czech content as part of CI/CD migrations; monitor GIN index bloat and schedule periodic reindexing/vacuum as needed.
- Keep the schema and queries search-engine-agnostic: encapsulate search in DB views/functions to allow future migration to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch if recall/precision requirements outgrow PostgreSQL FTS.

This decision meets the requirement for robust multilingual full‑text search with strong Czech support while keeping a single operational datastore. It balances relevance, performance, and operational simplicity, and preserves an exit path to a dedicated search engine if needed.

Decision:

Rufus will provide explicit, compiler-enforced visibility and export controls at both package and module levels to guarantee encapsulation:

- Default visibility is private. Identifiers are not visible outside their declaring module unless explicitly exported.
- Module-level export lists: Each module declares an explicit export block enumerating public types, constants, and functions. Only exportable, immutable interfaces are allowed; implementation details remain inaccessible.
- Package manifest exports: A package manifest contains an explicit exports section listing which modules are public. Non-exported modules cannot be imported by external packages.
- Visibility modifiers: public (visible to any package), internal (visible only within the same package), and private (module-local). No “friend” or cross-package exceptions.
- Opaque types: Support for opaque/abstract type declarations that expose a type’s name and operations while hiding its representation, enabling information hiding across module and package boundaries.
- Controlled re-exports: Modules may re-export selected public identifiers from other public modules, preserving a curated public surface without exposing sources’ privates.
- Reflection constraints: Reflection and introspection APIs are restricted to public surfaces; no bypass of visibility constraints is allowed.
- Tooling alignment: Documentation generators, API diffing, and semantic versioning analysis operate solely on the public API (manifest exports + module export lists). Linters flag unused or accidentally public identifiers.
- Binary/source boundaries: Compiled artifacts include only the public interface metadata; private symbols are not link- or import-addressable across packages.

These facilities ensure that users can import only declared public modules and access only explicitly exported identifiers, while authors retain strict control over internal structure and evolution.

Adopt ETag-based optimistic locking with the If-Match precondition for all mutating operations on versioned resources.

- Every GET of a single resource returns a strong ETag representing the exact stored state (derived from an incrementing version or content hash; no weak ETags). The ETag changes on any persisted modification.
- All PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests must include If-Match with the latest known ETag. Requests without If-Match are rejected with 428 Precondition Required.
- If the If-Match ETag does not match the current resource ETag, the server rejects the request with 412 Precondition Failed and returns a problem payload containing a meaningful message, the current representation, and its current ETag to enable the client to reload and reapply changes.
- For create operations, no If-Match is required. For bulk or batch updates, each entity must include its own If-Match; if any mismatch occurs, the server responds with 412 detailing conflicted items without applying partial unintended updates (apply-all-or-none unless explicitly designed otherwise).
- ETag generation is deterministic and cheap (e.g., version number or lightweight hash of persisted fields). Store a version column to avoid recomputing full hashes and to ensure atomic increments within the same transaction.
- Caches remain safe: clients may use ETags for conditional GETs (If-None-Match), but writes enforce If-Match.
- Rollout: introduce ETags on reads first; then enforce 428/412 on writes after client updates.
- Document response shapes, error codes, and client recovery flow; provide SDK helpers to propagate and require ETags automatically.

Adopt 1Password as the canonical, human-accessible store for development secrets via a shared “EASi Dev Secrets” vault.

- Scope: Local development and manual testing secrets only. Runtime/infra secrets for deployed environments continue to live in their respective systems (e.g., AWS SSM/Parameter Store); when needed for local dev, their current values are mirrored in 1Password.
- Access: Grant vault access to the EASi engineering group with least-privilege roles; owners are the Platform/Infra team. Offboarding removes vault access immediately.
- Structure and naming: One item per secret with fields for ENV_VAR_NAME, value(s) per environment (if applicable), source-of-truth location (link), rotation/expiry date, last-verified timestamp, and notes. Item titles must match the ENV var name to simplify discovery.
- Usage: Engineers retrieve secrets using the 1Password desktop/mobile apps or browser extension. Power users may use the 1Password CLI, but it is optional. Secrets must not be shared via email, Slack, or committed to repositories.
- Rotation workflow: When a secret rotates, the owner updates the 1Password item immediately, sets last-verified and expiry fields, and posts a heads-up in the team Slack channel with a link to the item. If rotation is detected elsewhere (e.g., SSM), the same process applies.
- Auditing and hygiene: Quarterly review of vault contents for validity and access. Archive superseded items instead of deleting to preserve history. Enable 1Password auditing features for access logs.
- Developer ergonomics: Provide sample .env templates referencing the item names. Document how to copy values safely and how to use the optional CLI for scripting.

This balances security, a single source of truth, ease of use, and minimal friction for engineers to stay current with rotating secrets.

Adopt a single-label-per-ml-aoi policy. Each ml-aoi Item must link to exactly one STAC Label Item and must copy the essential label metadata such that the ml-aoi Item is also a valid STAC Label Item. This ensures first-class compatibility with existing STAC label tooling, simplifies consumer logic (no catalog crawling or meta-label synthesis), and enables predictable, efficient training pipelines. Multi-class use cases are supported via an explicit preprocessing step that merges multiple source labels into a single composite STAC Label Item per ml-aoi (e.g., via unioned FeatureCollections or a derived label asset bundle). Producers are responsible for this merge; consumers can then operate uniformly over single-label ml-aoi Items.

To minimize friction:
- Provide a reference preprocessor to compose multiple label sources into a single Label Item per ml-aoi.
- Encourage publishing derived ml-aoi collections that materialize common multi-label combinations.
- Enforce the rule via JSON Schema/validation (exactly one label link with required metadata mirrored).

We defer native multi-label on ml-aoi to a possible future extension (e.g., ml-aoi-multilabel) if strong demand emerges, preserving backward compatibility while keeping the core spec simple and performant today.

We will extend the service to support communal defects by introducing a first-class Location model with two types: Property and CommunalArea. Defects must reference exactly one Location.

- Property locations reference a canonical property identifier and address metadata. We will resolve and persist external identifiers where available (Property API ID, UPRN) and cache the display address for resilience. We will not integrate with the Repairs API.

- CommunalArea locations are scoped to a user-maintained Scheme and capture the minimum viable data needed for contractors to find the fault: scheme name, optional block/core/level/landmark descriptors, map coordinates if supplied, free-text location description, and access instructions. Where a communal area is clearly associated with a known addressable point (e.g., a shared entrance), we will optionally capture a UPRN to improve downstream reuse, without requiring a complete hierarchy.

To decouple from fluctuating hierarchies, all reads/writes of external property/address data will go through a LocationGateway abstraction. Initially, the gateway will:
- Use the Property API for property lookups and identifiers.
- Use no external source for communal hierarchy; Schemes are created/maintained in the service by the New Builds Team.

We will design the Location schema and outbound events to be provider-agnostic and reusable by other services:
- Stable internal LocationId and SchemeId.
- Normalized external identifiers (PropertyApiId, UPRN), when known.
- Structured fields for access info and geo/human-readable descriptors.
- Versioned event payloads to support future enrichment.

Non-goals:
- We will not attempt to define or enforce a universal hierarchy (estate/scheme/block/core) now.
- We will not duplicate a master source of property/addresses.

Migration path:
- When the Addresses API becomes the strategic source of truth, we will switch the LocationGateway to it, backfilling UPRNs/addresses for existing records where possible. Internal IDs remain stable; external identifier mappings are updatable.

This decision enables immediate support for communal defects and high-quality contractor location/access data, while minimizing coupling and technical debt, and preserving a clear path to align with a future authoritative address hierarchy.

We will extend the bindings API to explicitly support bi-directional operations by introducing an operation contract and capability discovery, while maintaining backward compatibility.

- Add an operation field to binding invocation requests to declare intent. Define an enum OperationType with values: Out (default, current behavior), In (read/receive), and InOut (bi-directional). For granular semantics, an optional action string (e.g., "get", "put", "delete", "list") may further qualify the operation per binding.

- Default operation to Out when omitted to preserve existing behavior. Requests specifying In or InOut must be validated against the binding’s advertised capabilities.

- Introduce binding capability discovery: bindings declare supported operations and actions via metadata (e.g., capabilities: ["Out:put", "In:get", "InOut:copy"]). The runtime rejects unsupported combinations with a clear error.

- Define a consistent response contract for In and InOut:
  - data: payload or resource bytes (e.g., blob content)
  - metadata: key/value map for headers/properties (e.g., content-type, etag, length)
  - status: standardized code and message for transport-agnostic handling
For Out, responses remain optional and map to status/metadata only.
