- Versioning: release as a backward-compatible minor API version (e.g., v1.1). Older clients omitting operation continue to function. Servers advertising capabilities must tolerate clients without capability probing.

- Transport parity: apply the same request/response shapes across HTTP and gRPC. Document the canonical JSON/proto fields for operation, action, data, metadata, and status.

- Security and policy: enforce per-binding authorization on In and InOut operations, and allow policy-based restriction of actions (e.g., disallow "list").

- Telemetry: tag traces/metrics with operation and action for observability.

This decision enables explicit, safe bi-directional binding use cases (e.g., get blob) without breaking existing integrations.

## Decision
Adopt a standardized, human-readable, and machine-parseable GitHub repository naming convention using lowercase kebab-case with a consistent structural pattern:

Pattern:
<domain>-<product>-<component>-<artifact>[-<qualifier>...]

Rules:
- Allowed characters: a–z, 0–9, hyphen (-). No underscores, spaces, dots, or camelCase.
- domain: Primary business or platform domain (e.g., payments, identity, data, platform).
- product: Product or program/initiative name (e.g., checkout, merchant, analytics).
- component: Logical unit (e.g., api, web, worker, cli, batch, ingestion).
- artifact: Type of repository (svc, lib, app, infra, ops, doc, demo, template).
- qualifier (optional, repeatable): language/runtime/cloud/provider when necessary (e.g., go, js, k8s, lambda, aws, gcp). Avoid environment or region in names; use branches, directories, or GitHub environments instead.
- Experimental work must be prefixed with exp- and follow the same structure (e.g., exp-data-ml-featurestore-lib-py).
- Archived repositories must be prefixed with archived- and made read-only.
- Templates must be prefixed with template- and include a short artifact descriptor (e.g., template-svc-go).
- CI/CD, IaC, and ops repos use artifact=infra or ops and may include a narrow scope qualifier (e.g., platform-delivery-infra-terraform, data-lake-ops-k8s).
- Monorepos, if approved, must use artifact=mono and a concise domain/product scope (e.g., platform-devex-mono).
- Names should be ≤50 characters when feasible; abbreviate consistently if needed.
- Enforce via repository creation workflow checks; document exceptions in ADRs linked from repo descriptions. Add GitHub topics for env/region/classification metadata instead of encoding them in names.

We will adopt a unified, structured logging strategy and API across the codebase and deprecate all ad-hoc logging/printing.

- Introduce a lightweight logging facade with macros: ELEKTRA_LOG_TRACE, ELEKTRA_LOG_DEBUG, ELEKTRA_LOG_INFO, ELEKTRA_LOG_WARN, ELEKTRA_LOG_ERROR, and ELEKTRA_LOG_FATAL.
- Provide zero-cost abstractions: TRACE/DEBUG code is compiled out unless ELEKTRA_ENABLE_LOGGING is set; arguments are lazily evaluated inside macros to avoid runtime overhead when disabled.
- Enforce consistent, structured, single-line output by default (JSON Lines): fields include timestamp (UTC ISO-8601), level, component/module, file:line, function, message, error_code (if any), and optional key=value context pairs. Human-readable format may be selected at runtime.
- Runtime configuration via KDB and environment variables: ELEKTRA_LOG_LEVEL, ELEKTRA_LOG_FORMAT (json|text), ELEKTRA_LOG_DEST (stderr|file|syslog|journald), ELEKTRA_LOG_FILE, ELEKTRA_LOG_COMPONENTS (include/exclude lists), ELEKTRA_LOG_CONTEXT (enable file:line/function). Defaults: INFO, json, stderr.
- Standardize message content: short, action-oriented English sentences; no secrets or PII; stable message IDs (e.g., ELK-XXXX) for diagnostics; include error codes and relevant keys. Avoid multiline logs.
- Provide component tags (e.g., “kdb”, “plugin/<name>”, “tools/<name>”) for filtering. Include correlation IDs when available to tie operations across modules.
- Backward compatibility: existing logging calls are deprecated and replaced via mechanical refactoring; a compatibility shim is provided for one release cycle.
- Tooling and governance: add CI linting to forbid printf-style output in production code; supply a formatter helper for key/value context; document usage guidelines with examples; enable sampling for high-volume TRACE.
- Platforms: default to stderr; integrate with syslog/journald when available; thread-safe implementation.

This decision makes logs consistent, useful as living documentation, and efficient by default.

Adopt styled-jsx as the default approach for component styling. Co-locate styles with components using <style jsx> to ensure scoping and prevent class/name collisions. Avoid BEM or other naming conventions for component-scoped styles; reserve BEM only for unavoidable global CSS.

- Default: write scoped styles within each component via styled-jsx.
- Global styles: allowed only for app-wide resets, typography, design tokens, and third‑party systems (e.g., GOV.UK). Load these once at the app root (e.g., _app) and wrap any necessary overrides with :global.
- Design tokens: define CSS variables in a global :root and consume them in styled-jsx for consistency and theming.
- Reuse/composition: prefer extracting shared UI into components over sharing classes. Avoid deep selector chains.
- Dynamic styling: pass props into styled-jsx templates as needed; avoid runtime style mutations that bypass React.
- GOV.UK integration: import the GOV.UK stylesheet globally; author minimal, explicit :global overrides to integrate with our components.
- Performance: keep component styles minimal and colocated; remove unused global CSS.
- Accessibility: ensure global resets and typography respect GOV.UK guidance and WCAG. Do not override focus styles without providing accessible alternatives.
- Enforcement: add linting/PR checks to (a) flag use of :global in styled-jsx without justification, (b) discourage new ad-hoc global stylesheets, and (c) encourage colocation near components.
- Migration: new code uses styled-jsx by default; legacy global CSS may remain temporarily but should be reduced incrementally.

This decision standardizes on scoped, colocated styles to minimize clashes, while permitting controlled global CSS for shared foundations and third‑party frameworks.

Adopt layered configuration with explicit support for environment variables and command-line flags overriding file/default configuration.

- Precedence: command-line flag > environment variable > config file > built-in defaults.
- Scope: flags and env vars may set any documented configuration key; unknown keys are rejected with a clear error.
- Naming: environment variables use upper snake case with prefix APP_ (e.g., APP_DB_HOST), mapping 1:1 to config keys; booleans accept true/false/1/0; lists use comma-separated values unless otherwise documented.
- Discovery: all flags are discoverable via --help; a command prints the effective configuration with sensitive values redacted; provide a sample config and an env var reference.
- Validation: unified schema validation after merge; type conversion occurs before validation; failures are fatal with actionable messages.
- Immutability: configuration is loaded once at startup; hot-reload is out of scope for now.
- Security: discourage sensitive values via flags; allow secrets via environment variables or external secret providers; redact secrets in logs and diagnostics; support APP_CONFIG_FILE to point to a file path but do not allow inline secret material in flags.
- Determinism: overrides are explicit; we log the source for each effective setting at debug level for traceability.
- Portability: behavior aligns with 12-factor principles to ease container/orchestration use.
- Backward compatibility: changes to keys or semantics follow a deprecation window with warnings when overridden keys are used.

This decision enables flexible deployments without code changes while retaining predictability, observability, and security.

We will implement a multi-tenant, hierarchical role-based access control (RBAC) model with five primary actor types and explicit tenancy boundaries:

- Instance administrators (Marsha admins): Full control over the Marsha instance and global configuration. No default access to tenant content.
- Consumer site integrators (Consumer site admins): Manage the linkage and integration settings for their consumer site(s) within an instance. No default access to organization content unless explicitly granted.
- Organization managers: Manage organizations within a consumer site, including author accounts, groupings, and sharing policies across authors within the same organization and with other organizations when explicitly allowed.
- Authors: Create and manage their own media assets within their organization. Access to other authors’ assets only via explicit shares or organization-level policies.
- Viewers: End users who consume media. Access is limited to published assets or assets shared with them via signed access mechanisms.

Tenancy model and scoping:
- Organizations are the primary tenant boundary under a consumer site. All content and author identities are scoped to an organization.
- Cross-organization sharing is opt-in and controlled by organization managers with auditable grants.
- Consumer site boundary enforces isolation of organizations across different sites.

Authentication and authorization:
- Authentication is performed by either the Marsha instance (for instance administrators) or delegated to consumer sites for organization managers, authors, and viewers.
- Consumer sites issue signed tokens (e.g., JWT) conveying user identity, organization, and role claims; Marsha enforces authorization via RBAC policies scoped to those claims.
- Viewers receive time-bound, least-privilege access via signed playback tokens/URLs.

Operational considerations:
- Every action is auditable with actor, scope, and resource.
- Default-deny; privileges are additive via role assignment and explicit shares.
- Fine-grained permissions evolve under the RBAC model without changing actor taxonomy.

We will provision one dedicated, organization-controlled mailbox per AWS account, created automatically during account provisioning, using a deterministic, collision-free naming scheme: <account-alias>.<12-digit-account-id>@aws-root.example.com. The subdomain aws-root.example.com is reserved exclusively for AWS root-user email and has no catch-alls or mailing lists.

Mailboxes are non-human identities managed in our corporate IdP, not in third-party email silos. Access is SSO-only with phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 security keys), no passwords, no shared credentials, and no auto-forwarding. Each mailbox is assigned to a small break-glass access group; access is granted JIT via approved workflow, time-bound, and fully audited. All mailbox authentication, access, and configuration changes are logged centrally and retained per compliance policy.

Creation, validation, and lifecycle (suspend/close on account decommission) are automated to ensure control and avoid drift. Uniqueness is guaranteed by including the AWS account ID; operators cannot override the pattern. SPF/DKIM/DMARC are enforced on the domain; inbound filtering allows AWS sender domains while blocking bulk/unsolicited mail. No mailing lists or shared inboxes are permitted.

This design ensures exclusive purpose use, strong and uniform security aligned with our AWS controls, clear principal attribution, and eliminates collisions and operator error.

Persist all game records in PostgreSQL as the system of record, using an append-only, event-centric model optimized for reporting. Core decision points:
- Model game activity as immutable fact tables (e.g., game_events, game_sessions) with strict timestamps and surrogate keys, and normalize reference data into dimension tables (players, games, devices, regions) to ensure data integrity and reuse.
- Enforce ACID transactions, foreign keys, and check constraints; prohibit in-place updates/deletes of facts—apply corrections via compensating events for full auditability.
- Implement time-based partitioning on large fact tables (e.g., by day/week) for performance, maintenance, and data lifecycle management.
- Create a reporting-oriented star schema via database views and materialized views over the normalized OLTP structures, with pre-aggregations for high-traffic metrics (e.g., DAU, retention, session length, revenue).
- Index on common reporting dimensions (player_id, game_id, session_id, event_type, occurred_at, region) and use covering/partial indexes where beneficial; maintain generated columns for canonicalized values when needed.
- Use schema versioning via migrations and additive evolution; allow optional attributes using typed columns first, with JSONB only for sparse/extensible fields, coupled with generated columns for indexable metrics.
- Separate PII into a restricted dimension with keys only in facts; apply row-level security where required.
- Expose change data via CDC (e.g., logical replication/Debezium) to feed downstream BI/warehouse if needed, keeping PostgreSQL as the authoritative source.
- Establish retention and archiving policies per partition to control storage while preserving reporting accuracy.

Adopt a split deployment architecture for Snippets Service:

- Production snippet-serving instances will be stateless redirectors that perform URL manipulation and issue redirects to CloudFront-backed S3 bundle URLs. They will not run the Django application and will have no dependencies on database or cache services.
- A dedicated Snippets Admin environment will run the Django application with required database and cache backing services to pre-generate bundles and publish them to S3. Admin will be the sole writer to the S3 bucket; production instances will not require S3 access.
- Remove all support for pre-ASR Snippets and the legacy on-the-fly bundle generation code paths from the production serving tier.
- Update deployment and infrastructure definitions to:
  - Eliminate DB/Cache resources and related networking from production snippet-serving instances.
  - Restrict IAM and network policies so only Admin can write to S3; CloudFront serves bundles from S3; production instances only handle redirects.
  - Enable versioned, immutable bundle publishing to S3 to simplify rollbacks.
- CI/CD will build and validate bundles in Admin, then publish to S3; production deployments become configuration-only with zero app/runtime migrations.
- Monitoring will focus on redirect health for production and bundle generation/publish success for Admin.

This decision reduces operational complexity and cost for production serving, isolates risk to the Admin path, and ensures continued delivery of bundles even if Admin is unavailable.

We will adopt explicit API versioning with the following policy:
- Introduce URI-based major versioning (e.g., /api/v1/…), freezing current behaviour as v1. All breaking changes will only be released under a new major version (v2, v3, …).
- Use semantic versioning for releases of each major line. Minor versions are strictly backwards compatible and may introduce additive, optional fields and endpoints. Patch versions are limited to backwards-compatible bug fixes and non-functional changes.
- Provide version metadata in responses via an API-Version header and publish an OpenAPI specification per major version under a stable, versioned URL and tagged release.
- Maintain at least one previous major version concurrently for a defined window (minimum 6 months) after the release of a new major, subject to security and operational constraints.
- Implement a formal deprecation process: announce deprecations in release notes and public changelog; include Deprecation and Sunset headers on affected endpoints, with a minimum 90-day notice before removal; provide migration guidance.
- Prohibit breaking changes within a major version (including removing or renaming fields, changing semantics, status codes, or contracts). Newly added fields will be optional and defaultable; ordering of fields is not significant.
- Require all consumers (in-house and third parties) to pin to a major version in the base URL and to validate against the corresponding OpenAPI contract.
- Establish an approval and communication gate for any change that impacts external contracts, including API review and scheduled announcements.
- Begin by releasing the current API as /api/v1 and scheduling migration of the in-house client to use the versioned base path.

Introduce a dedicated Signing Gateway as the sole path to the HSM and implement tamper-evident, application-level auditability for every signing operation.

- All signing requests must traverse the Signing Gateway via mTLS and authenticated client identity (certificate-bound). The gateway assigns a monotonic sequence number and idempotency token per key and writes a write-ahead audit record before invoking the HSM; it refuses to sign if the pre-log write fails.
- Each audit record contains: gateway timestamp, sequence number, connector identity, request ID received, cryptographic hash of the payload-to-be-signed, key identifier, operation type, outcome, returned signature, and gateway instance identity.
- Audit logs are append-only and tamper-evident: persisted to S3 with Object Lock (compliance mode, retention and legal hold), and mirrored to an immutable ledger (e.g., AWS QLDB or CloudWatch Logs with integrity validation). Daily Merkle roots of the audit stream are computed and anchored externally (e.g., published to an independent timestamping service or public transparency log) to establish proof-of-time and prevent retroactive alteration.
- Alarms and analytics are applied over the audit stream to detect anomalies (sequence gaps, unexpected connector usage patterns, replayed request IDs, volume spikes).
- HSM access is isolated to the gateway IAM role and network segment; direct HSM access by connectors is prohibited. Key usage policies and per-key sequence counters are enforced in software until HSM-native usage logs become available; rotate keys regularly and segregate duties for log administration vs. key custody.

This decision provides defensible, independently verifiable proof of what was signed and when, despite the absence of native HSM usage logs.

We will decouple issue aggregation from the request/response path and serve precomputed metrics.

- Introduce a background aggregation pipeline that iteratively materializes “issues average age” per repository into a persistent store (materialized metrics). The HTTP endpoint returns the last computed value immediately; if missing or stale, it enqueues/refreshes asynchronously and returns 202 or the stale value with freshness metadata.

- Perform rate-aware, incremental ingestion:
  - Page with per_page=100 and respect rate limits with adaptive backoff.
  - Use conditional requests (ETag/If-None-Match) and since/updated filters to fetch only deltas after initial backfill.
  - Maintain a checkpoint per repo (latest seen issue updated_at and page cursors) to support resume without restarting from page 1.
  - Cap pages per run (e.g., 10–20) to avoid bursty 200+ request sequences; continue in subsequent jobs until convergence.

- Use a job queue with concurrency controls and global rate-limit coordination to serialize/slow down calls when approaching GitHub limits; centralize token usage with pooled GitHub app/installation tokens or user tokens to increase quotas.

- Cache results with TTL and versioning:
  - Short TTL (e.g., 5–15 minutes) for popular repos; longer for low-activity repos.
  - Invalidate or incrementally update when webhook events (issues opened/closed/edited) arrive; fall back to scheduled refresh if webhooks unavailable.

- Minimize payload by requesting only required fields (created_at, closed_at, state) via REST or GraphQL; prefer GraphQL for field-level selection when advantageous, retaining REST as fallback.

- Provide graceful degradation:
  - If initial backfill not complete, return best-known partial metric with a completeness indicator; optionally gate via a minimum coverage threshold.
  - Expose status endpoints/headers (lastComputedAt, coverage, nextRefreshAt) for observability.

- Enforce hard safeguards:
  - Per-request max pages/latency budget.
  - Circuit breaker on repeated 403 secondary rate limits.
  - Repository-level allowlist/denylist to avoid pathological sources.

This design ensures fast, predictable endpoint latency, respects GitHub API rate limits, and converges to accurate metrics through continuous, incremental computation.

Adopt Yarn v3+ (Berry) with Plug’n’Play (PnP) and the workspace: protocol for internal packages to eliminate yarn link and surface missing dependencies at install and build time. Enable PnP across the monorepo, migrate all internal cross-package references to workspace:* ranges, and configure constraints to enforce explicit dependency declarations. Add the Workspaces Tools plugin to support focus/partial installs and speed up local development. Disallow yarn link via linting and pre-commit checks.

We will adopt a single, repository-root Taskfile (go-task) as the canonical task runner for all developer, build, and CI/CD operations.

- Tooling: Use go-task (“task”) with a version-pinned wrapper script (./bin/task) to ensure consistent execution across developers, build agents, and operating systems.
- Canonical entry points: All workflows are invoked via task targets. Standard targets include: bootstrap, deps, fmt, lint, test, build, package, scan, generate, migrate, run, dev, clean, release, ci.
- CI/CD integration: Pipelines invoke task ci (and other targets as needed). The ci target composes lint/test/build/scan and produces versioned artifacts. No pipeline step reimplements logic contained in tasks.
- Local development: Developers use task commands exclusively (task --list for discovery). Pre-commit hooks and IDE tasks call task targets to avoid duplication.
- Monorepo/module structure: Subprojects define Taskfile.yml files and are included by the root Taskfile (using includes and dir-specific tasks). Namespaced targets (e.g., task api:test) avoid collisions.
- Environment standardization: Tasks handle environment bootstrapping (tools, language runtimes, .env loading) and may run within containerized contexts via Docker/Compose when necessary (task docker:*).
- Determinism and caching: Tasks are idempotent where possible, leverage incremental builds/caches, and fail-fast with consistent exit codes suitable for CI.
- Documentation and conventions: Target naming is consistent across services. Every target has a description. Any new operational workflow must be exposed via a task target.
- Governance: Changes to Taskfile(s) require review. The wrapper script enforces the required task version and installs it if absent.

## Decision
Adopt “Where Away” as the product name and publish the npm package as “where-away”.

- NPM package name: where-away (kebab-case, unscoped), selected for availability and clarity.
- Alternative alias “whereaway” will be reserved for future use (e.g., CLI alias or scoped variant) if needed, but “where-away” remains the canonical package name.
- Repository name: where-away.
- Package name in package.json: "name": "where-away".
- Import usage: import { ... } from "where-away".
- CLI (if provided): primary command “where-away”; optional short alias “wa” if not conflicting.
- Keywords and description will emphasize bookmarks, keyboard navigation, and single-key hinting to improve discoverability.
- Semantic versioning will be used; publish as a public package on npm.
- The name will remain stable unless legal/trademark conflicts arise or npm availability changes; in such cases, fallback to “whereaway” or a scoped name (e.g., @org/where-away).
- Branding and documentation will use “Where Away” consistently to align the product identity with the npm artifact “where-away”.

We will implement a centralized Identity Provider using Keycloak as the organisation’s IAM platform. The Library Members system remains the system of record; identities and entitlements will be synchronised into Keycloak via a secure, event-driven or scheduled integration, with Keycloak acting as the authoritative source for authentication and authorization decisions at runtime.

The platform will expose standards-based protocols:
- OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect for modern web, mobile, and API clients (Authorization Code with PKCE; JWT access tokens; refresh token rotation).
- SAML 2.0 for legacy service providers requiring SSO.
- SCIM 2.0 for user and group provisioning where supported; otherwise via API connectors.

Authorization will use RBAC and claims-based policies:
- Realm/client roles and OAuth scopes mapped to Wellcome services.
- Attribute/claim-based access control for fine-grained decisions (e.g., membership status, reader types, consent flags).

Security controls:
- MFA (WebAuthn/passkeys and TOTP) enforced per-risk policy.
- Account recovery aligned with membership verification flows.
- Token lifetimes and session policies tuned per client risk.
- Consent management for data sharing with relying parties.

Integration:
- Read-only sync from the Library Members pool (and other authoritative sources as needed) into Keycloak user store; bi-directional updates only where explicitly required.
- Group/role mappings derived from membership attributes.
- Support for federation with external IdPs if required (e.g., SAML/OIDC trust).

Operations and reliability:
- Highly available deployment (containerised on Kubernetes) with multi-AZ PostgreSQL, automated backups, and disaster recovery.
- Secrets managed via Vault/KMS; audit logs exported to the central SIEM.
- Configuration managed as code (GitOps), with environments for dev/test/stage/prod.

Adoption and migration:
- Phased rollout: new services integrate via OIDC; existing services migrate from bespoke auth to OIDC/SAML adapters.
- Backward-compatible SSO during transition; decommission legacy auth endpoints once consumers are migrated.
- Developer enablement via SDKs, templates, and self-service client registration under guardrails.

This decision standardises authentication and authorization across Wellcome Collection, integrates with the existing library membership base, and ensures interoperability through recognised, standards-based protocols.

Adopt error-wrapping with full error preservation and structured, redacted logging. Replace current ValidationError and CommercetoolsError constructors to accept an original error (err) and optional context, and use native Error cause to link the original error: new ValidationError(message, { cause: err }), new CommercetoolsError(message, { cause: err, statusCode, context }). Do not manually set stack; rely on V8’s stack and retain original stack via cause chain. Preserve and expose original error properties by:
- Storing the original error as cause and on originalError for backward compatibility.
- Merging enumerable properties from the original error (e.g., code, statusCode, name, details, request, response).
- Keeping existing fields (message, retry, statusCode) for compatibility; compute retryable using original or provided statusCode and network errors.

Introduce a standardized error serializer (toJSON or serializeError) used by the logger that outputs: name, message, stack, retryable, statusCode, code, context, and a recursive cause chain (limited depth/size). Include request/response metadata when present (method, url, status, correlationId, response body excerpt). Redact sensitive fields (Authorization, tokens, PII, PANs, CVVs) via a central redaction map before logging.

Update logging to always log the serialized error object; avoid logging only message/stack. Enforce size limits with truncation and mark as truncated. Maintain current retry logic semantics but source statusCode from original error/response when absent; network/DNS/timeouts are retryable. Add unit/integration tests for: cause preservation, property merging, redaction, serialization limits, and retry evaluation. This change improves debuggability without exposing secrets and remains backward compatible.

We will implement event transformers as processors, not backends.

- Rationale: Processors integrate directly into existing router/logger pipelines, minimizing configuration nesting and reducing cognitive and implementation complexity. This yields higher composability, reuse across multiple backends, and clearer execution ordering.

- Scope: All transformation logic (enrichment, redaction, normalization, schema mapping) will be delivered as stateless, idempotent, thread-safe processors. Any transformer-specific options will be expressed as processor-scoped configuration blocks, with optional per-pipeline overrides.

- Execution model: Transformers are appended to the processor chains of the target backend(s). Ordering is explicit and deterministic. Fail-fast behavior is configurable per processor (drop, quarantine/dead-letter, or propagate with error tag). Backpressure semantics follow the hosting pipeline.

- Configuration: Introduce a processor registry with typed schemas and validation. Support composition (chaining), parameterization, and feature flags. Provide sane defaults to keep common cases terse. Avoid deep nesting by prohibiting sub-backend configs inside processors.

- Observability: Each processor emits metrics (throughput, latency, error rates), structured logs with correlation IDs, and optional sampling. Traces will annotate spans with processor names and outcomes.

- Performance: Favor zero-copy/mutating transforms when safe; otherwise clone minimally. Batch-aware processors must preserve event ordering and respect batch size/time constraints.

- Compatibility and migration: Deprecate any existing transformer backends. Provide a migration guide and an automated config transformer where feasible. Maintain a compatibility shim during a deprecation window.

- Extensibility: Define a stable Processor interface, versioned configuration, and capability discovery to allow third-party transformers.

This decision standardizes transformation at the processor layer for simpler configuration, better reuse, and consistent operational behavior.

Adopt a single, authoritative global state per agent, owned and mutated by a dedicated state manager, with all other components interacting through explicit commands/events and receiving derived, immutable views.

- Introduce a State struct as the canonical, comprehensive in-memory model of the agent’s data. No other module holds long-lived mutable references to subparts.
- Centralize mutation through a State Manager (single owner task/actor). All state transitions occur via well-defined Commands producing Events and applying deterministic Reducers. No module mutates state directly.
- Expose read access via snapshot/queries that return immutable views or copies. Derived data is computed from State or cached inside the manager, invalidated by Events.
- Isolate side effects: networking, crypto, storage, and host I/O are adapters that emit Commands and consume Events; they never reach into State. This prevents implicit dependencies and cyclical coupling.
- Concurrency model: one owning executor (single-threaded or a dedicated actor on Tokio) serializes mutations; other tasks communicate via channels. This avoids shared mutable state and locks across modules.
- Persistence: append-only event log with periodic snapshots for fast recovery; State is reconstructed by replaying Events, ensuring determinism and auditability.
- Interfaces: modules depend on narrow service traits (Command submitter, Query provider, Event subscriber). Cross-module communication occurs through these interfaces only.
- Determinism and testability: reducers are pure and deterministic; property tests and replay tests validate invariants across p2p scenarios.
- Serialization: canonical formats for Events and State snapshots to ensure compatibility across versions and network peers.

This architecture reduces implicit coupling, clarifies ownership, and balances local coherence with the distributed p2p model.

Adopt an explicit, first-class attribute to distinguish definition axioms from simplification axioms, and update function evaluation to consult this attribute.

- Introduce an axiomKind attribute with values definition or simplification (or equivalently two boolean attributes isDefinition/isSimplification; mutually exclusive).
- Function evaluation prioritizes definition axioms for unfolding/evaluation and uses simplification axioms only in the rewriting/simplification phase, preventing unintended evaluation order changes and loops.
- In absence of an explicit attribute, apply conservative inference: a complete, non-overlapping, total set of equations for a symbol defaults to definition; otherwise defaults to simplification. Emit warnings for ambiguous/overlapping cases and encourage explicit annotation.
- Maintain backward compatibility: existing axioms continue to work under the inference rules; teams can incrementally annotate to remove warnings and gain deterministic behavior.
- Provide tooling/lints to detect conflicting annotations, overlapping definitions, and potential non-termination if a simplification is mistakenly marked as definition.
- Evaluation engine changes: (1) consult attribute to select candidate rules; (2) ensure definitions are confluent and terminating within function evaluation; (3) apply simplifications as orthogonal rewrites after/between evaluation steps with configurable strategies.
- Document precedence: definition axioms must not be preempted by simplifications on the same head symbol unless explicitly ordered; allow opt-in local precedence overrides where needed.

This decision makes evaluation semantics explicit, predictable, and optimizable while still allowing the engine to operate with both axiom types.

## Decision
We will standardize the dotcom-owned model.liveblog as the canonical contract for liveblog rendering and maintain an explicit adapter layer that maps CAPI responses into this model. Rendering code must depend only on model.liveblog and must not consume CAPI shapes directly.

- Introduce and own a versioned model.liveblog schema (with clear semver). Any breaking changes require a new version and a migration path.
- Implement a dedicated, testable transformer from CAPI -> model.liveblog, including:
  - Lossless mapping of essential fields and explicit handling of unsupported/unknown fields.
  - Deterministic defaults and feature flags for optional/experimental fields.
  - Strict runtime validation of inbound CAPI payloads and outbound model.liveblog (e.g., schema validation) with telemetry on validation failures.
- Keep component-level renderers aligned with model.liveblog types, enabling independent evolution of rendering concerns without leaking CAPI details.
- Encapsulate live updates (polling/WS) behind the adapter, emitting only model.liveblog-compliant deltas/events to the frontend.
- Document the mapping and edge cases, and provide contract tests to prevent regressions when CAPI evolves.
- Enforce the contract at boundaries (type-checking, lint rules) and prohibit direct CAPI access in the frontend.
- Provide fallbacks for partial data and a graceful degradation policy, ensuring resilience under CAPI variability or omissions.

This decision decouples rendering from upstream volatility while preserving strong typing, testability, and evolvability.

Adopt a pluggable template assembly strategy with two first-class strategies: (1) LegacyPathFallback (current path-based fallback) and (2) ManifestDriven (explicit assembly via a declarative manifest describing template parts, inheritance, and overrides). Selection of strategy will be configurable at the collection level with an environment-wide default; absent configuration, collections continue using LegacyPathFallback to ensure backward compatibility.

Introduce a StrategyResolver that chooses the assembly strategy per request based on collection config, with an optional request-scoped override for testing and controlled rollout. The ManifestDriven strategy will validate manifests at load time, support versioned components, and define deterministic precedence rules. On assembly failure in ManifestDriven, the system will log and, if configured, fall back to LegacyPathFallback to prevent outages during migration.

Provide common interfaces for template discovery, composition, caching, and diagnostics so both strategies share caching and observability. Emit structured logs and metrics tagging the selected strategy, cache hits, and fallback events to support monitoring and rollout control.

Ship a migration toolkit: a linter to generate/validate manifests from existing layouts, a dry-run mode comparing outputs across strategies, and feature flags to enable canary deployments per collection. Document the strategy selection and precedence rules, and add CI checks to validate manifests.

Plan to deprecate LegacyPathFallback once uplift coverage reaches agreed thresholds, with a staged timeline and removal criteria approved by stakeholders.

We will standardize code sharing via versioned internal packages within a pnpm workspace, orchestrated by Turborepo and TypeScript project references.

- All shared code resides in packages/* as standalone packages with clear package names, exports fields, and compiled dist outputs. Consumers import by package name only; cross-package relative imports and ad-hoc path aliases are prohibited.
- Use pnpm workspaces with the workspace:* protocol to link internal dependencies during local development. Each package builds to dist (tsup/tsc) and supports watch mode for fast feedback.
- Use TypeScript project references to enable incremental builds and accurate type boundaries. tsconfig paths are not used for runtime resolution; they are limited to project references/types.
- Turborepo coordinates build, test, and lint tasks in dependency order, enabling caching locally and in CI to ensure consistency and speed.
- In CI, we build from the workspace graph and run tests against the compiled outputs. For release, we use Changesets to manage versions and changelogs, then publish internal packages to our private npm registry. Versioning is required for all shared packages; no unpublished, symlinked code is allowed in production.
- Production applications depend only on published versions of internal packages. Docker builds restore the lockfile, install from the registry, and compile apps against released artifacts to ensure reproducibility.
- Enforce this via repo rules: no path-based imports across package boundaries, shared code must live in packages/*, packages must compile to ESM/CJS as needed with proper exports, and CI checks fail on violations.

This decision provides a single, consistent mechanism that works in local dev (workspace links), CI (cached graph builds), and production (versioned, published packages).

Adopt JUnit 5 (Jupiter) as the sole unit-testing framework and deprecate/remove JUnit 4. All new and existing unit tests must target JUnit 5. We will:
- Standardize dependencies on junit-jupiter (API, engine, params) and remove JUnit 4 from the compile/test classpath. Temporarily allow junit-vintage-engine only to run legacy tests during migration, then remove it by the migration deadline.
- Enforce via build: fail the build on new JUnit 4 tests (e.g., forbid org.junit.* imports via static analysis), and run only Jupiter engines in CI once migration completes.
- Provide a migration path: convert @Test, @Before/@After, @BeforeClass/@AfterClass to Jupiter equivalents; replace Rules/Runners with Extensions; update assertions and assumptions; migrate parameterized tests to Jupiter; and adapt category/tags to @Tag.
- Update project templates, examples, and documentation to JUnit 5; configure IDEs and CI (Surefire/Failsafe/Gradle Test) for Jupiter and parallel execution as needed.
- Set a firm cutoff date after which JUnit Vintage is removed and any remaining JUnit 4 tests must be migrated.

Success is defined as 100% of tests executing on JUnit 5 with no JUnit 4 dependencies, consistent developer experience, and a simplified, faster test pipeline.

We will provide cluster-wide logging via a node-level DaemonSet using Fluent Bit to collect all container stdout/stderr streams from the container runtime logs. Fluent Bit will enrich events with Kubernetes metadata (cluster, namespace, pod, container, labels, annotations) and normalize to JSON where possible. Logs will be forwarded to an in-cluster Elasticsearch deployment, with Kibana as the default UI for search, filtering, and browsing.

Indexing will use a predictable scheme (e.g., logs-<cluster>-<env>-<namespace>-yyyy.MM.dd) with Index Lifecycle Management for retention and rollover; default retention will be set (e.g., 30 days) and configurable per environment. Reliability is ensured via backpressure handling, on-disk buffering, retries with exponential backoff, and bounded memory usage; oversized or malformed records will be truncated or dropped according to a clearly documented policy. Security will include TLS in transit, restricted credentials for Fluent Bit to Elasticsearch, and NetworkPolicies; Kibana access will integrate with SSO and use Spaces (or equivalent) for multi-tenancy.

Logging is enabled by default for all workloads without requiring sidecars; teams may opt out per pod/namespace via an agreed annotation. For EKS Fargate workloads (where node agents are not available), we will use the AWS-managed log router/sidecar to ship to CloudWatch and forward to Elasticsearch via a supported AWS path (e.g., Firehose or Logstash integration).

This design allows future redirection to a central GDS log store by changing Fluent Bit outputs without application changes.

## Decision

Persist all business-significant Interventions (CRS) domain events in an immutable, append-only event stream and treat this stream as the authoritative historical record for reporting and analysis. Every published operational event (e.g., referral submitted, first supplier assessment booked, first action plan version submitted) will be durably captured via an outbox/event store and replicated to a long-retention event history store. Reporting read models and timelines will be materialized by replaying and aggregating these events, not by inferring from mutable current-state tables.

Events must include: aggregate identifier (e.g., referral ID), event type, occurred_at timestamp (UTC), actor identity (user/service), sequence/version for per-aggregate ordering, correlation/causation IDs, and a versioned payload schema. Ordering is guaranteed per aggregate; consumers must be idempotent.

Corrections are expressed as compensating events—historical records are never rewritten. Read models will compute key milestones (e.g., first occurrences) and actor attribution and can be re-built deterministically from the stream. This enables accurate reconstruction of past states and timelines even as operational state mutates.

Retention will meet regulatory and analytical needs; access is controlled and audited, with encryption in transit/at rest. Event schemas are forward-compatible (additive changes) with explicit versioning. This decision avoids lossy state mutation, ensures post-hoc examination of events, and provides a reliable foundation for performance reporting.

Adopt compile-time code generation to produce a transparent, interceptor-enabled layer for user classes, avoiding runtime Proxy-based interception. We will introduce a build-time generator (annotation processor/CLI) that scans opted-in classes and emits companion wrappers/subclasses that:

- Expose the identical public API as the original class (method signatures and visibility).
- Invoke an interceptor chain (before/after/around) with minimal overhead, then delegate directly to the underlying implementation via direct calls (no reflection).
- Preserve semantics such as generics, nullability, and checked exceptions.

Generation strategy:
- Prefer subclassing when the class/methods are non-final and have accessible constructors; otherwise generate a composition-based wrapper that delegates to an injected instance.
- Emit deterministic sources/bytecode into a dedicated module/namespace with stable naming (e.g., Foo_Interceptable) and a factory to obtain instances seamlessly.
- Support opt-in via annotations/config; per-method inclusion/exclusion; and compile-time validation for unsupported patterns (final/private methods, dynamic proxies required).

Runtime integration:
- A lightweight factory selects the generated type at runtime; if generation was not possible, configurable fallback is either: (a) no interception, or (b) Proxy-based interception (feature flag).
- Interceptor SPI supports ordered chains, context propagation, and async/await/coroutines where applicable.
- Thread-safe, reentrant interceptor invocation with zero reflection on hot paths.

Build and ops:
- Integrated into the CI/CD pipeline; incremental recompilation and caching to keep build times minimal.
- Versioned generator with compatibility checks; generated code is treated as build artifacts, not hand-edited.
- Diagnostics include mapping from generated code to source for debugging, with source maps/line directives where supported.

Non-functional outcomes:
- Performance target: within ~0–5% of native direct calls and substantially faster than Proxy-based interception.
- Maintainability via explicit, testable generated code and compile-time failures for unsupported cases.
- Observability hooks for metrics/tracing without introducing Proxy overhead.

Adopt a declarative, schema-driven approach to CLI argument specification and generation. All subcommands, options, flags, types, defaults, validation rules, and mutual-exclusion/required groups will be defined in a single versioned schema (e.g., YAML/JSON). A thin generation layer will consume this schema to construct the CLI using a mature, language-appropriate framework with first-class subcommand support, automatic help/usage, shell completion, and robust validation (e.g., Typer/Click, Cobra, or Clap).

We will:
- Centralize all argument definitions in the schema; prohibit ad-hoc/manual parsing in subcommand implementations.
- Generate parsers, contextual help, examples, and completions from the schema at build-time (preferred) or startup (fallback).
- Expose a lightweight registration API so new subcommands are added by contributing a handler and corresponding schema entry, enabling plugin-style extensibility.
- Enforce consistent UX (naming, defaults, error messages) via schema linting and CI checks.
- Maintain backward compatibility by honoring existing flags where feasible; issue structured deprecation warnings and provide migration aliases in the schema.
- Add contract tests that validate the generated CLI against the schema (types, constraints, conflicts) and snapshot the help output.

This decision reduces bespoke parsing logic, scales with growing complexity, improves consistency and testability, and decouples CLI surface design from implementation details.

We will discontinue use of Create React App (CRA) and react-scripts and adopt a first-party, repository-owned build toolchain. Specifically:
- Replace CRA with a custom Webpack 5 configuration (and Babel) that we version and maintain in-repo.
- Explicitly configure Node polyfills and shims required by the MilMove client (e.g., process, buffer, crypto) via Webpack 5’s resolve.fallback and appropriate plugins, eliminating breakages introduced by CRA’s hidden configuration.
- Manage ESLint (and related tooling such as Prettier, Jest/Testing Library) via explicit project-level configuration files, decoupled from CRA.
- Remove reliance on upstream CRA releases and policies; do not fork CRA or use react-scripts overrides (e.g., craco/react-app-rewired), as these are brittle and prolong dependencies we cannot control.
- Establish documented ownership for the build configuration, including versioning, changelogs, and upgrade procedures to keep Webpack, loaders, and plugins current.

This decision provides immediate control to address webpack 5 polyfill removals and future ecosystem changes without waiting on CRA. Migration will be executed incrementally: introduce the new build alongside the existing app, validate parity (dev server, HMR, lint/test, production builds), then retire react-scripts. We will also evaluate Vite as a potential future replacement, but the near-term path is a custom Webpack 5 setup to unblock current issues and stabilize the pipeline.

Adopt a layered, ports-and-adapters (hexagonal/clean) architecture with strict platform abstraction to decouple application logic from hardware and RTOS specifics.

- Define stable, versioned interfaces (ports) for all platform-dependent capabilities: time, threading/synchronization, interrupts, memory, logging, files/storage, networking, and device buses/peripherals (GPIO, I2C, SPI, UART, ADC/DAC, PWM, DMA).
- Provide concrete adapters per target platform:
  - OS Abstraction Layer (OSAL) for RTOS primitives.
  - Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) for MCU/peripheral access.
  - Board Support Package (BSP) for board-level wiring and pin maps.
- Enforce dependency direction: application and domain layers may depend only on interfaces; only adapters depend on RTOS/MCU headers. No direct hardware or RTOS calls outside adapters.
- Use dependency injection and factories to bind implementations at build time (preferred) or at startup, enabling per-platform selection without changing domain code.
- Enable unit/host testing with mock/fake implementations of all ports; provide simulator stubs where timing/peripheral behavior is required.
- Coding rules:
  - Prohibit inclusion of vendor/RTOS headers outside adapter layers (checked via CI/lint).
  - Keep interfaces small, synchronous by default; model async with callbacks/queues abstractions.
  - Separate real-time critical paths into narrowly scoped interfaces to preserve determinism.
- Build structure:
  - interfaces/: headers only, no platform includes.
  - domain/ and application/: logic using interfaces only.
  - adapters/<platform>/: OSAL, HAL, BSP implementations.
  - tests/: mocks/fakes and contract tests for ports.
- Performance: design for zero/low-overhead abstractions (inline, constexpr, function tables) and allow optional compile-time configuration (feature flags) to remove unused ports.
- Acceptance: CI enforces architecture rules; contract tests validate adapter conformance for each platform.

Route IIIF manifest requests authored by Meadow directly to the Meadow origin and bypass Donut entirely. We will implement deterministic, edge-level routing at the CDN by introducing a dedicated, stable namespace for Meadow manifests (e.g., /iiif/meadow/{id}/manifest or a distinct ID prefix/hostname). The CDN will match on this namespace/prefix and forward to the Meadow IIIF origin (service or S3), applying Meadow-defined cache headers and purge semantics. Donut will continue to handle legacy/non-Meadow manifests and S3 re-cache behavior.

For backward compatibility, Donut will detect Meadow-origin manifests (via ID namespace or embedded provenance flag when resolving) and respond with a 302 redirect to the corresponding Meadow IIIF URL, ensuring existing clients that still hit Donut do not break while enabling progressive migration. Once client adoption reaches target thresholds, the redirect can be removed and traffic enforced at the edge only.

If a Meadow-routed manifest is not found (4xx/5xx), the CDN will not fall back to Donut to avoid stale or incorrect recaching; failures will surface and be monitored. Operational ownership of caching and invalidation for Meadow manifests moves to Meadow: manifests are published with strong immutability (versioned URLs or ETags) and long TTLs; updates use new versioned URLs and/or CDN purges scoped to Meadow paths.

Summary of routing:
- CDN: route /iiif/meadow/* (or meadow ID prefix/host) to Meadow origin; route all other IIIF manifest paths to Donut.
- Donut: on Meadow IDs, issue 302 to Meadow URL; otherwise continue current behavior.
- No Donut re-caching for Meadow manifests; Meadow manages cache headers and purge.

This decision isolates concerns, prevents unintended re-caching, preserves stable URLs via redirects during transition, and provides a clear operational boundary and monitoring surface for Meadow-authored IIIF manifests.

Use PUT with idempotent upsert semantics to synchronize routes.

- Endpoint: PUT /route-tables/{customTableId}/routes/{destinationCidr}
- Semantics:
  - Adds or replaces the specified route in the target custom route table.
  - Treats the route as a canonical resource identified by destinationCidr within a table.
  - Supports limited-information triggers: if the request body is empty or includes a directive (e.g., {"source":"main"}), the service derives next-hop and attributes from the main route table at execution time.
  - When a body is provided, it may optionally include explicit next-hop and attributes to override main-table values.
- Idempotence and retries:
  - Safe for log-driven replays and at-least-once delivery.
  - Returns 201 Created on first creation, 200/204 on replacement with identical or updated values.
- Conflict and validation:
  - 409 if constraints prevent adoption (e.g., destination reserved or policy violation).
  - 404 if the custom table does not exist.
  - 422 for invalid CIDR or unsupported next-hop type.
- Concurrency:
  - Optional ETag/If-Match on the route resource to guard against concurrent writes if explicit attributes are provided.
- Rationale:
  - PUT best matches deterministic add/replace behavior and avoids PATCH ambiguity when the full desired state can be computed server-side from the main route table using minimal input.
  - Avoids introducing action-style POST endpoints while preserving clear resource modeling and predictable behavior.

We will replace the callback-based response mechanism between Handle and Supervisor with a typed, per-request reply channel sent as part of the event. Each request carries a bounded(1) reply Sender (oneshot semantics), and the Supervisor must complete the request by sending exactly one response on that channel. This removes the Callback abstraction and its associated try/scope/borrow complexity, and aligns the design with CSP-style concurrency and explicit backpressure.

The canonical Handle API will be synchronous: issuing a request enqueues the event to the Supervisor and then blocks (or awaits, internally) on receiving from the reply channel. Errors such as a dropped Supervisor are surfaced via closed-channel errors mapped to domain-specific error types.

We will deprecate and remove existing callback-based paths. Async variants of Handle methods will be minimized: we will provide a single async entry point that mirrors the synchronous semantics (awaiting the reply channel), but we will not proliferate separate async APIs without concrete use cases. Concurrency guarantees will remain conservative: Handle methods provide serialized access via the Supervisor’s mailbox; we make no additional promises about concurrent Handle method invocation beyond what the mailbox enforces. If wider concurrency is needed, multiple Handles or explicit higher-level coordination should be used.

Channel choices:
- Request queue: bounded MPSC to the Supervisor for backpressure.
- Response: typed oneshot (bounded capacity 1) per request.

We will monitor for real-world limitations and revisit async surface area and concurrency guarantees as use cases emerge.

Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for the Ditto project and make them a required artifact for any decision that affects system architecture, cross-cutting concerns, data models, external interfaces, runtime topology, security, performance, or long-term maintainability.

- Use the MADR template (v3 or later) for consistency.
- Store ADRs in the repository at docs/adr/, one file per decision, filename format: YYYY-MM-DD-short-title.md.
- Maintain a chronological decision log with incremental numbering in the filename header.
- Define lifecycle states: Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Deprecated, Superseded.
- Require every non-trivial architectural change proposal to include an ADR in Proposed state within its pull request; the ADR must capture context, decision, options considered, and consequences.
- Approval of the associated PR moves the ADR to Accepted; later changes that replace a decision must create a new ADR marked Accepted and set the prior one to Superseded with cross-links.
- Minor clarifications allowed as non-functional updates; substance changes require a new ADR.
- Tag ADRs with relevant domains (e.g., security, data, infra) and link to related RFCs, issues, and diagrams.
- Automate scaffolding with adr-tools or repository templates and validate via CI (lint check for template completeness and status).
- Make ADRs part of release notes and onboarding, ensuring decisions are discoverable and auditable over time.

Adopt a shared ingress model per cluster and retire the “one ingress controller per app/tenant” approach. Each cluster will run a minimal set of ingress controllers: one external (public) and one internal (private), each fronted by a single AWS NLB. Applications will share these controllers via host- and path-based routing, isolated by ingressClass, namespaces, and network policies. TLS will use SNI with per-host certificates managed centrally.

Where stricter isolation is required, teams must either:
- Use dedicated routing at the virtual host level (separate hostnames/certificates) on the shared controllers, or
- Escalate to a separate cluster/VPC for hard isolation.

We will not create additional ingress controllers beyond the public/private pair without explicit approval tied to quota availability. Existing per-app ingress controllers will be migrated to the shared controllers and decommissioned. Quota increase requests for NLBs will be pursued only to sustain the two-controller pattern across AZs, not to re-enable per-app controllers.

This decision supersedes [018] due to AWS NLB per-VPC/AZ limits, reduces LB sprawl, simplifies operations, and aligns with provider constraints while preserving multi-tenancy through logical isolation.

Decision:
We will remove all Localization dependencies from JabRefPreferences and make the preferences layer strictly locale-agnostic. Default values will be defined as immutable, language-neutral primitives or stable identifiers (e.g., enum constants, canonical codes, or resource bundle keys), never localized strings. Any text shown to users will be localized only at the point of use (UI/presentation layer) by resolving these identifiers via the Localization API.

Concretely:
- Define defaults in a central, typed DefaultValuesRegistry (or DefaultProvider) used by JabRefPreferences. This registry must not call Localization and must expose only deterministic, locale-independent values.
- For user-visible options, store stable identifiers (e.g., enum name or message key like “pref.general.importMode.auto”), not their localized display text. The UI translates identifiers to human-readable strings at render time.
- For free-form, user-editable strings (e.g., file patterns), store raw values as-is; defaults are canonical, non-localized literals.
- Prohibit/ban Localization usage in preference definitions via code review and tests. Add unit tests ensuring defaults do not vary by locale.
- Migration: On first run after upgrade, detect previously stored localized values and map them to canonical identifiers using a per-preference mapping table derived from known translations. If no mapping exists, retain the stored value and treat it as a custom user value.
- Backward compatibility: continue reading existing keys; only transform values as needed. Document the invariant schema and identifier-to-localization contract for contributors.

This decision guarantees stable defaults, predictable behavior across locales, and clear separation of concerns between configuration storage and presentation.

Deprecate and remove User.va_profile and any methods that expose the raw MPI profile. Replace them with narrowly scoped, documented getter methods on User that return only vetted attributes required by application features (e.g., icn, edipi, given_names, family_name, birth_date, gender, addresses, phone_numbers, email). These getters encapsulate source lookups, normalization, error handling, and caching, preventing direct coupling to MPI structures and minimizing overexposure of PII/PHI.

Implementation decisions:
- Introduce explicit getters with clear contracts (types, nilability, fallbacks) and consistent normalization.
- Disallow access to the underlying MPI profile from application code; only service adapters may query MPI.
- Add static enforcement (RuboCop rule) and runtime guards to block new calls to va_profile; log warnings initially, then raise after the deprecation window.
- Migrate all call sites to the new getters; delete va_profile and related helpers after verification.
- Align authorization with least-privilege: expose only attributes needed for the current request context; avoid returning composite/raw documents.
- Centralize attribute-level caching and staleness policies within the getters; remove memoization of the full profile.
- Provide metrics and logs to monitor getter usage, cache hit rates, and deprecation violations.
- Update tests to assert on getter behavior and to forbid references to va_profile.
- Document the attribute catalog, guarantees, and migration guide.

This decision confines identity access behind stable interfaces, reduces security risk, and decouples application code from MPI schema changes while improving testability and observability.

We will use RFC 4151 tag URIs as the canonical identifiers for all ODH data elements. Each URI will be immutable, globally unique, human-readable, and derived from stable business attributes where possible.

Format:
- tag:<authority>,<assignment-date>:<path>
- authority: a domain under ODH control (e.g., vwt.digital)
- assignment-date: date the authority first became valid for ODH tagging (YYYY-MM preferred)
- path: organizational namespace and resource hierarchy built from stable business identifiers

Construction rules:
- Path segments use meaningful, stable attributes (e.g., organization, catalog, resource type, business key): tag:vwt.digital,2020-01:mycompany/catalog/articles/313
- Use lowercase ASCII; words separated by hyphens; reserved characters percent-encoded
- Do not include PII or volatile attributes
- If no stable natural key exists, append an opaque UUID as the terminal segment
- Versions represent distinct resources (append /v/<version> when versions must be addressed)
- Multitenancy/domain contexts appear explicitly in the path to ensure uniqueness

Uniqueness and governance:
- The tuple (authority, assignment-date, path) must be unique; collisions are prevented via a central registry and automated linting in CI
- Once minted, a URI never changes. If business keys change, mint a new URI and record relationships (e.g., supersedes/superseded-by)
- Deprecated resources retain their URIs; tombstones may be published with status metadata
- Only authorized services/components may mint URIs under the controlled authority; local testing may use a sandbox authority/date

Interoperability:
- Tag URIs are non-resolvable identifiers; resolution, dereferencing, and metadata are provided via separate catalogs/HTTP APIs that map from tag URIs
- Where external systems require HTTP URIs, provide reversible mappings while preserving the tag URI as the primary key within ODH systems

We will implement High Privilege Access (HPA) for production support using a just-in-time, time-bound, least-privilege model:

- All developer access to production requires a ticketed request with a clear incident/health-check reference, manager/on-call approval, and explicit scope (systems, roles, commands).
- Access is granted via federated SSO with MFA, brokered by a PAM/JIT service issuing ephemeral, per-session credentials; no shared or persistent admin accounts, keys, or local users.
- Authorizations are enforced through fine-grained RBAC/ABAC and constrained to the minimum required: read-only by default; write privileges only when justified; data access masked unless unmasking is approved and logged.
- Sessions are fully audited (who/what/when/where), with command/console recording where feasible. Immutable logs are centralized, tamper-evident, and retained per policy; real-time alerts fire on elevation, sensitive actions, and policy violations.
- Access automatically expires at the end of the approved window; early revocation is supported. Out-of-hours or elevated scopes require additional approval.
- A controlled break-glass path exists for emergencies, with minimal pre-authorization, immediate notification, and mandatory post-incident review and retroactive approval.
- Periodic access reviews, metric reporting (frequency, scope, duration), and control tests are conducted to ensure least-privilege adherence and to tune policies.
- Tooling and policy changes will be applied consistently across all production environments and components; any exceptions are time-limited, documented, and reviewed.

## Decision
The Digital Object Store (DOS) will not persist descriptive metadata. DOS will store only administrative and structural metadata required for object management, preservation, and access control. Descriptive metadata will be maintained in authoritative external systems (e.g., catalog, DAMS) and referenced from DOS via persistent identifiers and resolvable URIs.

- DOS metadata model excludes descriptive fields. Allowed linkage fields: externalMetadataId, sourceSystem, schemaUri/schemaVersion, and optional integrity marker (e.g., ETag or hash).
- Ingest requires a valid reference to authoritative descriptive metadata; DOS will validate presence, schema, and resolvability but will not import or persist descriptive content.
- DOS APIs will return administrative/structural metadata and the external descriptive metadata reference. On-demand enrichment of responses with descriptive metadata is performed by a separate federation/edge layer that dereferences the reference; any cache is ephemeral, non-authoritative, and optional.
- Descriptive metadata updates occur solely in the source system. DOS remains unchanged unless the reference itself changes. Versioning is handled by the source (e.g., versioned URIs); DOS may record the referenced version identifier for traceability.
- Search and indexing within DOS are limited to administrative/structural metadata. Descriptive search is delegated to the authoritative system or to a cross-system index/aggregator.
- Backups, exports, and migrations from DOS exclude descriptive metadata content, preserving only references.
- If the external metadata system is unavailable, DOS continues serving digital objects and internal metadata; descriptive metadata is omitted until the source is reachable.
- Access control for descriptive metadata is enforced by the source system; DOS enforces least-privilege access to references and does not replicate permissions.

## Decision
Adopt Imo as the primary patient notification channel for Bangladesh, with SMS as a fallback and optional email where available. Implement a country-aware, channel-orchestrated messaging service that routes Bangladeshi patient notifications to Imo first, then degrades to SMS if Imo delivery is unavailable, the patient is not reachable on Imo, or consent is absent.

Integrate with an approved Imo business-messaging provider or official API, ensuring support for:
- Patient consent management, opt-in/opt-out, and preferences.
- Bengali language templates (with English fallback) and template approval flows.
- Delivery/read receipts, retries, and failure callbacks.
- Sender verification/branding to improve trust and open rates.

Introduce message templates for key use cases (appointment reminders, follow-ups, recalls, missed visits, education) and maintain parity with India’s WhatsApp content strategy where appropriate, localized for Bangladesh.

Roll out in phases:
- Pilot in a limited region/cohort behind feature flags.
- A/B test channel and content variants to optimize read/response and visit return.
- Expand nationally after meeting success criteria (delivery/read > X%, opt-out < Y%, return rate uplift > Z%).

Implement observability and governance:
- Per-channel metrics (send, delivery, read, response), cost per delivered/read, conversion to visit.
- Alerting, rate limiting, abuse prevention, and audit logging.
- Data retention aligned with Bangladesh regulations and company policy; encrypt PII at rest/in transit.

Architecture updates:
- Extend the notification service with a pluggable channel adapter for Imo.
- Persist per-patient channel eligibility and preferences.
- Centralize content, localization, and compliance checks.

Reassess channel mix quarterly; consider adding WhatsApp in Bangladesh if adoption or policy shifts improve its effectiveness.

## Decision
Adopt React with TypeScript as the primary frontend technology, using Next.js as the meta-framework to provide routing, SSR/SSG/ISR, automatic code splitting, and first-class performance features (image/font optimization). This choice maximizes developer productivity and modularity while leveraging the largest ecosystem and community support.

- Architecture: Component- and feature-sliced architecture (domain/feature/ui separation) to promote modularity, reusability, and parallel development. Co-locate tests, styles, and stories with components.
- Styling: Tailwind CSS for utility-first, performant styling; augment with Radix UI/Headless UI for accessible, unopinionated primitives where needed.
- State management: 
  - React Query (TanStack Query) for server state, caching, and request deduplication.
  - Redux Toolkit for cross-cutting client state when Context is insufficient; otherwise prefer local component state.
- Performance: Utilize Next.js dynamic imports for lazy loading, route-level code splitting, image optimization, and incremental static regeneration where applicable. Enforce Core Web Vitals budgets and bundle analysis in CI.
- API integration: REST/GraphQL supported via typed clients; prefer OpenAPI/GraphQL codegen for end-to-end type safety.
- Tooling: ESLint + Prettier + TypeScript strict mode; Jest + React Testing Library + Playwright for unit/integration/e2e tests; Storybook for component development and visual regression.
- Packaging: pnpm for efficient dependency management; consider a monorepo when sharing packages with mobile/web.
- Accessibility and i18n: Enforce a11y linting and testing; integrate i18next for localization.

This stack provides a rich UX, strong modularity, excellent performance primitives, and broad, mature community support.

## Decision
Standardize testing across the solution using a consistent strategy with language-specific frameworks and shared practices:

- Unit testing frameworks:
  - .NET: xUnit
  - JVM (Java/Kotlin): JUnit 5
  - Python: pytest
  - Node.js/TypeScript: Jest
- Integration testing: use Testcontainers for reproducible, containerized dependencies across all languages.
- Contract testing: Pact for consumer-driven contract tests between services.
- End-to-end/UI testing: Playwright for web applications; REST API E2E via Postman/Newman or REST-assured (JVM) consistently orchestrated in CI.
- Test doubles/mocking: Prefer built-in/mature libraries per ecosystem (e.g., Moq for .NET, Mockito for JVM, unittest.mock for Python, Jest mocks for Node).
- Code coverage: enforce minimum 80% line/branch coverage for unit tests; measure via Coverlet (.NET), JaCoCo (JVM), coverage.py (Python), and Istanbul/nyc (Node), all reported centrally in CI.
- Project structure: co-locate tests per module with a uniform naming convention (e.g., src/test, tests/), and “*Tests” suffix.
- Execution: all test suites run in CI on every pull request; nightly pipelines run extended integration/E2E suites. Flaky tests are quarantined with tracking.
- Tooling: standard test commands via package scripts or makefiles; results exported as JUnit XML for uniform reporting and trend analysis.
- Governance: a shared testing guidelines document and templates are maintained; new services must adopt these frameworks unless an exception is approved by architecture review.

Adopt an event-sourced architecture as the system of record. The authoritative state will be an append-only event store capturing domain events, not a mutable relational model. Read concerns (queries, reporting, integrations) will be served via projections/materialized read models built from event streams, following CQRS.

Key decisions:
- Model all state changes as explicit, versioned domain events; persist them immutably with strong ordering per aggregate.
- Use projections to produce task-optimized read models that can evolve independently as stakeholder needs change; rebuild projections deterministically from the event log when schemas or views change.
- Ensure exactly-once or effectively-once processing semantics with idempotent event handlers and correlation/causation metadata; apply optimistic concurrency on event appends.
- Employ snapshotting for long-lived aggregates to manage rehydration performance, without compromising the event log as the source of truth.
- Support event evolution through schema/versioning strategies (e.g., upcasters or tolerant readers) to preserve backward compatibility.
- Isolate writes and reads (CQRS), enabling independent scaling and deployment of command handlers (write side) and projectors/query APIs (read side).
- Integrate with external systems via outbox/relay patterns to guarantee atomic publication of events and side effects.
- Maintain observability with traceable event IDs and deterministic projection checkpoints; provide tooling to replay and audit.

We will still use relational/NoSQL stores where appropriate for projections, but they are disposable derivatives. This approach prioritizes adaptability to changing presentation and reporting needs, while keeping business behavior explicit, auditable, and reconstructable.

We will use TypeScript for the web front end and Python 3 for the server back end.

Front end:
- Language: TypeScript
- Framework: React
- GIS/mapping libraries: Mapbox GL JS (or OpenLayers/Leaflet as needed), deck.gl for visualization, Turf.js for client-side geospatial ops
- Rationale: Aligns with existing JavaScript/TypeScript skillsets, has strong industry adoption, rich ecosystem, and mature GIS tooling and community support.

Back end:
- Language: Python 3
- Framework: FastAPI (with option to use Django for admin-heavy needs)
- GIS libraries/tools: GDAL/OGR, Rasterio, Shapely/GEOS, Fiona, PyProj, GeoPandas; first-class integration with PostGIS; support for task queues (Celery/RQ) for heavy geoprocessing
- Rationale: Python’s geospatial ecosystem is the industry standard for server-side geoprocessing, widely supported, and matches team experience, enabling faster delivery and easier hiring.

This stack ensures broad industry support, deep GIS tooling coverage across client and server, and leverages current team competencies.

We adopt a project-wide, enforceable naming convention to accelerate onboarding and reduce cognitive load. The convention applies to code, APIs, data, infrastructure, and collaboration artifacts, and is backed by automation and review.

- Ubiquitous language: Maintain a living glossary of domain terms; prefer domain terms over technical slang. Avoid ambiguous synonyms.
- General rules: Clarity over brevity; no unexplained abbreviations; use consistent casing per medium; prefer full words.
- Code (language-specific casing per ecosystem): 
  - Classes/types: PascalCase (e.g., OrderService, PaymentGateway).
  - Variables/fields/params: camelCase (totalAmount).
  - Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS).
  - Booleans: is/has/should prefix (isActive).
  - Collections: plural nouns (orders).
  - Async methods: suffix Async (submitOrderAsync).
  - DTO/ViewModel: suffix DTO/ViewModel; interfaces without “I” prefix unless idiomatic for the language.
  - Events: past tense (OrderShipped), Commands: imperative (ShipOrder), Queries: “Get/Find…” (GetOrderById).
- Files/folders: Mirror types and namespaces; one type per file; tests mirror source structure with .tests suffix and methodName_condition_expected pattern.
- Database: Singular PascalCase table names (Order, OrderItem); snake_case column names (order_id); constraints/indexes prefixed (pk_, fk_, ix_). Migrations: timestamp + concise-kebab-case-description.
- APIs: Resource-oriented nouns; URLs kebab-case (/orders/{orderId}/line-items); JSON keys camelCase; events/topics kebab.case; HTTP verbs for actions; avoid verbs in resource names.
- Infrastructure/config: Environment variables UPPER_SNAKE_CASE; Terraform resources lower_snake_case; S3/buckets/k8s names kebab-case.
- Git/branching: feature/bugfix/chore/hotfix prefixes with kebab-case summaries (feature/checkout-flow).

Enforcement: Documented style guide, linters/formatters, schema/API linters, CI checks, and PR checklist; violations blocked unless waivered with justification.

We will introduce explicit bus binding for handlers and preserve current behavior by default:

- Handlers MAY declare one or more target buses (by identifier) in their definition (e.g., service tag/attribute/annotation).
- If a handler does not declare any target bus, it WILL be registered on all buses discovered at container compile time.
- A handler MAY be bound to multiple buses by listing multiple identifiers.
- If a handler references a non-existent bus, container compilation WILL fail with a clear error.
- We will not introduce an implicit “default bus”; absence of a bus declaration continues to mean “all buses.”
- Autoconfiguration/autodiscovery will keep the default behavior (register to all buses) unless a bus is explicitly declared.
- This decision applies uniformly across handler types (e.g., command, event, query) and does not change dispatch semantics.
- Registration order and handler method resolution remain unchanged; only bus scoping is affected.
- Documentation and examples will show both patterns:
  - Explicit bus binding for targeted routing.
  - Omitted binding for broad registration.

This maintains backward compatibility with the current single-bus setup while enabling clear, explicit scoping as additional buses are introduced.

## Decision
Adopt Selenium WebDriver as the standard browser automation framework for feature and end-to-end tests to enable a single test suite that runs consistently across developers’ machines and CI.

- Write tests once using Selenium WebDriver bindings in the primary application language and the team’s chosen test runner (e.g., JUnit/TestNG, Jest/Mocha, pytest), employing the Page Object Model for maintainability.
- Support local development via Chrome and Firefox (headed and headless) and CI execution via:
  - Selenium Grid for parallelization in containers (Dockerized nodes), and
  - Cloud cross-browser providers (e.g., BrowserStack) for OS/browser/version coverage not feasible in-house.
- Parameterize environment targets (dev/staging/production), base URLs, capabilities, and browser matrices via configuration and environment variables; no test code changes required to switch environments.
