- Enable CI parallelism and sharding to reduce wall-clock time; collect artifacts (logs, screenshots, videos) and JUnit-compatible reports for visibility.
- Implement stability practices: explicit waits over sleeps, idempotent test data setup/teardown, retry-once policy for known flaky tests with tagging to track and triage.
- Version and lock WebDriver binaries via driver managers; maintain a minimal supported browser matrix aligned with product support policy; review quarterly.
- Provide a thin adapter layer to abstract provider-specific capabilities so the same tests run locally, on Grid, and on BrowserStack with the same commands.
- Integrate into the CI pipeline as a required stage for pull requests (smoke subset) and nightly/full cross-browser runs on the complete matrix.

This decision standardizes on Selenium WebDriver to satisfy cross-browser parity, CI integration, and single-source test authoring.

Establish Staging as a production-like, regularly refreshed mirror of Production for ETL development and validation, while retaining Development for isolated engineering experiments.

- Staging will be the primary environment for Analysts/Engineers to build, modify, and test ETL processes against realistic datasets. It will be refreshed on a defined cadence (e.g., daily non-business hours or weekly) from Production using automated pipelines that:
  - Preserve schema parity with Production.
  - Mask/obfuscate PII and other sensitive fields consistently and deterministically to maintain referential integrity.
  - Downsample only where volumes are prohibitively large and do not impact transformation correctness; otherwise, full-fidelity replicas are used.

- Access controls in Staging will enforce:
  - Read-only copies of source datasets.
  - Write permissions restricted to user- or team-namespaced schemas/workspaces for ETL outputs and intermediate artifacts.
  - Guardrails to prevent cross-tenant impact and manage costs (quotas, warehouse sizing, job concurrency).

- Promotion flow:
  - ETL is developed and validated in Staging, including performance and BI compatibility checks.
  - Changes are peer-reviewed and promoted via CI/CD to Production with environment-specific configuration and data bindings.

- Development remains a sandbox for prototyping infrastructure, new services, and spikes that do not require production-like data fidelity.

Adopt a dedicated search engine (OpenSearch/Elasticsearch) and move all querying to a backend Search Service that exposes a typed query API and translates requests into the engine’s DSL. Define index mappings with multi-fields to support both exact and analyzed search: e.g., title, body, author, license, tags as text (analyzed) + keyword (exact). Add date fields (created_at, updated_at) as date type. Implement analyzers: standard + stemming for relevance; edge_ngram for startsWith; ngram for contains; lowercase keyword normalizers for case-insensitive exact matches. Manage synonyms via a versioned synonym set (domain-owned), applied in the analyzer chain for relevant fields; support locale-specific analyzers where needed.

Support complex queries via a structured request model: boolean AND/OR across fields (mapped to bool must/should), tag queries with AND/OR semantics, exact filters on keyword subfields, prefix queries (match_phrase_prefix or edge_ngram), contains queries (ngram analyzer), and date range filters. Expose operators (equals, contains, startsWith, in, range) per field type; validate at the API layer. Provide sorting options (relevance, date), pagination via search_after for deep paging, and optional highlighting.

Implement an ingestion/indexing pipeline: near–real-time indexing on writes; backfill job for historical data; idempotent upserts; soft-deletes with tombstones. Use index templates and aliases for zero-downtime reindexing when mappings/analyzers change. Add field-level boosts and query-time boosts for tuning; monitor via search metrics (latency, QPS, error rate), quality metrics (CTR, zero-result rate), and logs.

UI will use a query builder that constructs the structured API payload; the backend enforces ACL/tenant filters in queries to ensure authorized results only. Deprecate existing DB LIKE/exact searches after parity validation. Provide capacity planning and autoscaling for the search cluster; enable backups/snapshots.

Adopt Lombok to implement the builder pattern for EffectiveModel (and similar models), using @Builder (or @SuperBuilder for hierarchies) to minimize boilerplate while retaining Java. Prefer @Value (immutability) or @Getter with explicit fields; use @Singular for collection fields. Hand-written builders are disallowed except for exceptional edge cases justified in code review.

Scope:
- Apply Lombok to EffectiveModel and its subcomponents/aggregates that require many optional parameters.
- Maintain explicit validation in builder methods or a @Builder.Default + post-build validate().

Tooling and build:
- Add Lombok as a compileOnly dependency; enable annotation processing in IDEs and CI.
- Provide a delombok task to generate sources for downstream tools, code search, and Javadoc publishing.
- Ensure error-prone/spotbugs settings are compatible with Lombok; document local setup in CONTRIBUTING.

Serialization/interoperability:
- For Jackson, add @JsonPOJOBuilder if needed; prefer @AllArgsConstructor(onConstructor=@__(@JsonCreator)) when necessary.
- Avoid Lombok on public API boundary DTOs if consumers lack Lombok; use delomboked artifacts instead.

Constraints and risks:
- Accept Lombok dependency and annotation processing overhead.
- Mitigate debugging/stack-trace opacity via delombok artifacts and codegen mapping in IDE.

Rejected alternatives:
- Writing boilerplate increases LOC (~4k), maintenance burden, and defect risk with no functional gain.
- Migrating to Kotlin is out of scope due to language/tooling shift, training, and mixed-language maintenance.

Success criteria:
- LOC reduced vs handwritten builders; consistent builder API; no regressions in build, IDE, or serialization workflows.

Adopt a universal, DNS-based, cross-cluster service discovery and routing model using a multi-cluster service mesh with shared trust, enabling fully qualified names that include the cluster scope.

- Implement a multi-cluster service mesh (e.g., Istio multi-primary across networks) with:
  - Shared root of trust (SPIFFE/SPIRE or shared CA) enabling mTLS across clusters.
  - East-west mesh gateways for inter-cluster traffic.
  - A federated service registry synchronizing exported services.

- Standardize a universal FQDN scheme:
  - Format: <service>.<namespace>.<cluster>.<globalSuffix> (e.g., serviceb.default.cluster1.global).
  - Provide compatibility aliasing for requested pattern cluster1.serviceb where appropriate via DNS records.
  - Reserve a single global suffix (e.g., .global) across environments.

- Use Kubernetes Multi-Cluster Services (MCS) API to explicitly export/import services:
  - ServiceExport in source cluster; ServiceImport materialized in consumer clusters.
  - Annotate with cluster identifier and locality metadata for routing policies.

- Enforce secure connectivity and policy:
  - Strict mTLS, identity-bound authorization (service-to-service).
  - Network policies limiting east-west exposure to exported services only.
  - Per-cluster trust lists to ensure “trusted cluster” semantics.

- Routing behavior:
  - Local-first, then failover to remote clusters based on health and locality.
  - Traffic policies for edge intermittency: retries, circuit breakers, timeouts, outlier detection.
  - Weighted and canary routing to specific clusters for progressive delivery.

- Operational concerns:
  - Cluster identity is immutable and globally unique; managed via cluster-issuer and DNS zones.
  - Centralized, GitOps-managed registry of exported services and DNS records.
  - Observability unified across clusters (distributed tracing with cross-cluster propagation, mesh telemetry).
  - Backward compatibility: legacy clients can resolve through a bridging DNS zone until migrated.

This decision establishes a consistent, secure universal namespace and discovery mechanism enabling cloud-edge and multi-region cross-cluster invocation while preserving locality, resilience, and least-privilege exposure.

We standardize the Domain API on Domain.getAgent as the canonical and stable method to obtain an agent instance. Domain.getInstance is deprecated immediately and will remain as a thin shim delegating to getAgent until the next major release, after which it will be removed.

Actions:
- Introduce Domain.getAgent (restored) with no behavioral changes.
- Mark Domain.getInstance as @Deprecated, emit a runtime deprecation warning once per process, and document its replacement.
- Release a minor version with both methods available, followed by removal in the next major version in accordance with SemVer.
- Provide an automated codemod and lint rule to rewrite Domain.getInstance(...) to Domain.getAgent(...).
- Update all documentation, samples, and SDK references to use getAgent exclusively.
- Add contract tests ensuring both methods currently produce identical results, and that getAgent remains the compatibility baseline.
- For other factories, avoid ambiguous “instance” naming; prefer role-specific names (e.g., getRepository, createSession) to reduce confusion.
- Communicate the deprecation timeline in release notes and migration guide, including exact versions and examples.

This decision eliminates the ambiguous “instance” naming, aligns terminology with the domain concept of “Agent,” and provides a clear, low-friction migration path.

Adopt a standardized, version-controlled publishing checklist as a mandatory gate for releasing any crate in this repository.

- Location and format:
  - Maintain the canonical checklist in PUBLISHING.md at the repo root.
  - Provide an issue template (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/release-checklist.yml) to track completion per release.
  - Keep automation config in release.toml (for cargo-release or equivalent) alongside CI workflows.

- Enforcement:
  - A required “Release readiness” CI job must pass before tagging or publishing. It verifies:
    - Checklist issue exists and all mandatory items are checked.
    - Automated steps (lint/test/docs/audit/dry-run) succeed.
  - Exceptions require explicit maintainer approval and are recorded in the release issue.

- Minimum required items:
  - Version bumped per SemVer; no breaking changes without a major version.
  - CHANGELOG updated (Keep a Changelog format) and linked to commits/PRs.
  - README, crate-level docs, examples, and feature docs updated; no docs warnings (cargo doc --no-deps -D warnings).
  - Cargo metadata validated (name, description, categories, keywords, repository, homepage, license/license-file, readme, include/exclude).
  - MSRV declared and tested; CI matrix green (OS/arch/toolchain).
  - Code quality: rustfmt, clippy (deny warnings), tests, optional fuzz/benches as applicable.
  - Supply chain: cargo deny/audit/vet clean; dependency versions pinned as policy dictates.
  - Packaging: cargo publish --dry-run succeeds; package size reasonable; no untracked files included.
  - Security/privacy review for new features and telemetry (if any).

- Release and provenance:
  - Create an annotated, signed tag vX.Y.Z; generate GitHub Release notes from CHANGELOG.
  - Publish to crates.io after tag; verify availability and docs.rs build.
  - Post-release monitoring; define rollback/yank criteria and procedure.

- Governance:
  - Each release has an owner and a reviewer.
  - Checklist is living; changes require PR review by maintainers.

Adopt a temporary, offline-first persistence strategy to maintain application functionality while backend synchronization is being repaired. All writes will be captured locally and reads will prefer local data. We will introduce a local persistence layer using platform-appropriate, secure storage (e.g., IndexedDB/SQLite on web/desktop, Keychain/EncryptedSharedPreferences on mobile) with encryption at rest where supported.

Scope:
- Persist only data required for critical user flows and minimal metadata (timestamps, version, entity IDs).
- Avoid PII where possible; if unavoidable, encrypt and redact nonessential fields.

Behavior:
- Implement an append-only outbox for mutations (create/update/delete) with monotonic timestamps and client-generated IDs.
- Queue network operations; on sync service restoration, replay outbox in order. Interim conflict policy: last-write-wins using server-updatedAt where available; defer complex resolution to server rules.
- Provide UX indicators for “unsynced changes” and a manual “Retry Sync” action; prevent cross-device assumptions until sync resumes.

Controls and risk mitigation:
- Gate via a remote-config feature flag to enable/disable quickly.
- Enforce TTL (e.g., 7–14 days) and size quotas; purge on logout or when disabled.
- Add telemetry for queued ops count, replay success/failure, storage usage, and error codes.
- Protect data with device-level encryption where available; never write secrets/tokens to general storage.

Rollback and migration:
- On backend fix, progressively re-enable server as source of truth: complete outbox replay, fetch authoritative state, reconcile diffs, then disable local-first via feature flag.
- Provide a migration script to clear legacy local data safely after confirmation of successful sync.

Testing and ops:
- Include offline/airplane mode E2E tests, crash/restart durability tests, and replay idempotency validation.
- Document known limitations (potential stale cross-device data, limited conflict resolution) and communicate to stakeholders.

Adopt RabbitMQ (AMQP) as the messaging middleware for service composition, deployed as a highly available cluster using quorum queues. RabbitMQ natively supports core Enterprise Integration Patterns via exchange types and bindings: publish-subscribe (fanout/topic), content-based routing (headers/topic), competing consumers (work queues), message filter, splitter/aggregator (with consumer-side coordination), dead-letter channels, delayed/redelivery, and request-reply (replyTo/correlationId). We will standardize on topic exchanges for most flows, headers exchanges for content-based routing, and define dead-letter exchanges/queues with bounded retry policies per queue.

Reliability and scalability will be achieved through:
- Quorum queues for strong consistency and failover across 3+ nodes.
- Publisher confirms and mandatory routing to ensure delivery guarantees, combined with consumer acknowledgements for at-least-once semantics.
- Idempotent consumers and deduplication keys at the application layer.
- Consistent Hashing Exchange for balanced sharding where needed, and federation/shovel for cross-region bridging.

Operational concerns:
- Provision managed or Kubernetes-operator-based clusters with TLS/mTLS, per-tenant vhosts, and fine-grained permissions.
- Standardize message contracts (JSON/Avro) with versioning; enforce schema validation at the edge.
- Observability via Prometheus metrics, tracing with OpenTelemetry (correlationId propagation), and structured logging.
- Backup/restore and disaster recovery through mirrored quorum nodes and tested failover runbooks.

This decision aligns with EIP coverage, operational maturity, and horizontal scalability requirements while keeping latency and developer ergonomics favorable.

Decision

- Represent each member holding’s OCNs as a normalized, de-duplicated, unordered set (source-of-truth), retaining full provenance (submitted value, normalized value, timestamps).
- Eliminate the “pick one OCN at scrub time” behavior. Matching to HathiTrust items is computed as “any-of” over the holding’s OCN set and is re-evaluated whenever:
  - the holding’s OCN set changes,
  - a HathiTrust item is added/updated,
  - OCN equivalence/merge information changes.
- Persist computed matches as derived state (materialized for query performance) and make them recomputable/idempotent. Do not encode load-order–dependent side effects.
- Introduce a reconciliation service:
  - Event-driven recomputation on item/holding changes.
  - Scheduled backfill to catch missed events or updated OCN equivalences.
  - Commutative/idempotent logic to avoid order sensitivity; multiple runs must converge to the same state.
- Support OCN equivalence (merges/deprecations) via an authoritative mapping layer:
  - Prefer official OCLC services/feeds where available; otherwise maintain a local alias table seeded from trusted sources and member input.
  - During normalization, expand each submitted OCN to its canonical and known aliases; store both the submitted set and the resolved equivalence set for matching.
- Validation/normalization:
  - Normalize OCNs to numeric strings, strip punctuation, dedupe, and reject clearly invalid formats.
  - Remove dependence on “current maximum OCN”; stop scraping the OCLC web endpoint. Use configurable bounds/heuristics for sanity checks and optionally a licensed OCLC validation API behind a feature flag.
- Backwards compatibility: continue accepting multiple OCNs per holding; no requirement to collapse to a single OCN. Existing holdings will be reprocessed by the reconciliation job to correct prior “first OCN” choices.
- Observability: log decisions, emit metrics on reconciliation outcomes, and retain audit trails to support debugging and explainability.

Adopt a maintained, Docker-independent packaging and persistence model for CryptPad:

- Build and publish an official, reproducible flist directly from upstream CryptPad sources via CI, removing reliance on the deprecated Docker image.
- Define a single writable data root (/cryptpad/data) and a config root (/cryptpad/config) to decouple state from the immutable flist. All application state (blobs, databases, uploads, keys) must reside under /cryptpad/data.
- Provide persistence through the platform’s native writable storage (e.g., 0-DB/ZDB-backed filesystem or equivalent), mounted to /cryptpad/data at runtime by the orchestrator. Do not use Docker volumes.
- Configure CryptPad via environment variables and files under /cryptpad/config, ensuring idempotent startup and first-run initialization that creates required directories/migrations if absent.
- Implement CI pipelines to build multi-arch flists, run smoke/integration tests, embed SBOMs, and sign artifacts. Version flists aligned with upstream releases; maintain a rolling “stable” tag and immutable versioned tags.
- Deprecate the prior Docker-based solution; freeze it to security-only updates and document an assisted migration: export existing Docker volume data, map it to /cryptpad/data, validate integrity, and cut over with rollback instructions.
- Standardize health checks, logs to stdout/stderr, and minimal default permissions for the writable mount.

Adopt explicit major-versioning for HTTP App Callback contracts to preserve compatibility post v1.0 and enable controlled evolution.

- Versioning scheme: major-only semantic version applied to the callback surface. Breaking changes require a new major; additive/optional behavior must be backward compatible within the same major.
- Version transport: include the major version in the URL base path (/v{major}/...) and advertise the same via a dapr-api-version header. The runtime negotiates using the header when present; the path is authoritative for routing and supports side-by-side endpoints.
- Default and compatibility: v1 remains the default if no version is specified, ensuring existing apps continue to function unchanged. New runtimes must always send an explicit version. Apps MAY implement multiple major versions concurrently.
- Negotiation: the runtime selects the highest mutually supported major version discovered via initial capability probing or a configured supported-versions list. If negotiation fails, the runtime falls back to v1 and logs a clear warning.
- Deprecation policy: maintain support for at least the two most recent majors across their corresponding LTS windows. Announce deprecations with a minimum one LTS’ notice and a published migration guide; no in-place behavior changes within a major.
- Scope: this decision applies to HTTP App Callbacks; gRPC contracts follow their existing versioning policy independently.

## Decision
Adopt Hive-compatible folder-based partitioning for S3 datasets to enable partition pruning by Athena (and similar engines), thereby reducing scanned data and improving query performance and cost.

- Layout: s3://<bucket>/<domain>/<dataset>/<table>/<partition_key1>=<value>/<partition_key2>=<value>/... with data files only in leaf partitions. No mixed datasets in a prefix; no non-data files in partition folders.
- Partition keys: choose low-to-medium cardinality, high-selectivity columns that match common query predicates. Default to temporal partitions (year/month/day[/hour]) as the primary key; add at most one or two domain-specific secondary keys (e.g., region, tenant) when they materially improve pruning. Avoid extremely high-cardinality keys (e.g., user_id) unless justified by workload and file sizing.
- File sizing: write few large files per partition (target 128–512 MB) to minimize small-file overhead. Implement periodic compaction to maintain target sizes and merge small files.
- Format and compression: store datasets in columnar formats (e.g., Parquet) with block compression (e.g., Snappy) to maximize scan efficiency within pruned partitions.
- Catalog and discovery: register and manage partitions in AWS Glue Data Catalog at write time. Writers must upsert partitions as part of the ingestion workflow; avoid expensive full repairs in production. Enable partition projection where appropriate to reduce catalog size and speed discovery.
- Query discipline: require queries and views to include explicit predicates on partition columns to ensure pruning. Provide canonical views that expose partition columns for easy filtering.
- Limits and governance: cap the number of partitions per table and per query (e.g., via partition projection constraints). Document chosen keys per dataset with rationale; periodically review based on access patterns.
- Lifecycle and backfill: use S3 lifecycle rules scoped to partition prefixes for retention and cost control. Support safe historical backfills by writing to the correct partition paths and updating the catalog accordingly.

We will use a system-generated, immutable surrogate key (CitizenId, UUID v7) as the primary key for citizens. The Fiscal Code (FC) will be modeled as domain data, not as the primary key.

- All internal and external references (foreign keys, APIs, events) will use CitizenId. CitizenId is never reassigned or changed.
- FC will be stored in a separate CitizenFiscalCode assignment table with fields: CitizenId, FiscalCode, ValidFrom, ValidTo, Status (Active | Revoked | Conflicted), Source, and Audit metadata.
- Constraints:
  - At most one Active FC per CitizenId.
  - At most one Active assignment per FiscalCode globally (unique index on (FiscalCode) filtered by Status = Active), except when an administrative conflict is detected; in that case, Status = Conflicted is used and the unique constraint does not apply until resolution.
  - FC values are validated for format; FC is nullable to support missing/foreign cases.
- History:
  - Changes to FC (revocations, corrections, renames) create new time-bounded assignments; previous assignments are closed (ValidTo set) and retained for audit/traceability.
- Lookup:
  - Queries by FC resolve to the current Active assignment; if multiple Conflicted assignments exist, the system returns an explicit conflict error requiring manual resolution.
- Integration:
  - Incoming data that only provides FC will attempt to match the Active FC; if none or conflicted, the record is queued for resolution rather than creating/merging automatically.
- Exposure:
  - Public APIs expose CitizenId as the stable identifier; FC is exposed as an attribute with its status and validity period.
- Migration/merging:
  - In the event of duplicate citizens or FC corrections, records are merged under a single CitizenId with FC history preserved; downstream systems are informed via events keyed by CitizenId.

This approach ensures immutability and referential stability, accommodates FC changes and rare non-uniqueness, and preserves full auditability and temporal history.

Adopt tombstones for all hard-deleted items to enable discovery and restoration by metadata.

- On every delete operation, persist an immutable Tombstone record in a dedicated table/collection within the primary datastore, created atomically with the delete (same transaction) to guarantee existence.
- Tombstone schema (minimal snapshot): original_item_id, stable external/source IDs, title, type/kind, key identifying metadata (e.g., canonical slug, checksum/hash, collection/project), deletion_timestamp, deleted_by (actor/service), delete_reason/code, preservation_pointer (URI to preserved artifact, if any), original_created_at/updated_at, and tenant/partition keys. No full payload/content is stored in the tombstone.
- Index tombstones for searchability by title (text), source ID(s), checksum, type, deletion date, and tenant. Support exact and fuzzy search where available.
- Expose a read-only Tombstone Search API and admin UI to discover deleted items by metadata; results include links to preservation artifacts and restoration actions.
- Restoration uses the tombstone to locate the preserved artifact and rehydrate the record. Prefer restoring to the original_item_id when not conflicting; otherwise create a new item and link both via the tombstone. Record restore_timestamp, restored_by, and restore_target_id on the tombstone.
- Tombstones are immutable except for append-only lifecycle fields (restored flags/timestamps). All operations are auditable.
- Retention: keep tombstones for 24 months by default; immediately purge upon legal erasure requests or per data-retention policy. Preservation pointers are removed if the preserved artifact must be destroyed.
- Access control: restrict tombstone visibility and restore operations to privileged roles; tombstones inherit tenant scoping.
- Performance/storage: keep fields minimal; no binary blobs; enforce size limits.

## Decision
Adopt Redux as the single source of truth for application-wide state in the React application, and use redux-thunk as the middleware for handling asynchronous logic and controlled, conditional dispatching.

- Scope: Manage cross-cutting, shareable state (e.g., authentication, authorization/roles, user profile, feature flags, global notifications, cached server data that is reused across views) in Redux. Keep purely local/UI-ephemeral state (e.g., controlled inputs, transient toggles) within React components.
- Patterns:
  - Use pure reducers and serializable actions/state.
  - Use redux-thunk for async workflows (API calls, sequencing/conditional dispatch, retries) and side-effects; business logic for these flows resides in thunks, not in components or reducers.
  - Access state via React-Redux hooks (useSelector/useDispatch); wrap the app with Provider.
  - Configure middleware to include redux-thunk by default; add dev-only logger/immutability checks as needed.
- Rationale: Predictable state transitions, improved testability (reducers and thunks are unit-testable), easier reasoning about global state consistency, and broad ecosystem support. Chosen over MobX to maintain explicit, traceable updates and a stricter unidirectional data flow model aligned with team practices.
- Constraints/Guidelines: Avoid storing non-serializable data in Redux; keep reducers side-effect free; co-locate slice logic with feature domains; define typed action creators/selectors. Revisit middleware strategy if side-effect complexity grows beyond thunks’ ergonomics.

We will adopt a publish/subscribe event-driven architecture with a highly available, durable event bus based on Apache Kafka (or the managed equivalent in the target cloud) as the platform for integration events. Topics will be organized by bounded context and event domain, with naming conventions and partitions sized for throughput and scalability. Event contracts will use Avro with a Schema Registry to enforce compatibility; JSON may be permitted for external-facing events with documented schemas.

Delivery semantics will be at-least-once; consumers must be idempotent and support deduplication via event IDs and producer sequence numbers. Producers will implement the transactional outbox pattern to ensure atomicity between local state changes and event publication. Event versioning will follow backward-compatible evolution; breaking changes require new event versions/topics.

Operationally, the event bus will be provisioned as a managed, multi-AZ service with automatic failover, encryption in transit and at rest, and access control via ACLs. Retry policies, dead-letter topics, and replay procedures will be standardized. Observability will include centralized logging, metrics, tracing correlation (trace IDs in headers), and lag monitoring with alerting.

Retention policies will support bounded replay windows for recovery while controlling storage costs. Governance will include an event catalog, contract review, and CI/CD checks for schema compatibility. This platform will serve as the single integration backbone for cross-service communication via integration events.

We will standardize on UTF-8 encoding across the system and explicitly handle Excel’s UTF-8 BOM behavior. For CSV uploads, the importer will accept UTF-8 with or without a BOM. If a BOM is present, it will be stripped prior to parsing to avoid polluting the first header/field. If a file cannot be decoded as UTF-8, the upload will be rejected with a clear, actionable error message instructing users to save/export the file as UTF-8. We will not attempt lossy auto-detection or silent re-encoding.

For CSV templates and exports generated by the application, we will include a UTF-8 BOM to maximize compatibility with Microsoft Excel and similar tools. Export responses will set Content-Type with charset=utf-8 and Content-Disposition for proper handling by browsers and Excel.

For web form submissions, all inputs will be treated as UTF-8 end-to-end (client charset meta, server request parsing, persistence layer), ensuring consistency with CSV handling.

We will add automated tests covering BOM-present and BOM-absent CSVs, header normalization (first column), multibyte characters, and round-trip export/import via Excel. Documentation will clearly state the UTF-8 requirement, note the inclusion of a BOM in exports for Excel compatibility, and provide guidance for saving files as UTF-8 in common tools.

Adopt reflection-based JUnit 5 tests as the primary validation mechanism for the TOSCA YAML builder, driven by service-template fixtures augmented with metadata-based assertions. Each test fixture will include a metadata.assert block where each line encodes a dotted path to a target property and an expected value (e.g., repositories.rp1.url = http://github.com/kleinech; node_types.ntp1.requirements.0.rqr1.capability = cbt1). The test harness will parse the template, build the Java TOSCA model, and evaluate each assertion via reflection against the resulting instances.

Scope:
- Use reflection tests to verify structural mappings, field population, collections/indexed elements, maps, and simple value semantics (equals, null, presence).
- Retain a minimal set of manual tests for edge cases, complex behavior, and algorithmic logic not expressible via the assertion DSL.

Constraints and conventions:
- Define a strict, documented path grammar supporting objects, maps (by key), lists (by index), and nested properties.
- Support base operators: = (equals), != (not equals), isNull, notNull, contains (for collections/strings), size=, and boolean literals.
- Provide type-aware coercion for primitives, enums, URIs, numbers, and booleans; treat untyped values as strings by default with explicit markers when needed.
- Emit precise failure diagnostics including the path, actual value, expected value, and nearest resolvable segment.
- Make tests deterministic and environment-independent; prohibit reliance on network or clock.

Maintainability:
- Co-locate fixtures with subject modules; add a golden sample for each new TOSCA construct.
- Version the assertion DSL; validate and lint metadata before execution.
- Cache reflection lookups to minimize overhead; forbid setting accessible on non-public members unless justified.

This approach yields high coverage with concise, readable fixtures, acts as executable documentation, and scales with new TOSCA features while keeping manual tests focused on non-structural logic.

Adopt a manually authored OpenAPI (Swagger) 3.x specification as the single source of truth for the REST API documentation.

- Author and maintain the spec in YAML under version control (e.g., /docs/openapi.yaml), updated in the same pull requests as API changes.
- Enforce documentation parity via CI: validate and lint the spec (e.g., spectral/openapi-cli), fail builds on breaking or undocumented changes, and require review by API owners.
- Publish interactive documentation by serving the static OpenAPI spec through Swagger UI at a well-known endpoint (e.g., /docs) in all environments; include downloadable openapi.json/yaml.
- Provide comprehensive request/response examples, reusable schemas, standard error model, pagination, filtering, authentication flows, and explicit status codes.
- Manage versioning and deprecation in the spec (semantic version in info, deprecated flags on operations/fields, and a changelog). Host multiple versions if needed (e.g., /docs/v1, /docs/v2).
- Use the spec to generate client SDKs and server stubs where beneficial, but keep the spec authoritative over generated artifacts and annotations.
- For Spring-based services, serve the static spec from resources and avoid runtime coupling to code annotations; annotations may complement but must not diverge from the spec.
- Establish contribution guidelines: required sections, naming conventions, error catalog, and example completeness. Treat undocumented endpoints as non-public.
- Automate publishing of docs on release and ensure links from README and developer portals.

This approach maximizes accuracy, language/framework neutrality, and reviewability, while providing interactive, discoverable documentation without relying on Springfox.

Build a server-rendered web application using Node.js (LTS) with Express and Nunjucks templates, adopting the GOV.UK Design System (govuk-frontend) for accessibility, consistency, and usability. Prefer server-side rendering with progressive enhancement over client-side SPA frameworks (e.g., React/Vue/Angular), limiting JavaScript to targeted enhancements (validation, upload progress, resumable uploads) to reduce complexity and improve reliability in constrained government environments.

Implement secure, large-file uploads via direct-to-object storage (e.g., S3 multipart uploads) using server-signed URLs and resumable/chunked upload support (e.g., tus/S3 multipart), with clear progress feedback and robust error recovery. The application server will coordinate upload initiation, metadata capture, validation, and integrity checks (e.g., checksums), without proxying file data.

Use session-based auth with CSRF protection and standard OWASP controls; integrate with existing government identity/SSO where available. Ensure accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA), performance, and graceful degradation without JavaScript.

Rely on common, well-supported packages, minimal bespoke client code, and conventional Express architecture to optimize maintainability, onboarding, and operational simplicity. This approach aligns with common government technology stacks and deployment practices, lowers risk, and supports future extension without framework lock-in.

Adopt configuration-gated service wiring with no per-entity runtime dispatch. When federatedPropertiesEnabled = true, all Property-scoped entity data access services (e.g., EntityLookup, TermLookup, StatementLookup, EntityRevisionLookup, ChangeOps, Serialization/Deserialization, RDF builders, Search indexers) are bound at bootstrap to their federated, API-backed implementations. When federatedPropertiesEnabled = false, the same service contracts are bound to the local storage implementations. No service ever needs to branch at call time based on an entity identifier.

To avoid impacting non-Property entities, we provide Property-specific service registrations/aliases that only affect the Property entity type. Services for Items (and other local entity types) continue to use local implementations regardless of the flag. In federated mode, creation or use of local Properties is disallowed at the application layer; attempts to create or resolve a local Property are rejected early with explicit errors.

This decision intentionally excludes mixed-mode operation: there is no dynamic dispatch between local and federated Properties within a single wiki. As switching modes is not supported, we do not implement migration logic or data backfills; service bindings are chosen once at bootstrap based on configuration and remain constant for the life of the process.

Caching, persistence, and indexing layers follow the same binding: Property-related caches/indexes are populated only via federated fetches in federated mode and only via local reads in local mode; cache keys are unchanged because the backing implementation is global per deployment and not mixed within a process.

This approach minimizes complexity and risk in the MVP by:
- Eliminating per-request checks and entity-based branching.
- Constraining the federated behavior strictly to the Property entity type.
- Localizing the mode decision to service registration/factories in the MediaWiki service container, enabling clear, testable wiring and straightforward observability.

Adopt React with TypeScript as the primary front-end framework for Akvo DASH, avoiding alternative languages that transpile to JavaScript (e.g., ClojureScript) for the core application. Standardize on the following stack and conventions:
- Build tooling: Vite for development/build, Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for E2E, ESLint + Prettier for code quality.
- State and data: TanStack Query for server-state and caching; lightweight local state via Zustand (or React Context where trivial). Avoid global mutable stores unless justified.
- UI: Material UI (MUI) as the base component library with a theme system; adopt a design tokens approach to enable future theming/branding. Charting via Apache ECharts or Recharts, selected per visualization need.
- Type safety and APIs: Strict TypeScript with incremental type boundaries; OpenAPI/GraphQL codegen where applicable.
- Styling: CSS variables + MUI theming; avoid bespoke CSS-in-JS beyond what MUI requires.
- Architecture: Modular feature folders, route-based code-splitting, and a plugin-friendly composition pattern to enable future extensions.
- Interop: Allow Web Components where necessary; encapsulate third-party widgets behind adapters.

We will not adopt ClojureScript or other transpiled languages due to ecosystem constraints, hiring/training overhead, integration friction with widely used tooling, and reduced community support. This decision favors a large ecosystem, long-term maintainability, and faster onboarding.

Reevaluation checkpoint: reassess framework and supporting libraries in 18–24 months or upon major React ecosystem shifts (e.g., new stable React features significantly affecting architecture).

Adopt AWS CloudFormation as the standard mechanism to provision all AWS infrastructure required by ACS (EKS cluster, S3, Amazon MQ, Aurora, networking, IAM), while continuing to deploy ACS workloads to EKS via Helm. We will structure infrastructure as code using modular CloudFormation (nested stacks/StackSets as needed) and expose required outputs (endpoints, ARNs, credentials, config) for consumption by Helm through parameter stores/secrets and CI/CD integration.

Rationale:
- Aligns with our AWS-first strategy and leverages existing team expertise to minimize delivery risk and time-to-value.
- Provides full coverage of required AWS services without introducing custom controllers or new operational complexity.
- Avoids the learning curve and governance overhead of Terraform at this time and the immaturity/risk of building or operating custom Kubernetes controllers/CRDs for cloud resources.

Scope and constraints:
- This decision covers AWS resource provisioning and lifecycle management and the EKS control plane creation. Helm remains the mechanism for application-layer deployment within the cluster.
- Non-AWS resources are out of scope for now; if a cross-cloud or on-prem requirement emerges, we will re-evaluate introducing Terraform in a controlled pilot.

Implementation notes:
- Enforce guardrails via IAM roles, tagging, stack policies, and drift detection.
- Integrate with CI/CD to ensure reproducible, auditable deployments.
- Optionally use AWS CDK to author CloudFormation where it improves developer ergonomics, with CloudFormation as the deployment artifact.

Review in 6–12 months or upon multi-cloud/on-prem requirements.

## Decision

Adopt hermetic, containerized builds as the single, canonical build path. All compilation, testing, packaging, and tooling will execute inside a pinned OCI image (defined in /build/Dockerfile) to eliminate host OS and toolchain variance. Developers and CI will invoke builds via a simple wrapper (e.g., make build or ./scripts/build.sh) that runs docker/podman to mount the workspace and produce artifacts, ensuring identical results across macOS, Windows, and Linux.

Key elements:
- Pin all toolchain versions and OS base image in the Dockerfile; commit language/package-manager lockfiles; vendor critical build dependencies where feasible.
- Pre-resolve and cache dependencies within the image to enable offline, deterministic builds; disallow network access during build steps that should be reproducible.
- Standardize environment variables, locales, and timezones in the image; set deterministic build flags (e.g., SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH) where supported.
- Avoid reliance on host-installed tools; all required CLIs and linters are included in the image. Output artifacts and caches are written to mounted volumes for host access and build acceleration.
- CI pipelines use the same image to guarantee parity. Publish the image with a content-addressable tag (digest) and update via controlled release process.
- Provide a devcontainer configuration for editor integration and a minimal cross-platform wrapper script that gracefully falls back between Docker and Podman.

This approach makes the only prerequisite for building an OCI-compatible runtime, removing environmental differences from consideration and delivering consistent, reproducible builds across all basic environments.

Decide to introduce a platform-abstracted PathService that returns a user-facing “save location” appropriate to each OS, instead of assuming a universal Downloads folder. The service exposes a single API getUserSaveDirectory() with platform-specific implementations:
- Android: Resolve to the public Downloads directory. Use path_provider.getDownloadsDirectory() when available; if unavailable or null, use a lightweight platform channel to Environment.DIRECTORY_DOWNLOADS. Handle runtime permissions where applicable (pre-Android 10) and respect scoped storage on Android 10+.
- iOS: Resolve to the app’s Documents directory via path_provider.getApplicationDocumentsDirectory(), as iOS has no public Downloads folder. Do not attempt to emulate a Downloads folder.

Provide an optional export flow on iOS to let users pick an external destination (Files/iCloud/On‑device) using the system document picker/share sheet, rather than writing directly to arbitrary external paths.

Expose both getUserSaveDirectory() and getAppPrivateDirectory() to allow features that need app-private storage on either platform. The API returns a structured result including path, visibility (user-visible/app-private), and a flag indicating whether the location is shareable/exportable.

Fallback behavior:
- If Android Downloads is unavailable/not writable, fall back to app-private files and notify the user with an option to export.
- If iOS Documents is not writable (rare), fall back to app Support directory.

Rationale: Aligns with platform conventions, avoids broken assumptions on iOS, centralizes path logic, and keeps UX consistent by abstracting differences while enabling user export where a public Downloads folder does not exist.

## Decision
Adopt NetworkManager as the single, standardized abstraction for all network requests across the codebase, and deprecate the Fetchable protocol.

- Scope:
  - All new features must use NetworkManager.
  - Existing code paths using Fetchable will be migrated to NetworkManager.
  - Third-party or legacy components will integrate via an adapter layer when direct replacement is not immediately feasible.

- Deprecation and Migration:
  - Mark Fetchable as deprecated immediately; prohibit new usages.
  - Provide a FetchableAdapter that delegates to NetworkManager to minimize disruption during transition.
  - Incrementally refactor modules to call NetworkManager directly, removing Fetchable conformance as touched.
  - Remove Fetchable and its implementations after migration completes.

- Design and Usage:
  - Expose NetworkManager via dependency injection to support testability and mocking.
  - Standardize request building, error handling, retries, cancellation, timeouts, logging, and metrics within NetworkManager.
  - Define clear interfaces for authentication, interceptors/middleware, and response decoding to ensure parity with prior capabilities.

- Compatibility and Quality:
  - Maintain API compatibility at module boundaries via the adapter until fully migrated.
  - Add unit and integration tests around NetworkManager; replace Fetchable-based tests with NetworkManager mocks/stubs.
  - Centralize monitoring and tracing to NetworkManager to ensure consistent observability.

- Timeline and Governance:
  - Enforce adoption via code review checks and lint rules.
  - Track migration progress per module; target full removal of Fetchable by the agreed milestone.

We will remove client-side reliance on the PLAY_LANG cookie for the tracking consent banner and adopt a server-provided data-language attribute as the sole mechanism for language selection.

- The tracking consent script will read a data-language attribute (e.g., data-language="cy"|"en") rendered on the banner container.
- PLAY_LANG will no longer be read in the browser; teams may set PLAY_LANG as HttpOnly without impacting banner localisation or ZAP outcomes.
- Services using Play should populate data-language from the server-side i18n/language resolution (which may still use PLAY_LANG internally).
- Classic Java services must explicitly set the data-language attribute based on whatever language selection mechanism they implement.
- A short deprecation window will keep a best-effort fallback: if data-language is absent and PLAY_LANG is non-HttpOnly, Welsh (“cy”) will be honoured; this fallback will be removed in a subsequent major version.
- Documentation and integration guides will be updated with examples for Play and classic stacks, including defaulting to “en” if the attribute is missing or invalid.
- No other components should rely on client-side PLAY_LANG; align future components to data attributes for language.

Adopt XTDB as the primary graph-capable database instead of Neo4j. We will use XTDB’s bitemporal model to provide first-class time and complete historical auditability, and rely on its Datalog query capability to express graph traversals and relationships. XTDB’s open-source licensing and strong Clojure integration align with our ecosystem and reduce long-term licensing risk and library maintenance overhead.

Implementation details:
- Represent entities and relationships as documents with explicit edge documents where needed for higher-order relations.
- Enable bitemporal features for valid-time and transaction-time queries to support time-travel, auditing, and retroactive corrections.
- Use RocksDB for local storage in development; for production durability and scalability, use Kafka or a JDBC-backed transaction log (e.g., PostgreSQL) with S3-compatible object storage for index checkpoints.
- Standardize on Datalog for queries; provide thin Clojure wrappers for common graph patterns (neighbors, path expansion) to simplify usage.
- Migrate existing Neo4j data via an export-transform-load pipeline into XTDB documents, preserving timestamps and relationship semantics.

Operational considerations:
- Establish backup/restore procedures leveraging XTDB’s immutable log and checkpoints.
- Monitor index growth and configure compaction and retention policies appropriate to our audit requirements.
- Define performance SLOs and benchmark typical graph workloads (fan-out, path queries) to validate sizing.

We will not invest further in Neo4j-specific libraries. Revisit this decision only if we encounter non-negotiable requirements uniquely satisfied by a property-graph engine with native path algorithms that cannot be efficiently expressed in Datalog.

Adopt Azure DevOps Pipelines (YAML-based) as the standard CI/CD platform for the HEE National Website Platform, integrating with Azure services and enterprise controls. Pipelines will run on a hybrid agent model: Microsoft-hosted agents for ephemeral build/test workloads and self-hosted agents (in a locked-down subnet) for deployments and operations requiring private network access. We will use multi-stage YAML pipelines with distinct Build, Test, Security Scan, and Deploy stages, enforcing environment approvals and checks (including change management and CAB where required). Secrets and configuration will be sourced from Azure Key Vault via variable groups; artifacts and containers will be published to Azure Artifacts/ACR. Pull request validation, branch policies, and reusable pipeline templates will be mandatory to ensure consistency, quality, and reuse across services. Quality gates will include unit/integration tests, SAST/DAST/OSS license scanning, and code coverage thresholds. Deployment targets will use Azure-native integrations (e.g., App Service, AKS, Static Web Apps) with blue/green or canary strategies where applicable, and rollbacks will be automated via versioned artifacts. The decision standardizes on Azure DevOps for alignment with existing Azure tenancy, identity (Entra ID), security/compliance requirements, centralized auditing, and cost/governance efficiency, while allowing integration with external Git providers (e.g., GitHub) if needed through service connections.

We will resolve object graphs via constructor-based Dependency Injection using a single composition root per process and module-scoped registries. Each Command/Query is handled within an operation scope (child container) that resolves only the top-level handler; the container constructs the full graph transitively. We prohibit Service Locator and field/property injection.

- Lifetimes:
  - Singleton: stateless services, configuration, pure mappers, caches with explicit concurrency control.
  - Scoped (per Command/Query): unit-of-work, repositories, DbContext/transaction, request-specific services.
  - Transient: short-lived objects without shared state or expensive initialization.

- Registration:
  - Modules expose a bootstrap/installer that registers their handlers, repositories, policies, and factories.
  - Open-generic registrations bind ICommandHandler<T>, IQueryHandler<T> to implementations, enabling automatic handler discovery.
  - Cross-cutting concerns (logging, metrics, validation, authorization, retry) use container-supported decorators/middleware around handlers.

- Factories and runtime parameters:
  - Use typed factories/Func<T>/Provider<T> for runtime values and conditional creation.
  - Avoid injecting primitives; wrap in option/config objects or use IOptions-like patterns.

- Resolution rules:
  - Resolve only at the boundaries (command bus/query bus/web endpoint); no container access in domain code.
  - Fail fast on missing bindings and circular dependencies at startup.
  - Prefer interfaces over concretes; allow explicit concrete registration only for value objects.

- Scoping/transactions:
  - One operation scope per Command/Query; transaction lifetime aligns with scope.
  - Async flows capture and propagate scope correctly.

- Testing/verification:
  - Container verification at startup and module-level wiring tests.
  - Deterministic module registration order; no ambient/singleton mutable state.

This approach yields explicit, testable wiring, clear lifetimes, and isolation per operation while supporting cross-cutting concerns via decorators.

We will deprecate all core integrations that require direct access to host GPIO, SPI, or I2C (including Raspberry Pi–specific GPIO integrations and similar bus-based drivers) and remove them from core after a deprecation period. Effective immediately:
- No new GPIO/SPI/I2C host-access integrations will be accepted into core.
- Existing GPIO/SPI/I2C integrations will be marked deprecated and emit deprecation warnings with migration guidance.
- Official documentation will direct users to dedicated external solutions (e.g., ESPHome or other MCU/bridge projects) and, where applicable, community-maintained custom integrations.

Scope:
- Applies to integrations that depend on direct pin/bus access on the host or containerized environment.
- Exceptions may be considered only for integrations that:
  - Do not require host pin access (e.g., use network/USB bridges or standardized remote daemons) and
  - Are actively maintained, well-tested across platforms, and demonstrably stable in supported installation methods.

Timeline:
- Deprecate immediately; remove after a standard deprecation window spanning two regular release cycles (or the next major release, whichever is first), with clear communication in release notes.

Mitigations:
- Provide a migration guide to ESPHome and recommended hardware/firmware bridges.
- Facilitate transfer of unmaintained but desired integrations to community ownership (e.g., HACS) where feasible.

Reinstatement criteria:
- Any future proposal must demonstrate cross-platform stability without host GPIO access, active maintenance commitment, and test coverage meeting core standards.

## Decision
Parameterize identity across the zos SAL by introducing an explicit, optional identity parameter on all relevant SAL APIs and CLI/SDK commands. When provided, this identity is used to authenticate and authorize operations and to deploy workloads under that identity; when omitted, the system defaults to the node’s configured identity for full backward compatibility.

Implement an IdentityContext that can be passed per call, per session, or configured at component initialization, enabling safe runtime switching without process restarts. Provide an IdentityProvider abstraction supporting multiple sources (local key store, HSM, KMS, environment, config file), with pluggable resolvers and clear precedence rules. Identities are referenced by stable aliases; material is securely stored, encrypted at rest, and never logged. Add validation for key format, tenancy, and capability scopes before execution.

Propagate the effective identity through all layers (API -> scheduler -> executor) to ensure consistent signing, metering, and auditing. Extend audit logs to capture the identity alias and operation performed. Update CLI/SDK to accept --identity/<identity_alias> and session-level set-identity commands. Maintain a global default identity but mark implicit identity usage as deprecated; emit warnings and document a deprecation timeline before removing implicit behavior.

Provide feature flags to enable/disable identity switching per environment. Add comprehensive tests (unit/integration/e2e) for defaulting, override precedence, concurrent operations with different identities, and failure modes. Perform a phased rollout: introduce parameterization behind a disabled-by-default flag, migrate internal callers, then enable by default after validation.

## Decision
Adopt MultiFrameViewer as the canonical component for displaying multi-frame subjects in the lib-classifier, replacing the prior PagesViewer name. The first iteration will target multi-image transcription workflows and deliver:

- Core viewer supporting per-frame zoom/pan, image tiling where available, loading/error states, and per-frame annotation layers with persistence across frame changes.
- A minimal, extensible filmstrip component for frame navigation, providing lazy-loaded thumbnails, keyboard navigation, focus management, and selection; designed for future feature expansion (see decisions 6 and 7).
- Prefetching of adjacent frames and thumbnail virtualization for performance on large frame sets.
- Accessibility compliance (ARIA roles, logical tab order, visible focus, screen reader labels) for both viewer and filmstrip.

Architecture will be modular and composable:
- MultiFrameViewer orchestrates a FrameController, a MediaFrame renderer (initially images), an AnnotationLayer, and a Filmstrip. Communication occurs via explicit props/events to maintain testability and enable independent evolution of subcomponents.
- Media rendering will be media-type pluggable to support additional frame types in later iterations without breaking the API.
- Filmstrip is a replaceable subcomponent with a stable, documented interface to permit future domain-specific variants (e.g., ecology features).

Backward compatibility:
- Deprecate PagesViewer, exporting it as an alias to MultiFrameViewer for one release cycle with console warnings, then remove.

Configuration and data:
- Accept subjects with ordered frames; support frame-level metadata to influence thumbnail labels and default zoom.
- Provide sensible defaults; project-specific behaviors are opt-in via props.

Defers:
- Non-transcription features (e.g., domain-specific tooling for ecology, advanced filmstrip affordances) are deferred and will be added incrementally under the established interfaces, guided by decisions 6 and 7.

## Decision
Adopt SCSS (Sass, SCSS syntax) with CSS Modules as the primary styling approach.

- Use SCSS to enable variables, mixins, and partials for consistent theming and reusability.
- Use CSS Modules to provide local scoping of class names by default, preventing style leakage and reducing naming collisions.
- Co-locate component-specific .module.scss files with their components; reserve a small set of global SCSS files (e.g., variables, resets, typography) imported once at app entry.
- Configure the build (e.g., Vite/Webpack) with sass-loader and css-loader modules enabled; enable source maps in non-prod for developer experience.
- Establish a lightweight naming convention (e.g., camelCase exports; hashed class names in build) and a minimal linting/formatting setup (Stylelint + Prettier).
- Provide a shared tokens file (e.g., _tokens.scss) for colors, spacing, typography, and z-index layers; document usage in a brief style guide.
- Avoid advanced CSS-in-JS or runtime styling libraries to keep complexity low and ensure familiarity for future maintainers.
- Allow gradual adoption and easy onboarding by keeping plain CSS support where needed and offering clear examples for typical patterns (theming, responsive utilities, composition).

Decide to publish a single NPM package for the component library initially.

Rationale:
- Modern bundlers/tree-shaking will eliminate unused components, keeping consumer bundles lean without fragmenting the publishing strategy.
- A single package simplifies development, documentation, CI/CD, versioning, and releases, accelerating iteration.

Implementation:
- Provide ESM as the primary export, with type declarations; set "sideEffects": false to enable tree-shaking.
- Expose subpath exports for direct imports (e.g., @scope/ui/Button) alongside top-level named exports to support selective consumption without separate packages.
- Preserve module structure in the build (e.g., preserveModules) to aid tree-shaking and sourcemaps.
- Maintain consistent component-level entry files and test coverage to ease potential future extraction.
- Use semantic versioning with changesets/release notes to communicate changes clearly.

Re-evaluation criteria and triggers:
- Measurable pain signals: frequent consumer requests for per-component installs, issues with non-tree-shaking environments, or significant cold install size.
- Scale thresholds: >30 components, published tarball >10 MB, or sustained bundle-size complaints.
- Operational needs: desire for independent versioning/release cadence per component or differing peer dependency matrices.

Migration path if we split later:
- Adopt a monorepo with per-component packages; maintain the existing package as a meta-package that re-exports components to provide a non-breaking transition.
- Provide codemods and documentation for import path updates; deprecate legacy paths on a defined schedule.
- Automate publishing and changelog generation to manage multi-package complexity.

This approach optimizes for simplicity now while keeping a clear, low-risk path to per-component packages if usage and scale warrant it.

We will use OpenAPI 3.1 as the canonical, single source of truth for all HTTP APIs. The specification will be maintained in YAML within each service repository, versioned with the code, and authored contract-first. All server stubs, SDKs, tests, and human-readable documentation will be generated from this specification to ensure consistency and reduce drift.

Human-readable documentation will be published per release using Swagger UI/ReDoc, bundled with the service and available via an authenticated docs endpoint and the internal developer portal. The machine-readable spec will be exposed at a well-known path (/openapi.json and /openapi.yaml) for tooling consumption.

Machine clients for designated target languages will be generated via OpenAPI Generator in CI and published to internal package registries. The pipeline will also run spectral linting, schema validation, and breaking-change detection; merges will be blocked on violations. Specifications must include complete schemas (leveraging JSON Schema in OAS 3.1), examples, error models, pagination/concurrency conventions, and explicit versioning and deprecation metadata.

API versioning will follow semantic versioning. Backward-incompatible changes require a new major versioned path/host and deprecation windows for prior versions. A changelog is required for every spec revision.

For event-driven or streaming interfaces, AsyncAPI will be used under the same governance and CI rules, with corresponding docs and client generation.

This decision standardizes API documentation in both human- and machine-readable forms, enabling reliable automated client generation and consistent developer experience.

We will adopt a public, repository-based Architecture Decision Record (ADR) process, using a centralized “architecture-decisions” Git repository as the single source of truth and publishing it to the open web.

- Standard: All decisions use a lightweight ADR template capturing title, status, decision, context, options considered, decision drivers, consequences, authors, reviewers, and supersedes/superseded-by links. Each ADR receives a stable ID and permalink.
- Process: Propose via RFC pull requests. Discussion occurs in the PR and linked Discussions; decision is made through documented consensus or a recorded vote by the Architecture Working Group (AWG) with named approvers. Required reviewers are enforced via CODEOWNERS.
- Versioning: ADRs live in Git; all edits occur through PRs, preserving history. Status values: Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated, Superseded, Rejected. Changes update the decision log and cross-links.
- Centralization: A single repo indexes all ADRs across products and platforms, with labels/tags (domain, system, capability). Project repos may link to but not duplicate ADRs.
- Transparency: The repo is public by default; sensitive items use a private mirror with redacted public summaries. Meeting notes and rationale remain attached to ADRs.
- Discoverability: The repo is published as a searchable static site with full-text search, tags, and RSS. Each ADR has canonical URLs and is linked from engineering handbooks and onboarding.
- Stewardship: The AWG maintains the process, curates taxonomy, and reviews for consistency and accessibility.

## Decision
Adopt lightweight Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) to capture, communicate, and govern all significant architectural choices.

- Format and location:
  - Use MADR template (Concise 1–2 pages).
  - Store in repo at /docs/adr/.
  - Naming: YYYYMMDD-descriptive-title.md with incremental index.
  - Provide /docs/adr/README.md as an index with status and links.

- Scope and timing:
  - An ADR is required for any decision that materially impacts architecture, cross-cutting concerns, data models, interfaces, runtime topology, third-party selection, or SLAs.
  - Create ADRs before implementation; urgent cases may use “Draft” ADRs, finalized within 5 working days.
  - Routine refactors and non-architectural fixes are exempt.

- Lifecycle and governance:
  - Statuses: Draft → Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated/Superseded.
  - ADRs are immutable once Accepted; changes occur via a new ADR that supersedes the prior one.
  - Each ADR has an owner (feature lead or architect) and reviewers (at least 2, including architecture representative).
  - Approval via pull request review; discussion occurs in PR comments.

- Backfill and migration:
  - Within 4 weeks, produce ADRs for the top N (e.g., 10–15) past impactful decisions.
  - Tag unknowns as “Assumed” and iterate.

- Tooling and enforcement:
  - Provide a template and examples.
  - Add a PR checklist item: “Does this change require/affect an ADR? Link it.”
  - Optional CI rule to warn when architectural files change without an ADR link.

- Discoverability:
  - Tag ADRs with domains; cross-link to code, diagrams, and tickets; summarize in release notes.

We will adopt gin-gonic/gin as our primary HTTP router and request handling framework.

Rationale:
- Developer velocity: Gin’s routing, middleware, parameter binding, and error handling streamline adding and evolving endpoints, accelerating delivery versus net/http-only or custom routers.
- Performance and maturity: Gin offers proven performance with a large user base and active maintenance. gorilla/mux is archived and not recommended for new projects. Building our own router poses unnecessary complexity and risk.
- Ecosystem: Rich middleware (logging, recovery, CORS, rate limiting) and integrations (OpenAPI, validation) reduce boilerplate and standardize cross-cutting concerns.
- Maintainability: Route grouping, versioning, and conventions (Context-based handlers) support a clear, scalable API structure.

Scope and usage:
- Use Gin for all application endpoints, with route groups organized by domain and version (e.g., /api/v1). Reserve net/http only for minimal edge cases (e.g., health checks within Gin or via native handlers when required).
- Standardize on gin-gonic/gin v1.x, pinning via go.mod and enabling Dependabot/renovate for updates.

Operational and security considerations:
- Enable Recovery and structured Logging middleware by default; integrate request IDs and correlation.
- Configure timeouts, body size limits, and sane defaults (MaxMultipartMemory, JSON decoder DisallowUnknownFields where applicable).
- Validate inputs via binding/validation tags; return consistent error envelopes.
- Configure Trusted Proxies and enforce HTTPS/secure headers; add CORS and rate limiting where needed.
- Provide request metrics and tracing via middleware; expose pprof and health/readiness endpoints.

Architecture and testing:
- Keep handlers thin; delegate to services/use-cases. Inject dependencies via constructors.
- Use route contracts and golden tests for JSON responses. Provide httptest-based integration tests for route groups.
- Support graceful shutdown with context propagation and in-flight request draining.

Migration and extensibility:
- Establish deprecation policy per versioned route groups.
- Allow modular addition of new endpoints and middlewares without breaking existing routes.

This decision optimizes developer productivity and operational stability while avoiding the risks of deprecated or bespoke routing solutions.

We will standardize on an xUnit-style unit testing framework with a first-class mocking/doubles library to enable TDD and function-level isolation. All new code will be designed for testability via dependency inversion and seam creation:

- Functions and modules that call external services, I/O, time, randomness, environment, and global state must receive those collaborators as parameters (or via constructor/factory injection), enabling straightforward substitution with test doubles.
- We will prefer fakes/stubs over mocks where behavior is simple, and use mocks/spies only to verify interactions at architectural boundaries (I/O, network, message bus, persistence). Do not mock pure functions or data structures.
- Where legacy or third-party APIs prevent injection, we will use the framework’s patch/monkeypatch facility to replace functions for the duration of a test; such patches must be localized and cleaned up automatically.
- Hard singletons and hidden globals are prohibited in new code. Side-effectful utilities must be wrapped behind interfaces/ports to allow mocking.
- Tests must be deterministic and fast; avoid sleeping and real network/filesystem calls in unit tests. Use in-memory fakes for persistence and messaging where feasible.
- Organize tests co-located with source or in a parallel tree with matching names; one test file per unit under test, with descriptive test names expressing behavior. Follow red–green–refactor workflow.
- Code under test should expose minimal surface area required for testing; avoid adding test-only hooks beyond dependency seams.
- CI will execute the unit suite on every change; failures block merges. Coverage thresholds apply to unit tests, but do not incentivize mocking internals—focus on meaningful behavior coverage.

Tooling: adopt the language-idiomatic xUnit framework and its standard mocking library in each service; teams must not introduce ad-hoc mocking utilities outside the approved library without architectural review.

We will manage database schema and data migrations with Flyway using versioned, SQL-first migrations stored in the repository. All migrations are immutable, peer-reviewed, and applied automatically by CI/CD to each environment before application rollout.

Key practices:
- Tooling: Flyway with a dedicated schema history table; no ad-hoc/manual changes in shared environments.
- Location and naming: db/migrations with V{yyyyMMddHHmmss}__short_description.sql for versioned changes and R__name.sql for repeatable objects (views, functions, seeds).
- Strategy: expand-and-contract for zero/low-downtime releases (additive changes first; code toggles/compatibility; later contract/removal).
- Rollbacks: production rollbacks are forward-only via corrective migrations; optional U__ undo scripts permitted in local/dev only.
- Ordering and conflicts: timestamp-based versions; resolve merge conflicts by renaming to a new timestamp before merging to main.
- Data migrations: allowed in versioned scripts; long-running operations must be chunked/batched and run off-peak with safety guards and timeouts.
- Execution: CI/CD runs Flyway migrate on the target database prior to deploying the new application version; production migrations are explicitly approved. Application startup does not run migrations in production.
- Environments: same migration scripts across all environments; environment-specific configuration only for connection settings.
- Security: use a migration service account with required DDL permissions; application runtime uses least-privilege DML-only credentials.
- Observability: migration logs and schema history are captured and retained; alerts on failures.
- Backups: ensure recent backups/snapshots prior to production schema changes.

This approach provides deterministic, auditable, and backward-compatible database change management aligned with our deployment pipeline.

## Decision

Adopt TypeScript as the default language for all new application code and shared libraries to improve code confidence and self-documentation. Migrate existing JavaScript incrementally, prioritizing core/domain modules and public-facing interfaces.

Enforce strict type safety project-wide:
- Enable strict in tsconfig.json, including strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noImplicitThis.
- Disallow implicit any and ban ts-ignore; require ts-expect-error with a justification where unavoidable.
- Type all module boundaries (public APIs, I/O, network, storage, and inter-service contracts) explicitly using interfaces/type aliases.
- Prefer discriminated unions and string literal unions over enums, and readonly/immutable types where feasible.

Tooling and standards:
- Maintain a shared base tsconfig with path aliases and incremental compilation; consumers extend from it.
- Pin TypeScript and @types versions; update via scheduled maintenance.
- Use ESLint with @typescript-eslint and consistent-type-imports; format with Prettier.
- CI runs tsc --noEmit and lint checks; enforce type coverage thresholds for critical packages/modules.
- For packages, emit declaration files (declaration: true) and verify they compile in CI.
- Use a TS-aware test runner (e.g., Vitest/Jest with ts-jest/esbuild) with isolatedModules.

Migration approach:
- AllowJs only for transitional modules; disallow checkJs. Convert files to .ts/.tsx as they are touched.
- Introduce types at system boundaries first (API contracts, DB models, message schemas), then propagate inward.
- Provide shims for third-party libraries lacking types; prefer well-typed alternatives when available.

Developer workflow:
- Require editor type-checking enabled; supply project templates and examples.
- Document typing conventions (naming, generics, narrowing, error typing) and provide lint rules to enforce them.

## Decision
Adopt three explicit node runtime modes with strict capability boundaries and a single configuration switch for selection.

- Mode selection: --mode={full|validator|seed}. Defaults to full if unspecified.
- Keying: priv-validator keys are only loaded/accepted in validator mode. Nodes in full/seed mode will refuse to start if validator keys are present to prevent accidental consensus participation.

Full mode
- Purpose: state replication, block/tx validation, RPC and data serving, tx and block gossip.
- Constraints: never participates in consensus (no proposing/voting), never signs; cannot be promoted to validator at runtime. Transition to validator requires shutdown and restart with validator mode and keys.
- Sync: supports fast/snapshot/height-limited sync as configured.

Validator mode
- Purpose: identical to existing state machine behavior; participates in consensus only once fully synced.
- Behavior: sync without voting until caught up; on full sync, enable proposing/voting per validator set status.
- Networking: supports sentry/topology isolation; adheres to existing mempool, evidence, and consensus channels.
- Safety: double-sign prevention remains enforced; HSM/remote signer supported as in current system.

Seed mode
- Purpose: lightweight peer discovery service akin to TenderSeed; maintains address book and offers peer exchange/bootstrapping.
- Constraints: no consensus, no block execution/state, no mempool, no RPC, no storage beyond address book; minimal resource footprint.
- Networking: peer-exchange enabled; seeds do not relay transactions or blocks.

Enforcement and observability
- Capability gating at process init based on mode; consensus reactor ignores votes from non-validator modes.
- Metrics and logs are mode-tagged; readiness/liveness endpoints reflect mode-specific health.
- Configuration validation prevents conflicting settings (e.g., mempool enabled in seed mode).

Operational policy
- Mode changes require restart; no hot switching.
- Documentation and deployment profiles provided per mode, including security guidance (sentry for validators, public exposure for seeds, RPC for full nodes).

We will front Kibana with an authenticated reverse proxy using GitHub OAuth to provide SSO and controlled access.

- Deploy oauth2-proxy as the authentication gateway in front of Kibana. Configure it to use a GitHub OAuth App (client ID/secret) with our organization/team restrictions and approved email domains.
- Terminate TLS at the edge (AWS ALB or NGINX Ingress with ACM certificate). The ALB/Ingress routes only to oauth2-proxy; Kibana is reachable exclusively from oauth2-proxy via private networking and security group rules to prevent direct, unauthenticated access.
- On successful GitHub login, oauth2-proxy issues an encrypted, short-lived session cookie and redirects users to the Kibana dashboard URL (kibana-webconsole). Unauthenticated requests are redirected to GitHub, then back to the original Kibana URL to preserve user context.
- Propagate user identity to Kibana via configured headers (e.g., X-Forwarded-User, X-Forwarded-Email). Where Kibana supports it, enable multi-tenant/read-only views mapped by team using oauth2-proxy’s GitHub team filters; otherwise enforce coarse-grained access via proxy ACLs.
- Enforce security best practices: HTTPS-only, HSTS, secure/HTTPOnly/SameSite cookies, CSRF protection, minimal OAuth scopes (read:org if team filtering required), and key/secret rotation via AWS Secrets Manager. Configure short session TTL with refresh via OAuth, and explicit logout that clears sessions.
- Implement centralized observability: proxy access logs (success/failure, user identity, team) shipped to CloudWatch/ELK; alerts on anomalous access patterns.
- High availability: run oauth2-proxy in at least two AZs with health checks; stateless design using cookie sessions; infrastructure as code (Terraform/CloudFormation) and blue/green deploys.
- Block public Kibana endpoints; restrict ES/Kibana security groups to the proxy. Optionally place the stack behind a private VPC endpoint and expose via VPN or AWS Client VPN if further network hardening is required.
- Document onboarding: GitHub org membership, team mapping to Kibana spaces (if used), and support runbooks for OAuth app changes and certificate renewal.

This design provides GitHub-based SSO without modifying Kibana, centralizes access control, preserves user experience via post-auth redirects, and meets security and operability requirements.

Adopt a single, unified container image artifact for both Docker Swarm and Kubernetes. Implement a multi-stage Dockerfile that builds artifacts once (builder stage) and produces a minimal runtime image. Use Docker Buildx/BuildKit with layer caching and cache mounts (e.g., for package managers) to avoid re-downloading dependencies and re-building unchanged layers. Standardize a single CI pipeline that:

- Builds the image once per commit using Buildx.
