- Produces OCI-compliant images for linux/amd64 (and linux/arm64 if required).
- Publishes to a central registry with immutable digests and multiple tags: commit SHA, semantic version (if applicable), and a moving branch tag.

Split pipeline responsibilities: a “build and publish” stage runs once and pushes the image; “deploy” stages for Swarm and Kubernetes consume the same image reference (prefer digest pinning) without rebuilding. Enforce reproducibility with dependency lockfiles and deterministic build flags. Optimize for size and security by using slim runtime bases, copying only runtime artifacts from the builder, and integrating image scanning in the build stage.

All environments (dev, staging, prod) pull the same image artifact; configuration differences are injected via environment variables, secrets, and manifests/stack files. This approach eliminates duplicated work, reduces build time and bandwidth, ensures deployment parity across orchestrators, and creates a single source of truth for the application binary.

## Decision
Adopt a single, enterprise-wide pattern standard and governance model to ensure consistent format and structure across customer-facing, integration, and other architectures.

- Standard template: All patterns will use a unified Pattern Template v1.0 with the following sections and order: Title, Pattern ID, Status (Draft/Proposed/Approved/Deprecated), Summary, Problem/Forces, Context, Solution, Diagram(s), Variants, Constraints & Assumptions, Quality Attributes & Trade-offs, Security & Compliance, Operational Considerations, Integration Touchpoints, Dependencies, Known Issues, References, Example Implementations, Decision History, Changelog.
- Mandatory metadata: Owner, Reviewers, Domain, Tags, Version (SemVer), Created/Last Reviewed dates, Applicability (When to use/When not to use), Consumed/Produced contracts, SLAs/Non-functionals.
- Naming and taxonomy: Patterns will be categorized under a controlled vocabulary (e.g., UI, API, Integration, Data, Security, Observability) and named kebab-case with a stable ID (e.g., INT-API-GATEWAY-001).
- Docs-as-code: Author patterns in Markdown with embedded PlantUML/Mermaid for diagrams. Host in a central git monorepo under /patterns/<domain>/<pattern-id>. Auto-render to an internal site via CI.
- Versioning and lifecycle: SemVer for content changes; lifecycle managed via statuses and deprecation notices with migration guidance. Breaking changes require a new minor/major version and backward-compatibility notes.
- Governance: Architecture Review Board (ARB) owns the template and approves new/changed patterns via pull requests. Linting (markdownlint, template-checker) and CI gates enforce completeness and conventions. Domain Architects act as code owners for their areas.
- Reuse and discovery: Tagging and search enabled on the site; cross-links between related patterns. Reference implementations and sample repos linked in the pattern.
- Compliance: Security, privacy, and regulatory considerations are required sections; patterns must reference applicable policies and threat models.
- Adoption plan: Migrate existing patterns to the standard within two quarters. New patterns must use the template immediately. Provide a conversion guide and scripts to scaffold new patterns.

This decision establishes a consistent, governed pattern system that improves clarity, reuse, compliance, and cross-domain alignment.

Adopt TypeScript as the primary language for the browser-based visualization stack. TypeScript provides a familiar, class- and interface-based object-oriented model with static typing, enabling developers with OO backgrounds to be productive quickly and reducing onboarding time for frequently changing teams. We will compile TypeScript to JavaScript targeting the browser environment, using npm-based tooling and a standard build pipeline (e.g., webpack) to bundle assets. Typings (DefinitelyTyped or custom declarations) will be used to interoperate with the broader JavaScript ecosystem and existing visualization libraries. The codebase will follow an OO-centric architecture (modules, classes, interfaces) while allowing functional patterns where beneficial. Linting, formatting, and type-checking are mandatory in CI to ensure consistency and maintainability.

We will move the mymove repository outside of $GOPATH and use Go modules in module-aware mode by default, setting GO111MODULE=auto (or leaving it unset on Go versions where modules are default). This supersedes ADR0003’s guidance to keep the repo under $GOPATH with GO111MODULE=on.

Rationale:
- Resolves tooling conflicts (e.g., pre-commit hooks using Go libraries) observed when forcing module mode inside $GOPATH.
- Aligns local development behavior with our CI/CD configuration.
- Reduces contributor friction and eliminates the need for per-tool workarounds.

Actions:
- Update developer setup documentation to require cloning mymove outside of $GOPATH.
- Remove instructions that mandate GO111MODULE=on; recommend GO111MODULE=auto or unsetting the variable.
- Verify and update build scripts, Make targets, and tooling (pre-commit, linters, generators) to operate correctly outside $GOPATH in module mode.
- Ensure CI/CD and containerized environments mirror this layout and environment behavior.
- Provide a short migration guide for developers relocating existing checkouts.

Acceptance:
- All local builds, tests, and pre-commit hooks succeed with the repository outside $GOPATH.
- CI/CD runs use the same layout and environment configuration.
- No remaining dependencies assume $GOPATH-based paths.

Adopt a risk-based testing strategy anchored in the Testing Pyramid to balance cost and confidence:

- Mandate high-confidence unit testing for core business logic with 85–95% coverage on modules labeled critical and 70–80% on noncritical modules. Prefer deterministic, fast tests; use property-based testing where appropriate.
- Use consumer-driven contract tests at service boundaries (APIs, messaging) to lock interfaces and reduce brittle end-to-end reliance.
- Add focused integration tests for persistence, cross-service orchestration, and framework wiring; prioritize scenarios with stateful interactions and data integrity.
- Maintain a small suite of end-to-end smoke tests covering top user journeys and SLAs (e.g., signup, purchase, payment, P0 alerts). Keep E2E count minimal and stable; favor semantic selectors over UI snapshots to reduce brittleness.
- Treat defects as tests-first events: every bug fixed adds/updates a regression test.
- For external dependencies, use fakes/mocks by default; add a minimal set of contract-backed integration tests against sandboxes in CI/nightly.
- Enforce coverage gates per module: global floor 75%, critical modules 90%; waive only via architect-approved rationale documented in the PR.
- Make tests part of the Definition of Done: PRs must include appropriate tests; reviewers assess test scope and brittleness risk.
- Prefer deleting or refactoring tests over contorting production code to satisfy brittle tests; tests must assert behavior, not implementation details.
- Periodically audit the suite (quarterly) to prune flaky/brittle tests, review coverage hotspots, and adjust criticality tags as the system evolves.

This approach concentrates exhaustive testing where risk and change are highest, while keeping higher-cost tests lean and purposeful.

We will introduce a task-oriented, action-style endpoint to orchestrate route synchronization, rather than forcing it into a resource-centric REST URI. The API will expose POST /route-syncs to accept minimal, event-derived input (e.g., eventId, route identifier, operation=add|replace, and optional hints). The service will enrich and validate the request by querying authoritative sources (main route table and route catalog) to construct the full operation.

The endpoint will be asynchronous:
- Clients submit the request and receive 202 Accepted with Location: /route-syncs/{syncId} and a Job resource returning status, progress, and result details.
- The operation is idempotent using an Idempotency-Key derived from the log event (e.g., eventId), ensuring safe retries.
- The worker applies add/replace on all targeted custom route tables, with partial-failure reporting and compensating updates when applicable.

This explicit command endpoint avoids contorting resource URLs where no clear RESTful mapping exists, keeps the surface area focused, and cleanly separates orchestration from persistence. Authorization will require a scoped role (route.sync). Observability will include correlation with the source log event, structured audit logs, and metrics per sync. Errors follow application/problem+json; terminal states include succeeded, failed, and succeeded_with_warnings.

We will document the contract and constraints (minimal required fields, enrichment rules, conflict handling precedence) and version the action resource independently (e.g., /v1/route-syncs) to allow evolution without destabilizing resource-based APIs.

We will standardize on Liquibase for database versioning and safe migrations across all services.

- Tooling: Use Liquibase OSS with formatted SQL changesets and a master changelog (YAML). Prefer SQL for transparency and DB-native control; use XML/YAML only for orchestration. Use Liquibase Docker image/CLI in CI/CD; no ad-hoc execution.
- Structure: Each service owns its db/changelog with a single master file and per-feature/module changeset files. Naming: timestamped, descriptive IDs; authors map to Git handles. All changesets are immutable after merge.
- Safety and rollbacks: Every changeset must include explicit rollback statements and preconditions. Tag every successful deployment; support point-in-time and tag-based rollback. Use contexts/labels to scope environment-specific changes.
- Migration strategy: Enforce expand-contract pattern for backward-compatible releases (additive changes first; remove/alter only after code cutover). Zero-downtime patterns required for hot paths (online index creation, backfills via batched jobs).
- Validation: Enable checksums, fail-on-error, and databasechangeloglock enforcement. Run liquibase diff/drift checks in CI against a baseline schema snapshot. Block deployments on drift or missing rollbacks.
- Execution flow: 
  - Dev: updateSQL for review; apply to local containers automatically.
  - QA/Staging: dry-run (updateSQL) attached to PR; DBA/owner approval required for risky operations.
  - Prod: apply via pipeline with change window, tag before/after, and automated backup/snapshot when supported.
- Access control: Migrations execute with a controlled migration role; applications use least-privilege runtime roles. No application-initiated schema changes.
- Observability: Retain Liquibase audit tables; export logs/metrics to central monitoring; alert on failed locks, checksum mismatches, long-running migrations.
- Compatibility: Support for Postgres (primary) and MySQL (where applicable) with DB-specific guards via preconditions.
- Decommissioning: Schema drops require separate ADR and scheduled retention period.

We will implement a single, modular monolith backend that serves both “Hungry Person” and “Ghost Kitchen” clients via a versioned REST API. This backend will own domain logic for menus/food descriptions, discounts, feedback, and reporting, while integrating with Smart Fridge and Kiosk POS for purchases, inventory, and payment outcomes.

Key elements:
- Identity and access: Use a managed OAuth/OIDC provider (e.g., Auth0/Cognito) for user registration/login and role-based access (consumer vs. ghost kitchen staff/admin). Accounts enable discount eligibility.
- Purchase truth and verification: Treat POS as system of record for purchases and inventory. Receive purchase and inventory events via secure webhooks from POS; use these to validate “verified purchase” feedback and to update inventory and purchase aggregates.
- Content and sync: Maintain canonical food descriptions. Expose read APIs for clients and provide export/sync endpoints for POS systems; support delta-based updates. Discounts managed in backend and exposed to clients and POS via APIs.
- Reporting: Maintain operational store (PostgreSQL) and derive reports using materialized views and periodic ETL jobs for feedback, inventory, and purchase reports. No separate data warehouse initially.
- Client delivery: Host web SPA via CDN with edge caching for static assets; mobile apps consume the same API. Apply short-lived CDN caching for public menu data with cache-busting on updates.
- Non-functional: Prioritize simplicity for ~1,000 users; deploy as a single containerized service with horizontal scaling headroom. Use background workers for webhook processing and report refresh. Design modules with clear boundaries to enable future extraction into services if scale or team size requires.

Use a dual-representation strategy:

- Primary/internal representation: sample-based in integer sample frames to ensure channel-agnostic, bit-exact, and sample-accurate operations. Type: 64-bit signed integer (int64) “frames” for positions and durations. All engine/processing code and on-disk session state use frames.

- Secondary/external representation: time-based in integer milliseconds for rate-independent interchange and UI. Type: 64-bit signed integer (int64) “ms” for positions and durations. Public APIs, user-visible display, and configuration use milliseconds.

Conversions:
- frames = round_nearest(ms × sample_rate / 1000)
- ms = round_nearest(frames × 1000 / sample_rate)
Rounding uses nearest with ties to even to minimize bias; positions are clamped to valid ranges. All conversions operate on complete frames; channels are implicit in the frame concept (interleaved).

Rationale:
- Frames guarantee deterministic editing, alignment, and DSP across varying channel counts and avoid floating-point drift.
- Milliseconds offer readable, sample-rate-agnostic interaction and sufficient precision for UI and scheduling.

Constraints and guarantees:
- No floating-point seconds in public APIs or persisted data.
- 64-bit capacity prevents overflow for long sessions at high sample rates.
- Any API accepting time must also accept sample rate to enable precise conversion.
- Internal computations involving sub-frame timing are disallowed; the frame is the smallest unit of position/duration.

Decision: Measure customer-visible availability via synthetic checks of critical user journeys and public APIs, with clear success criteria, regional diversity, and dual reporting for improvement vs. contractual SLA.

- SLI definition: Availability = successful_checks / total_checks.
  - A check is successful when:
    - HTTP 2xx/3xx is returned,
    - end-to-end p95 latency ≤ defined SLO per journey/endpoint,
    - TLS/hostname is valid, and
    - response contains required functional assertions (e.g., login completes, item can be added to cart, API returns valid schema).
- Scope:
  - Tier-0 user journeys (web/app) and Tier-0/1 public APIs enumerated in a service catalog.
  - Dependencies that impact these journeys are included (failures of our dependencies count if they break the journey).
- Measurement mechanics:
  - Synthetic probes from at least 6 geographically distributed regions every 30 seconds per journey/endpoint.
  - A “downtime interval” begins when ≥2 regions fail consecutively for ≥2 minutes and ends after 5 consecutive minutes of success in ≥5 regions.
  - Partial outages count proportionally: if 3/6 regions fail, only the failing regions’ checks are considered unsuccessful.
- Aggregation and period:
  - Report in UTC over rolling 30 days and per calendar month.
  - Calculate overall availability as the weighted mean of journey/endpoint availability, weighted by observed traffic share (updated monthly).
- Dual views:
  - Internal availability (for improvement): includes all causes.
  - SLA availability (for compliance): excludes pre-announced maintenance windows, customer-caused issues, force majeure, and outages solely attributable to third-party providers explicitly carved out in contracts. All exclusions are tagged and auditable.
- Validation:
  - Correlate synthetics with server-side telemetry (error rate, saturation) and customer support signals for incident confirmation but do not replace synthetics as source of truth.
- Reporting:
  - Publish monthly percentage, downtime minutes, error budget burn, and top contributing incidents on a shared dashboard; trigger post-incident reviews for any ≥5-minute downtime.

We will name the “global MADRs” Decision Guidance Catalogs (DGCs).

A DGC represents a problem-space artifact: it describes a recurring decision problem, enumerates known solution options, and lists their global pros/cons and applicability conditions without making a project-specific choice. Local, project-level ADRs (MADR) remain solution-space artifacts; they link to the relevant DGCs, add project context and additional forces, and record the selected option.

Conventions:
- Scope: One DGC per decision problem (e.g., “Build Tool Selection”).
- Content: problem statement, assumptions/applicability, option list, global pros/cons, known trade-offs, references.
- No decision/choice recorded in a DGC.
- Naming: dgc-<nnn>-<kebab-title>.md; stored under /decision-guidance/.
- Cross-linking: Local ADRs must reference the governing DGC(s); DGCs may reference related DGCs.
- Format: Lightweight Markdown template optimized for option catalogs; ADRs continue to use MADR.

Examples:
- DGC: Build Tool Selection (options: Maven, Gradle, Ant)
- ADR (local MADR): selects Gradle, referencing the above DGC and adding local forces and consequences.

Adopt a purpose-built reporting data mart in Postgres centered on denormalized, partitioned summary tables (e.g., patient_facility_month, region_month, facility_quarter) as the primary source for dashboards, replacing materialized views for new reports.

- Data model: Star-like schema with a small set of wide, additive fact tables at monthly/quarterly grain and stable dimension tables (facility, region, date). Store precomputed metrics as columns to minimize runtime joins/aggregations.
- Storage: Native Postgres partitioning by period (month/quarter) with appropriate indexes; retention and vacuum tuned per partition; compression where available.
- Ingestion: Idempotent, incremental ETL jobs driven by updated_at/watermarks; support backfills by partition. Jobs run on a schedule (e.g., nightly) and on-demand for corrections; computed in SQL with versioned transformations.
- Stability and scale: Run ETL on the primary, write to reporting tables on a reporting replica or dedicated schema, and serve reads from a read replica. Avoid long-running locks and MV refresh contention.
- Quality and evolution: Include reconciliation checks (row counts, metric deltas, sampling). Version fact tables to enable schema evolution with dual-writing/cutover. Maintain lineage and definitions per metric.
- Rollout: New dashboards read from the data mart immediately; existing MV-based reports remain until migrated. Provide a migration path and deprecate MVs over time.

This simplifies queries, improves stability, and scales by controlling compute in ETL and partitioning data for efficient access.

We will eliminate AngularJS-specific $rootScope broadcasts and consolidate all shared UI/application state into a single source of truth managed by NgRx (@ngrx/store with selectors and effects). New Angular components and services must read state via selectors and mutate state exclusively by dispatching actions. The currently broadcasted selections (e.g., selected building in threeSceneService) and similar cross-component state will be modeled as NgRx feature slices.

To enable an incremental migration, we will introduce an Angular Store Facade service that encapsulates selectors and action dispatching. Using Angular’s UpgradeModule, this facade will be downgraded for AngularJS so legacy code can subscribe to observable selectors and dispatch actions instead of using $rootScope. $rootScope usage is deprecated immediately and must be removed as each area is migrated.

Where state is still held in the legacy Redux store, we will migrate slice-by-slice to NgRx. During the transition, a temporary synchronization layer will bridge critical events between the legacy Redux store and NgRx to prevent split-brain state. Each migrated slice becomes authoritative in NgRx and the corresponding Redux slice is frozen, then removed once consumers are migrated. No new functionality may be added to the legacy Redux store.

All new Angular features must use NgRx (store, effects, selectors, entity where applicable). We will adopt linting, schematics, and devtools for NgRx and train contributors on basic RxJS/NgRx patterns. Success criteria: no $rootScope broadcasts remain; all shared state resides in NgRx; legacy Redux and related connectors are removed; AngularJS code, where still present, interacts only via the downgraded facade until it is fully retired.

Adopt Ruby on Rails as the default application framework for all new Ruby applications in this programme. Rails will be used for both user-facing web applications and APIs, preferring Rails’ conventions over bespoke patterns to maximise consistency, speed of delivery, and maintainability across teams.

- Default to Rails 7.x (current stable) and API-only mode for services that do not require server-rendered views; use full-stack Rails for applications with HTML UIs.
- Use Active Record with PostgreSQL as the default persistence layer.
- Prefer Rails’ built-in components (Active Job, Action Mailer, Action Cable, Active Storage) unless there is a clearly evidenced need for an alternative.
- Follow standard Rails project structure, generators, and configuration; align with MOJ templates where available.
- Apply secure-by-default settings (e.g., CSRF protections, parameter filtering, encrypted credentials).
- Permit deviations from Rails defaults only via a documented ADR with clear operational or domain justification.

This decision standardises the stack, simplifies onboarding and support, and aligns with existing MOJ practices.

We will require verified digital identity before approving or disbursing any claim, implementing a risk-based, privacy-preserving identity assurance model:

- Primary approach: Federated authentication and proofing via the national digital identity service (e.g., GOV.UK One Login/eIDAS) at assurance equivalent to NIST IAL2/AAL2 (or local equivalent). We will reuse existing verified identities where available to minimize friction.
- Secondary approach (fallback): In-house remote identity proofing through an accredited provider, combining government-issued document verification, biometric facial match with liveness detection, and address verification, with manual review for edge cases and assisted digital channels.
- Authentication: Enforce MFA for claimant access (passwordless or OTP + device-bound factor), with step-up verification for high-risk actions (e.g., bank detail changes, large payouts).
- Risk engine: Apply risk scoring using device intelligence, IP/geolocation, behavioral signals, and claim context to adapt verification requirements and flag anomalies for review.
- Data minimization and privacy: Store only verification assertions, timestamps, and risk outcomes; do not retain document images or biometrics beyond legally required windows. Comply with GDPR/UK DPA and accessibility standards.
- Operations and audit: Maintain immutable audit trails, periodic re-checks before payment release or sensitive changes, and continuous monitoring with alerting for suspected fraud.
- Integration: Use standards-based protocols (OIDC/OAuth2), with clear SLAs and fallback processes to ensure availability and consistent claimant experience.

## Decision

Adopt an opt-in model for workflow command echoing to reduce log noise and improve signal-to-noise in user logs.

- Default behavior:
  - Disable command echoing by default.
  - Automatically enable echoing when the ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG secret is set to true.
- User control:
  - Introduce two explicit runtime commands to control echoing within a job/step:
    - ::echo::on — enables command echoing from the invocation point forward.
    - ::echo::off — disables command echoing from the invocation point forward.
- Error handling:
  - When a command fails to process or returns an error, echo the relevant command output regardless of the echo setting to provide sufficient context for troubleshooting.
- Scope:
  - This change applies to workflow command echoing only and does not affect normal stdout/stderr output produced by user processes unless such output is part of a workflow command.
- Persistence and precedence:
  - The most recent ::echo::on/off command dictates the current echo state for the remainder of the step or until overridden.
  - ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG determines the initial state at step start; user-issued ::echo:: commands can override it at runtime.
- Backward compatibility and migration:
  - Existing workflows will see reduced command echoing unless ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG is enabled or ::echo::on is invoked.
  - Documentation and examples will be updated to direct users to ::echo::on when verbose logs are desired.

Adopt a multi-relation input model with optimizer-managed arrangements and schema-aware layouts.

- Replace the single (e a v) input with a Catalog of named logical relations, each with an explicit schema and its own time domain. External sources (Datomic, Kafka, files, etc.) are integrated via ingestion adapters that expose one or more relations.

- Remove the hardcoded DB/ImplContext indexing. Indexes become first-class arrangements defined over logical relations (keys, projections, and predicates). All arrangements are declared in a common interface and built/maintained by an optimizer that decides reuse, materialization, and eviction. The current DB indexes are re-expressed as optimizer-managed arrangements (no special-case constructs).

- Introduce a time model that supports per-relation clocks. Cross-source computation uses explicit reclocking/join operators with well-defined as-of frontiers; a global time is optional and provided via adapters when required. The engine remains correct with heterogeneous time axes.

- Adopt schema-aware, attribute/columnar-native layouts per relation. Support columnar storage with dictionary/nullable encodings and selective materialization of referenced attributes. Provide a row-oriented Vec<Value> view only at API edges and for compatibility; internal operators consume typed/columnar batches to avoid layout inefficiencies.

- Define a stable ingestion interface: relation schema, time semantics, watermark/frontier reporting, and backfill/catch-up. Enable predicate/column pushdown from the optimizer to adapters.

- Maintain backward compatibility by shipping a compatibility adapter that publishes the legacy (e a v) stream as a set of logical relations (e.g., datoms, entities, attributes) and by providing shims that map legacy DB/ImplContext accessors to optimizer-declared arrangements. Migration can be incremental per feature.

This decision decouples inputs from execution, generalizes indexing into optimizer-planned arrangements, and unlocks performance by moving from generic tuples to typed, schema-aware layouts while supporting heterogeneous sources and time domains.

## Decision
Adopt a single source of truth for the project version, stored as a plain text file named VERSION at the repository root, containing a Semantic Version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[-PRERELEASE][+BUILD]).

The build process will generate language-specific artifacts from the VERSION file to ensure the version is embedded and accessible at runtime:

- C++: Generate an auto-managed header (version.hpp) via the build system (e.g., CMake configure_file) exposing:
  - constexpr int PROJECT_VERSION_MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH
  - constexpr char PROJECT_VERSION[] (full string, including pre-release/build metadata)
  - A function const char* getProjectVersion()
  For platforms supporting resources (e.g., Windows), also embed the version into a resource file for binary metadata.

- MATLAB: Generate a version.m function returning the version string and a parsed struct, e.g.:
  - function [v, info] = version(); where v is the full string and info has fields major, minor, patch, prerelease, build.

Tooling:
- Provide a script (tools/bump_version.[py|m]) that validates Semantic Versioning, updates the VERSION file, and triggers regeneration of artifacts.
- Generated files (version.hpp, version.m, optional .rc) are not manually edited and are either git-ignored or committed only via the generation step to support environments without the build system.

Process and enforcement:
- CI validates that generated artifacts match the VERSION file and fails if inconsistent.
- Releases and packaging invoke the generation step to guarantee executables, libraries, and MATLAB packages carry the correct embedded version.
- Public APIs in both languages expose getVersion() to retrieve the version at runtime; documentation references this API.

Rationale:
- Centralizes version management, avoids divergence across languages, and works in environments without VCS metadata.
- Semantic Versioning supports clear compatibility signals and automation in CI/CD.

## Decision
Adopt re-frame as the single source of truth and define a canonical, normalized app-db with clear separation between domain data and UI/session state.

- App-db structure:
  - :entities — normalized maps keyed by entity type (e.g., :users, :posts) with {:by-id {id -> entity} :all-ids [...] :indexes {...}}.
  - :ui — ephemeral view state (loading flags, dialogs, sorting, pagination).
  - :session — user/session/auth, feature flags, runtime config.
  - :meta — request status, errors, last-updated timestamps, version.

- Access policy:
  - No direct deref of app-db outside subscriptions.
  - All reads via reg-sub (layered/derived where needed).
  - All writes via reg-event-db/ reg-event-fx; side effects via fx/cofx only.
  - Public API per domain namespace exposing:
    - queries: (subs/ query fns returning subscription ids)
    - commands: (events/ dispatchable event ids)
  - Consumers import only the public API; internal keys are private.

- Conventions:
  - Namespaced keys (e.g., :user/id) and stable entity ids.
  - Normalization at ingestion; denormalization in subscriptions.
  - Path-based events for localized updates; batch events for bulk changes.
  - Schema validation of app-db and events using malli/spec in dev/test.
  - Versioned app-db (:meta :version) with migration fns.

- Migration:
  - Introduce re-frame alongside Redux; create a thin adapter to read from Redux as initial cofx and to mirror critical updates until parity.
  - Incrementally port slices: define schema + subs + events per slice, switch call sites from Redux selectors/actions to re-frame API, then retire adapters.
  - Deprecate Redux APIs with lint guards and compile-time warnings.

- Testing/observability:
  - Unit-test subs/events with fixture dbs.
  - Instrument fx/cofx; log event lifecycle in dev; time-travel via re-frame-10x in development.

This decision standardizes state shape and access, isolates consumers behind a stable API, and enables a safe, incremental migration off Redux.

- We will prefer command tests as the primary source of behavioral verification; integration tests are reserved for verifying cross-component wiring and critical end-to-end flows.
- Command tests:
  - Scope: command behavior in isolation—flag/arg parsing, user-facing output/messages, validation, error mapping, retries/backoff semantics, and interactions with collaborators.
  - Dependencies: use fakes/mocks; no real network, filesystem, or external services.
  - Coverage: exhaustive edge cases and negative paths; platform/version matrix where feasible.
- Integration tests:
  - Scope: end-to-end interactions across layers/components, real side effects, and environment-dependent behavior.
  - Dependencies: real or realistic external systems (e.g., API server, filesystem, auth), or contract-backed test doubles at process boundaries.
  - Coverage: happy-path smoke for each command, cross-command workflows, permission/role interactions, OS/filesystem effects, and backward-compatibility of wire contracts.
- Non-duplication rule: a behavior is tested at one level. Detailed logic and edge cases live in command tests; integration tests do not repeat them. Integration adds value only when behavior depends on wiring, environment, or contracts that command tests cannot represent.
- New/changed command workflow:
  - Implement comprehensive command tests first.
  - Add a single integration happy-path and any necessary cross-command or environment-specific scenarios.
  - If a scenario can be fully and reliably expressed with fakes, keep it at the command level.
- Migration/cleanup:
  - Remove or narrow integration tests that duplicate command-level assertions.
  - If a bug escapes due to wiring/contract mismatch, add/adjust an integration test; if due to command logic, add/adjust a command test.
- Test design conventions:
  - Name tests to reflect scope: Command: command/v7/<cmd>_command_test.go; Integration: integration/v7/<area>/<workflow>_test.go.
  - Keep integration tests coarse-grained and few; keep command tests fine-grained and many.
- CI gates: command tests must pass on all PRs; integration tests may run in a slower lane but must cover the documented smoke and workflows.

Adopt fabric8io’s kubernetes-assertions (with the Fabric8 Kubernetes Client) as the primary framework for end-to-end validation of transformed Kubernetes artifacts. Tests will run against an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster (e.g., kind in CI, minikube locally), applying the generated manifests and asserting both syntactic validity and operational readiness (e.g., resources created, controllers reconcile, Pods become Ready, Services endpoints available, required labels/annotations present, RBAC bindings effective).

Implementation outline:
- Test harness: JUnit 5 + Fabric8 Kubernetes Client + kubernetes-assertions.
- Cluster lifecycle: provision ephemeral cluster per test suite in CI; namespace-per-test isolation; deterministic cleanup.
- Apply: use Fabric8 client to create/update resources from generated YAML; fall back to kubectl only for bootstrap (e.g., kind cluster setup) where needed.
- Assertions: readiness waiters with bounded timeouts; resource existence and field-level assertions; events/logs inspection for diagnostics; negative tests for invalid inputs.
- CI: GitHub Actions runners with kind; parallelization via namespace sharding; artifacts (logs, describe, events) collected on failure.
- Quality gates: tests must pass for merge; version pinning of Fabric8 and K8s API; deprecation checks baked into assertions.
- Non-goals: replacing all operational scripts; only minimal shell usage for cluster bootstrap.

This decision favors maintainability, expressiveness, and rich, type-safe assertions over ad hoc shell scripting, reducing flakiness and improving readability and debuggability of end-to-end tests while remaining close to real cluster behavior.

We will continue to produce and publish two Docker image variants for Wikibase:
- Base: MediaWiki + Wikibase only
- Bundled (Wikibase Suite): MediaWiki + Wikibase + curated extensions/components

Both images will be built by the release pipeline and published exclusively to Docker Hub under the repository defined in ADR0001, using semantic version tags, immutable digest references, and maintained latest tags per stream as applicable. Images will conform to OCI standards and include SBOMs and metadata to ensure traceability.

We will not produce or distribute a tarball (or other manual installation archive) of the bundled Wikibase Suite. Distribution will be via container images only. Any non-container artifacts generated during build (e.g., intermediate extension packages) are considered internal and will not be published for end-user installation.

This decision preserves the existing delivery options (base and bundled images) while focusing maintenance, security updates, and user guidance on Docker-based distribution.

We will eliminate per-update reads and deserialization by aggregating all field-level mutations for a document and applying them in a single atomic MongoDB update via bulkWrite. During load, updates are buffered per document key and merged into a single update spec using atomic operators ($set, $inc, $addToSet, $push with $each, $min/$max as needed), with upsert: true. We will execute unordered bulkWrite batches to maximize throughput and avoid head-of-line blocking, targeting at most one read (only when necessary to resolve conditional logic) and one write per document.

To ensure correctness and performance:
- A per-document update builder merges incoming deltas, coalescing redundant operations and resolving operator conflicts deterministically (e.g., $set overrides prior $set for the same path; $inc values are summed).
- Updates for the same document are affinity-routed to the same worker to prevent interleaving; otherwise, we use optimistic retry on write-conflict errors.
- Batches are flushed on size/time thresholds and before exceeding MongoDB’s 16 MB document limit or batch size limits.
- Write concern is configurable; default is w:1, j:disabled for bulk loads, overridable for stronger durability.
- Validation guards prevent illegal operator combinations and enforce schema constraints without materializing the full document.

This approach removes the polynomial slowdown from repeated reads as documents grow, converting many small updates into a single network round-trip and write, while preserving atomicity at the document level and providing predictable, scalable load performance.

Adopt an off-chain entity metadata registry that serves self-certifying entity statements linked to on-chain identities. Each statement is a versioned, schematized payload (JSON or CBOR) signed by the entity using keys provably bound to its on-chain identifier. Statements are content-addressed and retrievable via multiple transports (HTTPS and optional decentralized storage), while the registry provides an index/discovery API but is not a trust anchor.

Clients obtain entity statements by resolving the entity identifier to authorized verification keys (from on-chain data or a well-defined key binding mechanism), fetch the latest statement references from the registry, retrieve the content from storage, and verify signatures before use. Verification MUST succeed for consumers to accept metadata; unsigned or unverifiable content is ignored.

We will support statement rotation and revocation through: immutable statements with monotonic sequence numbers, “supersedes” references, optional expiry/validity windows, and key rotation paths anchored in the on-chain binding. Multiple concurrent statements by type are allowed; conflict resolution is by highest sequence within type and valid time window.

The schema is extensible and versioned to allow additive fields and new statement types without breaking clients. Privacy is preserved by keeping sensitive data out-of-band or encrypted to intended verifiers. Operationally, we will provide caching, ETag-based freshness, rate limiting, and audit logs. The design keeps on-chain operations unchanged, while delivering authenticated, tamper-evident, optional metadata with graceful degradation when the registry is unavailable.

Adopt an “explicit data loading per action” policy: discontinue using before_action (and similar filters) to load domain data for controller actions. Limit filters strictly to cross‑cutting concerns that are cheap and universally applicable (e.g., authentication, authorization, request context/logging, feature flags, locale), and never for fetching business entities.

Each controller action must explicitly load only the data it needs, preferably via:
- Local variables within the action, or
- Private, memoized query/helper methods explicitly invoked by the action.

Avoid instance variable sprawl. Prefer passing explicit objects to render/serializers instead of relying on implicitly set @ivars. Shared loading logic should be extracted into POROs (query objects/services/form objects) called from actions, not into controller concerns or filters.

Additional conventions:
- Name query/helper methods to clearly convey scope (e.g., course_for_edit vs course_for_show) and include eager loading to prevent N+1s.
- Keep data fetching side‑effect free; no writes in data loaders.
- Use policy scopes/authorization explicitly within actions after data retrieval.
- Do not use except/only to conditionally apply data‑loading filters.

Guardrails:
- Add a linter rule to flag before_action/after_action that load domain data (e.g., names matching load_/set_/find_ on AR models).
- Code review checklist item: “Are all data dependencies explicit within the action?”
- Prefer controller tests/request specs that assert action‑specific behavior without relying on global setup that hides implicit data loading.

Migration path:
- Replace each load_* before_action with an explicit call in the actions that use it.
- Convert shared lookups into query/service objects and call them inline.
- Remove unused instance variables uncovered during refactor; measure and verify reduced DB calls.

Adopt AWS Systems Manager Session Manager as the sole access mechanism for MSK test client EC2 instances. Do not generate or distribute SSH key pairs for these instances; inbound SSH (port 22) will remain closed in security groups and NACLs. Where the launch workflow mandates a KeyName, a non-distributed, pipeline-created placeholder key pair will be referenced but never used for authentication. Instances will include the SSM agent, required IAM instance profile (AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore), and VPC endpoints for SSM/EC2 Messages as needed for private access. This decision eliminates key management overhead and reduces credential sprawl while enabling audited, just-in-time, role-based console/CLI access. For break-glass scenarios, access remains via Session Manager with elevated, time-bound IAM roles; no persistent SSH is permitted. Naming/tagging convention: Name=msk-test-client, Environment=<env>, Access=SSMOnly. Enforcement via launch templates and CI/CD ensures consistency across environments.

Decision:
- Use location_id for location assignment; do not rely on location_path for any API calls.
- Implement a client-side/location-service cache that periodically and on-demand synchronizes the full list of locations from /locations without filters, using pagination to bypass the 100-result limit.
- Build and store a human-readable canonical path (e.g., “Company/Region/Site/Building/Room”) for each location in the cache, derived from parent relationships returned by the API, and index both path and name for fast lookup.
- PowerShell cmdlet autocompletion sources from the local cache, performing client-side filtering/fuzzy matching over the canonical path and name, never using server-side filters on location_path.
- Employee creation flow becomes a two-step atomic operation:
  1) Create the employee without location (as per API constraints).
  2) Immediately update the employee with the selected location_id via the supported update endpoint.
- If step 2 fails, perform compensating action: delete the newly created employee or flag for retry according to idempotent retry policy and business rules.
- Maintain a mapping of path → location_id in durable storage with a short TTL (e.g., 24 hours) and background refresh; allow a manual refresh command to handle urgent taxonomy changes.
- Validate selected locations against the latest cache prior to create/update; if the chosen location is stale/missing, prompt the user to refresh or select an alternative.
- Log and monitor API anomalies (pagination failures, update errors) and expose metrics for sync freshness and autocomplete hit-rate to ensure reliability.

We will implement a mixed frontend-backend OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow (Alternative 3).

- The frontend initiates authentication by redirecting the user to GitHub’s authorization endpoint and includes state for CSRF protection. For browser-based clients, PKCE will be used (frontend generates code_verifier/challenge).
- GitHub redirects back to a dedicated callback with status and authorization code (and state). The frontend validates status/state and sends the code (and PKCE verifier when used) to the backend over HTTPS.
- The backend exchanges the authorization code with GitHub using the client credentials (and PKCE verifier when applicable), obtaining the access token (and refresh token, if enabled).
- The GitHub access token is not exposed to the browser. The backend stores it securely (encrypted at rest) and associates it with the authenticated user’s session.
- The backend issues an application-scoped session token (e.g., HTTP-only, secure cookie or opaque token) to the frontend. All GitHub operations are proxied through backend APIs using the stored GitHub token.
- Token lifecycle management (scopes, refresh, revocation) is handled server-side. Logout clears the application session and revokes the GitHub token when feasible.

This approach minimizes exposure of GitHub credentials, preserves a clean UX with a browser redirect, centralizes security controls and rate limiting on the server, and aligns with GitHub’s recommended patterns for SPAs and web apps.

We will consolidate orchestration by migrating the ADR-12 execution model to Apache Airflow and deprecate the custom execution framework.

- Airflow becomes the single system of record for scheduling, dependency management, retries, SLAs, and observability of all workflows previously governed by ADR-12.
- All pipelines will be expressed as Airflow DAGs with idempotent, modular tasks; existing business logic will be wrapped in operators/sensors where feasible to minimize code changes.
- We will use the organization’s standard Airflow deployment and executor, standardizing secrets management, connections, alerting, and metrics via Airflow’s native mechanisms and our platform conventions.
- New workflows must be implemented in Airflow immediately; ADR-12 execution paths are feature-frozen.
- Migration will proceed incrementally: prioritize critical pipelines, run in parallel for validation, then cut over and decommission corresponding ADR-12 jobs. Provide a lightweight compatibility layer/adapters where needed to bridge command-line or API invocations.
- Define uniform DAG conventions (naming, retries, SLAs, timeouts), failure-handling policies, and rollout/rollback procedures.
- Ownership: Platform team provides Airflow platform, templates, and governance; domain teams migrate and maintain their DAGs.
- Success criteria: functional parity, improved operability, reduced duplicate tooling, and measurable reduction in incident load tied to the legacy execution model.

## Decision
We will standardize on Microsoft Playwright as the primary JavaScript end-to-end (E2E) web automation framework across projects. Playwright Test (the built-in runner) will be the default for E2E execution, parallelization, tracing, and reporting. Jest or Vitest remains the default for unit tests, complemented by React Testing Library (or Vue Testing Library) for component tests. API tests that support E2E flows will be implemented using Playwright’s Request API; standalone API suites may use Supertest with Jest/Vitest where appropriate.

Scope:
- Applies to all new web UI automation efforts.
- Existing Cypress, WebdriverIO, or Selenium JS suites may continue temporarily but must provide a migration plan to Playwright within two quarters unless a justified exception is approved.

Constraints and standards:
- Tests must run headless by default with cross-browser coverage (Chromium, WebKit, Firefox) configured via Playwright projects.
- TypeScript is mandatory for test code.
- CI orchestration will use Playwright’s test runner with sharding and retries; artifacts (videos, traces, screenshots) must be published on failure.
- Page Object or Screenplay patterns may be used; selectors must prefer role- or test-id-based locators.
- Flake budgets and test execution SLAs will be enforced; auto-waiting and network idling features must be leveraged before adding explicit waits.
- Accessibility checks will be integrated via axe-core where feasible.
- Mobile web will be covered via Playwright device emulation; native mobile testing is out of scope.

Governance and exceptions:
- Any deviation from Playwright for E2E requires Architecture approval based on documented gaps (e.g., unsupported environments).
- New framework evaluations are paused for 12 months; reassessment will occur annually or upon material platform changes.

Migration:
- New features: write E2E tests in Playwright only.
- Legacy suites: prioritize migration of critical paths first; reuse assertions and helper utilities where possible.
- Central templates, coding standards, and example repos will be provided to accelerate adoption.

## Decision
Adopt a dedicated Query side with denormalized, event-driven projections and a separate read store optimized for low-latency, high-throughput queries.

- Projections: Build read models via asynchronous, idempotent, replayable projection handlers that consume domain events from the event bus. Projections are versioned, backward compatible, and support full rebuild from the event log/snapshots. Failed events go to a DLQ with retry/backoff.

- Read store: Use a separate Postgres read database (distinct schema and connection pool from the write side) with optional read replicas for horizontal scaling. Create tailored, denormalized tables/materialized views per query use case. Introduce Elasticsearch later only for advanced free-text/search requirements; keep the initial footprint minimal.

- API: Expose queries via a dedicated Query Service with REST endpoints returning DTOs crafted to the use case (no domain entities). Support pagination, sorting, filtering, and field selection. Prevent N+1 via pre-joined projections. Enforce authZ at the query layer using application logic and, where applicable, database row-level security/tenant scoping.

- Consistency: Accept eventual consistency. Provide read-your-own-writes strategies for critical flows: sticky reads to primary read node, client-side retry with version tokens, and optional on-demand synchronous projection for narrow cases. Include projection lag headers/metadata where helpful.

- Caching: Apply layered caching—CDN/edge for public endpoints, in-process cache for hot keys, and coarse-grained TTLs. Invalidate or warm caches via event-driven cache hints from the projection pipeline.

- Operability: Instrument projection lag, throughput, and error rates; track per-projection health. Provide admin endpoints to rebuild projections, reprocess from checkpoints, and backfill fixes. Implement schema migration controls for read models that allow rolling updates without query downtime.

## Decision
We will adopt the Elite2 API as the primary source of NOMIS data for the MOiC allocation component, replacing our reliance on the Custody API for offender and staff data retrieval in the short-to-medium term.

- We will not add integrations to any other legacy NOMIS APIs; Elite2 will be the single integration point for general NOMIS data access for this service.
- Authentication will use service-to-service tokens; we will leverage Elite2’s caseload-based endpoints with specific parameters where necessary to meet data locality needs.
- We will implement an integration adapter/anti-corruption layer to encapsulate Elite2-specific models, pagination, and query patterns, enabling a future switch back to the Custody API with minimal impact on the allocation service.
- We will address performance concerns (e.g., N+1 request patterns) via batching, server-side filtering, judicious caching with TTLs, and resilient patterns (circuit breakers, retries, idempotency), in line with Elite2 usage limits.
- We will pin to known-stable Elite2 versions, apply consumer-driven contract tests, and coordinate with the Sheffield team for any new endpoint requirements.
- This is a tactical decision that does not alter the strategic direction of moving HMPPS services to the Custody API over time. We will review the feasibility of returning to the Custody API quarterly.
- Exit criteria for migrating back to the Custody API will include: available endpoints meeting our data needs, resolution of locality/performance issues, acceptable latency and throughput, and a stable deprecation path for Elite2.
- Once the Custody API achieves parity for our needs, we will deprecate the Elite2 integration and migrate via the established adapter layer with a controlled rollout plan.

We will represent stateless aggregates and processes as pure, stateless functions (policies) with existence modeled explicitly via events.

- Aggregates:
  - Implement command handling as pure functions: Command × History → Events.
  - The only persisted “state” is existence, derived from the presence/absence of a Created/Initialized event (and optionally a terminal/Archived/Tombstoned event for shutdown).
  - The repository will not materialize mutable state; it will stream event history (or existence flags) to the command handler and enforce optimistic concurrency using expected version checks in the event store.
  - A NullAggregate abstraction will be used to represent “non-existent” until a creation event is produced; creation commands are allowed only when no prior existence event is found.
  - Deletion/archival emits a terminal event; subsequent commands are rejected.
  - No snapshots are maintained; sharding/partition routing continues to use aggregate ID.

- Processes (sagas):
  - Stateless processes are modeled as policy/event handlers that react to events and emit commands without instance persistence.
  - Idempotency and at-least-once handling are enforced via event IDs and the outbox/inbox pattern; no saga state store is created.
  - When a process must track only existence/activation, it follows the same event-flag pattern as aggregates.

- Operational guarantees:
  - All handlers are deterministic, re-entrant, and side-effect free except for emitting commands/events.
  - Observability includes correlation/causation IDs on all produced messages.
  - Concurrency control relies solely on event store versioning; no in-memory locks or long-lived actors are used.

This approach minimizes storage and complexity for truly stateless domains, preserves auditability, and maintains CQRS/ES invariants while allowing seamless evolution to stateful models if future rules require persisted state.

Adopt a single, platform-managed, cluster-scoped NGINX Ingress Controller to serve ingress across all namespaces. Deploy the controller in a dedicated platform namespace (e.g., platform-ingress) with HA settings and configure it to watch all namespaces (no namespace selector). Define an IngressClass named platform and set it as the cluster default; all application Ingress resources, including Datalabs, will reference this class via ingressClassName: platform.

Remove the per-namespace ingress controller from the Datalabs deployment (e.g., drop the controller subchart/components). Datalabs will only deliver namespace-scoped Ingress resources and annotations appropriate to the shared controller. Ownership, lifecycle, and configuration of the controller (TLS termination, external DNS, rate limiting, WAF options, timeouts, access logs) are centralized under the Platform team, decoupled from application release cadence.

Migration will proceed by: deploying the platform controller; updating Datalabs Ingress manifests to use ingressClassName: platform; validating hostname/TLS coverage; then disabling and removing existing namespace-scoped controllers. Post-migration, enforce use of the platform IngressClass via policy to prevent drift.

This decision standardizes ingress, reduces duplication, enables multi-project/multi-namespace routing, and strengthens separation of concerns between platform and application.

Adopt a modular shell scripting architecture: replace the monolithic script with a suite of small, self-contained scripts with clear responsibilities and stable interfaces. Each script will be single-purpose, executable, and composable via a thin orchestration layer.

Key elements:
- Structure: scripts/<domain>/<action>.sh with an entrypoint (bin/tool) that routes subcommands.
- Interfaces: consistent CLI patterns (posix flags, --help, exit codes), no reliance on global state; inputs via args/env; outputs to stdout/stderr.
- Safety: shebang, set -euo pipefail, IFS handling, strict error propagation, traps for cleanup.
- Composition: orchestrate via Makefile or a dispatcher script; share common logic via sourced libs under lib/ with explicit, documented functions.
- Standards: naming conventions, function headers, usage blocks, argument parsing helpers, idempotency where applicable.
- Tooling: enforce shellcheck and shfmt in CI; minimal unit/integration tests for critical scripts; pre-commit hooks.
- Discoverability: top-level README and scripts/README with a command index, examples, and contribution guide; bin/tool --help to list subcommands.
- Backward compatibility: provide a wrapper for the legacy entrypoint to preserve existing workflows while delegating to new modules; deprecate progressively with clear timelines.
- Ownership and lifecycle: codeowners per domain, versioned changes to public-facing scripts, and changelog entries for breaking interface changes.
- Performance: avoid unnecessary process spawning; cache expensive calls where safe; prefer POSIX sh unless features require bash.

This decision reduces cognitive load, lowers change risk, and enables parallel development. Migration will proceed incrementally, splitting the monolith by feature area and adding tests as modules are extracted.

## Decision
Establish a lightweight, mandatory Architectural Decision Record (ADR) practice, stored alongside code in the main repository, as the single source of truth for technical decisions and their evolution.

- Create an /adr directory managed in version control; each ADR is a text file with a standardized template: Context (incl. status quo), Problem/Forces, Options/Alternatives, Decision, Consequences, Implementation Plan, References, and Status (Proposed/Accepted/Deprecated/Superseded).
- Require an ADR for any decision that meaningfully impacts architecture, cross-cutting concerns, data models, external interfaces, SLAs, security, or team-wide tooling/process (use a simple threshold checklist).
- Link ADRs to issues, RFCs, and pull requests; decisions are reviewed via normal code review. Acceptance is recorded by tagging Status=Accepted and the approving reviewers.
- Ensure traceability by tagging ADRs with components/domains and creating an index (README + tags) for discoverability. Use “Supersedes” and “Superseded by” fields to capture change over time.
- Make “status quo assessment” mandatory in the Context to document existing behavior and migration path. Require a “Consequences” section to capture trade-offs and risks.
- Automate with an ADR template and optional tooling (e.g., adr-tools, linters, PR checks ensuring ADR presence for qualifying changes).
- Assign ownership: tech leads curate ADR quality, and each team maintains their domain ADRs. Conduct periodic ADR reviews to deprecate or consolidate outdated records.
- Provide a short onboarding guide and examples; include ADR review in Definition of Done for qualifying changes.

We will adopt the Data Abstraction Layer (DAL) as the default mechanism for all application data access. Plain SQL is allowed by exception only, subject to strict controls.

- Default: All CRUD, transactional workflows, and common queries must use the DAL (ORM/query builder/repository interfaces) to ensure portability, consistency, security, caching, and maintainability.
- Exceptions for plain SQL:
  - Performance-critical paths where the DAL cannot produce optimal plans.
  - Complex reporting/analytical queries not expressible or efficient via the DAL.
  - Vendor-specific features (e.g., window functions, hints) required for correctness or SLAs.
  - One-off data migrations/maintenance scripts executed outside the app runtime.

- Constraints for plain SQL:
  - Must reside in the infrastructure/data layer behind DAL-compliant interfaces (repositories/gateways); no SQL in domain/presentation layers.
  - Must be parameterized/prepared; no dynamic string concatenation.
  - Must include explain/benchmark evidence and tests; reviewed and approved by the architecture/review group.
  - Must provide fallbacks or feature gates if dependent on vendor-specific behavior.
  - Must include observability (structured logs, metrics, tracing) and adhere to connection/transaction management policies defined by the DAL.
  - Must be documented with rationale, ownership, and deprecation criteria.

- Implementation notes:
  - Expose repository interfaces and query abstractions as the stable API; hide engine-specific details.
  - Provide a sanctioned SQL execution helper with standardized error mapping, retries, and timeouts.
  - Linting/CI checks will enforce DAL-first usage and flag raw SQL outside approved locations.
  - New features default to DAL; introduce plain SQL only after profiling demonstrates material benefit.

This decision ensures a DAL-first architecture for maintainability and portability while enabling controlled use of plain SQL where it measurably improves correctness or performance.

Adopt a provider-agnostic query layer backed by a canonical Code Review Domain Model, with pluggable source adapters per review system. Monocle queries will target the canonical model (changes, revisions, comments, reviewers, labels, states, metadata) and never reference provider-specific fields directly. Each supported system (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, Gerrit, Bitbucket, Phabricator) is integrated via an adapter that maps provider schemas and APIs into the canonical model, normalizes semantics (states, approvals, timestamps, users), and exposes a standardized capabilities contract.

Queries execute against the unified model via a stable API/DSL, with resolvers that either (a) read from a normalized persistence layer populated by incremental ingestion, or (b) federate live calls through adapters when freshness is required. Capability negotiation determines which query predicates and projections are executable per source; unsupported features must degrade gracefully with explicit, standardized errors or partial results metadata.

The query layer will define consistent pagination, sorting, filtering, and error semantics across providers. Provider-specific extensions are allowed only via namespaced fields that do not leak into core queries; extensions are discoverable through capability descriptors and versioned to avoid coupling.

Adapters must conform to a strict contract: idempotent upserts, deterministic mapping rules, time and identity normalization, retry/backoff, rate-limit handling, and audit-friendly change logs. All adapters will be test-gated by a shared conformance suite and golden datasets to ensure semantic equivalence. The canonical model and query API are versioned; breaking changes follow a deprecation policy.

Performance and freshness are managed by caching and change streaming where available; the system prefers event-driven ingestion but supports polling fallback. Observability is mandatory: per-adapter SLIs, query traces, capability coverage, and reconciliation metrics.

This decision ensures Monocle queries remain data-source agnostic while enabling broad provider coverage, predictable behavior, and incremental addition of new systems without impacting existing queries.

We will use Maven as the primary build tool and generate sources during the build, never committing generated code to VCS. Generated files will be written under target/generated-sources and added to the project’s source path via the Maven generate-sources/compile lifecycle, and excluded via .gitignore.

To avoid a two-pass compilation within the project, code generation will not be implemented as code compiled within the same module. Instead:
- Prefer Java annotation processing (JSR 269) for compile-time generation, delivered as a separately published processor artifact. The project will depend on the processor via annotationProcessor scope.
- For non-APT use cases, use a prebuilt, versioned JVM-based generator distributed as a Maven plugin or executable JAR, invoked in the generate-sources phase.

All codegen tools will be maintained and versioned in separate modules/repositories, published to a Maven repository (Maven Central) to ensure they are precompiled before consumption. Build configurations will pin exact versions of generators to guarantee reproducible builds.

Artifacts of this project (including generated outputs compiled into binaries) will be published to Maven Central via standard Maven publishing. No generated sources are checked into Git; local and CI builds must produce identical outputs from the same inputs.

Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as the canonical way to document significant architectural and design decisions. Each ADR will be a lightweight plain-text Markdown file, stored in-repo under docs/adr/, one decision per file, with a stable, incrementing identifier (e.g., 0001-meaningful-title.md), date, status (Proposed, Accepted, Superseded, Deprecated), and the standard sections: Context, Decision, Consequences, and Links.

ADRs will be created and evolved via pull requests, reviewed like code, and approved by at least one maintainer for the affected area. ADRs are append-only: updates that change a decision’s substance create a new ADR that supersedes the prior one, with cross-links between them. A generated index (docs/adr/README.md) will list all ADRs by status for discoverability.

Code comments may contain brief rationale but must reference the relevant ADR id when applicable; the ADR remains the single source of truth for the decision’s rationale. Authors are expected to write an ADR for changes that alter public interfaces or behavior, introduce/retire dependencies, impact data model or persistence, affect cross-cutting concerns (security, privacy, performance, reliability), or establish team-wide conventions.

We will not backfill all historical decisions; instead, we will add ADRs opportunistically for past critical decisions when touched. Provide a shared template and minimal linting/checks to ensure consistency.

## Decision
Adopt explicit constructor-based dependency injection. All components will declare their dependencies as constructor parameters (preferably as interfaces or well-defined structs), and the application will compose the object graph in main.go (or a small set of top-level wiring packages). No package-level globals or singletons will be used to hold runtime dependencies. Avoid init() side effects for wiring.

Guidelines:
- Constructors must accept all required dependencies and fail fast on invalid/missing ones.
- Prefer small, focused interfaces owned by the consumer to enable easy mocking in tests.
- Group related configuration into immutable config structs passed explicitly at construction time.
- Manage resource lifecycles (e.g., DB connections, HTTP clients) in main.go and pass handles to dependents; close resources centrally on shutdown.
- Detect and resolve cycles during composition; refactor responsibilities if a cycle appears.
- For optional behavior, use explicit optional parameters (e.g., functional options) rather than hidden globals.
- Tests construct units with fakes/mocks/stubs by satisfying the declared interfaces; avoid touching global state.

Rationale: This approach makes dependencies explicit, improves testability and clarity of the dependency graph, eliminates hidden coupling via package globals, and localizes composition concerns to the application entry point while keeping libraries/framework-agnostic.

We will not adopt a style linter for katas. Instead, we will enforce only automated formatting using language-standard formatters to ensure consistency with minimal friction for learners.

- Enforce formatting via language-native/defacto tools (e.g., Black for Python, gofmt for Go, rustfmt for Rust, Prettier for JS/TS, ktfmt/ktlint-format for Kotlin, clang-format for C/C++, dotnet format for .NET).
- Provide a unified “format” task/command in each kata template and a pre-commit hook to auto-format on commit. Include a CI job that verifies formatting (fails if diffs are produced), but does not run style linting rules.
- Provide a shared .editorconfig for baseline indentation, line endings, and whitespace to keep cross-editor behavior consistent.
- Exclude non-formatting lint rules (naming, complexity, pedantic style, import ordering beyond what the formatter handles). Linters may be documented as optional for maintainers or as stretch goals but must not block submissions or CI for participants.
- Allow limited correctness checks that overlap with formatting tools only when low-noise and auto-fixable (e.g., remove unused imports if supported by the formatter). Otherwise, defer to tests to drive feedback.
- Document the single “format” workflow prominently in each kata’s README to minimize setup and cognitive load.

This decision optimizes for approachability, determinism, and fast feedback for learners while maintaining consistent, auto-applied code style across all katas without introducing linter-related noise or configuration overhead.

Adopt Elektra-conforming array notation for storing multiple warnings. All warning entries will be stored under a single array key using canonical Elektra array indices (e.g., /warnings/#0, /warnings/#1, …, with Elektra’s dynamic underscore-based padding as needed for lexicographic ordering, e.g., #_10, #__100). The array’s last index will be tracked via the standard meta key “array”.

Writing logic will always emit the conforming format; reading logic will accept both the legacy “#00…#99” two-digit notation and the conforming notation. On read, any legacy-formatted indices will be normalized in-memory to conforming indices; on write, data will be persisted only in the conforming format, eliminating the 100-entry limit.

A one-time migration step will be provided to convert existing configurations from “#00…#99” to the conforming indices and to set/update the “array” meta key accordingly. After one stable release supporting mixed-read/normalized-write behavior, legacy parsing will be deprecated and subsequently removed.

This decision removes the artificial 100-entry cap, aligns with the established array design decision, ensures proper lexical ordering, and standardizes warning handling across components.

Adopt Ports and Adapters (Hexagonal) architecture as the primary application architecture.

- The domain (core) will encapsulate all business rules, modeled via entities, value objects, domain services, policies, and domain events. The Reservation module will be treated as a deep module with rich domain models and explicit invariants.
- An application layer will coordinate use cases, enforcing transactional boundaries and orchestrating domain operations without containing business logic.
- Ports (interfaces) will define all interactions with the outside world (persistence, messaging, external services, time/clock, email, payment, UI), owned by the application/domain. Adapters will implement these ports for specific technologies (e.g., ORM/repository, REST controllers, message consumers/producers).
- Dependency direction will always point inward (adapters depend on ports; domain depends on nothing), enabling technology-agnostic business logic and easy replacement of infrastructure.
- Testing strategy: business rules will be thoroughly unit-tested in isolation; application services will be tested with ports mocked; adapters will have focused integration tests; end-to-end flows will be covered with a minimal set of system tests. This maximizes testability and feedback speed for complex rules.
- Code organization will reflect layers and boundaries (domain/, application/, ports/, adapters/), with explicit module boundaries for the Reservation deep module to prevent leakage of invariants and to promote reuse.
- Where appropriate, read-side adapters may be optimized independently of the write-side (optionally enabling CQRS for complex queries) without compromising the core model.

This decision prioritizes maintainability, evolvability, and testability in the presence of numerous and complex business rules, and reduces coupling to frameworks and data storage. Layered architecture is not selected as the primary approach due to higher risk of domain-infrastructure coupling and harder isolation for deep modules and testing.

Adopt versioned, immutable data volumes for stateful services and enforce explicit migrations on datastore major upgrades.

- Encode the datastore major version in the Docker volume name (e.g., mongodb_data_v3, postgres_data_v13, elasticsearch_data_v7). Upgrading a datastore’s major version requires introducing a new volume name.
- Never reuse an existing volume across incompatible major versions. On upgrade, containers bind to the new, empty volume by default, avoiding opaque start-up failures due to on-disk format mismatches.
- Provide a deterministic migration path: supply make/CLI targets to export from the old volume and import into the new (e.g., mongodump/mongorestore, pg_dump/pg_restore, Elasticsearch snapshot/restore), and to opt-in to a clean slate.
- Add a startup guard: a lightweight entrypoint check (or sidecar) verifies the volume’s version via a label/file marker. If a mismatch is detected, abort early with a clear error and actionable guidance (migrate, recreate, or pin to the old stack).
- Retain old volumes by default to enable rollback; provide an explicit cleanup command to prune deprecated volumes.
- Document the policy and process: every major datastore upgrade PR must introduce the new volume alias, update migration scripts, and include release notes with steps and expected downtime for local environments.

This decision makes upgrades safe-by-default, reversible, and user-driven, replacing implicit, error-prone reuse of incompatible volumes with explicit, guided migration.

Adopt JSON as the manifest serialization format, validated against a versioned JSON Schema (targeting JSON Schema 2020-12). Publish and maintain an authoritative schema (semver’d) for the Wikibase Manifest that defines required/optional fields for metadata and configuration. Align field names and semantics with OpenRefine’s wikibase-manifest schema where feasible to ensure interoperability; when divergence is necessary, provide a stable mapping and document differences. Provide a namespaced extension mechanism using vendor-prefixed keys (e.g., x-wikibase-*, x-<org>-*) and allow additionalProperties only under such namespaces to preserve forward compatibility.

The manifest will not embed or require an OpenAPI document. Instead, it may include discoverable links (URLs) to API entry points (REST and Action API) and, if available, references to external OpenAPI artifacts for clients that can consume them. The schema will include versioning fields ($schema, manifestVersion) and explicit deprecation semantics for fields to support evolution without breaking existing consumers.

Distribution requirements:
- Manifests are served as application/json at a well-known path and may support ETag/Last-Modified for caching.
- A minimal, mandatory subset enables basic client functionality; optional capabilities are expressed via feature flags/capabilities arrays.

This decision decouples runtime configuration from full API descriptions, maximizes compatibility with existing ecosystem tooling (JSON Schema), and enables gradual enrichment without obligating deployments to maintain OpenAPI specifications.

Adopt Anvil (STFC’s centrally managed Jenkins service) as the primary CI platform for the project. We will implement build pipelines as code (Jenkinsfiles) and run builds on Anvil-managed agents configured with MATLAB and access to the STFC MATLAB license server. Credentials, tokens, and license-related configuration will be stored and managed via Anvil’s standard secrets/credentials facilities. Build artifacts and test reports will be published via Anvil-supported storage and retention policies.

Travis CI will not be used due to lack of secure access to on-premises MATLAB licensing and constraints around proprietary dependencies. A private Jenkins instance will not be created, avoiding the operational overhead and security/compliance burden of provisioning, patching, scaling, and auditing our own CI infrastructure and license integration.

Operationally, we will:
- Create per-repository Jenkins pipelines (multibranch where appropriate) with PR validation, tagged releases, and nightly builds.
- Use Anvil agent labels to target MATLAB-enabled nodes and to control concurrency and resource usage.
- Integrate with repository webhooks for commit/PR triggers; fall back to polling only if required by policy.
- Enforce build reproducibility via pinned MATLAB/toolbox versions and containerized/toolboxed dependencies where feasible.
- Monitor with Anvil’s job health metrics; define SLAs for queue times and agent availability with the Anvil team.

This decision ensures compliant access to MATLAB, reduces maintenance risk, and provides a scalable, supportable CI foundation.

We will deprecate Bower and adopt npm as the single source of truth for all frontend dependencies. All client-side packages will be installed from the npm registry and managed via package.json with a committed package-lock.json to ensure deterministic builds. We will introduce Vite as the standard dev server and bundler for building, transforming, and serving frontend assets.

Key actions:
- Replace bower.json with package.json dependencies; map Bower packages to their npm equivalents or maintained forks.
- Remove bower_components and associated wiring from source control, build scripts, and CI/CD pipelines.
- Update import paths to ES modules (or CommonJS where required) and configure Vite to handle legacy UMD globals as needed.
- Define Vite configuration for asset handling, transpilation targets, CSS preprocessors, and code splitting; produce versioned build artifacts.
- Enforce dependency hygiene: semver ranges aligned to caret by default, explicit resolutions for known conflicts, and periodic npm audit.
- Establish migration shims for globals formerly injected by Bower (e.g., window.$) using Vite aliasing or entry shims, then remove them once code is updated.
- Document the new workflows (install, dev, build, test) and update developer environment prerequisites to require Node.js LTS and npm.
- Block new Bower usage via CI checks and remove any Bower-related docs.

This decision consolidates tooling, aligns with the ecosystem standard, and ensures ongoing support, security updates, and improved developer experience.

## Decision
We will eliminate host-to-container bind-mounting of /app in production and instead deploy immutable, versioned container images that embed the application code at build time.

- The Dockerfile will COPY the application source (and built artifacts) into /app. Production images will be built by CI, tagged with the commit SHA and version, and pushed to the registry.
