- Scope: Prioritize unit tests over behavioral/spec-style tests. Each test targets a single unit with clear Arrange–Act–Assert structure and minimal setup.
- Isolation: Use dependency inversion, lightweight test doubles (protocol-based fakes/mocks), and XCTest expectations for async behavior. Avoid global state and shared fixtures.
- Assertions: Use native XCTest assertions and custom helpers where necessary; forbid matcher DSLs from third-party libraries.
- Coverage and quality: Establish baseline coverage for critical modules and enforce thresholds in CI. Emphasize determinism, repeatability, and speed.
- Test organization: Co-locate tests with modules, name tests by behavior under test (not scenarios), and keep test code explicit rather than hidden in DSLs.
- CI/CD: Configure the pipeline to run XCTest with parallelization and test plans. Generate reports using standard Xcode tooling.
- Migration: Freeze additions to third-party frameworks immediately. Migrate existing tests incrementally, starting with flakiest/slowest and most critical paths. Provide shims/adapters only to aid transition; remove third-party dependencies once migration completes.
- Tooling and linting: Add lint rules or precommit checks to prevent new third-party test imports. Provide templates/snippets for XCTest patterns (sync, async, error handling).
- Documentation and onboarding: Publish testing guidelines and examples, including patterns for async testing, mocking via protocols, and fixture creation.

This decision simplifies the toolchain, reduces maintenance and onboarding overhead, improves test reliability and performance, and aligns with platform-native practices.

We will architect and release all software as small, independently versioned modules (“minimally reusable products”) that each satisfy a single, well-defined responsibility. Every module exposes a stable, language-agnostic contract (e.g., JSON/HTTP, gRPC/Proto, or well-specified CLI/IPC), avoids global state, minimizes external dependencies, and can be composed interchangeably within applications.

To maximize reusability and community contribution:
- Publish early once a module fulfills its responsibility in isolation; iterate via minor releases.
- Use semantic versioning, strict deprecation windows, and clear compatibility guidelines.
- Provide reference implementations, adapters, and conformance test suites to ensure interoperability.
- Maintain small, focused repositories with concise READMEs, quick-starts, and well-scoped issues.

To ensure security without sacrificing modularity:
- Apply least-privilege defaults, reproducible builds, signed artifacts, and SBOMs for each module.
- Perform module-level threat models and security reviews; automate checks in CI.
- Isolate trust boundaries; restrict transitive dependencies; enforce pinned, vetted versions.

To sustain transparency and collective ownership:
- Default to open source; document module boundaries, contracts, and ADRs.
- Govern breaking changes via lightweight RFCs; require migration notes for any contract change.
- Provide templates, scaffolding, and tooling for creating new modules consistent with these principles.

We will prefer composition over integration-by-fork, discourage monolithic coupling, and measure success by interchangeability, contribution velocity, and reduced integration effort across the ecosystem.

We will introduce a production-like staging deployment workflow and environment to validate Next.js production builds before merging to master.

- Create a dedicated staging Kubernetes namespace mirroring production configuration (ENV, secrets, CDN/proxy, build flags). CI will produce a production-mode Next.js build (next build) and container image identical to production.
- For each pull request, CI will automatically deploy an ephemeral preview to staging under a stable, non-wildcard host using path-based routing: https://staging.zooniverse.org/previews/{repo}/{pr}/{app}/. Ingress will route by path prefix to the corresponding service, avoiding wildcard subdomains.
- Previews are created/updated on PR open/update, and automatically torn down on PR close/merge.
- Add required checks: staging deploy must succeed and pass smoke tests against the production build before merge. Changes that touch classification routes require manual QA sign-off on the staging preview.
- Provide a “design review” channel via the same path-based previews for non-PR branches (explicitly triggered in CI), with automatic expiry.
- Protect previews from indexing and unintended public access (robots.txt noindex, optional basic auth).
- On merge to master, production deploy proceeds only if the staging checks have passed.
- Monitor and cap preview concurrency; enforce TTL-based garbage collection to control cost.
- Revisit per-branch subdomain previews when ingress supports wildcards; until then, path-based previews on a single staging domain are the standard.

## Decision

Adopt a generalized hierarchical Region model to replace coarse FacilityGroup-based grouping and enable arbitrary geographic/administrative aggregation for reporting and mobile sync.

- Introduce Region as a first-class entity with fields: id, organization_id, parent_id (nullable), name, slug (unique per organization), description, type (enum, e.g., country/state/district/block/facility), and ancestry/materialized path for efficient subtree queries. Enforce an acyclic tree.
- Facilities are modeled as either:
  - a Region of type facility; or
  - a Facility entity linked 1:1 to a Region of type facility (preferred for minimal downstream change).
- All reporting and access control pivot to Region: users are granted access at a Region node; dashboards aggregate over that Region’s subtree; URLs use Region slugs.
- Mobile sync is scoped by a user’s assigned sync_region (a Region node). Devices sync only records associated with facilities within the sync_region subtree, reducing payloads to the relevant operational slice. Guardrails: per-user sync_region is required; server enforces subtree limits and can cap by patient count if needed.
- Backward compatibility and migration:
  - Create Region trees per organization, mapping existing FacilityGroups to type=district and linking all Facilities under their corresponding district Regions.
  - Provide compatibility views/APIs to derive FacilityGroup from Region during transition.
  - Mark FacilityGroup deprecated and remove after consumer migration.
- APIs: expose Region CRUD, subtree, and ancestry endpoints; add filtering by region_id and descendant_of to reporting queries; add user-to-region assignment and access policies.
- Data integrity: validate unique slugs per organization, enforce single-root per organization, and require a facility to be linked to exactly one Region of type facility.
- Performance: use indices on organization_id, ancestry/path, type; consider a closure table if subtree aggregations require heavy joins at scale.

This decision enables fine-grained, multi-level grouping for reports and safe, right-sized mobile synchronization.

We will physically isolate all components capable of interacting with an HSM from any internet-facing service.

- Deploy the Translator (and any future HSM-capable components) on dedicated physical machines in a restricted GSP tier/subnet with no public ingress and no direct east–west connectivity from the Gateway tier.
- Enforce a single, narrowly scoped integration path: the Gateway publishes validated, canonicalized messages to a secure broker/API; the Translator pulls from/accepts only this interface over mutually authenticated TLS with certificate pinning and strict allowlists. The Translator will not accept, parse, or process raw/untrusted SAML.
- Apply strong network segmentation and policy: layer-4/7 firewalls, private addressing, deny-by-default ACLs, and no administrative plane exposure from the Gateway tier. No SSH access from Gateway networks; out-of-band management only through a bastion in a separate admin tier.
- Harden the Translator hosts: minimal OS, SELinux/AppArmor enforcing, disabled kernel module loading, no container co-tenancy, dedicated service accounts with least privilege, read-only root where feasible, FIPS-validated crypto, and automatic patching windows coordinated with RE.
- Constrain HSM access: exclusive logical partitions, role-scoped credentials, audited PKCS#11 operations, and key material never leaves the HSM. Rotate credentials and enforce just-in-time access for operators.
- Implement comprehensive observability and controls: tamper-evident audit logs, syscall and process monitoring, IDS/IPS on the Translator tier, and alerting on policy violations. Regular penetration tests focused on cross-tier compromise paths.
- Define break-glass and incident response procedures, including rapid isolation of the Translator tier without impacting key custody.

This architecture adopts RE’s separation guidance to remove direct attack paths from the Gateway to kernel/HSM boundaries and constrains data flow to a verified, minimal interface.

Adopt a service-first directory structure with language-specific implementations nested under each service. Concretely:
- Top-level services directory with one folder per service: services/<service-name>/.
- Within each service, create a subfolder per language implementation: services/<service-name>/{go, java, python, node, ...}/.
- Centralize shared contracts/IDLs, API schemas, and test fixtures at repo root (e.g., contracts/, schemas/, test-data/), versioned and consumed by all implementations.
- Standardize naming and build entry points per language to enable uniform CI/CD matrices across services and languages.
- Enforce that cross-language code sharing happens only via contracts and shared libraries in dedicated top-level folders (e.g., libs/<lang>/), avoiding cross-service coupling.
- Deprecate and phase out the language-first directory layout; provide redirects and CI updates to reflect the new paths.
- Update tooling to support per-service, per-language targets (lint, build, test, package) and enable multi-language release workflows for the same service version.
- Document conventions (directory names, module/package names, artifact naming) to keep discoverability and enable side-by-side language versions of the same service.

We will standardize the ordering of common top-level keys in all V3 JSON responses.

- When present, the following keys MUST be the final keys of the top-level JSON object and MUST appear in this order: 1) relationships, 2) metadata, 3) links.
- links is expected to be present in most responses; relationships and metadata are optional.
- Absent keys are simply omitted; the relative order of any present keys is preserved, with links always last among them.
- This ordering requirement applies to all V3 endpoints for their top-level response object (including both single-resource and collection responses).
- Other top-level keys (e.g., data, errors, included, pagination fields) MAY appear before these keys and are unaffected by this decision.

Adopt OpenAPI (v3.x) as the mandatory specification format for all DOS API endpoints and artifacts in an API‑first workflow. The OpenAPI document will be the single source of truth for API contracts, driving design, documentation, mocking, client/server code generation, validation, and governance.

- Author and review APIs as OpenAPI specs before implementation; no API work starts without an approved spec.
- Maintain OpenAPI specs in the DOS repository (one spec per service), version-controlled, with semantic versioning aligned to API versions.
- Enforce consistency via a shared style guide and automated linting (e.g., spectral) in CI; block merges on violations and breaking changes.
- Generate human-readable docs, SDKs, and server stubs from the spec; host published docs in the API portal/registry.
- Use the spec to power contract tests, mock servers for consumer development, and backward-compatibility checks.
- Prefer OpenAPI 3.1 for new APIs; use 3.0.x where tool compatibility requires it, with a migration path to 3.1.
- Define extensions only when necessary and documented; avoid tool lock‑in by staying within the standard where possible.
- Publish stable, immutable versions; deprecate with clear timelines; communicate changes via changelog derived from spec diffs.
- Secure endpoints and schemas within the spec (securitySchemes, components) and validate examples/schemas as part of CI.

This standardization aligns with existing DLS practices, maximizes tool support, and improves interoperability, quality, and developer experience.

Decision:
- Standardize all UI applications and libraries on React 17 via a coordinated release to eliminate cross-version incompatibilities.
- Upgrade semantic-ui-react to the latest version and decouple from its removed Responsive component.
- Preserve backward compatibility by vendoring the last stable Responsive implementation into the UI repository as a temporary shim:
  - Exported as Responsive (deprecated) from decentraland-ui/legacy.
  - API-compatible, no runtime behavior changes.
  - Dev-only deprecation warning with migration hints.
  - Planned removal after a 6-month grace period or two minor releases (whichever is later).
- Introduce an organization-supported responsive solution to replace Responsive:
  - Add a new package @decentraland/ui-responsive based on react-responsive.
  - Expose:
    - <Media at|above|below="xs|sm|md|lg|xl"> for conditional rendering.
    - useBreakpoint() returning current named breakpoint.
    - useMediaQuery(query) for advanced cases.
  - Centralize breakpoint tokens in the design system (xs, sm, md, lg, xl) and ensure SSR safety via react-responsive’s configuration.
- Provide migration tooling and documentation:
  - Codemod to replace imports of Responsive with Media/useBreakpoint where applicable.
  - Cookbook with common recipes (show/hide, different components per breakpoint) and SSR guidance.
- Release plan:
  - UI repo: major version for React 17 + semantic-ui-react upgrade; includes legacy Responsive shim and new responsive package.
  - Downstream apps/libs: upgrade to React 17 and adopt @decentraland/ui-responsive during the grace period.
  - Enforce removal of legacy Responsive after the deprecation window via lint rule and CI check.

We will remove hook-based “scale” utilities from render-props and adopt a component-first API with explicit, simple data flow.

- Replace scale hooks with pure, stateless helper functions (e.g., createScaleBand/createLinearScale). Recompute scales per render; memoize only at component boundaries via useMemo when inputs are large. Favor clarity over premature optimization.
- Stop using hooks inside render props. Customization points will be React components (Cell/Header/Axis components) receiving well-defined inputs.
- Introduce an internal React Context (PivotDataContext) that provides the root DataFrame, a cursor resolver (getCursor), and other shared configuration. This removes prop drilling and the need to pass “root” data everywhere.
- Expose getCursor access consistently: either surface getCursor on substructures or always resolve via context-provided resolver. Avoid mixed patterns.
- Adopt explicit tagged unions for cell/header/axis variants with a discriminator field (type). Use straightforward pattern matching/switch logic instead of implicit/ambiguous inference. Prioritize readability and maintainability.
- Provide escape hatches: users can supply custom components that receive the resolved inputs (scales, cursors, dimensions) via props/context rather than recreating them ad hoc.
- Performance stance: measure before optimizing. If profiling identifies hot paths, add targeted memoization or scale caching keyed by stable inputs at the context level.

This decision simplifies the API, eliminates confusion from hook limitations, avoids root-data plumbing, and restores predictable, testable control flow with tagged unions.

Adopt clear, role-based, and transport-agnostic names for messaging interfaces, with a consistent verb/noun scheme and explicit sync/async semantics. Apply the following renames and conventions:

- Producer/consumer:
  - IProducer → MessagePublisher
  - IConsumer → MessageSubscriber
  - IBatchConsumer → BatchMessageSubscriber
- Message representations:
  - IMessage → MessageEnvelope
  - IEvent → DomainEvent
  - ICommand → CommandMessage
- Transport and routing:
  - IQueue → MessageQueue
  - ITopic → MessageTopic
  - IExchange/IRouter → MessageRouter
  - IDeadLetterQueue → DeadLetterQueue
- Serialization and middleware:
  - ISerializer → MessageSerializer
  - IMiddleware → MessageMiddleware
- Outbox/Inbox patterns:
  - IOutbox → OutboxStore
  - IInbox → InboxStore

Conventions:
- Use nouns for interfaces representing capabilities (Publisher, Subscriber) and precise domains (DomainEvent, CommandMessage).
- Use verb-based method names to reflect actions (publish, subscribe, acknowledge, deadLetter).
- Include Async suffix for methods that are asynchronous (publishAsync).
- Separate concerns by transport with namespaces: Messaging.Core, Messaging.Transport.Kafka, Messaging.Transport.RabbitMQ, etc.
- Avoid single-letter “I” prefixes unless required by language standards; when required, keep naming identical minus the prefix.

Deprecation and migration:
- Mark legacy names as deprecated immediately; provide shims and type aliases for two minor releases.
- Supply codemods and a migration guide; automated CI checks enforce new names (lint rules).
- Update public docs, API references, and code samples in the same release.
- Version bump to indicate non-breaking via compatibility layer; remove deprecated names after the deprecation window.

This decision standardizes messaging nomenclature, reduces ambiguity, and improves maintainability across services and transports.

We will implement a hybrid destination entry model: search-first with map-assisted selection.

- Primary input: a typeahead search box with autocomplete backed by a Places/Geocoding API, returning structured place objects (stable place_id, lat/lng, name, address, types). Supports addresses, POIs, coordinates, and user favorites/recent searches.
- Secondary input: click/tap on map to add a destination. A dropped marker triggers reverse geocoding to suggest the nearest canonical place; users can confirm the suggestion or keep raw coordinates. Markers are draggable with live reverse geocoding.
- The destinations list and the map remain synchronized (selecting an item highlights its marker and vice versa), preserving order for trips.
- Deduplication: prevent near-duplicates by place_id or proximity threshold; consolidate ambiguous geocodes to a canonical place when available.
- Precision: store canonical place_id and normalized lat/lng (snap to entry points when provided by the API; otherwise, geohash precision suitable for routing).
- Accessibility and usability: full keyboard support, screen-reader labels for search results and markers, clear undo/remove actions, and haptic/visual feedback on mobile.
- Performance and resilience: debounce queries, cache recent results, respect API rate limits/quotas, and provide offline/low-connectivity fallback for raw lat/lng entry. Support internationalization and localized search.
- Error handling: surface ambiguous matches with disambiguation UI; handle reverse geocoding failures by retaining coordinates with a “coordinates only” label.
- Telemetry: track entry method (search vs map), correction actions, and failure modes to inform future refinements.

This decision ensures broad user coverage (keyboard, touch, desktop, mobile), aligns with common user expectations, and provides a consistent, canonical representation for downstream routing, ETA, and pricing services.

Decision

Adopt the “bare repository with $HOME as work tree” pattern to track dotfiles and program configuration files in place.

- Create a bare Git repository stored outside the tracked files (e.g., $HOME/.cfg) and set the work tree to $HOME so that files like ~/.bashrc remain at their canonical paths and can be freely read/modified by external programs.
- Interact with the repo via a dedicated alias to avoid accidental use of the default Git context:
  - alias cfg='/usr/bin/git --git-dir=$HOME/.cfg/ --work-tree=$HOME'
  - cfg config --local status.showUntrackedFiles no
- Explicitly add only intended files (e.g., cfg add .bashrc .gitconfig .config/nvim/init.vim), keeping noise low and preventing accidental mass adds.
- External program edits will be visible as working-tree changes and can be committed normally (cfg status/commit/push).
- Bootstrap on a new machine without relocating files:
  - git clone --bare <remote-url> $HOME/.cfg
  - alias cfg='...'
  - cfg checkout
  - cfg config --local status.showUntrackedFiles no
  - If checkout conflicts with preexisting files, back them up and re-run checkout.
- For machine-specific differences, use Git features (branches, sparse-checkout) or config include patterns (e.g., includeIf.onbranch or per-host includes) while keeping shared defaults in main.
- Avoid symlink farms or relocating config files; files remain at their expected locations, preserving compatibility with tools that read/write them directly.

We will implement a centralized analytics platform for GOV.UK publishing data by building an AWS-hosted data warehouse backed by a governed data lake. Key elements:
- Establish an S3-based data lake (raw, staged, curated zones) with Lake Formation for governance, Glue Data Catalog for metadata, and Redshift as the primary analytics warehouse; Athena will support ad-hoc/exploratory queries.
- Ingest data from all publishing-related transactional systems via change data capture (CDC) using AWS DMS (or Debezium/Kafka where applicable) and scheduled API/file ingestions; standardize to open, schema-managed formats (Parquet) with schema evolution controls.
- Adopt an ELT workflow: land raw data unchanged, then transform within Redshift using dbt (or equivalent) to produce a canonical, conformed dimensional model (star/snowflake schemas).
- Capture historical changes using slowly changing dimensions (Type 2) and audit fields to support point-in-time and trend analyses.
- Define data products (subject-area marts) for publishing workflow KPIs and analytical reporting, with clear ownership and contracts (schemas, SLAs, quality checks).
- Implement data quality gates (profiling, validation tests, anomaly detection) in the pipeline; failures trigger alerts and do not promote to curated layers.
- Enforce privacy, security, and access controls (least privilege, row/column-level security, tokenization where needed) and align with GDS security policies and data retention requirements.
- Provide near-real-time freshness for critical operational KPIs (via streaming CDC micro-batches) and daily refresh for broader analytical datasets; publish freshness and reliability SLAs.
- Expose data via Redshift views, APIs, and BI connectors (e.g., Looker/Tableau/QuickSight) for self-serve reporting and standardized dashboards.
- Decommission direct analytical workloads on OLTP systems; all reporting and performance indicators will source from the warehouse/lakehouse.
- Establish a Data Platform team responsible for platform reliability, governance, and enablement; embed domain stewards to curate source-to-target mappings and semantics.
- Start with the highest-value publishing domains, iteratively onboard additional sources, and evolve the model based on usage and feedback.

## Decision
Adopt Mock Service Worker (MSW) as the standard mechanism for mocking network requests across all test levels (unit, integration, component, Storybook, and e2e where feasible). Deprecate direct fetch/XHR mocks and ad hoc stubs. All new tests must define request handlers using MSW’s express-style routing; legacy mocks will be migrated incrementally.

Key practices:
- Establish a shared handlers registry per service/domain with reusable factories for common scenarios and error states; allow per-test overrides and composition.
- In Node-based tests use @mswjs/node; in browser-based tests and Storybook use the Service Worker. Include a common test harness to start/stop/reset handlers automatically.
- Configure tests/CI to error on unhandled requests to surface missing mocks early; allow explicit opt-in passthroughs for true integration cases.
- For e2e, prefer MSW for deterministic network control when backend independence is desired; reserve real backend tests for a dedicated suite.
- Provide utilities for data builders and auth/session state to keep handlers declarative and maintainable.
- Version-pin MSW, document conventions (folder structure, handler naming, lifecycle hooks), and assign ownership for maintenance and updates.

This decision standardizes network mocking, reduces duplication, improves test reliability, and aligns with community and react-testing-library guidance.

Adopt a single, reusable Terraform module as the sole source of infrastructure definition, consumed by three environment-specific stacks (dev, uat, prod) that supply differing parameters to materialize distinct instances. Each environment will:

- Provide its own tfvars and backend configuration, resulting in fully isolated state files/backends and clearly separated lifecycles.
- Use standardized naming and tagging conventions with an environment prefix/suffix to avoid resource collisions.
- Consume a versioned release of the module (semver tags), enabling controlled promotion (dev → uat → prod) without code forks.

We will not create per-environment module copies or divergent code paths. Environment-specific behavior is expressed via input variables and minimal, intentional conditionals within the module. Secrets and sensitive values are injected from approved secret stores rather than hardcoded variables.

Operational controls:

- One module repo; one stack per environment repo/folder referencing a pinned module version.
- CI/CD validates plans per environment, with mandatory review gates for uat and prod. Promotion advances the module version pin, not the module code.
- Drift detection and policy checks (e.g., tagging, IAM) run per environment.
- Breaking changes require a new major module version with documented upgrade steps.

This approach enforces DRY, consistency, and parity across environments while preserving isolation, safety, and controlled evolution.

## Decision
Adopt Emory Shibboleth as the sole authentication mechanism for both Lux and Curate. Each application will continue to use its three existing Shibboleth endpoints (prod, test, arch) with the same approved attribute release policy across environments. Lux will implement just-in-time user provisioning: when a user successfully authenticates via Shibboleth, Lux will create or update the local user record using the released attributes; Curate will continue to rely on Shibboleth for authentication without offering new-user sign-up. No alternative or fallback authentication methods will be enabled in production for either application.

In non-production environments (test and arch), alternative authentication may be temporarily enabled for developer workflows and automated testing, but must be gated behind environment configuration and disabled by default.

Authorization in both applications will be enforced using attributes provided by Shibboleth and mapped to application roles/permissions; any additional attribute needs must go through the institutional attribute release process before use. Configuration, attribute mapping, and endpoint metadata will be version-controlled and consistently applied across both applications to minimize drift. Operational monitoring will be added to detect authentication/attribute failures, and change management will be coordinated with Emory IAM for any updates to endpoints or attributes.

Use UUIDs as the canonical primary identifiers across Meadow (not ULIDs), preserving DONUT’s existing UUIDs during migration without transformation. All domain entities, database primary keys, and externally visible API/resource IDs will be UUIDs. Meadow will not generate or require ULIDs in core systems.

To ensure compatibility and stability:
- Meadow will accept UUIDs in common textual forms (hyphenated/lowercase/uppercase) at APIs but will normalize and persist them in a canonical lowercase hyphenated form for consistency.
- Migration will carry over DONUT UUIDs verbatim; no rekeying or shadow IDs will be introduced.
- Any need for chronological ordering or aesthetic identifiers will be addressed via separate fields and indexes (e.g., created_at, database sequences, or composite indexes), not by changing the primary identifier type.
- If a sortable or user-facing identifier is later required, it may be added as a secondary, non-primary attribute, derived lazily and kept distinct from the UUID.

This decision applies to all new Meadow services and schemas to avoid dual-ID complexity. Any deviation (e.g., adopting ULIDs) requires an explicit ADR and a compatibility plan ensuring UUID continuity at data and API boundaries.

We will treat HTTP status codes as transport metadata and will always attempt to parse and surface the response body when present, regardless of status code. Client libraries will return a canonical Result object containing: status code, headers, raw body, parsed payload (if Content-Type is supported), and a normalized domain error (when applicable). Consumers must not discard bodies for non-2xx responses.

Behavior by class:
- 2xx: return Success with parsed payload. 204 has no body; 206 includes range metadata.
- 3xx: follow redirects up to N hops respecting method-preservation rules; expose final and intermediate locations. 304 yields CacheHit with validators; body is not expected.
- 4xx: return ClientError with parsed error schema when available. Do not retry except 408 and 429; honor Retry-After and backoff policy for those.
- 5xx: return ServerError; enable bounded exponential backoff retries for idempotent and safely retryable operations only.

Error payloads will be mapped to a common error model (code, message, details, correlationId) and preserve provider-specific fields. Unknown Content-Types will be surfaced as raw body bytes with best-effort text preview.

Logging/observability: log status, request id/correlation id, and error codes; sample bodies only when flagged and compliant with PII policies. Emit metrics by endpoint and status class.

Caching and ETags/Last-Modified will be honored per RFC; stale-if-error may be used for 5xx when configured.

APIs we expose will document their error schemas and include machine-readable fields. Feature flags will allow strict-2xx-only mode for legacy clients.

Wir implementieren folgende MVP-Entscheidungen:

- Nutzer-Assoziation: Jeder Eintrag speichert creator_id und last_editor_id. last_editor_id wird bei jeder Änderung gesetzt.
- Benachrichtigungen: Für eingeloggte Ersteller wird standardmäßig eine Benachrichtigung über zukünftige Änderungen aktiviert (per-entry subscription = true). Vor dem Speichern kann der Nutzer diese via Checkbox abwählen. Abo-Einstellung ist pro Eintrag persistiert und änderbar.
- Copyright/Lizenz: Keine erneute Zustimmung pro Eintrag; Registrierung enthält einmalige Lizenzzustimmung, die im Nutzerprofil gespeichert und systemweit geprüft wird.
- Attribution: In der Fußzeile jedes Eintrags wird der Username (Fallback: Nutzer-ID) des zuletzt eingeloggten Bearbeiters angezeigt.
- Vorabmoderation anonymer Änderungen: Pro Eintrag gibt es ein Flag moderation_required_for_anonymous (Checkbox beim Speichern). Ist es aktiv, werden anonyme Änderungen als status = pending gespeichert, sind bis zur Freigabe unsichtbar und erzeugen Freigabe-Benachrichtigungen.
  - Freigabeberechtigte: der Eintragsersteller sowie Rollen RegPi/ThemPi.
  - Freigabe-Workflow per signiertem E-Mail-Link (Approve/Reject). Aktionen werden auditierbar protokolliert.
  - E-Mail-Typen sind getrennt: “Eintrag bearbeitet” vs. “Aktualisierung wartet auf Freischaltung: {Eintragsname}”.
- Datenmodell/Prozess:
  - Entry: creator_id, last_editor_id, subscription_default, moderation_required_for_anonymous.
  - Change/Audit: change_id, entry_id, editor (nullable für anonym), status {pending|published|rejected}, timestamps.
  - Events/Notifications: EditNotification, ApprovalRequest mit eigenen Templates/Subjects.
- NTH-Funktionalität wird nach MVP geplant: Filter “nur veränderte Einträge” und visuelle Markierung (rote Pins) für Einträge im Pending-Status.

## Decision
The proposal is rejected. No changes will be made to the current architecture or delivery roadmap as a result of this proposal.

Rationale:
- Insufficient stakeholder engagement and review; no cross-functional validation or consensus was established.
- Lack of clear problem statement and measurable success criteria, making impact assessment inconclusive.
- Missing analysis of risks, operational implications, cost, and migration strategy; no proof-of-concept or benchmarking evidence provided.
- Misalignment with current strategic priorities and near-term delivery commitments; adoption would introduce undue delivery risk and opportunity cost.
- Unclear benefits relative to established alternatives already in use and supported by the team.

Consequences:
- The existing solution and standards remain in effect.
- The proposal may be reconsidered if resubmitted with a comprehensive problem definition, stakeholder sign-off, comparative evaluation against alternatives, risk/operability assessment, migration plan, and PoC results demonstrating material benefits aligned with our non-functional requirements and roadmap.
- Future proposals of similar scope must include early stakeholder involvement and objective evaluation artifacts before ADR review.

We will restrict all Datalabs workloads to private subnets within the JASMIN tenancy and prohibit any public-facing endpoints. Access will be provided exclusively via a hardened JASMIN-resident bastion (jump host) and JASMIN-managed VPN, ensuring that all management and user traffic remains on JASMIN internal networks.

Key elements:
- No public IPs on Datalabs servers; default-deny inbound firewall policy.
- Single ingress path: JASMIN VPN (with SSO + MFA) to the JASMIN network, then SSH to a hardened bastion.
- Bastion enforces short-lived, identity-bound credentials (e.g., SSH certificates) and mandatory MFA; password-based SSH disabled.
- Fine-grained allowlisting: only the bastion’s security group can reach Datalabs servers on required ports; east–west traffic is minimized via host-based firewalls and network ACLs.
- Administrative and developer access via SSH jump sessions and controlled port forwarding/SOCKS proxies for service interaction; no direct exposure of service ports.
- Internal web UIs and APIs are available only through an internal reverse proxy within JASMIN, protected by SSO, TLS, and optional mTLS; no external DNS records.
- All access is fully audited: central logging of bastion sessions, command logs, proxy access logs, and network flow logs.
- Automated machine-to-machine access uses service identities with least privilege and IP/SG restrictions; secrets are stored in a managed secrets service and never leave the tenancy.
- Temporary exceptional access (e.g., vendor support) must traverse the same VPN+bastion path, time-boxed and explicitly approved; no temporary public openings.
- Data egress/ingress occurs via designated transfer nodes or storage gateways inside JASMIN with malware scanning and policy checks; outbound internet access from workloads is egress-filtered and proxied.
- Regular hardening and patching of bastion and proxies; periodic penetration testing and review of firewall rules.

This approach enables necessary access to the Datalabs network while keeping all services non-public, reducing attack surface to a single, tightly controlled ingress inside the JASMIN tenancy.

We will adopt a Single-File Component pattern for Terraform to ensure each component is self-contained, discoverable, and understandable without cross-referencing multiple files.

- For each deployable component, create exactly one .tf file named <component>.tf in its module or environment folder. This file will contain all inputs, resources, and outputs for that component.
- File structure (strict order):
  1) Header doc block: Purpose, Creates, Inputs, Outputs, Usage example
  2) terraform and required_providers blocks (if needed)
  3) locals
  4) data sources
  5) variables (inputs)
  6) resources
  7) outputs
- The header doc block is mandatory and must list:
  - Purpose: one-sentence description
  - Creates: enumerated resources and key relationships
  - Inputs: name, type, required/optional, default (if any), sensitive
  - Outputs: name and description
  - Usage: a minimal module or resource usage snippet
- Variables and outputs must be declared in the same file as the resources they affect. Do not split variables.tf or outputs.tf across the repo for the same component.
- No implicit cross-file coupling: components reference each other only via module boundaries and explicit outputs/inputs, not via shared locals or data in other files.
- Naming conventions:
  - Variables: snake_case, prefixed when component-specific (e.g., lb_*)
  - Outputs: meaningful, stable names describing consumer intent (e.g., endpoint_url)
  - Resources: standard terraform provider naming and consistent tags/labels
- Documentation and quality gates:
  - Pre-commit hooks enforce terraform fmt, validate, and presence/order of required sections.
  - Use terraform-docs (or equivalent) to verify Inputs/Outputs in the header align with declarations.
- Scope and size:
  - Prefer one file per cohesive component. If a component grows large, it becomes a module directory with a single main.tf retaining the same single-file convention inside that module.
- Exceptions (rare) require ADR approval and must include rationale in the header.

This decision ensures every component is understandable from one file, with consistent documentation, inputs, and outputs visible upfront.

Adopt a modular, plugin-oriented architecture with a small, stable core and opt-in feature modules packaged and released as separate artifacts.

- Establish a minimal core that exposes clear SPIs/extension points and contains only shared domain models, contracts, and utilities. The core must not depend on any feature module.
- Extract each optional capability into an isolated module/plugin with its own artifact, dependencies, and lifecycle. Modules depend on the core and may depend on other modules only via declared, stable interfaces.
- Use dependency inversion and strict architectural boundaries enforced by build-time checks (e.g., module graphs, forbidden dependencies) to prevent regressions into a monolith.
- Provide discovery and integration via explicit registration (configuration) and/or runtime service discovery (e.g., service loader pattern) so features are loaded only when present.
- Publish a curated BOM or dependency bundle to simplify “à la carte” selection while keeping all modules independently consumable.
- Version the core and modules independently with semantic versioning; define compatibility policy for SPI changes and deprecations to allow gradual migration.
- Offer reference distributions that assemble common module sets without coupling them into a single artifact.
- Automate CI/CD per module, with contract tests validating module-core compatibility and backward compatibility across versions.

This decision reduces artifact bloat, clarifies boundaries, and enables precise feature selection by adding or omitting module artifacts.

Decision:
- Adopt a standardized schema taxonomy across environments:
  - APP_[system]: application-owned code and metadata (packages, procedures, types), no tables.
  - DATA_[domain]: normalized business data tables and constraints.
  - INT_[system]: integration/API surface (views, synonyms limited to API exposure, REST-enabled objects).
  - STG_[source]: ingestion and staging tables for ETL/ELT with time-bound retention.
  - MART_[subject]: curated/denormalized analytics/reporting structures.
  - REF_[scope]: reference/master data shared across domains.
  - UTIL_[team]: utility objects (pipelines, scheduler metadata) without business data.
  - SBX_[user/team]: sandboxes; no promotion to higher envs.
  - SEC_[scope]: sensitive/PII data when required; segregated access and encryption.
- Enforce single ownership and separation of concerns:
  - Each schema is owned by a dedicated Oracle role; objects are created only in their owning schema.
  - No cross-schema object ownership; cross-schema access only via INT_* surfaces (views/packages).
  - Public grants and cross-schema DML without an INT_* boundary are prohibited.
- Access control:
  - Standard roles: R_[schema]_READ, R_[schema]_WRITE, R_[schema]_EXEC with least-privilege grants.
  - Application connections use role-based credentials; humans use personal accounts with granted roles.
  - PII in SEC_* requires explicit approval and audited grants; use TDE/column-level encryption where applicable.
- Deployment and change management:
  - All DDL is delivered via migrations (e.g., Liquibase/Flyway) executed as the owning role.
  - Naming conventions, versioning, and environment suffixes (e.g., _DEV/_TST/_PRD) are standardized.
  - Synonyms limited to INT_* schemas; avoid global/public synonyms.
  - Backfills and bulk loads occur in STG_* with idempotent/promotable scripts.
- Interoperability:
  - For non-Oracle platforms, map schema taxonomy to native namespace constructs with equivalent RBAC.
- Governance:
  - Schema creation/change requires DBWG review; decommission with documented data disposition and revoke roles.

Adopt a single, reusable HMRC footer component with first-class Welsh (cy) support, delivered via the shared hmrc-frontend design system. Footer content will be fully externalised into locale message files (en, cy) with no hard-coded strings. Language will be determined by the existing language preference mechanism (e.g., PLAY_LANG/language cookie and/or explicit URL param), with runtime selection of the appropriate locale; if a Welsh key is missing, the component will gracefully fall back to English. All Welsh copy will be provided and signed off through the established translation workflow (Content Design + Welsh Language Unit), versioned alongside the component, and distributed via a library release so all consuming services gain consistent, compliant wording by upgrading dependency versions. The component will ensure accessibility and compliance: lang attributes set appropriately, no mixed-language strings, correct directionality and semantics, and parity of links (Welsh destinations where available; otherwise clearly signposted English). Services must not override footer text locally; any content changes occur centrally in the component and translation source. We will add automated i18n tests to prevent missing keys/regressions and document integration steps for services, including the minimum hmrc-frontend version required to render the Welsh footer.

We will implement the FlowKit HTTP API using Quart as the web framework.

- Rationale: Quart provides an async-native, ASGI-compliant framework with strong performance, first-class asyncio support, and built-in WebSocket handling. It offers broad compatibility with the Flask ecosystem while avoiding Flask/Django legacy and boilerplate.
- Server/runtime: Deploy under an ASGI server (Hypercorn preferred; Uvicorn acceptable) on Python 3.10+.
- Design constraints: Adopt an async-first architecture; prohibit blocking I/O on request paths (wrap unavoidable sync calls in thread executors). Use Quart blueprints for modularity. Prefer Flask-compatible extensions only when confirmed ASGI-safe.
- WebSockets: Enable server-native WebSocket endpoints for future interactive and streaming features without additional frameworks.
- Extensibility and exit strategy: Encapsulate framework dependencies behind a thin HTTP/ASGI adapter layer (routing, middleware, request/response, background tasks), avoiding Quart-specific APIs where a Flask-compatible equivalent exists. This allows low-impact migration to Flask or another ASGI framework (e.g., FastAPI/Starlette) if required.
- Observability and middleware: Use ASGI middleware for logging, tracing, CORS, compression, and rate limiting to maximize portability.
- Versioning: Target the latest stable Quart release, tracking minor updates; pin dependencies and run compatibility tests with key Flask-compatible plugins.

Adopt the AndroidX MenuHost/MenuProvider API as the single, consistent mechanism for fragment menus. Each fragment contributes its menu via a MenuProvider registered in onViewCreated and scoped to viewLifecycleOwner with Lifecycle.State.RESUMED. We will deprecate and prohibit setHasOptionsMenu, onCreateOptionsMenu, and onOptionsItemSelected in fragments.

Implementation pattern:
- Define a BaseMenuFragment that registers/unregisters a MenuProvider automatically in onViewCreated/onDestroyView.
- Fragments override onCreateMenu(Menu, MenuInflater) and onMenuItemSelected(MenuItem) (and optionally onPrepareMenu) to inflate and handle menu items.
- Register the provider on the activity MenuHost: requireActivity().addMenuProvider(provider, viewLifecycleOwner, Lifecycle.State.RESUMED).
- Store menus per fragment under res/menu with a naming convention menu_<feature>_<screen>.
- For dynamic state changes, trigger requireActivity().invalidateMenu().

Toolbar ownership:
- If the activity hosts the app bar, fragments still use MenuProvider via the activity MenuHost.
- If a fragment owns a Toolbar, set it as the supportActionBar in onViewCreated; menu contribution remains through the same MenuProvider pattern.

Testing and linting:
- Add a lint/checkstyle rule (or code review guideline) to reject setHasOptionsMenu usage.
- Provide a test helper to create a MenuProvider and assert onMenuItemSelected behavior.

Outcome: Uniform, lifecycle-aware menu handling that avoids deprecated APIs, prevents menu leaks across configuration changes, and centralizes menu logic per fragment.

## Decision
Encode sidecar/runtime dependencies as first-class, declarative metadata within each deployable image and enforce them at deploy time.

- Each image that requires sidecars MUST include a Runtime Dependencies Manifest (sidecars.yaml) packaged in the image and referenced via OCI annotations. The manifest lists required sidecars with:
  - Immutable image digests (primary requirement); optional semver ranges are allowed at authoring time but MUST be resolved to digests during publishing.
  - Configuration contract (env, args, ports, volumes, health checks, securityContext, readiness ordering).
  - Compatibility constraints (platform/arch, minimum API levels).

- Publishing policy:
  - Dependencies are pinned to verified digests before release to ensure reproducibility and supply-chain integrity.
  - Images and manifests are signed; signatures are verified at deploy time.

- Enforcement:
  - A Kubernetes admission webhook/operator reads the manifest and mutates Pods to inject sidecars, validates compatibility, and blocks deploys on violations. For non-Kubernetes targets, CLI tooling performs the equivalent resolution and composition.
  - CI validates that all referenced dependencies exist, are accessible, and pass basic policy checks.

- Backward compatibility and portability:
  - Images without a manifest deploy unchanged.
  - Consumers that do not support the manifest ignore it safely.
  - The manifest is versioned to allow evolution without breaking existing images.

This approach centralizes dependency intent with the image, ensures determinism via digest pinning and signing, and enables consistent, portable deployment of required sidecars across environments.

## Decision

Adopt declarative Infrastructure as Code (IaC) as the single source of truth for all infrastructure, replacing imperative/manual provisioning. All environments will be defined in version-controlled code, reviewed via pull requests, and applied through automated pipelines. We will standardize on Terraform (HCL) for its maturity, ecosystem, and multi-cloud support, organizing reusable, versioned modules and separating environments/workspaces. Remote state will be stored in a backend with locking (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB/Azure Blob + table/GCS + locking) to ensure consistency.

No direct, manual changes in cloud consoles are permitted; production write-access is limited to CI/CD runners. Every change executes plan and policy checks before apply. We will implement policy-as-code (e.g., OPA/Conftest or Sentinel) to enforce guardrails (e.g., no unintended public IPs, encryption, tagging, least privilege). Drift detection will run continuously (scheduled plan or drift tooling) with alerts and remediation via code.

Security and compliance are first-class: secrets are sourced from an approved secret manager; modules embed secure defaults; immutable patterns (e.g., blue/green or canary) are preferred over in-place mutation. Observability metadata (tags/labels) is mandated for cost, ownership, and traceability.

Branching and promotion flows will mirror environments (dev → staging → prod) with pinned module/provider versions and documented change windows for sensitive systems. Emergency changes follow the same IaC path with expedited review. This decision reduces configuration drift and human error, accelerates safe change, and ensures reproducibility and auditability of infrastructure state.

Adopt a two-tier rendering and caching strategy for Termbox v2:

- ParserCache continues to be used for entity pages and will include a fully server-rendered Termbox fragment for the default user context: interface language as in ParserCache, preferred languages equal to interface language only, and the “more languages” section in its default (collapsed) state.
- For requests whose user context deviates from the default (custom preferred languages and/or logged-in users with language settings differing from interface language), Termbox v2 is invoked at request time to render a per-request fragment that is injected into the output without writing back to ParserCache.
- The “more languages” toggle will not introduce cache key variance. The page will be cached with the default collapsed state; clients with a non-default toggle preference will adjust the UI post-render (client-side) to avoid cache fragmentation.
- CDN behavior remains public-cacheable for default context responses; responses that include per-user rendering are marked private and not shared. No Vary dimensions beyond existing interface language are added to shared caches.
- Implementation details:
  - ParserCache keying remains entity id + revision + interface language.
  - A lightweight runtime check computes whether the request matches the default context; if yes, use the cached Termbox fragment; if no, fetch from the Termbox service and inject.
  - Timeouts and graceful degradation are enforced for the per-request path; on failure, fall back to the cached default fragment.

This decision preserves high ParserCache hit rates for the vast majority of traffic while supporting correctness for the minority of user-specific configurations without introducing cross-service marker replacement.

Adopt a resilient, time-aware ingestion and validation strategy for Koshvani data:

- Timestamp model: persist three timestamps per record—event_time (platform transaction timestamp when available), posting_time (department upload/posting timestamp), and ingestion_time (our successful extract time). Use event_time as the analytic default; fall back to posting_time, then ingestion_time with a provenance flag.

- Incremental extraction with watermarks: maintain per-district/treasury watermarks keyed by the highest known event_time and posting_time. Implement idempotent, paginated pulls with retries. Schedule frequent incremental runs (e.g., hourly) and a nightly reconciliation job scanning a rolling backfill window (e.g., last 14–30 days) to capture late-arriving updates.

- Late data handling: allow record upserts based on stable business keys; reprocess partitions when late records arrive; version records (soft history) to preserve prior states. Establish a maximum allowed lateness SLA (e.g., T+3 days) after which aggregates are re-baselined.

- Validation and quality flags: compute per-source completeness and staleness metrics (e.g., last update age, delta vs. expected volume). Attach data_quality_status to each record and publish source-level quality dashboards. Do not block ingestion on quality failures; quarantine only malformed records.

- Source heterogeneity: configure per-district/treasury adapters with tailored parsers and extraction windows, honoring known posting schedules. Maintain a registry of source capabilities (which timestamps are reliable/available).

- Auditability: log every extraction with request/response hashes, counts, and watermarks. Store immutable raw snapshots and curated, deduplicated tables. Ensure reproducible rebuilds from raw.

- User-facing currency: surface dataset freshness and quality banners (latest event_time, posting_time spread, coverage by district) in downstream products to set expectations.

- Governance: define change control for backfill and schema changes; document assumptions when event_time is missing/irregular; coordinate with departments on posting schedules to refine windows.

This decision balances timeliness and accuracy despite inconsistent temporal data by capturing multiple time dimensions, embracing late-arriving data, and making data quality explicit.

We will adopt RFC 4122-compliant UUIDs across the Telemetry project and will not implement any custom UUID generation or parsing. The default identifier format will be UUID version 4 (random) generated from a cryptographically secure random source to maximize uniqueness and randomness. Where deterministic, namespaced identifiers are explicitly required (e.g., idempotent keys), we will use UUID version 5 with an approved namespace; any such use must be documented per service.

UUIDs will be represented externally and at rest in canonical RFC 4122 text form (lowercase, hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12). Inputs in other cases will be normalized to this format; non-compliant values will be rejected. Where storage or performance benefits are material, services may store UUIDs as 16-byte binary while preserving canonical string representation at interfaces.

We will exclusively use vetted, widely adopted libraries that default to CSPRNG and enforce RFC 4122 variants and versions. Preference order: platform standard libraries where available (e.g., Java java.util.UUID, Python uuid, .NET System.Guid); otherwise, well-maintained third-party libraries with permissive licenses (e.g., Node.js uuid, Go google/uuid, Rust uuid). Libraries must be version-pinned, monitored for security advisories, and centrally approved.

Generation occurs at the service boundary that creates the resource; downstream services must not regenerate IDs. All services must include UUID validation using the same library to ensure consistency.

Adopt lightweight, incremental architectural documentation using small, versioned Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) stored alongside the code. Each significant architectural decision will be captured as a single ADR that documents context, decision, options considered, rationale, consequences, and status. ADRs will be created just-in-time as decisions arise, rather than in a large, upfront specification.

Process and governance:
- Scope: Create an ADR for any choice that materially affects system qualities, interfaces, data models, runtime topology, or external commitments.
- Lifecycle: ADR statuses are Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Superseded/Deprecated as context evolves; superseding ADRs must reference predecessors.
- Placement: Keep ADRs in the repository under a well-known directory, reviewed via the same pull request process as code.
- Ownership: The team making the decision authors the ADR; the tech lead (or equivalent) is accountable for coherence and alignment.
- Currency: “Definition of Done” requires ADRs to be created/updated for impacted decisions. Release notes must list ADRs added/changed.
- Traceability: Link ADRs to user stories, non-functional requirements, incidents, and experiments/spikes; add cross-links to code modules and tests.
- Accessibility: Keep ADRs short (1–2 pages), self-contained, and titled for quick scanning. Provide an index and tags (e.g., security, data, performance).
- Review: Schedule lightweight periodic reviews to validate continued relevance; retire or update ADRs when context changes.

This approach minimizes valueless documentation while preserving decision intent and consequences, enabling teams to evolve architecture safely without blind acceptance or change.

Adopt a namespaced, non-merged column model for Kafka records. SELECT * expands only to the Value schema fields. Key and metadata are not implicitly merged into the tabular schema and must be explicitly projected using namespace qualifiers:
- value.<field> or value.* for Value fields
- key.<field> or key.* for Key fields
- meta.<attribute> or meta.* for engine/record metadata (e.g., topic, partition, offset, timestamp, headers)

Deterministic column ordering for JDBC is defined as:
1) Columns appear in the order they are referenced in the SELECT list.
2) For wildcards, expansion order is value.* first, then key.*, then meta.*.
3) Within each namespace wildcard, fields follow the schema-defined order; for metadata, a fixed canonical order is used.

Column naming in ResultSet metadata uses fully qualified names (e.g., key.id, value.userName, meta.offset) to avoid collisions and to enable retrieval by name or index reliably. No implicit merging of Key and Value schemas is performed; collisions are impossible due to namespaces. If Value or Key is schemaless, expose a single column (value.raw or key.raw) with bytes/string as applicable. If Value is null, value.* expands to zero columns; key and meta remain accessible.

This decision preserves intuitive SELECT * behavior for tabular consumers (Value-only), provides explicit, discoverable access to Key and metadata, ensures stable column indexing for JDBC, and avoids ambiguity and complexity from schema merging.

Adopt a formal Architectural Decision Record (ADR) process for archetypes-rules to ensure rigor, transparency, and revisability of major technical choices.

- Scope: ADRs are required for decisions affecting public APIs/contracts, data models, domain semantics, persistence/storage, cross-cutting concerns (security, observability, performance), external dependencies, deployment/runtime topology, and any change with medium/high blast radius. Minor/local refactorings are exempt.
- Repository and visibility: ADRs live in-repo under docs/adr/, are public by default, and are indexed via docs/adr/README.md with status and owners. Each ADR gets a stable ID (ADR-xxxx) and title.
- Template and content: Use the MADR-style template (Context, Decision, Alternatives, Consequences, Status, Review date, Owners). All ADRs must enumerate considered alternatives and trade-offs.
- Workflow:
  1) Open a GitHub PR adding a Proposed ADR and (optionally) a prototype/experiment.
  2) Announce in the team channel and open a linked GitHub Discussion (RFC).
  3) Require ≥2 maintainer approvals; for “Major” decisions add tsc-review label, notify TSC, and allow a 5-business-day review window (expedite with explicit justification).
  4) Merge as Accepted or Rejected; record dissent if unresolved.
- Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → (optionally) Deprecated → Superseded. Changes do not edit Accepted ADRs; create a new ADR that supersedes prior ones and cross-link.
- Review cadence: Each ADR includes a review date (≤12 months). The team runs a quarterly triage to confirm validity or trigger a superseding ADR if conditions have changed.
- Traceability: Link ADRs from code (README/docs), issues, and PRs; major releases include an ADR summary. CI enforces presence of ADR references for flagged PR labels (api-change, dependency, storage).
- Roles: Each ADR has an Owner and a Shepherd (review coordinator). The Shepherd ensures alternatives are explored and stakeholders consulted.
- Exceptions: Emergency changes may proceed with a “post-hoc ADR” within 5 business days.
- Non-compliance: PRs in scope without ADR references cannot merge unless explicitly waived by the tech lead with rationale recorded.

This decision institutionalizes shared understanding, TSC oversight, and disciplined revisiting of architectural choices.

We will provision CSI-based storage drivers by default, with a single “default” RWO block storage class per environment and an additional RWX shared file storage class for workloads that require multi-writer access. Defaults are:

- AWS:
  - RWO (default): EBS gp3 CSI (encrypted, volumeBinding=WaitForFirstConsumer, allowExpansion=true, snapshots enabled)
  - RWX: EFS CSI (encrypted, bursting, access points)
- GCP:
  - RWO (default): Persistent Disk Balanced CSI (encrypted, regional optional, WaitForFirstConsumer, allowExpansion=true, snapshots enabled)
  - RWX: Filestore CSI (Basic / Zonal by default)
- Azure:
  - RWO (default): Azure Disk Premium SSD v2 CSI (encrypted, ZRS optional, WaitForFirstConsumer, allowExpansion=true, snapshots enabled)
  - RWX: Azure Files Premium CSI (encrypted, AD DS optional)
- On‑prem:
  - RWO (default): Ceph RBD via Rook‑Ceph CSI (encrypted at rest via Ceph, replication per pool policy)
  - RWX: NFS (nfs-subdir-external-provisioner) or CephFS via Rook‑Ceph CSI where available

Global defaults and policies:
- Mark exactly one StorageClass as default per cluster (the RWO class above).
- Provide non-default “performance” classes (e.g., io-optimized / SSD / higher IOPS) and “cost-optimized” classes per environment; no default change.
- Enable encryption at rest for all classes; enforce in parameters/policy.
- Enable snapshots and PVC resize across all drivers that support it.
- Set reclaimPolicy=Delete by default; provide a “retain” variant for stateful production.
- Use volumeBindingMode=WaitForFirstConsumer to ensure topology-aware placement.
- Label and document access modes (RWO/RWX), performance, and cost in annotations.

Opt-outs and extensibility:
- Drivers are installed conditionally based on detected provider; clusters without the matching cloud will not install that driver.
- Additional drivers (e.g., local PVs) may be enabled per cluster via configuration without changing defaults.

This decision standardizes on CSI, provides sensible, secure defaults for the common RWO and RWX needs, and keeps room for environment-specific performance tiers without fragmenting the default experience.

Adopt a JVM-native, source-first text extraction strategy centered on Apache Tika. We will implement a TextExtraction SPI with per–MIME type handlers and a default Tika-backed handler to minimize external dependencies while covering a broad set of formats.

- Primary library: Apache Tika (parser + detector) for unified content detection and extraction across most document types.
- Specialized handlers (still JVM-only) where needed for fidelity/performance:
  - PDF: Apache PDFBox (direct), while retaining Tika PDF parsing as fallback.
  - Office: Apache POI for .doc/.docx/.xls/.xlsx/.ppt/.pptx (Tika uses POI; we allow direct use when precision is required).
  - HTML/XML: Jsoup/SAX for robust text extraction and sanitization.
  - Plain text/Markdown/Code: direct UTF-8 streaming with charset detection via Tika; optional flexmark for Markdown if needed.
  - Archives: Apache Commons Compress to iterate entries and delegate to the SPI per file.
- No PDF conversion: always extract from original source formats to preserve structure and reduce errors.
- Architecture: plugin-based handlers registered via MIME types; default route through Tika unless a specific handler is present. Handlers operate in streaming mode where possible, enforce size/time limits, and normalize to UTF-8 with consistent newline and whitespace policy.
- Dependencies: JVM-only by default; no native services required. Optional OCR for images/scanned PDFs via Tesseract (tess4j) is provided as a pluggable, off-by-default module with clear operational requirements.
- Operational concerns: sandbox parsing with resource limits, deny-lists for dangerous formats if necessary, and telemetry for handler selection, errors, and fallbacks. Provide deterministic outputs for the same inputs to aid caching and deduplication.

This decision maximizes coverage with minimal external dependencies, keeps the system extensible per file type, and ensures text is extracted from original sources rather than derived PDFs.

## Decision
Adopt a progressive, promotion-based deployment pipeline across integration → staging → production using a single, immutable, versioned artifact built once per change. The CI pipeline will compile, test, security-scan, and sign the artifact, then publish it to a centralized registry. CD will promote that exact artifact through environments without rebuilds or code changes.

Environment deployments will be automated with approval and quality gates:
- Integration: automatic deploy on merge to main; smoke, contract, and integration tests; fast feedback.
- Staging: automatic promotion on green integration; end-to-end, performance, and security tests; optional canary; product/QA sign-off.
- Production: manual approval gate; progressive rollout (canary or blue/green) with automated health checks and SLO/SLA guards; auto-rollback on regression.

Parity across environments will be enforced via infrastructure-as-code and identical deployment manifests with environment-specific configuration supplied externally (env vars, config maps, and managed secrets). No environment-specific code paths are allowed. Database changes will follow backward/forward-compatible migration patterns and be applied as part of deployment with automated verification and safe rollbacks.

Feature flags will be used to decouple deploy from release, enabling incremental exposure and rapid mitigation. All deployments will be observable (logs, metrics, traces), auditable (immutable change records and approvals), and reproducible. Semantic versioning will label releases; promotions will reference the artifact digest. This approach minimizes risk, shortens lead time, and ensures consistent, testable promotion through integration, staging, and production.

Adopt first‑party analytics only: instrument the website with standardized client events for user behaviors and task completion that are sent exclusively to our existing, approved internal telemetry pipeline (first‑party collection endpoint → ingest service → internal streaming/storage → internal BI). No third‑party/web‑beacon analytics, tags, or external endpoints (e.g., Google Analytics) are permitted.

Define and enforce a versioned event taxonomy (page_view, component_interaction, form_start, form_submit, task_start, task_complete, error, performance) with a shared schema (event_name, event_version, timestamp, user/session/device/page context, feature flags/variant, task_id, task_status, metadata). Implement client SDK wrappers that honor CMP consent and Do Not Track, and default to minimal collection until consent. Transport via our approved SDK to the first‑party ingest API with batching, backoff, and offline queueing; no PII in event payloads beyond approved pseudonymous identifiers. Enrich server‑side only using internal services.

Persist data in our approved internal data lake/warehouse with role‑based access, retention, and data quality checks; expose curated task/behavior datasets and metrics through our approved BI platform and notebooks. Provide standard dashboards for task completion, funnel/drop‑off, and behavior cohorts using only internal tools.

Operationalize with schema validation, observability (event volumes, error rates), and deployment guards via our tag manager limited to first‑party tags. Document governance (ownership, SLAs, retention, deletion), and review new events via the existing analytics schema review process.

Adopt Relay (Relay Modern) as the GraphQL client/runtime for v5 and deprecate Apollo (and our fork). Enforce strict data colocation via Relay fragments and compile-time validation with the Relay Compiler to prevent misuse and accidental performance regressions. Generate artifacts as part of the build/CI pipeline and gate merges on successful Relay compilation. Use Relay’s normalized store, fragment ownership, and hooks (useFragment, usePreloadedQuery, usePaginationFragment, useRefetchableFragment) to standardize data flow, pagination, and refetching. Enable persisted queries and query identifiers; implement a custom Network layer with batching, retries, caching policies, SSR/streaming, and error observability.

Define and enforce project-wide patterns:
- Colocate all data requirements with components via fragments; no ad-hoc “fat queries.”
- Compose data with fragment spreads; prohibit manual result distribution.
- Centralize mutations with updater functions and optimistic updates using Relay APIs.
- Maintain a single Relay Environment per app surface with clear boundaries for preloading and routing.
- Provide ESLint rules, code mods, and templates to prevent anti-patterns and simplify adoption.

Execute a phased migration: new features on Relay only; migrate high-traffic and complex views first; remove Apollo after parity and stability are reached. Pin Relay versions and upgrade via planned sprints. Deliver comprehensive documentation, examples, and training to internal and community contributors. This decision is mandatory for v5 and a release blocker for features that do not conform.

We will not re-platform Libero Publisher to a React SPA. Instead, Publisher will adopt an HTML-first, server-rendered front end with progressive enhancement to meet read-optimised performance goals, while aligning on the JavaScript/TypeScript ecosystem and phasing out PHP.

- Rendering: Server-side rendering in Node.js using a lightweight templating engine (e.g., Nunjucks) to produce semantic, cacheable HTML that works without JavaScript by default.
- Progressive enhancement: Layered, minimal JavaScript for interactivity; no hard client-side dependency for core reading flows. Enhancements delivered via small, framework-agnostic modules and Web Components where appropriate.
- Alignment: Standardise on JS/TS toolchain (package management, linting, formatting, testing, bundling), shared design tokens, and shared accessibility and performance practices across the Libero Suite.
- Reuse strategy: Shared UI delivered as framework-agnostic components (Web Components) with thin adapters for React (Reviewer/Producer) and vanilla use (Publisher), maximizing cross-product reuse without imposing a SPA runtime on Publisher.
- Backend language: Remove PHP from Publisher’s front end delivery path; use Node.js for rendering and asset delivery. Server-rendered HTML integrates with existing services via APIs.
- Performance: Prioritise TTFB, HTML payload efficiency, CDN/cache-friendliness, and minimal JS footprint; avoid mandatory hydration costs on read pages.
- Scope boundaries: React may be used selectively for isolated, high-interactivity islands only when justified by user needs and performance budgets, but is not the default rendering technology for Publisher.

This decision aligns technology choices where beneficial (JS/TS, tooling, components, CI/CD) while preserving Publisher’s read-optimised, progressively enhanced requirements and enabling reuse with Reviewer without enforcing a React-first architecture.

We will strengthen CloudHSM access controls by extending the Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy to require a dual label gate: traffic to the HSM is permitted only when both of the following are true:
- The originating Pod has label talksToHsm=true
- The originating Namespace has label talksToHsm=true

Implementation details:
- Update the existing GlobalNetworkPolicy governing egress to CloudHSM endpoints/ports to include both a podSelector (talksToHsm=true) and a namespaceSelector (talksToHsm=true). All other traffic to HSM CIDRs/ports remains denied by default.
- Namespace labels are change-controlled via the gsp/cluster-config repositories; tenants cannot self-serve this label. Pod labels remain tenant-controlled, preserving least privilege within approved namespaces.
- Only platform-owned namespaces that host HSM-integrated workloads will be granted the namespace label via PR and review. No user/ephemeral namespaces receive the label by default.
- Provide a controlled migration: apply in non-production first, then production after validation. Prior to enforcement, identify current HSM clients and ensure their namespaces receive the label to avoid disruption.
- Document the request/approval process for adding the namespace label, including security review and monitoring expectations.
- Maintain observability: add network policy metrics/logging and alerts for denied HSM egress to detect misconfigurations or abuse attempts.

This decision preserves tenant flexibility for pod-level intent while preventing unilateral HSM access enablement from tenant namespaces. The fail-safe default remains deny, and any expansion of HSM access requires explicit, auditable platform changes at the namespace level plus pod-level opt-in.

We will extract authentication from panoptes-javascript-client into a dedicated Panoptes Auth package within the Panoptes.js monorepo. The new module will provide both a headless core and optional UI components to deliver a consistent login experience across projects and replace the buggy OAuth client.

Key elements:
- Protocol: adopt OAuth 2.1 with OpenID Connect using Authorization Code + PKCE for third-party apps; maintain first-party session auth for Zooniverse domains.
- Token handling: access tokens stored in memory; refresh via rotating refresh tokens in secure, httpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookies for first-party; no use of localStorage or sessionStorage for tokens. Support silent refresh via iframe is explicitly not implemented; use refresh token and short-lived access tokens.
- UI: ship a minimal, accessible set of React components (LoginButton, LogoutButton, UserMenu, CallbackHandler) and a headless API for non-React consumers. Provide CSS-agnostic styles or design tokens.
- Client integration: expose a small, framework-agnostic core (TypeScript) that wraps fetch with auth headers and automatic retry on 401 with refresh. Pluggable storage and transport interfaces to support Node and browser environments.
- Security: PKCE mandatory, state/nonce validation, CSRF protection on first-party flows, strict domain scoping for cookies, and tenant-aware redirect URI validation.
- Migration: deprecate auth surfaces in panoptes-javascript-client, provide a compatibility adapter for a minor release, then remove in the next major. Document cutover steps and examples.
- Observability: standardized events and hooks for login/logout/errors and metrics.
- Browser support: evergreen browsers only; no IE.

We will deploy Nginx as the HTTP server and FastCGI gateway to PHP-FPM via Unix domain sockets on the same host. Nginx will serve static assets directly and forward only PHP requests to PHP-FPM, using a dedicated upstream pointing to a Unix socket for lower latency, reduced overhead, and no port exposure.

Key configuration points:
- Use fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php-fpm.sock (or distro-appropriate path) with a matching php-fpm pool configured to listen on that socket.
- Ensure socket ownership and permissions align with the Nginx worker user (e.g., www-data) via listen.owner, listen.group, listen.mode in the PHP-FPM pool.
- PHP handling: location ~ \.php$ { try_files $uri =404; include fastcgi_params; fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root$fastcgi_script_name; fastcgi_index index.php; fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php-fpm.sock; } to prevent path traversal and missing file execution.
- Static and index: location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string; } and separate locations for static extensions with caching headers.
- Tune FastCGI: set fastcgi_read_timeout, fastcgi_buffers, fastcgi_buffer_size, fastcgi_send_timeout appropriate to workload; enable gzip/HTTP/2 at Nginx; keepalive off for FastCGI.
- Security: disable .php execution in uploads, limit request body size (client_max_body_size), sanitize fastcgi_param PATH_INFO handling, and restrict methods if needed.
- Observability: access_log/error_log with distinct formats; PHP-FPM slowlog enabled.
- Operations: zero-downtime reloads (nginx -s reload) and rolling PHP-FPM restarts; provide a TCP fallback only when sockets are unsuitable (e.g., cross-host).

We will introduce a configurable retention policy for mail queue metadata and markers and enforce it via automatic expiration and blob garbage collection:

- Keep TimeWindowCompactionStrategy for enqueuedMailsV3 and deletedMailsV2, and set default_time_to_live on both tables to a configurable retention (e.g., 30–90 days). TTL will be applied to new writes; legacy rows will be rewritten with TTL by a one-off backfill job.
- Align TTL as a multiple of the TWCS window to enable efficient drop of entire SSTables; reduce gc_grace_seconds accordingly (while preserving repair safety) to accelerate space reclamation.
- Implement a periodic BlobStore GC that:
  - Computes the set of live blob references from non-expired rows in enqueuedMailsV3 and deletedMailsV2.
  - Deletes blobs that have no live references after a configurable safety delay beyond TTL (to accommodate clock skew and late repairs).
  - Runs incrementally and idempotently, with rate limiting and metrics.
- Do not persist indefinite “deleted” markers; deletedMailsV2 rows expire under the same retention, ensuring privacy.
- Provide configuration flags to enable/disable TTL application, set retention and safety delays, and tune GC cadence.
- Migration plan:
  - Deploy schema changes (TTL, gc_grace_seconds).
  - Run a controlled backfill to reinsert legacy rows with TTL.
  - Enable BlobStore GC after at least one full retention period has elapsed or when backfill completion is verified.
- Maintain observability: export metrics for row expirations, GC candidates, deletions, and storage savings; add alerts for GC lag and blob reference drift.

This decision bounds data lifetime for both privacy and cost, leverages TWCS-friendly TTL-based expiry, and reclaims unreferenced blobs safely.

We standardize on content-addressable preservation storage keyed solely by the SHA-256 digest of the exact AIP bitstream, eliminating the ULID component and any dependence on external identifiers for storage paths.

- Key derivation: compute the lowercase hex SHA-256 over the immutable, finalized AIP payload bytes (no normalization).
- Path layout: adopt a versioned algorithm namespace and pairtree derived from the digest:
  - Prefix: v1/sha256/
  - Pairtree: 2-character segments from the digest (e.g., ab/cd/ef/01/23/45/), with sufficient depth to keep directory fanout manageable (6–8 segments).
  - Leaf filename: the full 64-character hex digest (no extension).
  - Example: v1/sha256/ab/cd/ef/01/23/45/abcdef012345... (64 chars)
- Identifier mapping: the logical object identifier-to-storage key relationship is maintained in metadata/index services; identifiers do not appear in storage paths.
