Disabling certificate verification is prohibited in production and staging. For development and testing, only an approved internal CA may be used; any temporary bypass requires an explicit, time-boxed exception and is blocked from release builds.

For first-party and high-risk external services, we will implement certificate/public key pinning (SPKI pinning preferred) to further reduce man-in-the-middle risk. Pin sets must include at least one backup key to enable seamless rotation and must be versioned and distributed via secure configuration channels. Pinning violations will fail closed with clear telemetry.

Operationally, we will:
- Manage trust stores centrally with change control and automated distribution.
- Rotate certificates and pins proactively before expiry using overlapping validity.
- Log and alert on verification failures and pinning mismatches.
- Reject weak algorithms and enforce modern TLS settings consistent with organizational policy.

SDKs, services, and CLI tools must not expose options to skip verification in production contexts. Security reviews will verify adherence, and CI/CD will include automated checks preventing deployment with disabled or insecure certificate verification.

Adopt a convention-over-configuration strategy that minimizes the configuration surface and complexity for verification and metadata.

- Provide sensible, opinionated defaults covering the common 80% use cases, requiring zero configuration for standard scenarios.
- Consolidate settings into a single, human-readable config file with a minimal “core” section; move non-essential and expert options to an “advanced” section or separate profile.
- Offer curated presets/profiles (e.g., dev, CI, prod) that can be selected with a single flag and overridden incrementally.
- Automatically discover and infer metadata from project sources, environment, and repository when safe; only prompt for explicit fields when inference fails.
- Introduce a versioned configuration schema with strict validation, clear error messages, and actionable suggestions.
- Ship a guided CLI wizard and template generator to scaffold minimal configs and surface advanced options only on demand.
- Deprecate redundant/low-value options; maintain an escape hatch via plugin hooks or a custom verifier block for edge cases.
- Ensure backward compatibility by supporting legacy configs through a translator layer and emitting deprecation warnings with migration hints.
- Prefer immutable, declarative configuration; avoid imperative logic in configs.
- Establish a documented default-override precedence: defaults < preset < core config < advanced overrides < CLI flags/env.
- Commit to keeping defaults stable and evolving via semver-governed config schema versions.

We will adopt “first-occurrence full embed with subsequent summary stubs” for Expanded JSON-LD emission to control payload size while preserving regular-JSON consumption.

- For each document emission, we maintain a per-emission node registry keyed by @id.
- The first time a node appears, we embed its full expanded representation.
- On subsequent references within the same document, we embed a summary stub instead of re-embedding the full node. A stub includes at minimum:
  - @id
  - type(s) (@type)
  - a configurable set of summary properties (e.g., name, title) sufficient for common UI rendering
  - a marker flag (e.g., _summary: true) indicating a non-full embed
- No JSON-LD link-only references are emitted in Expanded mode; stubs remain regular JSON objects to preserve the “consume as JSON” goal.

Configurability:
- maxEmbedDepth: cap recursive embedding depth; beyond the cap, only stubs are emitted.
- summaryFields: per-type projection for stub content.
- maxDocumentSize / maxNodeSize: hard limits that trigger stub substitution when exceeded.
- determinism: stable traversal order ensures deterministic selection of the first full embed.
- mode toggles:
  - expandedStrict (legacy): always fully embed (may be large).
  - expandedDedup (default): first full, subsequent stubs.
  - flattened: single render per node with JSON-LD links (unchanged).

Documentation and contracts:
- Publish the stub schema and semantics of _summary to consumers.
- Guarantee that any @id present in a stub also appears once as a full embed somewhere in the same document unless prevented by depth/size limits, in which case we include a top-level includes array with full nodes pruned by limits.

This approach reduces duplication, bounds payload size, preserves regular JSON consumption, and remains backward-compatible via a strict mode.

We will standardize on Kotlin as the primary language for all new application code to ensure consistency, modern language features, and improved developer productivity. Kotlin will be the default for new services, modules, and features. Java remains supported only for maintaining existing components, leveraging third-party Java libraries, or when platform constraints require it.

Guidelines:
- All new repositories start in Kotlin; mixed-language projects are discouraged unless justified by integration needs.
- When touching legacy Java modules, prefer incremental conversion to Kotlin where feasible (file-by-file or module-by-module), validated by tests.
- Shared libraries and SDKs provided by our teams should offer Kotlin-first APIs; Java interop must be preserved as needed.
- Enforce Kotlin style, static analysis, and null-safety rules via ktlint/Detekt and CI gates; adopt coroutines for async workflows.
- Tooling: use Kotlin DSL for build scripts where supported; baseline on the current LTS Kotlin version with controlled upgrades.
- Training and onboarding: provide Kotlin guidelines, code examples, and pair programming support to upskill the team.
- Exceptions require an approved ADR addendum documenting why Java is necessary and plans to reconcile later.

This decision promotes a consistent, concise, and safer codebase while retaining seamless interoperability with the Java ecosystem.

We will adopt a progressive, backward-compatible release strategy for Dapr binaries and configurations to prevent user blockers.

- Versioning and compatibility: Use SemVer with majors for breaking changes only. Guarantee control plane compatibility with sidecars n-2 and sidecar compatibility with control plane n-1. Config schemas carry explicit apiVersion with defaults and feature-gated fields; deprecated fields retained for at least two minors with automated migration tooling.

- Release channels: edge, beta (RC), stable, and LTS. Stable releases follow a set cadence; LTS every two minors with 12–18 months security/backport support. RC window ≥2 weeks.

- Progressive delivery: Blue/green and canary rollouts across environments and clusters: 1%→10%→25%→50%→100% with health gates. Namespaces/workloads can pin versions via annotations/labels. Control plane is upgraded first; sidecars are auto-upgraded per policy; workloads opt-in per namespace. Immediate rollback to previous stable is supported.

- Safety and policy: Binaries and container images are SBOMed, reproducibly built, signed (Sigstore/cosign), and published with checksums. Admission policies verify signatures and enforce allowed versions. Default-off feature flags guard new capabilities until both control plane and sidecar advertise support.

- Distribution: Publish via OCI registries, Helm charts, Homebrew/apt/yum, and GitHub Releases. All artifacts are immutable; prior releases remain available.

- Telemetry and SLOs: Rollout gates on error rates, latency, crash loops, and compatibility probes. Automated halt/rollback if thresholds breach.

- Communication and deprecation: Publish compatibility matrix, upgrade guides, and deprecation notices with timelines. Provide config migration CLI and dry-run validators to ensure safe adoption.

We will treat the issue tracker as the single source of truth for outstanding work and use structured inline tags only as pointers and context.

- Tags
  - TODO: Small, near-term follow-ups discovered during implementation. If not resolved within the current PR, they must reference an issue. Lifetime limit: 14 days after merge.
  - FIXME: Known defects or incorrect behavior. Always requires a linked issue and should be prioritized; must not block release criteria unless explicitly waived.
  - NOTE: Non-actionable guidance or rationale. No issue required. Do not use XXX.

- Required format
  - TAG: concise imperative summary — context (Issue: PROJ-1234) [owner: initials] [yyyy-mm-dd]
  - Example: TODO: Extract validator into strategy — duplication in FooService (Issue: PROJ-2345) [ab] [2026-01-23]

- Workflow rules
  - Any actionable item expected to take >1 day or span sprints must have an issue and only a brief TODO remains in code linking to it.
  - All FIXMEs must have a failing test or clear reproduction steps in the linked issue.
  - No unlinked TODO/FIXME may be merged to main. NOTES are allowed without links.
  - TODOs older than 14 days or lacking an issue link will fail CI. FIXMEs without an issue link will fail CI immediately.

- Tooling
  - Configure linters/CI to enforce tag format, presence of issue links, and age thresholds.
  - IDE templates/snippets provided for consistent insertion of tags.

This decision ensures actionable work is tracked, code remains readable, and inline markers provide just-in-time context without becoming a parallel backlog.

Sirius Public API will expose and persist a single, immutable, system-generated unique identifier for each report record. On successful report creation, the API will return HTTP 201 with a response body containing reportId (opaque UUID v4) and will include the same reportId in all subsequent GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE operations for that report. The identifier is globally unique within the Sirius deployment, never reassigned or recycled, and remains stable regardless of changes to donor, period, or report metadata.

Supporting documents creation and association will require this reportId; endpoints that accept or return documents linked to reports will include reportId as the authoritative foreign key. For discovery, list and search endpoints (e.g., by donor and reporting year) will return arrays including reportId for each matching report, ensuring that multiple reports for the same donor and year are individually addressable.

We will not rely on composite/natural keys (e.g., donorId + year + version) for external integrations. A human-readable reference (e.g., donor/year/version) may be exposed for display but must not be used as an integration key.

All existing reports will be backfilled with a generated reportId. Eventing/webhooks and audit logs will include reportId to maintain traceability. The identifier format is opaque and may change in representation in the future without affecting semantics.

Adopt containerization as the standard runtime and packaging model for the Data Submission Service, using Docker to build immutable images for all application components and their runtime dependencies. Each service will have its own Dockerfile, with pinned base images and multi-stage builds to produce minimal, secure images. Local development and integration will use docker-compose to run the full stack (app, database, queues, test doubles) consistently across developer machines.

CI/CD will build, tag, and push images to a private container registry, run vulnerability scanning, and enforce reproducible builds via locked dependencies and deterministic build args. Deployments will target a managed container platform provided by the chosen cloud (e.g., ECS/Fargate, EKS, AKS, or Cloud Run), enabling clear separation from the host OS and compatibility with PaaS-like services. Runtime configuration will be injected via environment variables and externalized secrets/config stores (e.g., Secrets Manager, Key Vault), not baked into images.

Observability will be standardized via sidecar or agent-based logging/metrics exporters, and health checks will be implemented for readiness/liveness. Rollouts will use blue/green or rolling strategies supported by the orchestrator. VM-centric configuration management (e.g., Puppet/Chef) will not be used for application runtime; it may be retained only for legacy or base infrastructure provisioning where required. This decision enables repeatable builds, portable deployments, and scalable operations across environments.

We will not use feature flags within Storefront SCSS. All SCSS will be compiled unconditionally, and feature toggling will be handled exclusively at the markup/behavior layers.

To support incremental delivery without breaking consumers:
- Breaking changes in SCSS functions, mixins, and variables will be introduced via new, versioned identifiers (e.g., mixin_v2), while retaining existing ones until a scheduled major release. Old identifiers will be marked deprecated and maintained for compatibility.
- Style changes gated by features will be additive and opt-in via markup-driven scope or modifier classes (toggled via Twig/JS). The legacy styles remain in place until removal in a major release.
- Prefer CSS custom properties and BEM-style modifiers to allow coexistence of old and new styling without conditional compilation.
- Avoid relying on “made-up” classes solely for build-time gating; scope classes must reflect semantic/feature state and be applied at runtime by the feature flag.
- Accept that CSS for flagged features will be present but inactive when the corresponding DOM hooks are absent; remove dead CSS only during major cleanup.
- Provide clear deprecation notices and migration guides for theme developers, including timelines for removal.

This policy ensures deterministic builds, avoids brittle SCSS workarounds, and confines feature flag logic to layers that can be toggled at runtime.

Adopt the React Context API to provide the edition value application-wide and eliminate prop drilling of edition-related props. Introduce a strongly typed EditionContext and a top-level EditionProvider that is initialised from server/request data during SSR and passed unchanged through hydration. The context value is read-only for the client lifecycle of a page render and must be treated as immutable; components should consume it via useContext rather than receiving edition as a prop.

Do not introduce an external state-management library (e.g., Redux, MobX) for this use case. Context is sufficient for infrequently changing, app-wide configuration such as edition. We will revisit broader state management only if we encounter cross-cutting, frequently updated client state that cannot be handled with local component state and targeted contexts.

Scope this decision initially to edition only. Keep the context surface minimal and focused; avoid aggregating unrelated concerns into a “global” context. If additional global, low-churn configuration emerges (e.g., region, rendering flags), introduce separate contexts to preserve cohesion.

Implementation guidelines:
- Provide EditionProvider at the application root; memoise the value to avoid unnecessary rerenders.
- Maintain strict TypeScript types for the context value and default fallback to catch misuse at compile time.
- Migrate incrementally: new/updated components should read from context; legacy prop paths may remain temporarily until removed.
- Testing: supply a lightweight test helper and Storybook decorator to wrap components with EditionProvider.

Success is measured by reduced prop drilling, simpler component interfaces, and no hydration mismatches or performance regressions.

Adopt an event-driven, log-centric architecture with CQRS and event sourcing to decouple services, make data portable, and enable extensibility. The immutable event log is the system of record; services publish domain events to a broker and build query-optimized materialized views for consumption. Public data contracts are owned and versioned per domain through a schema registry to support backward/forward compatibility and independent evolution. Where request/response is needed (e.g., UX, partner integrations), provide thin adapters over materialized views and command endpoints rather than synchronous service-to-service calls.

Developer experience is a first-class concern: ship a reference implementation and project template that runs locally with a single command (docker compose up), provisioning broker, schema registry, event store, observability stack, APIs, and a minimal UI. Provide an optional zero-dependency in-memory profile for sub-minute onboarding, plus seed data, replay scripts, and fixtures. Include generators for new domains (events, handlers, projections, contracts) and golden-path documentation with runnable examples.

Operational guardrails are mandatory: schema governance, idempotent consumers, retries with DLQs, trace correlation, deterministic projections, and automated contract tests. Observability (tracing/metrics/logs) is embedded from the start to make distributed flows inspectable and debuggable.

Accepted trade-offs: embrace eventual consistency, increased operational/tooling complexity, and a steeper mental model in exchange for higher evolvability, loose coupling, auditability via replay, and faster feature delivery. To mitigate adoption risk, prioritize frictionless local setup, scaffolding, and clear guidance on modeling, schema evolution, and failure handling.

Decision:
- Split openHAB core into granular OSGi bundles that follow API/SPI/Implementation separation per domain (e.g., org.openhab.core.items.api, org.openhab.core.items.spi, org.openhab.core.items.impl). Stop producing a single “core” jar.
- Export only API/SPI packages; keep all implementation packages private. Disallow exporting .internal packages. Enforce with bnd instructions (Export-Package, -privatepackage) and OSGi Baseline checks.
- Make REST and other adapters depend strictly on API/SPI bundles, not on implementation bundles. Invert dependencies where needed so implementations depend on APIs, never vice versa.
- Introduce fine-grained Karaf features aligned with these bundles (e.g., openhab-core-items-api, openhab-core-items-spi, openhab-core-items-impl, openhab-core-rest-items), and provide optional aggregate features (openhab-core-base, openhab-runtime-base) for convenience only.
- Require extension bundles to depend on the minimal feature(s) they need (typically API/SPI), preventing activation of unrelated framework parts. Use Karaf feature verification to ensure dependency closure.
- Apply build-time enforcement:
  - Maven/bnd to restrict compile classpath to declared API/SPI; forbid impl leakage into API via enforcer rules and revapi/osgi-baseline.
  - Fail the build if public APIs reference implementation types or internal packages.
  - Version and import packages with semantic versioning and proper ranges; use ‘uses’ constraints to preserve class space consistency.
- Migrate existing modules incrementally by carving out API/SPI first, then moving implementations; provide temporary compatibility aggregators only during migration.
- Outcome: decoupled contracts, reduced dependency pollution, smaller transitive graphs for callers, minimal activation for extensions, and clearer, enforceable architectural boundaries.

We will adopt a GOV.UK-wide docs-as-code standard and service catalog to make system understanding self-serve and reduce handover meetings.

- Standardize repository documentation with mandatory files: README (purpose, how to run, how to deploy), Architecture Overview (system context, key flows, dependencies), Runbook (incident procedures, common tasks), Ownership (team, on-call, contact), ADRs (key decisions), and CHANGELOG. Each doc includes a review date and owner.
- Use a central service catalog (e.g., Backstage) as the single pane of glass aggregating metadata from repos: ownership, runtime links, APIs, deployments, health/status, SLOs, dependencies, and docs. All services must be registered.
- Automate freshness and completeness via CI checks: presence of required docs, valid owners, last-reviewed within SLA, status badges, and broken links. Failing checks block merges for critical repos and raise reminders otherwise.
- Adopt a lightweight RFC process in a shared repo for cross-team changes, with async review by default and time-boxed feedback to avoid meetings.
- Provide consistent onboarding packs and rotation checklists generated from the service catalog, ensuring new/rotating team members can self-serve context.
- Make this standard a default for new repos and retrofit high-impact systems first, tracked via the service catalog with visibility on compliance.

We will implement optimistic concurrency control with per-aggregate versioning.

- Each mutable aggregate/entity will have a monotonically increasing Version (integer or rowversion/timestamp). Version is incremented on successful updates within the same transaction.
- All update/delete operations must be conditional: WHERE Id = ? AND Version = ?. If the affected row count is 0, the server treats it as a concurrency conflict.
- The API will surface the Version as an ETag (or explicit version field). Clients must submit updates with If-Match (or the version value). On mismatch, the server returns 409 Conflict (or 412 Precondition Failed).
- Clients handle conflicts by reloading the latest state and reapplying changes; the server will not do “last write wins” merges by default. Domain-specific merge strategies may be introduced case-by-case behind explicit endpoints.
- For read-modify-write flows, the server applies a bounded retry policy for transient conflicts where the operation is pure and safe to retry; otherwise it surfaces the conflict immediately.
- Batch operations use per-item conditional updates; no long-held pessimistic locks. Where necessary, we may use snapshot isolation to reduce read/write contention.
- For event-sourced components, we will enforce expectedVersion on event append to guarantee stream consistency.
- Responses will include the new Version/ETag after successful writes; audit metadata (lastUpdatedAt/by) will be recorded to aid user-facing conflict resolution.
- Idempotency keys will be supported for at-least-once command delivery scenarios to avoid duplicate effects during retries.

Pessimistic locking is avoided except for narrowly scoped administrative maintenance where system-wide blocking is acceptable. This decision provides safe concurrent updates with minimal contention and clear conflict semantics.

We will start with a modular monolith implementing Domain-Driven Design and Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) architecture to prioritize a robust domain model and clear boundaries while deferring premature distribution. Business capabilities will be modeled as Bounded Contexts, each implemented as an isolated module with its own domain model, application services, adapters, and persistence layer abstractions. Cross-context interactions will occur via explicitly defined interfaces and asynchronous domain events to reduce coupling.

The core data model will be relational and normalized, backed by a single transactional database (e.g., PostgreSQL) managed via versioned migrations. Aggregates will encapsulate invariants; repositories will persist aggregates per context. We will use UUIDv7 identifiers, UTC timestamps, optimistic concurrency control, and soft-deletes only where business needs require recoverability; otherwise, hard deletes. Schema evolution will follow backward-compatible changes first, with deprecation windows and automated migration verification in CI.

We will apply CQRS selectively: simple CRUD flows will remain unified; read-optimized projections will be introduced only where justified by performance or UX requirements. Domain events will be raised within aggregates and published through an in-process event bus; outbox pattern will be adopted before introducing external messaging. Event schemas will be versioned and immutable.

External interfaces will be RESTful HTTP APIs with resource-oriented design and explicit versioning; GraphQL or gRPC may be added per consumer needs behind anti-corruption layers. Validation and business rules will live in the domain model; adapters will handle I/O concerns (persistence, messaging, HTTP). Each module will be independently testable, with a focus on domain unit tests and a small set of end-to-end flows.

Code will be organized by bounded context, not by technical layer, with shared kernel kept minimal and stable (cross-cutting types, primitives, and policies). Observability (structured logging with correlation IDs, metrics, traces) will be built in from the start. Security and privacy will be first-class (least privilege, input validation, audit trails).

We will plan for evolutionary decomposition: if a bounded context shows independent scaling, deployment, or ownership needs, it can be extracted into a service with minimal refactoring due to the existing module boundaries and event contracts.

We will standardize error handling across all Ockam Rust crates by adopting a layered, portable error model centered on a core error type and code system.

- Introduce ockam_core::Error as the canonical error, composed of:
  - domain: &'static str identifying the crate/subsystem
  - code: u32 stable numeric code (documented registry)
  - kind: lightweight enum for common categories (InvalidInput, NotFound, Io, Timeout, Internal, Unavailable, PermissionDenied, Canceled, Unsupported, Other)
  - message: optional human-readable message (alloc-enabled)
  - source: optional cause (std/alloc-enabled)
- Provide Result alias: type OckamResult<T> = core::result::Result<T, ockam_core::Error>.

Portability and environments:
- no_std-first design. When std is unavailable:
  - no allocation by default; message is optional &'static str
  - no std::error::Error impl; provide core traits and formatting via core::fmt
- With feature flags (std, alloc, backtrace):
  - implement std::error::Error
  - capture source errors and optional backtrace
  - integrate with anyhow via From<ockam_core::Error> and Try conversions

Ergonomics and agility:
- Derive helpers using thiserror (behind std/alloc) for crate-local error enums; map them to ockam_core::Error via From.
- Provide constructors and macros:
  - err!(domain, code, kind [, "fmt {}", arg])
  - bail!(...) and ensure!(...) convenience macros
  - with_code!/with_kind! helpers for adaption
- Ensure ? works naturally via From conversions from common std/alloc/io/serde errors into ockam_core::Error with appropriate domain/kind.
- Disallow panics for recoverable conditions; prefer returning OckamResult.

Interoperability and stability:
- Maintain a centralized, versioned error code registry to guarantee stable codes across crates and FFI.
- Define an FFI-safe representation (domain id + code + optional static message) for C/other language bindings.
- Provide guidelines for crate authors: define per-crate domain, local ErrorKind if needed, map all public errors to ockam_core::Error, avoid leaking foreign types.

Documentation and testing:
- Document codes and mapping rules; require unit tests for error mapping and no_std compatibility.
- Lint to prevent use of panic! in library code except in impossible conditions with debug_assert!.

We will refactor services into smaller, use‑case–oriented components without introducing a state machine.

- Create action-specific handlers/services per transition (e.g., UpdateDraftIntake, SubmitIntake, DecideIntake), each owning its validation, authorization, and side effects.
- Expose distinct endpoints mapped to each action to make intent, permissions, and auditing explicit:
  - PATCH /system-intakes/{id}/draft
  - POST /system-intakes/{id}/submit
  - POST /system-intakes/{id}/decision
  If routing must remain consolidated temporarily, dispatch to action-specific handlers via explicit command objects and deprecate the monolithic update path.
- Centralize authorization with policy checks per action (e.g., CanUpdateDraft, CanSubmit, CanDecide) and enforce least privilege at the handler boundary.
- Encapsulate side effects behind domain services and publish domain events for cross-cutting behaviors (notifications, analytics), using transactional guarantees where required.
- Encode allowable state transitions in a lightweight, declarative policy/guard registry (transition rules and preconditions) co-located with handlers to ensure consistency and readability without FSM runtime overhead.
- Strengthen testability with unit tests per handler (validation, auth, effects), endpoint contract tests, and policy tests for transition rules.
- Improve observability and security with action-scoped logging, metrics, and audit records tied to the specific handler and outcome.
- Migration plan: maintain backward-compatible behavior for the existing endpoint, add warnings/metrics, document new endpoints, update clients incrementally, and remove the deprecated path after adoption.

This approach achieves clearer boundaries, targeted permissions, and simpler maintenance while avoiding the complexity and coupling of a full state machine.

- Use RESTful resource-oriented design with plural noun paths (e.g., /v1/orders), camelCase fields, and stable IDs.
- API versioning via URI prefix (/v1); breaking changes require new major version. Deprecations signaled via Deprecation and Sunset headers with timeline.
- JSON only for request/response bodies (Content-Type: application/json). Nulls omitted unless semantically required.
- Timestamps in ISO 8601 UTC (e.g., 2026-01-23T12:34:56Z). Monetary and decimal values as strings to avoid precision loss.
- Standard HTTP methods and semantics: GET safe/idempotent, PUT full-replace idempotent, PATCH partial update (JSON Patch or Merge Patch; prefer Merge Patch), POST create/non-idempotent actions, DELETE idempotent. Use 201 with Location on creates.
- Standard status codes: 200/201/202/204 success; 400 validation, 401 auth, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 412 precondition failed, 415/406 negotiation, 422 semantic validation, 429 rate limit, 5xx server.
- Errors use RFC 7807 (application/problem+json) with type, title, status, detail, instance, and machine-readable error codes; include field-level violations array.
- Filtering, sorting, and pagination via query parameters: filter[field]=value, sort=field,-field, page[size], page[number]. Return pagination metadata and HATEOAS-style links (self, next, prev, first, last).
- Concurrency control via ETag/If-Match for update/delete; support GET caching with ETag/Last-Modified.
- Consistent resource expansion via include=related and sparse fieldsets via fields[resource]=a,b.
- Idempotency-Key header required for POST operations that should be idempotent (e.g., payments).
- Observability: include Correlation-Id header echo; log it; return Request-Id in responses.
- Security: OAuth2 Bearer tokens over TLS 1.2+ only; reject plaintext; PII redaction in logs.
- Rate limiting: enforce and communicate via X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset and Retry-After on 429.

## Decision
Adopt S3 Presigned URLs for direct client uploads to S3. The API will expose an authenticated endpoint that validates user permissions and requested file metadata (size, type, intended bucket/key prefix), then issues a short-lived presigned URL (and fields for POST policies when applicable). Clients will upload files directly to S3 using this URL, bypassing the application servers.

Rationale:
- Scalability and performance: removes server as a file data plane bottleneck, reduces latency, and eliminates server CPU/memory pressure for large files.
- Cost efficiency: avoids server egress and bandwidth costs; leverages S3’s optimized ingress path.
- Reliability: supports resumable multipart uploads for large files and client-side retries without impacting API availability.
- Security: upload is constrained by time-limited, scope-limited URL/policy tied to specific bucket/key, content-length, and content-type; API enforces authorization and ownership before issuing URLs.

Implementation notes:
- Provide both single-shot PUT/POST and multipart upload flows; default to multipart for large files (e.g., >50 MB).
- Enforce validations in the signing request: max size, allowed MIME types, key prefixes/namespacing per tenant, server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), content-MD5 if needed, and short expiration (e.g., 5–15 minutes).
- Configure S3 CORS to allow browser uploads from approved origins.
- Return upload metadata (key, etag/parts) and require client to notify completion; optionally verify object existence and size before persisting domain records.
- Provide a server-side fallback endpoint (multipart form) only for legacy or restricted environments and rate-limit it.
- Plan for observability and security: log sign requests, enable S3 access logs/Object Lambda or event-driven scans if malware scanning is required, and handle lifecycle policies/retention.

Adopt a unified, docs-as-code Technical Toolkit with a shared taxonomy, standard templates, and a single source of truth repository to standardize, decentralize, and raise the quality of architectural material.

- Establish a canonical Toolkit model comprising: Principles, Reference Architectures, Patterns, Building Blocks, Implementation Guides, Runbooks, ADRs, Standards, and Compliance Checks, each with required metadata (owner, version, lifecycle, applicability, dependencies).
- Consolidate material into a central monorepo (read-only mirrors allowed) with versioning, changelogs, and deprecation policy; retire/merge duplications.
- Mandate standardized templates and tagging across all architecture spaces; content outside the model or lacking metadata will not be endorsed.
- Implement a lightweight governance and review workflow: proposal via RFC/ADR, peer review by cross-centre maintainers, automated quality gates (linting, link checks, schema validation), and periodic audits.
- Define ownership per artifact (accountable steward, backup) and maintenance SLAs (review at least quarterly); stale items auto-flagged for archival.
- Enable broad contribution via transparent contribution guidelines, issue templates, and open pull requests; appoint “Toolkit Champions” in each delivery centre to seed content, mentor contributors, and drive adoption.
- Integrate the Toolkit into delivery pipelines (checklists, policy-as-code, template scaffolding) to make compliance the path of least resistance.
- Provide onboarding and short-form training; publish usage analytics and quality KPIs to drive continuous improvement.
- Enforce that new initiatives consume from and contribute to the Toolkit as a definition-of-done criterion.

## Decision
Adopt a theming-first design system implemented as framework-agnostic Web Components built with Lit, powered by design tokens and CSS custom properties.

- Implementation: Build UI primitives as Lit-based Web Components to ensure cross-framework reuse (React, Vue, Angular, plain Web) and optimal platform interoperability. Expose all visual styling via CSS variables mapped from design tokens.
- Theming: Establish a single source of truth for tokens (color, typography, spacing, radii, motion, shadows) and generate platform artifacts using Style Dictionary (CSS variables, JSON for apps, optional iOS/Android exports). Support dynamic runtime theme switching and multi-brand strategies via token aliases and theme packages.
- Accessibility: Bake in a11y fundamentals (focus states, contrast-safe palettes, ARIA patterns) at the primitive level; provide sensible defaults per theme.
- Composition: Offer headless behaviors where appropriate and styleable shells via tokens to avoid component-level customization sprawl; encourage composition over overrides.
- Tooling: Document and preview themes and components in Storybook; add visual regression and theme-coverage tests. Provide a token playground and theme switcher.
- Performance: Use Lit’s small runtime, template caching, and scoped styles; leverage tree-shaking and lazy-loading per component. Prefer CSS variables for zero-reflow theme updates.
- Integration: Provide thin adapters for popular frameworks (React wrappers with typed props) without duplicating logic. Publish as versioned packages (tokens, components, adapters).
- Governance: Introduce a token change process with semantic versioning and automated release pipelines to propagate changes safely across platforms.

Rationale: This approach centers on themes rather than per-component customization, maximizes reuse across platforms and stacks, simplifies runtime theming, and reduces long-term maintenance risk while aligning with modern front-end trends.

We will pin the project’s TypeScript version to 3.4.5 to maintain compatibility with the current TypeScript ESLint plugin until an updated plugin supports ≥3.5.0.

Actions:
- Set devDependencies "typescript": "3.4.5" and enforce via package manager resolutions/overrides to prevent accidental upgrades.
- Regenerate lockfile and verify lint, build, and IDE tooling operate correctly with 3.4.5.
- Add a CI guard that fails if TypeScript ≥3.5.0 is installed (e.g., a prelint script checking tsc -v).
- Note the constraint in CONTRIBUTING/README and in engines/peerDependencies as appropriate.
- Track upstream plugin compatibility and schedule an upgrade task; reassess within one release cycle. If a compatible plugin version is not available in a reasonable timeframe, evaluate migrating to a supported @typescript-eslint parser/plugin version or decoupling lint from the compile TypeScript version (e.g., containerized lint environment).
- If any dependency mandates TS ≥3.5.0, prefer isolating lint to TS 3.4.5 (separate toolchain) over raising the project-wide TS version until plugin support lands.

This decision prioritizes a stable linting toolchain with minimal disruption while providing a clear path to upgrade once support is available.

Adopt RFC 3986–compliant URIs as the canonical identifier format for all resources across services, ensuring uniform syntax while preserving extensibility via a hierarchical naming scheme. All externally exposed resources will use the https scheme with an authority under our organizational domain. Paths will model resource hierarchy (collection/item/sub-resource), avoiding file extensions; query parameters are reserved for filtering, pagination, and projection; fragments are not used by servers.

We will enforce normalization rules: scheme and host are lowercase; percent-encoding follows RFC 3986; no superfluous dot-segments; a consistent policy on trailing slashes (collections end with “/”, items do not). Resource identifiers are stable and opaque to clients; internal implementation details are not embedded. For multi-tenant or versioned APIs, version and tenant context appear early in the path (e.g., /v{n}/{tenant}/...), with a migration/deprecation policy.

If custom schemes are required for non-HTTP contexts, they must be registered in a team-maintained scheme catalog, document authority semantics, and conform to URI syntax. All services must validate and generate URIs using shared libraries, and contract tests will verify URI structure, normalization, and reversibility. Documentation must specify allowed characters, reserved parameters, and examples. This decision standardizes interoperability, discoverability, and long-term evolvability of resource identifiers.

We will deprecate and remove GraphQL from Nimbus UI and backend, consolidating all data access on Django REST Framework (DRF).

- Immediately freeze GraphQL: no new features; security fixes only. Publish a deprecation notice and migration guide.
- Build first-class DRF endpoints to cover all current GraphQL use cases with explicit, task-oriented resources. Adopt server-side pagination, filtering, and sorting; avoid over-generic aggregation endpoints.
- Replace Apollo Client with a lightweight REST data layer (e.g., React Query or RTK Query + fetch/axios) and standardize on JSON over HTTP with ETag/Last-Modified for caching.
- Generate and publish an OpenAPI 3 spec from DRF (e.g., drf-spectacular) as the single source of truth for contracts, client generation, and testing.
- Optimize performance: eliminate GraphQL resolver overhead and N+1 queries; use select_related/prefetch_related; add query-level caching where beneficial; enable conditional requests and gzip/br compression.
- Improve maintainability: single API surface (REST) reduces duplicate implementations, tests, and tooling. Establish contract tests against OpenAPI and performance budgets (e.g., p95 endpoint < 300 ms, payloads < 200 KB).
- Migration plan: ship REST endpoints in parallel; adapt UI feature-by-feature to REST; run dual-read (UI configurable) for 1–2 releases; monitor with metrics and logs; remove GraphQL schemas, resolvers, and Apollo once parity and SLOs are met.
- Risk mitigation: keep a minimal read-only GraphQL compatibility layer behind a feature flag during migration; document breaking changes; version REST endpoints (v1) and provide deprecation windows.

Success is defined by reduced latency, lower error rates, simplified code paths, and retirement of graphene-django, graphene, and apollo-client from the dependency graph.

## Decision
Defer architectural selection and solutioning until a concrete context and problem statement are provided. No design, implementation, procurement, or vendor engagement will proceed without a succinct (2–3 sentences) problem definition that includes stakeholders, key constraints, and measurable success criteria. This ADR remains in “Pending Context” status and will be elevated to evaluation only after the requestor supplies the required context. Engineering leaders will enforce a merge gate requiring a linked ADR with an approved context section before any architecture-impacting changes are merged. If context is not provided within the agreed timeframe, this ADR will be closed as “No Decision—Insufficient Context,” and the initiative will be deprioritized. This guardrail minimizes rework, avoids premature optimization, and ensures that any subsequent decision aligns with explicit goals, constraints, and trade-offs defined by stakeholders.

We will explicitly model a single Primary Household Member per household. The data model will add Household.primary_person_id as a foreign key to Person(id), constrained to reference a Person belonging to that Household. This guarantees exactly one designated primary per household (once populated) and removes ambiguity compared to list-only representations.

Key rules and behaviors:
- Uniqueness: Only one primary per household; enforced by FK plus membership validation.
- Lifecycle:
  - Creation: primary_person_id may be null until at least one member exists; must be set before household submission or routing.
  - Deletion/Move: if the primary person is removed from the household, a new primary must be selected transactionally; operations removing the primary will fail unless a replacement is provided in the same request.
  - Merge/Split: merging households triggers a required selection of a single primary in the resulting household; splitting preserves the primary in the originating household and requires selection in the new one.
- API: expose GET/PUT /households/{id}/primary-person to retrieve/set; include primary_person_id in household payloads; Person includes computed is_primary for convenience.
- Routing: routing engine uses primary_person_id to apply primary-specific flows; non-primary members follow existing paths.
- Validation: server-side checks ensure the referenced person belongs to the household; audit log records all changes (who/when/old/new).
- Migration/rollout: add nullable column, backfill using deterministic rule (e.g., earliest added adult or first member), then enforce NOT NULL for active households. Provide admin tooling to resolve exceptions.
- Events: emit PrimaryPersonChanged for downstream synchronization.

This decision maintains backward compatibility while enabling unambiguous identification and differential routing of the primary person.

Adopt BlazeMeter Taurus as the standard framework to author, run, and orchestrate performance and benchmarking tests for the cluster.

- Author tests in Taurus YAML, primarily targeting JMeter as the load engine; optionally integrate Selenium for end-to-end/browser scenarios. Store all test specs, data files, and artifacts under version control in the performance repo.
- Provide a Dockerized Taurus execution environment to ensure reproducibility across developers, CI, and ephemeral runners. Default images include JMeter and Selenium drivers as needed.
- Integrate with CI/CD: run lightweight smoke performance tests on pull requests; execute full benchmark suites on scheduled runs and on release candidates. Gate merges/releases via Taurus pass/fail criteria (SLAs/thresholds for latency, error rate, throughput).
- Standardize outputs and artifact retention: JMeter JMX (generated), JTL/CSV/JSON metrics, Taurus consolidated reports, and JUnit/XML for CI visibility. Publish artifacts to centralized storage and surface key metrics/dashboards; ensure compatibility for import into JMeter and analysis in Jupyter/other tools.
- Enable scalable load generation by distributing Taurus runs across multiple executors/nodes when higher throughput is required; document patterns for horizontal scaling and environment provisioning.
- Establish configuration conventions: environment-specific variables injected via CI and environment files; secrets supplied through vault/CI secret stores (never committed). Use tagged datasets and deterministic seeds where applicable for reproducibility.
- Provide a baseline library of reusable scenarios (login, read/write, long-running, spike, soak, stress) and shared include files for headers, correlations, and common assertions.
- Maintain versioned SLAs per service/component, reviewed periodically and adjusted based on capacity planning.
- Allow exceptions for direct JMeter authoring only when necessary; such tests must still be runnable via Taurus and adhere to artifact/CI standards.

This decision standardizes on Taurus to simplify setup, improve repeatability, enable multi-tool orchestration, and streamline reporting/analysis while preserving compatibility with JMeter and downstream data tools.

- Adopt a new type system hierarchy: retain Type, Command, and State as interfaces; introduce AbstractBaseType as the single superclass for all concrete Types to enable extensibility and uniform metadata (e.g., security context, source, priority).
- Remove ComplexType and PrimitiveType from the public model to reduce complexity and avoid ambiguous semantics.
- Replace reliance on java.lang.Number with a new NumberType base class that extends AbstractBaseType. DecimalType, QuantityType, and other numeric types will extend NumberType. All framework numeric checks must use instanceof NumberType (not instanceof Number).
- Refactor enum-based Types (e.g., OnOffType, UpDownType) into final classes extending AbstractBaseType while preserving their public constants and semantics via static instances and valueOf/parse APIs. Ensure equals/hashCode/toString remain stable to preserve behavior.
- Maintain backward compatibility at the interface level: existing bindings using Type/Command/State continue to compile. Provide adapters and deprecations where necessary (e.g., bridge helpers for code paths that previously depended on enum identity or java.lang.Number).
- Prohibit framework-level wrappers around Command/State for metadata; instead, embed extensible metadata capabilities into AbstractBaseType (and/or attach immutable typed attributes) to support advanced features without core rework.
- Provide a migration guide and tooling:
  - Replace instanceof Number with instanceof NumberType.
  - Replace enum identity checks with equals or explicit predicate methods.
  - Use factory/valueOf methods for constructing Types instead of enum literals.
- Versioning and rollout: introduce changes in a major release with a compatibility layer and deprecations over at least one cycle; add compile-time checks and runtime warnings for deprecated patterns.
- Testing and serialization: ensure binary and wire compatibility for type names and serialized forms; add conformance tests for equality, ordering, serialization, and metadata propagation across all Types.

We will request storage access using the platform-recommended flow to avoid always showing an explanation dialog on first request:

- On upload attempt, check permission. If granted, proceed with upload.
- If not granted:
  - If ActivityCompat.shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(...) returns true, show a non-blocking rationale (dialog/sheet) explaining why access is needed, then request permission.
  - If shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(...) returns false:
    - If this is the first request for this permission, request permission directly without showing a rationale.
    - If we have previously requested and the user denied with “Don’t ask again” or policy prohibits, do not show the system request. Instead, present a dialog explaining the need and provide a deep link to App Settings to enable the permission.
- We will persist “hasRequestedReadStorageOnce” (boolean) in SharedPreferences to distinguish first request from post-denial cases.
- We will adopt the Activity Result API (registerForActivityResult with RequestPermission/RequestMultiplePermissions) rather than onRequestPermissionsResult for clearer lifecycle handling.
- Platform targeting:
  - API 33+: request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES/READ_MEDIA_VIDEO/READ_MEDIA_AUDIO as applicable instead of READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE.
  - API 29–32: use READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE.
  - For scoped access alternatives (e.g., user-picked files via SAF/MediaPicker), prefer picker flows that do not require broad permissions when product requirements allow; otherwise follow the above permission flow.
- UX specifics:
  - Rationale appears only when shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(...) is true.
  - Settings-redirect dialog appears when permission is required but shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(...) is false and hasRequestedReadStorageOnce is true.
  - All dialogs are asynchronous and do not block the UI thread; upload is resumed automatically after grant.

This approach ensures the system permission prompt is shown on first request, prevents unnecessary rationale on first run, handles “Don’t ask again” gracefully, and aligns with modern Android permission models.

We will integrate ORCID as an external identity provider via a centralized Auth Gateway that brokers OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code with PKCE for all applications (e.g., Journal). Applications will not manage ORCID client secrets; they will redirect to the Auth Gateway, which will handle the authorization code exchange, enforce state, PKCE, and CSRF protections, and return a signed first-party JWT to applications containing the user’s subject, ORCID iD, and required claims.

The Auth Gateway will request only minimal scopes needed for authentication (e.g., ORCID iD, verified email where permissible) and will store access/refresh tokens encrypted and scoped per user/provider, with rotation and revocation support. ORCID profile retrieval will be performed server-side and normalized.

To support future data combination, we will introduce a canonical Person aggregate with linked ExternalIdentity records (provider, subject/id, scopes, tokens metadata, claims snapshot). Domain data (e.g., affiliations, works) will be mapped into a provider-agnostic schema and versioned. Account linking will be supported by: (1) deterministic linking via verified email or ORCID iD when safe; (2) user-driven linking flows when ambiguity exists.

The Auth Gateway will expose a normalized userinfo endpoint and publish standardized identity events for downstream services. Data refresh will be via scheduled sync and/or provider webhooks, with idempotent upserts. All operations will be audited.

This design isolates provider specifics, enables multi-source aggregation later (additional providers plug into the same interface), keeps applications simple and consistent, and adheres to least-privilege and security best practices.

We will decommission the Discourse forum and consolidate user support and discussion into Slack and the documentation site.

Actions:
- Retire the Discourse infrastructure (application, database, object storage, backups, monitoring) and remove it from the platform’s operational scope and cost center.
- Export and archive the Discourse content (full site backup) and retain it in secure storage for 12 months for reference/compliance; delete thereafter per data retention policy.
- Migrate any valuable knowledge (FAQs, how‑tos) from Discourse into the documentation site, preserving URLs where feasible.
- Implement permanent redirects from forum URLs/domains to the documentation landing page or support overview.
- Update onboarding, website, in‑app links, and runbooks to point users to Slack channels and documentation for support.
- Define and publish Slack support guidelines (channels, hours, escalation paths) and add a lightweight “request help/feedback” entry point from the docs.
- Monitor support load and satisfaction via Slack analytics and doc feedback to ensure no degradation in user experience.
- Reassess the need for an async forum if requirements change (e.g., increased external/community participation or need for threaded, searchable discussions) and be prepared to reintroduce a forum solution if justified.

We will expose the cluster’s Ingress controller (nginx-ingress by default; Ambassador as an alternative) via a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer, terminating TLS at the Ingress controller and managing certificates with cert-manager.

- Cloud deployments: Use the cloud provider’s managed L4 load balancer (e.g., AWS NLB/ELB, Azure Load Balancer, GCP Load Balancer) to forward TCP 80/443 to the Service. The LB performs only TCP forwarding; TLS is terminated by the Ingress controller. Health checks target the standard readiness path. HTTP (80) is enabled solely for HTTP→HTTPS redirects.

- Bare-metal/on-prem: Provide the external virtual IP via MetalLB (L2/BGP) or an external HA pair (e.g., HAProxy/Keepalived) forwarding TCP 80/443 to the Service’s NodePorts. The Ingress controller remains the TLS termination point.

- Security/compliance: Only 80/443 are exposed publicly; 80 redirects to 443 and HSTS is enforced. Certificates are provisioned/rotated by cert-manager per Ingress. Optionally support TLS passthrough or mTLS per service as policy requires. Network policies and firewall rules restrict access to the Ingress namespace/pods.

This approach standardizes the traffic path as: External L4 LB/VIP -> Kubernetes Service (LoadBalancer/NodePort) -> Ingress controller -> backend Services, satisfying encryption-at-rest-in-transit requirements while remaining portable across environments.

We will distribute the template as a LaTeX class (.cls) via CTAN as the primary channel. The class abstraction matches a document template’s purpose (layout, structure, defaults) and enables users to adopt it via \documentclass with automatic availability through TeX Live/MiKTeX package managers. The CTAN release will include a properly documented .dtx/.ins source, example documents, and a .cls artifact, follow semantic versioning, and provide a clear changelog. Source code, issue tracking, and development releases will be maintained on GitHub, with tagged releases mirrored as convenience ZIPs, but CTAN remains the authoritative distribution for end users.

Adopt a flexible RDF export that (1) reuses established vocabularies (CIDOC CRM/FRBRoo where applicable, plus Dublin Core and PROV-O for metadata and provenance), and (2) introduces a versioned, SDBM-owned namespace for interim terms needed until the MMM unified model is finalized. Implement the export through a configurable mapping layer (SPARQL CONSTRUCT/R2RML-style templates) that translates the SDBM internal schema to RDF, with mappings externalized and version-controlled to allow rapid iteration and future replacement when the MMM model is agreed.

Publish persistent HTTP URIs for core resources (manuscripts, agents, places, works, events), with stable identifier policy and content-negotiation. Provide JSON-LD as the primary serialization and Turtle as an alternative. Include record- and dataset-level provenance (generation time, software and mapping versions, data snapshot identifiers) and explicit links to source records. Partition outputs by named graph per dataset release to support re-ingestion and diffing.

Deliver two artifacts per release: (a) the RDF dump and (b) the mapping specification/application profile documenting term usage and equivalences to MMM/CIDOC CRM. Commit to maintaining backward compatibility for published URIs and to deprecating interim SDBM terms via owl:equivalentClass/Property and owl:deprecated once the unified MMM model is adopted.

We will require a file attachment at the time of record creation and restrict record creation to authenticated users with the appropriate role.

- The backend will enforce a non-null file_reference on record creation; records without an attached file cannot be persisted.
- Record creation will follow a two-phase flow: (1) request upload URL, upload file, receive file_reference; (2) submit record metadata with file_reference to finalize creation. The API will reject finalization without a valid file_reference.
- The UI will prevent submission until the file upload completes and will display validation for file type/size constraints.
- We will use pre-signed uploads to object storage, with server-side validation of content type/size and virus scanning where available. Failed or abandoned uploads will be auto-expired and cleaned up.
- Access control: only authenticated users with create permission can initiate and finalize records. Anonymous record creation is disabled.
- Schema change: make file_reference required, add indexes/constraints to ensure referential integrity.
- Existing metadata-only records will be flagged as incomplete; owners will be prompted to attach a file within a defined grace period. After the grace period, incomplete records will be archived or deleted per retention policy.
- Telemetry and alerts will be added for upload failures and rejected creations to monitor impact post-deployment.

We will maintain a single mono-repo that contains both production code and end-to-end tests as the system’s source of truth, and establish a one-way, read-only public mirror for community collaboration.

- The internal mono-repo remains the authoritative repository. All development occurs there, with branch protections, CODEOWNERS, and full CI (including e2e) enforced.
- A CI-driven mirroring pipeline will publish a curated subset of the mono-repo to the public mirror. Only approved paths are mirrored; proprietary assets, secrets, internal tooling, and compliance-restricted content are excluded via allowlist filters. History is preserved; tags and release artifacts are mirrored post-compliance checks.
- Mirroring is triggered on merges to the default branch and on tagged releases after license scanning, secret detection, and SBOM generation pass.
- The public mirror is read-only with respect to direct pushes; community contributions flow via forks and pull requests against the mirror.
- A bot-based bridge will ingest approved community PRs from the mirror into the internal mono-repo as canonical PRs, preserving authorship metadata. These PRs must pass the full internal CI (including e2e) and owner reviews before merge.
- Upon merge in the internal mono-repo, changes are propagated back to the public mirror on the next mirroring cycle, ensuring community visibility and a single consistent history.
- Security hardening includes signed commits/tags on internal and mirrored releases, mandatory DCO/CLA checks on the public mirror, and automated license policy enforcement.
- Issue tracking remains internal for sensitive topics; the public mirror tracks community-facing issues and discussions. We will link issues across systems where appropriate.
- We will document contribution guidelines, path ownership, and the synchronization cadence in both repositories to set clear expectations.

This approach preserves a single trusted codebase with comprehensive testing while enabling safe, transparent community engagement through a controlled mirror.

We will adopt environment-variable–based proxy configuration for all outbound network traffic and subprocess execution. Specifically:
- Recognize and support http_proxy, https_proxy, and no_proxy environment variables as the primary configuration mechanism.
- Accept both lowercase and uppercase variants (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY); if both are provided, the lowercase variant takes precedence and will be used internally. Values are treated case-insensitively for keys, not values.
- Propagate the effective proxy-related environment variables to all child processes (e.g., tools invoked by the runner) without modification, unless explicitly overridden per-invocation.
- Honor no_proxy semantics using a comma-separated list of hosts, domains (leading dot implies domain-wide), IPs, and CIDR ranges. Localhost and loopback addresses are not implicitly exempt; exemption must be specified via no_proxy as needed.
- Do not introduce additional CLI flags or config-file options for proxies in this iteration; environment variables are the single source of truth. We may revisit richer configuration if enterprise demand emerges.
- Do not log proxy values; redact credentials in diagnostics. Never persist proxy credentials.
- Defer to underlying HTTP libraries’ standard proxy handling where available; otherwise, implement minimal resolution logic that respects the above rules.
- Document precedence, examples, and security guidance (including credential embedding formats, e.g., http://user:pass@host:port) and provide troubleshooting steps.

This decision aligns with common industry practice, minimizes configuration burden for enterprises already using these conventions, and ensures compatibility with widely used tooling.

Adopt automated, workspace-based versioning and release management for all Origin SDK packages to eliminate manual dependency updates. Consolidate all packages in a monorepo with pnpm workspaces and declare all internal dependencies using the workspace protocol (e.g., "workspace:^" ranges). Introduce Changesets for independent package versioning and changelog generation, enabling automatic propagation of version bumps to dependents based on semver impact. Configure Changesets to:
- Detect dependency changes and bump dependents accordingly (major -> at least minor/major as required; minor -> dependent patch/minor when API surface is consumed; patch -> no dependent bump unless types/peer contracts are affected).
- Generate a versioning PR that updates package versions, internal dependency ranges, changelogs, tags, and publishes artifacts.

Integrate this flow in CI:
- On merge of changesets: compute affected graph, run build/test for impacted packages only (Nx/Turborepo optional), apply versioning with Changesets, publish to the registry, and push tags.
- Protect main with required checks and enforce changeset entries for any public-facing change.

Standardize dependency policies:
- Internal deps: "workspace:^" with no hard-pinned versions.
- External deps: caret or tilde per policy; peers declared explicitly where appropriate.

This decision ensures consistent, automated dependency updates across the SDK, reduces human error, shortens release cycles, and maintains clear traceability via generated changelogs and tags.

We will standardize all Shopware events around a canonical, versioned event contract to ensure consistency, predictability, and backward compatibility.

- Adopt a base EventEnvelope (interface + final implementation) required for all new and revised events, containing:
  - eventName (domain.resource.action.vX)
  - version (semantic, tied to payload schema)
  - occurredAt (UTC ISO-8601)
  - eventId (UUID, idempotency key)
  - correlationId / causationId
  - tenant/shop/context (sales channel, language, currency)
  - actor (user/system/app) and origin (service/component)
  - metadata (string→string map for non-critical extensions)

- Define a payload contract per event as a strongly-typed, immutable DTO with:
  - Required fields explicitly defined and documented
  - Optional fields nullable and documented with defaults
  - No mixed/array-of-mixed; use typed collections
  - Referential identifiers (UUIDs) instead of entire aggregates unless explicitly justified

- Establish domain event catalogs with curated namespaces and naming:
  - Domain: Sales, Product, Order, Customer, Inventory, Catalog, Payment, Shipping, System
  - Name format: Domain.Resource.Action (e.g., Order.Payment.Captured)
  - Topics/dispatch names mirror eventName; version suffix (v1, v2, …) on breaking changes only

- Enforce validation at dispatch time via Symfony Validator; events failing validation do not dispatch. Provide factory methods/builders to avoid invalid construction.

- Introduce PHP interfaces (EventEnvelopeInterface, DomainEventInterface) and abstract base classes to enforce required data and typing. Add a light ExtensionBag for controlled extensibility.

- Provide BC strategy:
  - Freeze legacy events; mark deprecated with end-of-life dates
  - Emit both legacy and canonical events during transition (adapters)
  - Document migration guides and mapping tables

- Tooling and governance:
  - Add event schema docs generated from PHP attributes
  - Add static checks/lints in CI for naming, versioning, typing, and required fields
  - Require “Event Contract Review” in PRs that add/modify events

This decision unifies event structure across domains while allowing domain-specific payloads, enabling safer integrations and evolvable contracts.

Adopt hashicorp/go-metrics as the unified telemetry abstraction for the Cosmos SDK and application modules. Telemetry is disabled by default; when enabled, metrics are recorded via a no-op to active sink switch to ensure negligible overhead when off.

Implement a fan-out MetricsProvider that supports multiple concurrently configured sinks:
- Built-in in-memory sink as the default when telemetry is enabled.
- Optional Prometheus sink as the first external sink, selected via configuration.

Expose metrics via the API server at /metrics?format={text|prometheus}. The endpoint returns the in-memory text format by default and Prometheus exposition format when requested and configured. The endpoint is read-only; exposure scope (bind address, TLS, and auth) is governed by existing API server controls.

Standardize metric usage across modules by:
- Requiring modules to depend only on go-metrics interfaces (counters, gauges, histograms, timers) with no direct Prometheus client usage.
- Providing a lightweight SDK helper to register module-scoped metric sets and common tags (e.g., module, chain_id, version).
- Enforcing conventions to limit cardinality (bounded label values, no unbounded user input) and providing configurable histogram buckets.

Configuration options include:
- enable: boolean (default false)
- sinks: list [inmem (default when enabled), prometheus]
- global_tags: map[string]string (e.g., chain_id)
- sampling_rate / percentiles for timers and histograms
- in-memory retention/window and max series limits
- prometheus-specific settings (scrape path, namespace/prefix)

Backwards compatible integration ensures existing modules can adopt metrics incrementally with minimal friction. Future sinks (e.g., StatsD, OTLP) can be added by implementing the sink interface and registering via configuration.

We will license all first-party source code under the Apache License, Version 2.0. This permissive license enables broad adoption (including commercial use), encourages contributions, and provides an explicit patent grant and patent termination provisions that protect users and contributors while minimizing friction for organizations with IP policies.

Project documentation, guides, and non-code content will be licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) to enable reuse with attribution. Project branding assets (name, logo) will be reserved under a separate trademark policy and not covered by the open-source license.

All inbound contributions will be made under the same outbound licenses. We will require a Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) sign-off on all commits instead of a CLA to reduce contributor friction while maintaining clear provenance. The repository will include LICENSE, NOTICE, and CONTRIBUTING files, standardized source headers, and a clear trademark policy.

Third-party dependencies will retain their original licenses; we will avoid copyleft-licensed dependencies that impose reciprocal obligations on the project as a whole, unless isolated and compliant. Any exceptions require approval via the governance process.

This licensing approach is intended to maximize community and industry participation, simplify redistribution, and set clear expectations for use, modification, and warranty disclaimers.

We will make asynchronous operations testable and deterministic by exposing explicit completion signals and prohibiting bare sleeps.

- Every asynchronous command must return a correlation/job ID that is propagated through all downstream work.
- The system will publish a domain “completion” event (success/failure) with that ID on the event bus when processing finishes. Events must be emitted exactly-once or deduplicatable (idempotent) and include sufficient context for diagnostics.
- In addition, each job ID must be queryable via a status/read-model endpoint to provide a polling-based fallback (e.g., PENDING, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED) with last-updated timestamps and error details.
- The test harness will include a WaitUntil/Eventually utility that:
  - Subscribes to the event stream and awaits the matching completion event, or
  - Polls the status endpoint with bounded timeouts, exponential backoff, and jitter.
  - Fails with clear diagnostics if the timeout is exceeded or a failure status is observed.
- We will ban Thread.sleep and similar fixed waits in tests and production readiness checks; code reviews and linters will enforce this.
- Definition of Done: any new async flow must (a) propagate correlation IDs, (b) publish completion events, (c) update the status/read model, and (d) include tests that await completion via the utility.
- Observability: logs and traces must include the correlation ID; metrics will track job durations and outcomes to aid debugging and flakiness triage.

This approach provides deterministic synchronization, reduces test flakiness, and yields actionable failure signals without relying on nondeterministic timing.

We will standardize all React applications in a single repository using npm Workspaces and a canonical directory structure. Each application will live under apps/<app-name> and conform to the following layout: src/, public/, tests/unit/, tests/e2e/, config/ (env, build, lint), scripts/, and README.md. Shared code, tooling, and configuration will live under packages/ (e.g., packages/ui, packages/config-eslint, packages/tsconfig, packages/testing).

We will adopt Vite for new apps and migrations, with a common Vite config package consumed by all apps. TypeScript is required; tsconfig extends from packages/tsconfig. ESLint, Prettier, and Stylelint configs are centralized in packages/config-* and consumed via root-level .eslintrc.cjs/.prettierrc.js that extend the shared packages. Path aliases and testing setup are standardized across apps.

We will use npm (not Yarn) as the package manager:
- Rationale: first-class Node support, simpler CI/CD, broad ecosystem compatibility, and reduced tooling friction. We will use npm@>=10 with lockfileVersion 3 and enforce via the packageManager field, .npmrc, and CI checks. Workspaces enable hoisting, shared scripts, and deterministic installs without Yarn-specific features.

Enforcement and scaffolding:
- Provide a plop/generator script (or Hygen) to scaffold new apps and packages to the exact structure.
- Add a validate-structure script (Node) to check required files/folders and config inheritance; run in CI.
- Enforce consistent scripts in each app (dev, build, test, lint, typecheck, preview).
- Use lint-staged and Husky to guard formatting and lint on commit; run full validation in PR CI.
- CODEOWNERS and required reviews for changes under packages/config-*.

Repository layout:
- apps/*: individual React apps.
- packages/*: shared libraries and tooling configs.
- .github/workflows: CI with matrix builds per app plus affected-only builds using workspace filters.
- docs/: standards and migration guides.

Migration: New apps must follow this structure immediately. Existing apps will be migrated incrementally with templates and CI enforcement enabled after each app adopts the shared configs.

Adopt the Python scientific stack (NumPy + SciPy) as the authoritative statistics/algorithms engine and Matplotlib as the canonical plotting reference, exposed behind a thin service/API consumed by the existing GUI. For interactive client-side plots, mirror visuals with Plotly (using server-produced canonical data/series) to retain a consistent visual vocabulary while decoupling correctness from rendering.

Rationale for selection centers on algorithmic correctness: SciPy/NumPy provide mature, well-vetted, numerically stable implementations with extensive test coverage and reproducible behavior in double precision. Matplotlib serves as the baseline rendering to verify numerical outputs and chart semantics independent of client interactivity. The service boundary enforces a single source of truth for computations, enabling deterministic runs, version pinning, and traceable results.

Implementation decisions:
- Pin NumPy/SciPy/Matplotlib versions and record exact build metadata for reproducibility.
- Add property-based and golden-master tests that compare library outputs against published references and synthetic invariants.
- Use strict input validation and explicit dtypes to avoid implicit casting and platform variance.
- Emit computation metadata (algorithm, parameters, seed, versions) alongside results to the GUI for auditability.
- Where client-side plotting differs, validate against Matplotlib-rendered baselines in CI.
- For any algorithm not covered by SciPy, defer to StatsModels or scikit-learn; if unavailable, implement with reference tests against R or academic datasets.

This decision prioritizes correctness and verifiability while keeping the GUI responsive and implementation portable.

Adopt a stable, namespaced module entry point for Core JavaScript components and prohibit deep relative imports. Core components will be packaged and exposed as an npm-consumable package (e.g., @core/components) with proper exports and semantic versioning. Modules must import via this package or via a configured module alias resolving to the same source in development/monorepo setups.

Key elements:
- Publish Core components as an npm package with ESM (and CJS if needed) builds, tree-shaking, and type definitions where applicable.
- Provide a bundler-agnostic alias (e.g., @core/components) configured in webpack/vite/rollup resolve.alias and tsconfig/jsconfig paths for local development to avoid brittle relative paths.
- Update all imports to absolute form:
  import { TranslatableInput } from '@core/components/translatable-input';
- Add ESLint rule/custom lint to forbid ../../-style imports into Core internals.
- Maintain a short deprecation window with a compatibility alias; remove deep import paths afterward.
- Version and distribute via package registry; in monorepo/CI use workspaces/lockfiles to ensure deterministic resolution; in containers/symlinked environments rely on module resolution instead of filesystem depth.
- Document the public API surface and change management; breaking changes require a major version.

This decision ensures robust imports across CI/CD, symlinked, and containerized environments and decouples modules from Core’s directory layout.

Adopt Docker named volumes for directories with high I/O churn that developers do not edit (at minimum node_modules and tmp) and mount them inside containers instead of reading from the macOS bind-mounted workspace. This removes these paths from the slow shared mount and leverages the faster container filesystem, significantly improving Sassc/asset pipeline performance on macOS.

Implementation:
- For each app in GOV.UK Docker, define named volumes (e.g., appname_node_modules, appname_tmp) in docker-compose and mount them at /app/node_modules and /app/tmp.
- Ensure container entrypoints/scripts install dependencies into the volume when lockfiles change (e.g., run yarn install or npm ci if node_modules is empty or if checksums differ).
- Provide make/tasks to reset volumes (e.g., make clean-node-modules, make clean-tmp) to handle corruption or major dependency changes.
- Keep application source code on the standard bind mount to preserve live-edit workflows.

We will not adopt NFS-based shared mounts or docker-sync: both add setup complexity, platform variance, and ongoing maintenance burden for contributors, and they do not target the specific high-churn paths as effectively as volumes.

This decision is transparent to Linux users (who are not impacted by macOS bind-mount performance) and improves the first-run and iterative build times on macOS without changing developer workflows or requiring host-level configuration.

Adopt Google Cloud Storage (GCS) as the primary image storage backend and decommission the self-managed Cassandra cluster.

- Store images as objects in GCS with deterministic object keys (e.g., bucket/<namespace>/<imageId>) and persist the GCS URI in Elasticsearch documents for retrieval.
- Use Multi-Region or Dual-Region buckets for high availability; enable object versioning and lifecycle rules (transition to Nearline/Coldline/Archive based on access patterns) to optimize cost.
- Serve images via signed URLs; front with Cloud CDN for low latency and reduced egress; enable CMEK encryption and enforce restricted access (IAM + VPC-SC).
- Leverage GCS autoscaling and managed operations to achieve real-time scalability without manual node management or capacity planning.
- Implement a thin storage abstraction in the service layer to encapsulate GCS operations (upload, get, delete, signed URL generation), enabling future portability.
- Migration plan:
  - Export images from Cassandra and bulk upload to GCS using parallelized tooling (gsutil/Storage Transfer Service).
  - Backfill ES records with GCS URIs; run a dual-read period (GCS primary, Cassandra fallback) with observability.
  - Validate integrity (checksums, counts), then finalize cutover and decommission Cassandra after retention window.
- Observability and SLOs:
  - Monitor latency, error rates, egress, and cache hit ratios; set availability SLO aligned with GCS/Cloud CDN SLAs.
  - Implement retries and idempotent uploads; enforce content-length and checksum validation.
- Security and compliance:
  - Private buckets by default; signed URL expiry policy; audit logging; lifecycle/delete policies aligned with data retention requirements.

This decision reduces operational burden, improves elasticity and availability, and better matches our current access pattern (object retrieval only).
