A central Lifecycle Orchestrator interprets LDL definitions and enforces transitions in an event-driven manner, decoupled from domain logic.

Key aspects:
- Versioned lifecycle schemas stored in a registry; resource instances bind to a specific lifecycle version at creation.
- Transitions are triggered by domain events, scheduled timers, or explicit API calls, with policy-based authorization, guard evaluation, and idempotent execution.
- Side effects are executed via pluggable action handlers per domain, keeping lifecycle semantics abstract while enabling use-case-specific behavior.
- State is persisted with the resource as first-class metadata, with complete auditing (who/what/when/why), metrics, and tracing.
- Validation ensures only LDL-compliant lifecycles are deployed; static analysis detects dead states, unreachable transitions, and missing handlers.
- Backward-compatible evolution is supported through versioning and controlled migration strategies (opt-in per instance, bulk migration jobs, or aliasing).
- Default lifecycles are provided per archetype, but tenants can override or extend via configuration within guardrails.
- Failure handling includes retries, compensations, and quarantine states; time-based SLAs can escalate or auto-transition.
- Access control integrates with platform RBAC/ABAC, scoped by state and transition.

This decision separates lifecycle semantics from implementation, enabling consistent, auditable, and reusable resource lifecycles across heterogeneous use cases while preserving extensibility and policy control.

Decision: Adopt a vertical micro-frontends architecture, with one micro-frontend per business domain, loaded per page and owned by a single team. A container “shell” application will provide global concerns (authentication, authorization, routing, navigation, header/footer, layout, error boundaries) and orchestrate which micro-frontend renders for a given route.

Integration will be performed at runtime using Webpack Module Federation (or equivalent), with each micro-frontend exposed as a remote module. The shell will declare React, React Router, the design system, and other common libraries (analytics, auth SDK) as singletons to avoid duplication and ensure consistency. Micro-frontends will be independently built and deployed, versioned, and registered in an environment-specific manifest consumed by the shell.

UX consistency will be enforced through a shared design system and component library published as a versioned package; deviations require architectural review. Cross-micro-frontend communication will use a minimal, documented contract: shell-managed client-side routing for navigation, and a typed, namespaced event bus for loosely-coupled interactions. Shared state is prohibited across micro-frontends; data sharing occurs via backend APIs. Direct DOM manipulation across boundaries is not allowed.

Performance will be addressed via route-based code splitting, lazy loading, prefetching of high-traffic domains, and caching of remotes. Accessibility, security, and observability are mandatory: WCAG-compliant components, centralized auth in the shell, CSP and permission boundaries, standardized logging/metrics/tracing, and feature flags.

Migration from the current deep-link approach will be incremental: map existing pages to shell routes, wrap legacy apps as transitional remotes where feasible, and progressively replace with domain micro-frontends. Continuous delivery pipelines will support independent releases with contract tests and canary deployments.

## Decision
Adopt a layered, renderer-agnostic architecture centered on a canonical ADR Domain Model to maximize adr-viewer usability while preserving flexibility for additional output formats.

- Define a stable ADR Domain Model (versioned JSON schema) produced from CommonMark ADRs with YAML front matter and conventional headings. Implement an adr-core library that parses, normalizes, enriches (linking, status, supersedes), and exposes this model.
- Establish explicit extension points:
  - DataSource interface (filesystem, Git, HTTP, mixed) returning the Domain Model.
  - Renderer interface consuming the Domain Model to produce outputs (static HTML, SPA, CLI, live web server).
  - Plugin hooks for metadata enrichers (e.g., cross-references, tags) and link resolvers.
- Deliver adr-viewer as the default Renderer with top-tier usability: accessible, responsive UI; full-text search; filters (status, tags, date); deep linking; permalinks; keyboard navigation; and theming via design tokens/CSS variables.
- Keep the UI framework-agnostic by using Web Components and progressive enhancement over pre-rendered HTML templates. Support both:
  - Static export (SSG/prerender) for zero-runtime hosting.
  - Optional hydration for richer interactions in the browser.
- Provide an HTTP API adapter exposing the Domain Model (read-only JSON) to enable a live web server and future integrations.
- Version and document the Domain Model and Renderer contracts; maintain backward compatibility via adapters and deprecation policy.
- Package as a CLI with subcommands (build, serve, validate) and as libraries for embedding.

We will provide PersistentVolumeClaims in storage-less clouds by bundling an in-cluster, CSI-compliant, open-source storage backend by default: Rook-Ceph.

- Deploy Rook-Ceph operator and Ceph-CSI in every cluster lacking a suitable cloud storage CSI. Use node labels/taints to dedicate storage nodes and local disks to Ceph OSDs.
- Expose two default StorageClasses:
  - csi-ceph-rbd (default): ReadWriteOnce block volumes for stateful workloads.
  - csi-cephfs: ReadWriteMany file shares for multi-pod access.
- Configure pools with:
  - Replication factor ≥3 (or erasure coding when appropriate) across failure domains (rack/zone) for durability.
  - At-rest encryption via dm-crypt/LUKS and in-transit encryption with Ceph mTLS.
  - Quotas and per-tenant namespaces for multi-tenancy isolation.
- Integrate with Kubernetes primitives:
  - Dynamic provisioning, snapshots, and cloning via CSI.
  - StorageClass parameters enforced via admission policy; resource requests/limits and PVC quotas per namespace.
- Operations and compliance:
  - Monitoring and alerting via Ceph Dashboard, Prometheus, and alerts integrated into cluster SLOs.
  - Day-2 ops (scaling, upgrades, rebalancing) automated through Rook.
  - Backup/DR via Velero to S3-compatible object storage using CSI snapshots and periodic volume backups; documented restore procedures.
  - Auditability through Kubernetes and Ceph logs; regular health checks and disaster-recovery runbooks.
- Fallbacks:
  - Where disks are unavailable or footprint must be minimal, optionally support Longhorn or OpenEBS-LocalPV as alternative CSI backends with documented trade-offs. Non-production clusters may use NFS-provisioner for RWX.

This decision ensures multi-cloud portability, security, and compliance without relying on provider-managed storage, while remaining open-source and vendor-neutral.

We will implement all client-side functionality of Libero Reviewer in JavaScript as the primary language. We will standardize on modern ECMAScript (ES2019+), using native ES modules, async/await, and the Fetch API, while transpiling to maintain compatibility with our supported browsers (latest two versions of Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge). Babel will be used for transpilation and polyfills as needed; bundling will support tree-shaking and code-splitting to optimize load performance.

We will not adopt a static type system (e.g., TypeScript/Flow) at this time; this may be revisited in a future ADR. Code quality will be enforced via ESLint (with our shared config) and Prettier for formatting. Unit and component testing will be implemented with Jest and Testing Library; integration/e2e coverage may be added with Cypress as needed.

Package management will use npm with lockfiles committed; release builds will be reproducible and pass our CI quality gates. Browser APIs will be accessed via standards-first approaches, with minimal, carefully chosen polyfills to meet our support matrix. Public-facing code will adhere to accessibility best practices (WCAG) and internationalization readiness.

This decision establishes JavaScript as the canonical client-side language for Libero Reviewer, enabling a consistent development model, broad ecosystem support, and efficient delivery of features to modern browsers.

Adopt AWS ECS on Fargate for containerized deployment with an Application Load Balancer, using Terraform for infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions for CI/CD. Container images will be built via GitHub Actions, scanned, and pushed to Amazon ECR. Deployments will target ECS services running on Fargate in private subnets across at least two AZs, fronted by an ALB in public subnets. Routing, health checks, and zero-downtime rolling updates will be managed by ECS with ALB target groups; blue/green can be enabled later via CodeDeploy if needed.

Networking will be provisioned with a dedicated VPC, public and private subnets, NAT gateways for egress, security groups with least-privilege rules, and optional WAF on the ALB for edge protection. Application configuration and secrets will be managed via AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (SecureString) and/or AWS Secrets Manager, injected at runtime. Observability will use CloudWatch Logs and Metrics, Container Insights, and ALB/access logs to S3; alarms will be configured in CloudWatch and routed via SNS.

Stateful dependencies (databases, caches, queues) will use managed AWS services (e.g., RDS/Aurora, ElastiCache, SQS) and connect within the VPC. Environments (dev, staging, prod) will be isolated via separate ECS clusters and Terraform workspaces/stacks. This decision avoids server management, scales automatically with workload, and standardizes deployment while remaining cost-aware and portable across regions.

Adopt a centralized runtime lifecycle manager that orchestrates initialization, start, and stop of application services based on an explicit dependency graph derived from the Arachne configuration. Each module- and user-defined runtime element must declare:
- A unique identity
- The services/resources it provides
- Its dependencies on other services/resources
- Lifecycle functions implementing init, start, and stop (idempotent where feasible)

The lifecycle executes in ordered phases:
1) Init: Construct instances and wire dependencies without performing side effects that assume availability of external systems.
2) Start: Activate services in topologically sorted dependency order.
3) Stop: Deactivate services in the reverse order to guarantee no running service outlives its dependencies.

The manager validates the graph (DAG), detects cycles/missing dependencies at boot, and provides deterministic ordering. Failures during start trigger automatic rollback: already-started services are stopped in reverse order; failures during stop continue best-effort and surface aggregated errors.

Provide a uniform API:
- init(config) -> runtime
- start(runtime) -> running-runtime
- stop(running-runtime) -> stopped-runtime
Optionally, start/stop accept a subset of targets to support partial lifecycles when dependencies are satisfied.

Support extensibility via standardized lifecycle hooks (pre-init, post-init, pre-start, post-start, pre-stop, post-stop) for modules, and event/log emission for observability. Allow readiness signaling for asynchronous services (e.g., a start function may return a handle/promise or register a readiness predicate) so dependents only start once prerequisites are ready.

Register an optional JVM shutdown hook that invokes stop to ensure orderly teardown on process exit, while remaining decoupled from JVM startup. This decision ensures predictable, configurable, dependency-aware startup and shutdown across Arachne applications and modules.

Adopt a canonical, declarative dependency manifest paired with a generated, immutable lock file as the single source of truth for releases. The manifest captures human-authored intents (names, semantic version ranges, optional features, platform markers), while the lock file records the fully resolved dependency graph, including exact versions, transitive dependencies, and integrity hashes. Release builds and CI/CD will consume only the lock file to guarantee reproducible, deterministic installs across environments.

Operationally:
- All changes to dependencies are made in the manifest; the resolver updates and commits the lock file.
- Platform/architecture-specific constraints are encoded via manifest markers; the lock file may contain conditional entries to support multi-platform releases.
- Integrity (hash) pinning is required in the lock to mitigate supply-chain risk.
- CI enforces lock/manifest consistency and fails builds on drift.

Transitional plan:
- Deprecate the alternative representation; convert existing definitions into the manifest, generate the initial lock, and freeze it for the release.
- Document the workflow (add/update/remove dependency → resolve → review diff in lock → commit).
- Provide tooling to diff, validate, and reproduce installs locally and in CI.

This decision prioritizes determinism, security, and auditability for releases while preserving flexibility during development through manifest-level version ranges that are concretized at lock time.

Adopt the AWS Load Balancer Controller (ALBC) as the standard ingress/egress mechanism for the cluster. Use it to provision:
- Application Load Balancers (ALB) for Kubernetes Ingress resources (L7 HTTP/HTTPS)
- Network Load Balancers (NLB) for Kubernetes Service resources of type=LoadBalancer (L4 TCP/UDP)

Key decisions:
- Replace in-tree AWS cloud provider features with ALBC to align with out-of-tree provider best practice.
- Terminate TLS at the ALB using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates referenced via Ingress annotations.
- Manage DNS records in Route 53 for ALB/NLB endpoints using ExternalDNS, sourced from Ingress/Service resources.
- Enable both Ingress and Service patterns to support near-term flexibility and GOV.UK Router integration/experimentation:
  - Use Ingress+ALB for L7 routing, name-based virtual hosts, path-based routing, redirects (HTTP->HTTPS), and WAF integration if required.
  - Use Service(type=LoadBalancer)+NLB for L4 connectivity and pass-through scenarios.
- Standardize deployment via Helm with IRSA for controller permissions; scope IAM policies to least privilege.
- Enforce security by only exposing required ports externally, using managed security groups on ALBs/NLBs, and private subnets for nodes.
- Prefer internal NLBs for east-west or Router adjacency when appropriate; use internet-facing ALBs for public endpoints.
- Defer final responsibility boundaries with GOV.UK Router; ALBC provides the necessary options to front Router or route around it during transition.
- Deprecate NodePort and direct internet exposure of cluster nodes.

This decision provides immediate capability for TLS termination, Route 53 integration, and both L4/L7 ingress, while keeping options open to evolve the edge architecture alongside the GOV.UK Router.

We will implement a dedicated Searches bounded context that exposes a search endpoint per domain and manages a single AWS Elasticsearch/OpenSearch domain with multiple indices (one index per domain that requires search). Each domain remains the source of truth for CRUD and publishes domain events (or CDC streams) consumed by the Searches context to build denormalized, query-optimized read models in Elasticsearch. The Searches context owns index design, analyzers, relevance tuning, query DSL, and result shaping, and provides domain-specific search APIs that abstract Elasticsearch from consumers.

Key constraints and choices:
- One OpenSearch domain shared across indices for operational efficiency, consistent security, unified observability, and cost control; shard/replica settings per index based on domain scale and SLA.
- Separate indices per domain (and per environment), with optional sub-indices or index aliases to manage schema evolution and zero-downtime reindexing.
- Event-driven ingestion pipeline with idempotent upserts and enrichment to support cross-bounded-context fields (e.g., joining person, asset, tenure attributes) within the Searches context.
- Consistent analyzers (language, n-grams, partial matching, wildcards), field-level mappings, and relevance strategies governed centrally; domain stewards collaborate on search schema contracts.
- Explicit eventual consistency guarantees documented for each endpoint; retries and dead-letter handling on the ingestion side.
- Fine-grained IAM: read-only for consumers, write access restricted to the Searches pipeline; VPC integration and encryption at rest/in transit.
- Backpressure and scaling via managed OpenSearch scaling and decoupled ingestion (e.g., SNS/SQS/Kinesis).

Exception: a domain may own its dedicated index and endpoint only when strict autonomy or unique performance/regulatory needs justify it; such exceptions require approval and alignment on shared standards.

Adopt a rank-aware flux measurement strategy. For any given network, determine the number of independent flux degrees of freedom by analyzing the stoichiometric matrix (e.g., via SVD/QR rank or null-space analysis). Require that the set of flux measurements intended for inference does not exceed this rank; measurements along dependent directions must be either (a) excluded from the inference set or (b) explicitly marked as validation-only checks. In the A -> B -> C chain, measure either reaction 1 or reaction 2 for inference; use the other only for validation.

Implement automated diagnostics that:
- Compute the design matrix rank and identify linear dependencies/near-collinearities (condition number threshold).
- Classify the system as determined, overdetermined, or underdetermined.
- Warn on redundant measurements and propose a minimal independent subset.

For overdetermined cases, retain at most one representative measurement per dependent subspace for inference. If multiple are kept for quality control, model their correlation to avoid double-counting evidence or inflate uncertainty accordingly.

For underdetermined cases, proceed with Maud’s Bayesian inference using informative priors and hard constraints (stoichiometry, thermodynamics, bounds). Encourage adding orthogonal measurements and report posterior identifiability metrics (e.g., marginal variances, parameter correlations) to guide additional data collection.

Codify this policy in the pipeline: dependency checks are mandatory pre-inference; priors/bounds are required for underdetermined systems; validation-only measurements are excluded from likelihood by default; all decisions and diagnostics are logged with the run.

Rebuild the DECODE demo as a TypeScript-based Node.js application, replacing the Python/Flask/Flask-SocketIO stack. Use Express (or NestJS for opinionated structure) with Socket.IO for real-time messaging between components and the dashboard to avoid prior socket instability and improve maintainability. Deliver a small React dashboard (Vite/Next.js optional) consuming a documented REST/Socket.IO API. Structure the service as modular domains (core messaging, component adapters, dashboard API, auth) to enable incremental extension (e.g., adding user login with Passport.js or NextAuth using JWT/OAuth).

Adopt 12-factor app practices with environment-based configuration, stateless processes, and centralized logging. Provide a Dockerfile and a Heroku-ready Procfile; default to a single dyno with optional Redis add-on for Socket.IO’s Redis adapter when scaling to multiple instances. Use PostgreSQL (via Heroku Postgres) only if persistence becomes necessary; otherwise remain stateless for the demo. Include health checks and basic observability (request logs, Socket.IO connection/error logs).

Define a thin integration layer for each DECODE component with clear interfaces, keeping transport concerns (HTTP/WebSocket) separate from business logic to simplify maintenance and testing. Secure by default (HTTPS-only behind Heroku, CORS restrictions, rate limiting), with stubs for future authentication/authorization. Provide CI workflow to run linting/tests and build Docker images, enabling quick deployment to public environments and easy future extension.

Adopt the Excelize library (github.com/xuri/excelize) as the standard package for parsing XLSX baseline rate workbooks for the 400NG Tariff import pipeline.

- Justification: Excelize provides high performance and low memory usage via StreamReader for large worksheets; robust XLSX spec support (shared strings, merged cells, date/number formats, errors); active maintenance and feature velocity; good cross-platform support without CGO; and an Apache-2.0 license suitable for our use. It enables deterministic, reproducible imports required by the rate engine.

- Implementation: Pin to a specific major/minor (v2.x) and commit SHA. Wrap Excelize behind an internal Parser interface to isolate third-party API details and enable future swaps. Use StreamReader for all large sheets; avoid loading full workbooks into memory. Normalize cell types (dates, numbers, text) explicitly. Validate worksheet names and ranges against a schema per tariff year. Add golden-file fixtures and benchmarks to guard performance and correctness.

- Operational considerations: Run in read-only, strict mode; reject volatile formulas and external links; log and surface schema/parse errors with row/col context. Document supported Excel features and known limitations (e.g., no macros; require prior normalization of xlsm). Cache shared strings if needed to meet SLAs.

- Re-evaluation triggers: Major upstream API/maintenance changes, material performance regressions, or new XLSX requirements not supported by Excelize.

Rebuild the Schoenberg Database of Manuscripts as a modular monolithic web application using a modern, open-source stack to enable flexible data modeling, user-contributed editing, and advanced search. Implement the core application in Ruby on Rails to accelerate delivery and leverage a mature ecosystem. Use PostgreSQL as the primary datastore with a normalized schema for core entities (manuscripts, sources, people, institutions, places) and JSONB columns for extensible, community-contributed attributes. Provide robust auditing, versioning, and rollback of all edits via PaperTrail, with role-based access control and moderation workflows (Devise + Pundit).

Support complex, faceted, and full-text search with Elasticsearch (or OpenSearch) integrated via asynchronous indexing (Sidekiq + Redis) and tuned analyzers for multilingual data. Expose a documented REST API for interoperability and future integrations; reserve GraphQL for a later iteration if needed.

Deliver a responsive, accessible UI using Rails server rendering augmented with React components in high-interactivity areas (search, editing forms). Containerize with Docker, automate CI/CD (GitHub Actions), and deploy to a cloud environment (e.g., AWS) with managed PostgreSQL and search services. Migrate legacy ColdFusion data via scripted ETL with validation checks, and preserve provenance metadata. Adopt open-source licensing and community contribution guidelines to sustain user-based editing and long-term maintainability.

## Decision
Adopt a modular, artifact-first distribution model and decompose the current multipurpose Docker image into versioned, composable components.

- Build each hamlet component (bash, freemarker, java) as an immutable, versioned release artifact (e.g., tarball/zip for bash/freemarker templates, Maven/Gradle artifacts for Java) published to standard registries and/or GitHub Releases. Eliminate git-based source pulls from images; only consume released artifacts.
- Introduce a lightweight cross-platform hamlet CLI that:
  - Resolves component versions via SemVer rules and a project lockfile.
  - Fetches, verifies (checksums/signatures), caches, and executes required components locally, enabling use outside Docker and supporting offline builds.
  - Manages upgrades/downgrades per project and reproducible builds via lockfile pinning.
- Provide slim, task-scoped Docker images (e.g., hamlet-base, hamlet-build, hamlet-deploy) that:
  - Layer a minimal runtime and fetch pinned artifacts at container start from the lockfile/cache.
  - Reuse OCI layers to reduce size and speed updates, avoiding image rebuilds for component version changes.
- Maintain the current monolithic image as “legacy” for a limited deprecation window while documenting migration to the CLI + slim images.
- Enforce semantic versioning, signed releases, and SBOMs for all artifacts; publish checksums and provenance metadata.
- Distribute the CLI via common channels (e.g., Homebrew, Chocolatey, apt, curl installer) to simplify adoption.

This decision reduces image size, removes the Docker-only constraint, enables rapid version switching without pulling full images, and improves reproducibility, security, and operational flexibility.

We will expose subscription status to Relying Parties via OpenID Connect claims augmented by a reconciliation API and change notifications:

- Include a namespaced subscription claim in ID tokens and Access tokens at user authentication. Claim contains: product/plan identifiers, status (active, trialing, past_due, canceled), entitlements, seats/limits, effective/expiry timestamps, and tenant/context identifiers where applicable.
- Keep tokens short-lived (≤5 minutes) and signed; RPs may cache within token lifetime but must treat token data as advisory beyond exp.
- Provide a protected Subscription Status endpoint (GET /subscriptions/:userId or /me/subscriptions) that returns authoritative, up-to-date status for all products/entitlements scoped to the RP, using the Access token for authorization. Responses are versioned and include ETags for efficient polling.
- Emit subscription.updated events via webhooks (or a message bus where supported) whenever a user’s subscription materially changes (activation, cancellation, downgrade/upgrade, payment state transitions, entitlement changes). Events are idempotent and contain minimal pointers; the RP must call the Subscription Status endpoint to fetch current truth.
- For session continuity, RPs should re-validate status on significant actions and on receiving webhook events; background polling is permitted with sensible backoff.
- Backward compatibility: RPs may start with the API only; OIDC claims and webhooks are additive. Multiple products and multi-tenant contexts are supported through claim scoping and per-tenant entries.
- Security and privacy: expose only RP-authorized product scopes; PII is excluded from claims/events. All endpoints require TLS and JWT validation.

Adopt dynamic route discovery with an authoritative route registry and expose a versioned summary endpoint to ensure complete, up-to-date route visibility across services.

- Implement a centralized, canonical Route Registry populated from each service’s OpenAPI/metadata at build time and refreshed at runtime via heartbeat/self-describe endpoints.
- Require each service to host a /routes/self-describe endpoint (JSON) and publish an OpenAPI document; registration occurs on deploy, with periodic re-validation.
- Provide a read-optimized, cached /routes/summary endpoint (v1) per gateway and per environment, aggregating from the Route Registry, including route path, methods, auth scopes, owners, deprecation status, and version.
- Enforce CI checks to validate new/changed routes against the registry (naming, conflicts, auth tags), failing builds if routes would be “invisible.”
- Enable runtime drift detection: alert when a route is live but not registered, or registered but not live.
- Support gradual adoption: legacy services onboard by supplying minimal self-describe JSON; full OpenAPI integration becomes mandatory within two release cycles.
- Keep discovery passive (no dynamic proxying) to avoid latency/regression risk; gateways consume the registry for routing hints and documentation only.
- Version the summary schema and registry entries; deprecations require a sunset date and owner approval.
- Roll out behind a feature flag per service; success metric is zero missed-route incidents and complete parity between live routes and the summary.

## Decision
We will automate enforcement of test coverage and test quality in the development workflow and CI/CD, eliminating reliance on manual checks.

- Gate merges with CI coverage thresholds: initial targets are 85% global line coverage and 70% per-file coverage; changed-code (diff) coverage must be ≥90%. Builds fail if thresholds are not met.
- Enforce test-on-change: CI computes coverage for modified lines/files and blocks PRs that decrease coverage or introduce untested code paths.
- Run fast unit/integration tests on each PR; run the full suite (including slower end-to-end and cross-browser, if applicable) on main and nightly.
- Introduce mutation testing on critical/core modules in nightly builds with an initial mutation score threshold of 60%, increasing over time; report but do not fail the pipeline during the ramp-up phase.
- Publish coverage and mutation reports as PR checks and dashboards; add a coverage badge to the repository for visibility.
- Pre-commit hooks run linting, type checks, and a targeted subset of unit tests (no coverage gating locally to keep feedback fast).
- Define and document explicit coverage exclusion rules (e.g., generated code, config, trivial data classes) with mandatory inline annotations and reviewer approval.
- Manage flaky tests via quarantine with time-boxed remediation; quarantined tests do not count towards coverage until fixed.
- Increment thresholds by 5% per quarter (or team-agreed cadence) until reaching 90% global and 80% per-file; diff coverage remains at 90%+.
- Ownership: Each team maintains coverage for its modules; the Developer Productivity team owns shared tooling, CI policies, and reporting.

This policy is enforced uniformly across repositories via shared CI templates and will be revisited quarterly.

Decision:
- Target SDK 30+ for all releases.
- Refactor the download feature to be compliant with scoped storage by eliminating direct file path access and WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE. All file I/O will use URI-based APIs via ContentResolver.
- Default behavior: use Android’s DownloadManager to download into the public “Downloads” collection, ensuring files are user-visible and managed by the system. Where DownloadManager is insufficient (custom metadata/streaming), insert into MediaStore.Downloads (API 29+) and write via ContentResolver openOutputStream.
- For app-private downloads (temporary or non-user-facing), save to the app-specific external storage (getExternalFilesDir) without additional permissions.
- For user-selected custom locations, use the Storage Access Framework: ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT for single-file save; ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT_TREE for exporting a folder structure. Persist URI permissions as needed.
- Access all downloaded content via content URIs; remove any reliance on absolute file paths. Share files using FileProvider or content URIs.
- Permissions: do not request WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE. For API 30–32, request READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE only when reading user media outside the app scope. For API 33+, migrate to granular READ_MEDIA_* when applicable (future-proofing).
- Backward compatibility: keep existing behavior for API <29 where safe, but route through the same URI-based code paths to minimize divergence.
- Telemetry and UX: surface download location (Downloads/app-specific/custom) to users; provide in-app open/view actions using Intent.ACTION_VIEW on content URIs.

Adopt the GDS Supported Platform (GSP) as the sole hosting and runtime environment for the proxy node. The proxy node will be deployed as Docker containers orchestrated by Kubernetes on AWS instances managed by GDS.

Enforce image provenance by mandating that only cryptographically signed Docker images are built, stored, and deployed; admission policies on GSP will block any unsigned or tampered images from entering the cluster. Restrict workload colocation by using Kubernetes scheduling controls (e.g., taints/tolerations, node selectors, affinity/anti-affinity) and namespace/tenant isolation to ensure only approved applications can share a host with proxy node components.

Leverage GSP-provided capabilities for CI/CD, monitoring, logging, and networking as the default operational toolchain. All build, test, and deployment pipelines will run on GSP CI/CD, publishing signed images to an approved registry. Operational telemetry will be captured via platform-standard logging and monitoring stacks, and service connectivity will use GSP-managed networking and ingress controls.

No external hosting or bespoke platform components will be introduced for this service. Exceptions to platform standards are not permitted without formal review and approval. This decision ensures compliance with GDS internal hosting requirements, consistency across services, and alignment with security controls for signed images and controlled colocation, while minimizing undifferentiated platform work by relying on GSP’s managed features.

We will store pixel data on disk as single-precision (float32) but promote to double-precision (float64) for computation by default.

- Default execution mode: On data load or at algorithm entry points (especially long call chains such as TobyFit and Horace core routines), all pixel arrays are explicitly cast to double. Mixed-precision inputs are normalized to double to avoid MATLAB’s implicit single propagation and to minimize accumulated rounding error.
- Performance mode (opt-in): For algorithms proven numerically stable and performance-critical, provide a documented single-precision execution path. This path requires explicit user or pipeline selection and will be limited to functions validated by precision/accuracy tests.
- Binning and cross-language consistency: Pixel binning will compute indices and accumulation in double precision in both MATLAB and C++ with an identical, documented rounding policy (nearest, ties-to-even) and consistent epsilon handling. Only after binning/aggregation will results be cast to the requested precision. Conformance tests will verify MATLAB/C++ parity bitwise where feasible.
- I/O boundaries: Data are written to disk as single. In-memory precision is controlled by the selected execution mode; results destined for persistence are downcast to single with range checks and overflow diagnostics.
- API and configuration: Provide a global precision setting (default: double) with per-call overrides, and enforce precision promotion at public entry points. CI will include precision regression tests to detect qualitative result changes.

We will decouple unreliable functional tests from release gates and invest in a new, more reliable testing stack with explicit reliability and cost targets.

- Effective immediately, PR merges and CD will be gated only by fast, deterministic checks (lint, unit, contract tests, and a minimal smoke suite). The current functional suite will run as non-blocking on PRs and as a blocking post-deploy verification only after it meets the reliability SLO below.
- We will time-box a 4-week evaluation and migration spike to replace our current functional test stack with Playwright-based E2E tests, Testcontainers-managed dependencies, and ephemeral, hermetic environments per run. Shortlist alternatives: Playwright (primary), Cypress (fallback). Selection criteria: auto-waiting stability, parallelization, traceability, flake detection, and CI resource usage.
- We will implement a quarantine lane for flaky tests, automatic flake detection, and per-test reliability telemetry. Quarantined tests run on a schedule and do not block merges.
- We will standardize on deterministic test data, network virtualization for third-party calls, fixed time sources, per-test isolation, and sensible global timeouts/retries at the transport layer (not at assertion level).
- Success criteria (SLOs) to re-enable gating: ≥90% pass rate in CI across 14 days, ≥95% pass rate in stage across 14 days, and ≥50% reduction in CI reruns/credits for PRs.
- Cost target: reduce PR CI credits by ~50% within 60 days by eliminating reruns and leveraging Playwright’s parallelism and tracing to speed triage.
- Governance: create a Flake Review weekly, require a rollback or quarantine within 24 hours for newly flaky tests, and track SLOs on a public dashboard.
- If the evaluation fails to meet SLOs, we will adopt the fallback (Cypress) or further scope the functional surface into smaller, stable smoke and contract suites.

We will re-interrupt threads in production code to comply with RSPEC-2142 and proper interruption semantics, but intentionally exempt test code from this rule to avoid leaking interruption state across JUnit’s thread reuse.

- Production/runtime code:
  - When catching InterruptedException, either propagate it (preferred) or immediately call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and exit/cleanup promptly. Do not swallow the interruption.
  - Long-running loops must check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() and stop cooperatively.
  - Code reviews will enforce this policy.

- Test code (unit/integration) and test-only utilities:
  - Do not call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() in catch blocks for InterruptedException to prevent contaminating JUnit worker threads and causing nondeterministic downstream failures.
  - Prefer to fail the test immediately (e.g., Assertions.fail with context) or propagate the exception to the test runner.
  - Configure SonarQube to exclude test sources from rule S2142, or locally suppress with @SuppressWarnings("java:S2142") and a justification comment where exclusion is not feasible.

- Shared libraries used by both production and tests must follow production policy; tests should wrap such calls to avoid propagating interrupts back into JUnit threads.

This approach preserves correct interruption semantics in production while ensuring deterministic test execution and avoids brittle builds caused by stale interrupt flags.

## Decision

Adopt a Kubernetes-based platform as the runtime for all microservices to ensure elastic scalability, high availability, and operational consistency across environments.

- Provisioning and configuration will be fully automated using Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) and configuration management (Helm). Delivery will follow GitOps with Argo CD for declarative, versioned, and auditable rollouts.
- Multi-AZ cluster topology is mandatory; use node pools with zonal spread, anti-affinity, and Pod Disruption Budgets to remove single points of failure at the node and workload levels.
- Traffic management is centralized via an API Gateway (Kong) and a service mesh (Istio) for mTLS, traffic shaping, retries, timeouts, and circuit breaking without code changes.
- Autoscaling: HPA/VPA/KEDA to scale on CPU/memory and custom/event metrics; enable cluster autoscaler for node scaling under load.
- Resilience patterns are standardized: idempotent handlers, exponential backoff, bulkheads, timeouts, and circuit breakers enforced at the mesh and SDK levels.
- Messaging uses Apache Kafka with multi-broker clusters, partitioning, and replication across zones; producers/consumers use at-least-once semantics with dead-letter queues.
- Data layer requires managed or operator-backed HA (e.g., Postgres with Patroni or cloud-managed equivalents) with synchronous replication across zones, automated backups, PITR, and routine restore testing.
- Observability is unified with OpenTelemetry tracing, Prometheus metrics, Loki/ELK logs, and Grafana dashboards; SLOs, error budgets, and alerting are defined per service.
- Chaos engineering (Litmus) and failure injection through the mesh are used to proactively identify SPOFs and validate failover paths in CI and scheduled game days.
- Progressive delivery (canary/blue-green) is standard for all services; feature flags manage runtime risk.
- Security and secrets: Vault/KMS, least privilege (RBAC), network policies, and image signing with policy enforcement (OPA/Gatekeeper).
- Documentation of ADRs is continuous; every platform capability and deviation requires an ADR entry linked to runbooks and readiness checklists.

Adopt asynchronous, non-blocking connection initialization and reconnection, decoupling reconnect loops from global lifecycle synchronization.

- Per-connection lifecycle execution: move connection init/start/stop/close into dedicated executors so a blocked/retrying connection does not hold the global state transition lock. Global lifecycle operations orchestrate via futures and time-bounded coordination, not synchronized blocking.
- Interruptible reconnection: reconnection loops run in background threads with interrupt/cancel support. Any admin/UI-triggered lifecycle change (stop/close/restart/apply-config) first signals a quiesce, cancels active reconnect attempts, and then proceeds with the requested transition.
- Bounded initialization: introduce a configurable max-initialization duration independent of retry counts. If exceeded, transition the connection to FAILED_INIT (degraded) while allowing the container to complete startup and other components to progress.
- Non-blocking apply-config: the UI applies configuration and receives an acknowledgement once the new model is validated and accepted; startup continues asynchronously. Readiness/health endpoints are split so the UI does not wait for full startup to succeed before returning.
- Timeouts on lifecycle coordination: replace indefinite synchronized waits with try-lock + timeout semantics. If a component cannot transition within the timeout, the operation degrades gracefully (reporting pending/failed state) without blocking the process.
- Administrative overrides: provide “force close”/“disable connection” operations that immediately cancel reconnect and move the connection to CLOSED/DISABLED, enabling configuration changes even under fault conditions.
- Backoff and retry remain per-connection but are supervised by a ReconnectManager that enforces cancellation, backoff jitter, and metrics.
- Backward compatibility: gated behind a configuration flag (e.g., lifecycle.async.enabled=true). Default enabled for new deployments; legacy behavior available for rollback.

This decision ensures the platform can start, stop, and apply configuration under connection failures, eliminates UI hangs, and provides clear operational controls and observability over reconnect behavior.

Adopt a separate Lucene-backed search service (e.g., OpenSearch or Apache Solr) for full-text indexing and querying, instead of using RDBMS full-text features. The search component is optional and isolated: the core application must remain fully functional if the search service is unavailable; only search capabilities degrade.

Implement an asynchronous, eventually consistent indexing pipeline: persistence events enqueue indexing jobs to a durable queue; the indexer performs idempotent upserts/deletes with retries and dead-letter handling. Provide on-demand and scheduled full reindexing, plus index versioning to enable zero-downtime reindex (build new index, then alias switch).

Define a narrow search abstraction in the application to allow swapping providers or disabling search via configuration. Apply circuit breakers, timeouts, and graceful fallbacks for search endpoints; non-search flows must not depend on the search service. Expose health checks and metrics for indexing lag, errors, and query latency.

Index only necessary fields (content, key metadata) to control storage and cost. Secure connections with TLS and authentication. Document deployment as an optional component with sensible defaults, and provide migration scripts and operational runbooks for backup/restore and reindex procedures.

We will enforce all business invariants within aggregate command methods and treat the aggregate as the authoritative boundary for invariant validation. Each command will validate relevant invariants before any state mutation; on violation, the operation will fail fast: no state changes, no domain events emitted, and the surrounding transaction will be rolled back. The error will be returned immediately to the caller.

Implementation details:
- Aggregate methods return a Result/Either type (preferred) or throw domain-specific exceptions to signal invariant violations; application layers map these to consistent API errors (e.g., HTTP 400/409 with machine-readable codes).
- Any preliminary input validation may occur at the edges (API/UI), but the aggregate remains the single source of truth for business invariants to prevent bypass and race-induced inconsistencies.
- All invariant checks execute synchronously within the same transactional boundary as the aggregate update to guarantee atomicity.
- No retries or compensations are attempted on invariant failures; callers are responsible for corrective action and may resubmit commands once preconditions are satisfied.
- Errors are logged with correlation IDs and metrics for observability, without leaking sensitive data.
- Cross-aggregate or eventually consistent constraints are not enforced within a single aggregate; if needed, they are handled via process managers/sagas and out-of-band policies, while keeping aggregate-local invariants strict.
- Idempotency keys are honored to avoid duplicate processing when clients retry after failures.

Decision:
- Default base: Debian bookworm-slim (or current stable -slim) for general-purpose runtimes. Rationale: glibc compatibility, broad ecosystem support, predictable CVE patches, good balance of size and debuggability.
- Language/runtime-specific: Use the official vendor-backed image for the target runtime for build and, when appropriate, runtime:
  - Java: eclipse-temurin:<version>-jre/jdk (slim) for runtime/build respectively.
  - Python: python:<version>-slim for runtime; -build or full for building native deps.
  - Node.js: node:lts-slim for build; copy built artifacts to a slimmer runtime.
  - .NET: mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/* appropriate ASP.NET/runtime and SDK images.
  Pin minor version and prefer digest pinning for reproducibility.
- Production runtime hardening for compiled apps: Prefer distroless (gcr.io/distroless/base or static) or debian:bookworm-slim with removed tooling. Use non-root user. Provide minimal CA certs/timezone if needed.
- Scratch: Use only when delivering a fully static binary with no shell/libc needs, minimal runtime dependencies, and when operational tooling (shell, package manager, certs) is unnecessary or explicitly provided.
- Alpine: Avoid as default due to musl/glibc incompatibilities, DNS/musl quirks, and ecosystem friction. Use only when musl is required or dependency-proven. If used, ensure compatibility testing and note CVE triage differences.
- Multi-stage builds: Always build in a larger official SDK image and copy artifacts into a minimal runtime base (slim/distroless/scratch where applicable).
- Security and supply chain: Pin image digests, enable regular base rebuilds for CVE patches, include SBOM/attestations when possible, and prefer images with clear maintenance policies and multi-arch support.
- Exceptions: Document justification when deviating from defaults (hardware needs, vendor mandates, performance, licensing).

Adopt immutable, content-addressed versioning for declarations and filters, with append-only history and deterministic regeneration. Each declaration and filter change produces a new versioned artifact with a stable identifier derived from a canonical serialization hash (plus an incrementing human-readable version for UX). Snapshots persist the exact declarationId@version and filterId@version (and the transformation/renderer engine version) used at creation time. Regeneration resolves these IDs to immutable payloads and replays the same transformation pipeline, guaranteeing reproducibility independent of current state.

Implementation:
- Append-only “DeclarationVersions” and “FilterVersions” stores holding full canonicalized payloads, metadata, effective dates, and parent links; optional diffs are stored for audit/inspection, but full payloads remain retrievable.
- Canonical, deterministic serialization and hashing to ensure identical content maps to the same ID; any semantically relevant change yields a new version.
- Strong referential integrity from Snapshots to versioned artifacts; no snapshot can reference mutable/live entities.
- API exposes read-only access by versioned ID and read-write operations that always create new versions (no in-place edits).
- Migration path to backfill initial versions and to lock historical snapshots to resolved versions.
- Governance: schema evolution is versioned; breaking transformation/runtime changes are captured as engineVersion in the snapshot to preserve reproducibility across code upgrades.

## Decision
Adopt Kotlin as the primary JVM language for new development, with continued support for Java where appropriate. We will not adopt Scala.

This decision optimizes for developer onboarding, maintainability, and pragmatic use of modern language features while preserving seamless interop with the Java ecosystem. Kotlin’s syntax and semantics are close enough to Java to minimize ramp-up time, yet provide significant safety and productivity gains (null-safety, data classes, concise syntax, extension functions, sealed hierarchies).

Guidelines:
- Use Kotlin for all new services and modules; existing Java codebases may remain in Java and be incrementally migrated when there is clear value.
- Avoid overly esoteric language features that hinder readability (e.g., excessive operator overloading, complex DSLs); prioritize clarity and Java-friendliness.
- Standardize on Kotlin coroutines for asynchronous workflows where appropriate; document concurrency patterns.
- Adopt Gradle with Kotlin DSL, and standardize formatting (ktlint/Detekt) and static analysis in CI.
- Maintain strict null-safety and prefer immutable data structures by default.
- Provide a lightweight enablement plan: Kotlin fundamentals training, code templates, and review checklists focused on idiomatic but accessible usage.
- Interoperate with Java libraries as needed; wrap APIs to enforce null-safety and reduce leakage of Java-specific patterns.

Scala is excluded to avoid a steep paradigm shift to advanced functional programming, fragmented style choices, and increased onboarding and maintenance costs relative to our team’s current Java-centric skill set.

Adopt a token-driven, scoped styling strategy using styled-components on web and styled-components/native on React Native, backed by a shared design token source.

- Default styles: Each component ships with baked-in styles authored via styled-components, using tokens for color, typography, spacing, and radii, ensuring attractive defaults and consistency with the Style Guide.
- Theming/overrides: Expose a ThemeProvider-driven theme with a constrained surface area (e.g., brand colors, font families, radii, spacing scale). On web, also expose a limited set of CSS custom properties at the component root for common overrides without rebuilds. Provide an sx (style overrides) prop per component that maps to tokenized style properties; reject arbitrary CSS/className to preserve consistency and isolation. In RN, sx maps to StyleSheet-compatible props using the same tokens.
- Isolation from app/global styles: 
  - Web: No global CSS from the library; all styles are component-scoped with hashed class names. Avoid tag selectors and descendant selectors that could leak. Neutralize inheritable properties prone to external overrides (e.g., font, line-height) at the component root. Do not depend on any external resets. Namespaced data-attributes are used to reduce collision risk and enable targeted testing.
  - RN: Styles are inherently scoped; no global leakage.
- Compatibility with foreign CSS (e.g., Bootstrap): Components explicitly set critical properties (box-sizing, font, line-height, button/input defaults) and avoid relying on UA or global resets to ensure consistent rendering even when third-party CSS is present.
- Cross-platform source of truth: Use a centralized design tokens package (e.g., Style Dictionary) to generate platform-specific artifacts (CSS variables and JS theme for web; JS/TS theme for RN). Versioned tokens ensure stable theming boundaries.
- Extensibility: Allow component slot-level sx overrides where applicable; disallow deep arbitrary selectors. Provide a documented escape hatch for web via styled(Component) extension for advanced cases, with warnings about isolation trade-offs.
- No dependency on global CSS frameworks; the library remains self-contained and non-invasive.

We will eliminate the “global” barcode scope and make all barcodes organization-scoped. Each barcode value must be unique within an organization and map to exactly one Base Item owned by that organization.

Barcode lookup will be deterministic and local: on scan, resolve by (org_id, value). If no match exists, users can (a) link the value to an existing Base Item or (b) create a new Base Item and link it. Optionally, the UI may suggest candidates from a read-only system catalog or from imported packs, but adoption creates an org-scoped barcode and does not depend on cross-org data at runtime.

To support reuse without coupling, we will replace “Share (global)” with explicit publish/import flows:
- Organizations may export a curated pack of barcode-to-Base Item mappings.
- Other organizations may import these packs, creating independent, editable copies within their own scope.

Data model and constraints:
- Remove global flag.
- Barcode fields: id, org_id, base_item_id, value, metadata.
- Enforce uniqueness on (org_id, value).
- Enforce one-to-one mapping of value→Base Item per org; prevent multiple Base Items sharing the same barcode in the same org.

Migration:
- Convert existing global barcodes into org-owned records for organizations that reference them; if none reference them, move them to a system catalog for optional adoption or archive them.
- Update APIs and UI to remove global endpoints/actions and to add import/export and local linking flows.

This decision clarifies ownership, ensures predictable lookup tied to Base Items, and decouples cross-organization reuse from runtime resolution.

Decision:
- Adopt a semantic ID as the primary identifier for synchronization and automatic matching. UUIDs remain for internal storage only and are not used for sync identity or name-based matching.
- Add a source attribute to all items:
  - Optional; empty for items created via GUI (editable).
  - If set, must be the fully-qualified class name (FQCN) of an Extension that acts as the provisioner (non-editable via GUI).
- Enforce namespacing of provisioned items to avoid collisions:
  - Provisioners MUST prepend their provisioner identifier to the item’s local ID when constructing the semantic ID (for example, <provisionerId>/<localId>).
  - The provisioner identifier is derived from the provisioner and should align with or be derivable from the source FQCN.
- Uniqueness rules:
  - Semantic IDs must be unique globally across all items.
  - Creation/update requests that would cause a semantic ID collision are rejected.
- Matching rules:
  - Synchronization and cross-references use the semantic ID as the canonical identity.
  - For provisioned items, the combination of source and the namespaced semantic ID ensures deterministic identification and avoids name-only ambiguity.
- Editability rules:
  - Items with a non-empty source are considered provisioned and immutable via GUI or API, except by the owning provisioner.
  - GUI-created items (source empty) are editable and use a non-namespaced semantic ID.
- Migration:
  - Existing items receive a semantic ID derived from their current name and a default “gui” namespace when source is empty; provisioned items must be updated by their provisioners to adopt the namespaced semantic ID.

We will enforce referential integrity with database-level foreign key (FK) constraints for all intra-database relational associations.

- Scope: Apply FKs within a single service/database boundary. Do not use cross-database or cross-service FKs; integrity across services is handled via IDs and application workflows or asynchronous validation.
- Defaults: Use NOT NULL on required relationships; allow NULL only for optional relationships. Default to ON DELETE RESTRICT/NO ACTION and ON UPDATE RESTRICT. Explicitly justify and document any CASCADE/SET NULL.
- Cascades: Use ON DELETE CASCADE only for true ownership/containment (child has no meaning without parent). Use SET NULL sparingly for optional references. Never cascade across large/high-value aggregates without review.
- Many-to-many: Use junction tables with a composite primary key of (fk_a, fk_b) and FKs to each side.
- Indexing: Create supporting indexes on all FK columns. Ensure composite FKs have matching leftmost index prefixes.
- Soft deletes: Prefer hard deletes where cascades are defined. If soft deletes are required, enforce via application logic and disallow soft-deleting a referenced parent unless alternative integrity rules are implemented.
- Migrations: Add FKs with backfills and validation steps (e.g., create NOT VALID then VALIDATE in Postgres) to avoid outages. Never drop constraints to perform data fixes; fix data, then add/validate constraints.
- Performance: Monitor lock/validation impact during large backfills; use batched updates and off-peak windows. Consider DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE for complex transactional inserts; do not globally defer constraints.
- Tooling/ORM: ORM mappings must reflect database constraints; application validations complement but do not replace FKs.
- Exceptions: Analytical/warehouse schemas may omit FKs for load performance but must maintain integrity via ETL checks and data quality rules.

We will adopt a resource-oriented JSON/REST API as the primary external interface.

- Contract-first development using OpenAPI 3.1 for schema, documentation, client/server code generation, validation, and test scaffolding.
- Standard HTTP semantics: GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE; pagination, filtering, and sorting via query parameters; hypermedia links where useful.
- Consistent error model using RFC 7807 (application/problem+json).
- Authentication/authorization via OAuth 2.1/OIDC bearer tokens; fine-grained scopes; rate limiting and quota enforcement at the gateway.
- Caching via HTTP caching headers, ETags/If-None-Match, and cache-aware gateway/CDN.
- Backward-compatible evolution with versioning at the URI level (/v1) and a documented deprecation policy; additive changes preferred.
- Performance optimizations: sparse fieldsets (fields=), include/expand for related resources, bulk/batch endpoints for high-throughput operations, and server-driven pagination (cursor-based where appropriate).
- Observability baked in: structured logging, distributed tracing, metrics, and audit trails at gateway and service layers.
- Tooling: automated contract checks in CI, mock servers for consumers, and SDK generation for key languages.

We will not expose a GraphQL API at this time. We will revisit a GraphQL gateway for specific aggregation/composition needs once we have clear client-driven query patterns and performance requirements, ensuring it layers over the canonical REST resources.

We will standardise on Ruby Smart Answers as the single implementation and deprecate Smartdown.

- Effective immediately, no new Smartdown flows will be created. All new and existing work will use Ruby Smart Answers.
- We will migrate the 2 published and 2 draft Smartdown flows to Ruby, refactoring as needed to express rules and outcomes clearly. During migration, we will maintain a minimal compatibility layer to keep existing Smartdown flows running without feature development.
- After migration, we will remove Smartdown (grammar, parser, rendering pipeline, and CI) from the Smart Answers codebase and archive the Smartdown repository as read-only with a deprecation notice.
- We will prioritise enhancements to Ruby Smart Answers to address authoring pain points that motivated Smartdown, including:
  - Improved content editing ergonomics (e.g., clearer separation of content and rules, richer templates, preview tooling).
  - Support for multiple questions per page where justified by user research.
  - Better test helpers and linting to make content changes low-cost and safe.
- We will provide migration guidelines, examples, and code mods where feasible to assist teams in converting Smartdown flows.
- Ownership and maintenance will consolidate under the Ruby Smart Answers maintainers, with product guidance to ensure content designers can efficiently collaborate on changes.

Adopt Python Scrapy as the primary framework for crawling and data extraction from the Koshvani platform, augmented with Scrapy Playwright for JavaScript-rendered content. Implement structured item definitions and validation via Pydantic, with Scrapy Item Pipelines responsible for serialization and persistence.

Storage will follow a dual-path approach:
- Operational store: PostgreSQL for normalized, queryable entities (e.g., agencies, schemes, allocations, transactions) with idempotent upserts keyed by stable natural/composite keys.
- Data lake: Object storage (S3/MinIO/Azure Blob) for raw and curated datasets, versioned per crawl, stored as Apache Parquet (preferred) and newline-delimited JSON for interoperability.

For non-HTML sources encountered (e.g., PDFs), integrate targeted extractors (pdfplumber/tabula-py) behind a Scrapy pipeline stage, emitting the same item schemas.

Crawl behavior will include incremental fetching via checksum/ETag/date heuristics, politeness (robots.txt, rate limiting), and comprehensive logging/metrics. The solution will be containerized (Docker) and schedulable (e.g., cron, Airflow), with secrets/config managed via environment variables. Artifacts (schemas, mappings) will be version-controlled and migrations handled via Alembic.

Success criteria: consistent machine-readable outputs with schema guarantees, reproducible crawls, and reliable storage in both PostgreSQL and object storage, enabling downstream analytics without additional scraping logic.

We will not implement a single, monolithic Gradle project. Instead, we will use a modular Gradle multi-project build within a single repository. Each subproject will expose a clearly defined API, minimize transitive dependencies, and be versioned independently. Modules intended for reuse will be published as artifacts to our internal Maven repository to enable consumption outside this codebase.

To preserve easy integration and developer workflow, we will:
- Compose modules under an umbrella build with consistent conventions (version catalogs, shared plugins).
- Use Gradle composite/included builds and dependency substitution to enable local, multi-module development without publishing.
- Establish CI pipelines that build, test, and verify the full graph and also support per-module releases.

To enforce boundaries and code quality, we will:
- Define explicit API vs. implementation dependencies (api/implementation configurations).
- Optionally use Java Platform/JPMS or ArchUnit rules to prevent forbidden dependencies and cycles.
- Maintain module-level contracts and documentation.

This approach balances integration simplicity with strong API boundaries and enables reuse outside the project, mitigating the risks of a monolithic build producing tightly coupled, harder-to-reuse code.

We will use Jest as our primary test runner, assertion, and mocking framework for all automated tests. For component integration tests, we will use @testing-library/react (react-testing-library) with @testing-library/user-event, testing components through the DOM as a user would interact with them. We will not use Enzyme.

Tests will focus on observable behavior and rendered output rather than component internals (state, props, instance methods, lifecycle). Queries should prioritize accessible selectors (byRole, byLabelText, byText, byPlaceholderText) to reflect user-facing semantics and encourage accessible markup. Interactions will be simulated via user-event to model real user behavior.

Unit tests (libs/helpers) will use Jest in isolation with fine-grained, deterministic assertions. Component integration tests will render components with realistic providers and context where needed, minimizing mocking of the DOM and avoiding shallow rendering.

We will avoid assertions tied to implementation details (e.g., testing private functions via component instances, inspecting internal state/props), prefer resilient queries over brittle snapshots, and treat snapshot testing as a last resort for stable, intentionally structured output. The default environment will be jsdom, and tests will run in parallel via Jest to maintain speed and reliability.

Adopt a unified, cross-language error handling standard for Hamlet Deploy.

- Standard schema (Hamlet Error Specification v1) for all handled errors:
  - fields: error_code (namespaced, stable), message (human-friendly), component (e.g., freemarker-wrapper, bash-executor, click-cli), severity (error|warn), category, timestamp, version, correlation_id, context (key/values), cause (chained code/reference), stack_trace (optional), remediation (optional), docs_url (optional).
- Output format and channels:
  - Default machine-readable JSON emitted to stderr for all components.
  - CLIs print a concise human summary to stdout by default and support flags: --format=json and --verbose for full detail; continue writing full JSON to stderr for tooling.
  - Non-interactive executors always emit JSON to stderr; summaries are optional and disabled by default.
- Language support:
  - Provide minimal libraries/wrappers to emit the schema:
    - Java: exception mapper and logger for Freemarker wrapper.
    - Freemarker: macros to wrap/normalize error details into schema.
    - Bash: sourced shell library (err_emit) to create JSON with jq-free fallback.
    - Python: dataclass/exception hierarchy and click error handler.
- Error code governance:
  - Central registry in repo with namespacing per component; unique per error; documented semantics and remediation.
  - CI validation to prevent duplicate or undocumented codes; mapping tests ensuring specific exceptions map to stable codes.
- Propagation rules:
  - Preserve correlation_id across layers; add context without losing original error_code; only wrap with cause when rethrowing.
  - Do not convert specific codes back into generic messages.
- Backward compatibility and migration:
  - Legacy messages are wrapped into the schema with a transitional code and original_message in context; deprecate generic codes over two releases.
- Logging/observability:
  - Central log collectors ingest JSON; dashboards/alerts keyed on error_code and component.
- Versioning:
  - Schema versioned; consumers must tolerate unknown fields; breaking changes only in major versions.

Adopt trunk-based development with a single long-lived main branch and optional release/* branches for supported versions. Eliminate “sprint branches” and branch folders used for grouping; sprints are managed in the tracker only, not as branches. Standardize sprint names to Sprint-YYYY.WW (ISO week), e.g., Sprint-2026.05, and require all work items to reference a sprint via tracker linkage, not branch paths.

Standardize branch naming using semantic prefixes and work-item IDs:
- feat/<scope>-<workId>-<short-desc>
- fix/<scope>-<workId>-<short-desc>
- hotfix/<scope>-<workId>-<short-desc>
- chore/<scope>-<workId>-<short-desc>
- spike/<scope>-<workId>-<short-desc>
- release/<version> (long-lived)
Examples: feat/payments-1234-add-3ds, fix/api-5678-null-order.

Operational policies:
- Short-lived branches only; target lifetime ≤ 10 business days.
- Auto-delete branches on merge; protect main and release/* with required reviews and status checks.
- Stale branch pruning: warn at 14 days inactivity; auto-archive/delete at 30 days unless explicitly exempted.
- Enforce naming via repository rules/pre-receive hooks and CI checks; reject nonconforming branch names.
- Tag releases with v<semver> and avoid creating additional long-lived folders/prefixes.
- Use PR templates to capture the linked work item and sprint (Sprint-YYYY.WW).
- Provide a dashboard showing active branches by prefix and age to detect drift.

This decision removes folder-based branch grouping, prevents naming collisions, limits branch proliferation, and creates a consistent, enforceable convention across teams and sprints.

## Decision
Adopt Codeception as the primary framework for functional and integration testing, while retaining Lumen’s built-in PHPUnit for fast, isolated unit tests. Codeception will enable end-to-end and database-backed tests via its Lumen/Laravel, REST, and Db modules, supporting realistic workflows (database read/write, authentication, middleware, queues) that the out-of-the-box PHPUnit setup does not cover.

Implementation details:
- Maintain separate suites: unit (PHPUnit), api (REST), and integration (Lumen/Laravel + Db).
- Use a dedicated test database with .env.testing; run migrations and seeds (or factories) per suite.
- Prefer transactional tests (Db module / transactions) for speed; fall back to refresh database for cases requiring persistence across requests.
- Mock external services via Codeception stubs or HTTP fakes; isolate side effects (mail, queues) with fakes.
- Integrate into CI with composer scripts and parallelization; produce JUnit and coverage reports.
- Keep test code colocated with app modules, and enforce deterministic data setup/teardown.

We will not migrate to a full standalone PHPUnit framework at this time, as Codeception builds on PHPUnit and provides the missing higher-level capabilities with less custom plumbing. Reevaluate if Codeception support, performance, or ecosystem becomes a blocker.

## Decision
We will adopt lightweight, version-controlled Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) to document all significant architectural choices throughout this exploration project.

- Format: Use MADR (Markdown Any Decision Records) v3.x template to ensure consistency and brevity.
- Location: Store ADRs in the repository under docs/adr/, committed to source control with the code.
- Naming/Numbering: Use sequential numbering (e.g., 0001-use-foo.md). Titles are short, action-oriented.
- Scope: Record any decision that materially affects quality attributes, interfaces, dependencies, data models, deployment, or team/process for architecture.
- Status Lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Superseded/Deprecated. Superseding ADRs must reference predecessors.
- Authoring Rules: Each ADR captures context, decision, options considered, consequences, and links to evidence/spikes. Keep to ≤2 pages; prefer clear, testable consequences.
- Process: New or changed architectural decisions require an ADR in the same PR as the code change (or as a preceding PR). Reviews are mandatory by at least one architect/lead.
- Traceability: Link ADRs in README/Architecture Overview and reference them from code/docs where relevant.
- Tooling: Use adr-tools (optional) or repo templates to scaffold records; enforce via PR checklist and CI lint for folder/filename conventions.
- Cadence: Revisit open/proposed ADRs in weekly architecture sync; close or supersede promptly after experiments.
- Openness: Encourage exploratory ADRs for spikes with time-boxed validation and explicit criteria for promotion to “Accepted.”

We will adopt Express.js as the primary web framework for the Node-based application. Express provides a minimal, flexible core with first-class routing and middleware composition that aligns with our need to quickly establish HTTP handling, request/response lifecycle management, and modular extensibility. This choice enables straightforward integration of GOV.UK Design System components by pairing Express with a server-side templating engine (e.g., Nunjucks) and serving govuk-frontend assets via static middleware, ensuring consistent UI, accessibility, and design compliance. The application will structure routes as feature modules, apply a layered middleware stack for security (e.g., Helmet), parsing, session/cookie handling, and logging, and expose health and readiness endpoints. This decision keeps the framework surface area small, reduces vendor lock-in, and preserves the option to introduce additional libraries (validation, authentication, caching) incrementally. Express will serve as the HTTP interface behind which we can later introduce domain services and adapters without constraining architectural evolution, supporting both server-rendered pages and JSON APIs as needed.

Use ActiveRecord migrations exclusively for schema changes; perform data migrations via idempotent, restartable Rake tasks (or background jobs) executed after deploying compatible application code.

Rationale:
- Keeps schema migrations fast, deterministic, and safe to run automatically during deploys.
- Avoids long-running or failure-prone data operations blocking deploy pipelines and holding locks.
- Allows batching, throttling, retries, observability, and rollback strategies suited to large datasets.
- Enables safe sequencing: deploy code that can read/write both old and new shapes, then backfill data, then flip flags/remove shims.

Policy and constraints:
- No non-trivial data changes in AR migrations; only minimal, metadata-safe tweaks tightly coupled to schema (e.g., seeding enum values) are permitted, and must be fast and reversible.
- Data tasks must be idempotent, resumable, and auditable; process in small batches, with progress checkpoints and metrics.
- Gate behavior with feature flags; maintain dual-compatibility during backfills; verify completeness before removing shims.
- Wrap batches in transactions when feasible; avoid full-table locks; use appropriate indexes beforehand (via AR migrations).
- Provide a runbook and explicit invocation (e.g., rake data:backfill_x) for post-deploy execution and reruns.
- Testing is required in staging with production-like volumes.
- Rollback: revert feature flag, stop task, and/or deploy previous code; schema rollbacks remain separate via AR reversible migrations.

Adopt a mandatory malware scanning control in the user-upload path that quarantines all uploads and promotes only files that pass scan results. All externally supplied files will be stored in an isolated, non-executable quarantine bucket upon receipt. An event-driven scanner (managed multi-engine service preferred; otherwise a maintained AV engine such as ClamAV with daily signature updates) will scan each file. Files that pass are tagged “clean” and atomically promoted to trusted storage for downstream processing; files flagged malicious or suspicious are rejected, quarantined for forensic retention, and never exposed to consumers. The system fails closed: unscanned, timed-out, or scanner-error cases are treated as non-compliant and blocked.

To ensure coverage and performance, we will:
- Integrate the scanner as a mandatory gate in every upload path (API, batch, backfills).
- Maintain auto-updating signatures and engine versions; schedule periodic re-scans on definition changes for cached artifacts above a risk threshold.
- Deduplicate scans via SHA-256 hashing and a signed scan-result cache with TTL.
- Enforce file size/type limits and stream scanning for large files; apply rate limiting to protect capacity.
- Emit immutable, timestamped audit logs of scan inputs, engine versions, and outcomes to meet RA-5 evidence requirements; alert on detections and systemic failures.
- Define SLAs: P95 scan latency under agreed threshold; backlog alarms; quarantine retention and secure deletion policies.
- Protect data in transit/at rest and minimize retention of content; store only necessary metadata and hashes for audit/compliance.
- Provide an appeal/review workflow for false positives with security approval.

This decision blocks distribution of any user-uploaded file until malware scanning completes successfully, providing demonstrable RA-5 compliance.

We will enforce an atomic, single-writer, alias-driven blue/green indexing pattern with strong concurrency control and automated cleanup.

- Atomic alias switch: Updaters create a new versioned index (<base>-v<Timestamp/UUID>), validate it, then perform a single _aliases request that simultaneously:
  - Adds the write/ read alias to the new index (is_write_index=true where applicable).
  - Removes aliases from the prior index.
  - Fails the entire operation if any step cannot be completed.
- Distributed lock: Before any update, an updater acquires a lock document in a coordination index with a short TTL and lease renewal. Only the holder may mutate aliases for a given base alias. If lock acquisition fails, the updater exits and retries with backoff.
- Idempotency and generation guard: The target alias stores the current generation in its metadata. Each updater run carries a generation token; alias updates validate the expected generation to prevent stale writers from overwriting newer state.
- Orphan and duplicate remediation: On startup and post-run, a cleanup task:
  - Identifies indices matching the managed pattern that have no alias or are not the current generation and are older than a grace period; deletes them.
  - Detects multiple indices bound to the same alias; keeps the newest valid generation and detaches/deletes others.
- Namespace isolation for parallel environments: PR and long-lived test updaters use prefixed namespaces for indices and aliases (e.g., pr-<id>-<base>), preventing collisions with mainline/prod.
- Resilience: All Elasticsearch operations use bounded retries with exponential backoff and circuit-breaking on repeated timeouts. Partial failures are surfaced and do not leave the system in an intermediate alias state.
- Monitoring/watch indices: Continue daily date-stamped monitor and watch indices, but manage them under ILM (hot rollover + retention) and explicit index templates. These indices are excluded from alias cleanup and use fixed metric export aliases to avoid duplication.
- Observability: Emit metrics and logs for lock acquisition, alias updates, cleanup actions, and deletions; alert on repeated lock contention or cleanup of unexpected duplicates.

We will standardize on an established, highly adopted mocking framework that supports auto-generated mocks, fine-grained control over parameters/return values, and minimal code intrusion. Concretely:
- JVM: Mockito (with Mockito-Kotlin where applicable)
- .NET: Moq (or NSubstitute if syntax preferences dictate)
- JavaScript/TypeScript: Jest (built-in mocking) or Sinon.js where more granular control is needed
- Python: unittest.mock with pytest-mock plugin

We will use dependency injection and interface/contract-driven design to enable seamless mocking without production code changes. A thin, shared test-utilities layer will provide common patterns (factory helpers, argument matchers, verification shortcuts) to ensure consistency and reduce boilerplate. Teams will prefer auto-mock generation and fluent APIs for rapid test authoring, and avoid custom hand-written fakes unless behavior is complex and better served by explicit test doubles.
