Clear documentation will enumerate required records, validation steps, and security considerations. This decision ensures compatibility with external DNS providers and cross-account patterns while retaining a simple opt-in path for managed Route 53 setups.

We will format files programmatically using a repository-managed toolchain invoked via a single command. All authoritative formatting will be performed by scripts (e.g., npm run format and npm run format:check) that call pinned versions of formatters and linters (Prettier for code/docs/config files; ESLint with --fix for JS/TS as applicable). Tool configurations and ignore lists will be committed in the repo (.prettierrc, .eslint{rc}, .prettierignore, .eslintignore, .editorconfig). Version consistency will be enforced via package.json and the lockfile; the expected Node version will be declared (e.g., .nvmrc).

A pre-commit workflow will automatically format changed files using lint-staged (wired via Husky or equivalent). CI will verify formatting with a non-mutating check command and fail on diffs. IDE/editor plugins are optional for on-save convenience but are non-authoritative and must respect the repo configs.

Scope: all supported source and text formats (e.g., JS/TS, JSON, Markdown, YAML, CSS/SCSS) will be formatted; generated, vendored, and third-party code will be excluded via ignore files. Developers can run the single format command locally; no per-IDE setup is required.

Migration: introduce the scripts and configs, run a repo-wide format once, and commit the changes. Ownership for maintaining formatting configuration and scripts: @sublimesneaks.

Adopt a contract-first, schema-driven validation strategy with a single source of truth shared across backend and clients. Define all request/response contracts in OpenAPI 3.1 using JSON Schema for constraints. Generate server-side validators (middleware at the API ingress) from these schemas to enforce strict validation before any business logic runs. Front-end/mobile clients consume the same schemas for type generation and client-side validation to ensure coherence.

Validation rules are strict: no type coercion; unknown/extra fields are rejected; required fields and value constraints are enforced. The backend returns machine-readable errors only, using a standardized envelope:
- HTTP 400 for malformed payloads; HTTP 422 for schema/semantic violations.
- error_code (stable, documented), message (brief), and details[] items containing path, constraint, expected/actual (when safe), and a localization_key for client UX.

All endpoints must integrate the validation middleware; no endpoint-specific bypasses. Schemas are versioned; only non-breaking changes (e.g., adding optional fields) are allowed in place. Breaking changes require a new API version. Deprecation windows are announced and enforced. Any server-side data normalization is explicit in the schema (e.g., formats) and visible to clients.

Observability is required: validation failures are logged with correlation IDs and summarized metrics to detect client regressions. CI gates ensure schema linting, backward-compatibility checks, and regeneration of validators/SDKs. This decision ensures consistent, fail-fast validation, coherent cross-platform behavior, and predictable error handling for asynchronous clients.

We will provide distributed tracing propagation by default at the platform boundary and keep tracing configuration and span creation within user code. Specifically:
- Propagation standard: adopt W3C Trace Context (traceparent, tracestate) and Baggage for both HTTP headers and gRPC metadata; deprecate any non-standard correlation headers over time while continuing to accept them for backward compatibility.
- Sidecar behavior: if inbound requests include valid W3C context, Dapr sidecars will continue and propagate it to downstream calls; if absent, sidecars will generate a new trace context. Sidecars will inject correlation IDs into outbound requests prior to handing control to user code. Propagation is best-effort and non-blocking.
- Sampling and span lifecycle: sampling decisions are respected if present; otherwise no-op sampling is assumed by the platform. The platform will not automatically create application spans; user services are responsible for configuring OpenTelemetry (or equivalent) SDKs, creating/continuing spans, setting attributes, and exporting traces.
- Tooling: provide optional middleware/helpers and reference configurations for major languages/frameworks to simplify OpenTelemetry setup, but do not make them mandatory.
- Observability hygiene: do not propagate PII or secrets in trace attributes or baggage. Enforce size limits and drop oversize baggage silently.
- Compatibility and migration: maintain support for existing correlation mechanisms during a transition period; prefer W3C headers for all new integrations. Failure to propagate tracing must not impact request processing.

## Decision
Adopt Algolia as the primary search-as-a-service solution for the platform. Algolia best meets the stated requirements out of the box: flexible and hierarchical facet management, configurable synonyms, query suggestions, typo/misspelling tolerance, and natural-language-style query handling. It provides a robust administrative UI enabling non-developers to manage synonym sets, relevance tuning, and ranking rules, and offers prebuilt frontend components that accelerate delivery while supporting customization. Algolia’s connectors and APIs enable integration with external sources beyond the CMS, satisfying the integration requirement.

We will not use the native Bloomreach Lucene search for the final solution due to limited configurability (notably synonyms and advanced relevance controls). We will not adopt Bloomreach Search & Merchandising at this time; while powerful, it is optimized for commerce use cases and carries uncertainty for this non-commerce scenario pending ongoing POCs. Azure Cognitive Search and Amazon Kendra/Elasticsearch remain viable alternatives but would require greater engineering effort to match Algolia’s admin experience, rapid UI enablement, and turnkey features.

We will proceed with an MVP on Algolia, implement index governance (schema, pipelines, relevancy tests), and conduct a cost/performance review post-MVP. We will monitor the NHS Digital brSM POC; if it demonstrates parity for content search needs and strategic alignment, we may reassess in a future ADR.

## Decision

Adopt JSDOM as the HTML parsing and DOM implementation for test code. We will:
- Add jsdom as a devDependency and configure the test runner to use a JSDOM-based environment (e.g., Jest testEnvironment: "jsdom") or provide a small utility (parseHtml(html: string): Document) that constructs a DOM via JSDOM for direct unit tests (e.g., transform.js).
- Standardize test assertions on web-standard DOM APIs (innerHTML, querySelector, textContent, etc.) exposed by JSDOM.
- Keep the existing XML parser for production/runtime and for XML-specific parsing; JSDOM will not be bundled with the app and must not be referenced by runtime code.
- For tests that previously used the XML parser to parse HTML, migrate to the JSDOM helper to avoid gaps (e.g., innerHTML support). Do not implement or maintain shims for innerHTML on the XML parser.

Constraints and guardrails:
- Use only web-standard DOM APIs in tests to avoid coupling to JSDOM internals; if behavior differs from browsers, prefer browser-aligned semantics.
- Disable or avoid network/resource loading in JSDOM during tests; no external requests are allowed.
- Pin to a stable major version and monitor changelogs for breaking changes; update the helper or test config as needed.
- For non-HTML XML test cases, continue using the existing XML parser to validate XML-specific behaviors.

Success criteria:
- Tests can parse and assert on rendered HTML snippets easily and reliably using familiar DOM methods.
- No production bundle size or runtime impact from this decision.

We will standardize repository placement across five GitHub organizations and apply explicit selection rules:

- Open-source: Public code intended for community use/contribution resides in github.com/<company>-oss. License, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, and CODEOWNERS are mandatory. Community-facing forks should also live here.
- Core proprietary: Company-owned product/platform and shared internal libraries reside in github.com/<company>. Default private visibility; public mirrors allowed only via CI to -oss.
- Labs/experiments: Short-lived spikes, PoCs, and research prototypes reside in github.com/<company>-labs. Private by default, time-boxed (e.g., 90 days) with a required disposition (graduate, open-source, or archive).
- Customer/engagements: Client-specific deliverables, code with contractual constraints, or repositories requiring external collaborator access reside in github.com/<company>-eng. Repositories must be private and restricted to engagement teams.
- Archived/deprecated: Sunsetted repositories move to github.com/<company>-archive with read-only permissions.

Selection rules:
- If the code contains or depends on non-shareable IP, secrets, or regulated data, it must not be public and must go to <company> or <company>-eng per above.
- If the primary intent is community distribution/contribution, place in -oss; otherwise default to <company>.
- Experiments with unclear destiny start in -labs and must declare an owner and review date; graduation requires security review and license decision.
- Customer-specific forks should live in -eng; upstreamable work should be contributed from -oss or <company> per visibility.
- Personal forks are disabled; team forks occur within the target org.

Governance and controls:
- Every repo must define: owning team, CODEOWNERS, README, SECURITY, license (where applicable), lifecycle state, and data classification.
- Access via SSO and GitHub Teams; least-privilege; external collaborators only in -oss and -eng.
- Mandatory protections in all orgs: branch protections, secret scanning, Dependabot, required reviews.
- Naming convention: <domain>-<product>-<component>; avoid ambiguity and reserved names. Repos with the same artifact name may not exist across orgs without qualifier.
- Migration on scope change (e.g., lab graduation, open-sourcing) is required; preserve history when feasible. Architecture Board approval is required for exceptions and for open-sourcing proprietary code.

Adopt a standardized base-image strategy to eliminate variability and reduce defects:
- Default runtime base: debian:bookworm-slim (glibc) for all services, unless a documented exception is approved.
- Builder stage: official language images aligned to Debian Slim (e.g., node:<ver>-bookworm, golang:<ver>-bookworm) in multi‑stage Dockerfiles; copy only artifacts into runtime image.
- For minimal production images where shell and package manager are not required, use Distroless (gcr.io/distroless/<lang>) as the runtime base; fall back to debian:bookworm-slim when interactive debugging or native tools are needed.
- Alpine is disallowed for new images due to musl/glibc incompatibilities and behavior differences; existing Alpine/Fedora images will be migrated to the approved bases.
- Pin base images to minor versions/digests; automate monthly base refreshes and rebuilds to pick up security updates.
- Enforce via CI policy: lint Dockerfiles for allowed bases, verify pinned digests, and run vulnerability scans on final images.
- Provide a formal exception path for workloads requiring non‑Debian bases (e.g., vendor dependencies), with time‑boxed review and mitigation plan.
- Deliver multi‑arch images (amd64, arm64) from the standardized bases; document common OS packages and hardenings (non-root user, minimal locales, CA certs).
- Migration plan: convert all services within two release cycles; deprecate nonconforming images after the deadline.

Adopt AngularJS 1.x as the primary frontend framework and migrate the existing plain JavaScript codebase incrementally. Bootstrap an Angular application alongside the legacy code and replace features module-by-module to minimize risk and maintain continuous delivery. Continue using the SoundCloud JavaScript SDK, encapsulated behind an Angular service/factory to standardize access, enable mocking in tests, and isolate vendor-specific behavior.

Apply “controller-as” syntax and prefer component-style directives (angular.component where available) to promote one-way data flow and clearer boundaries. Use a single root module with feature modules for routing, playback, search, and user interactions; introduce ngRoute or ui-router for navigational state management. Establish shared services for state, caching, and error handling.

Introduce unit testing with Karma/Jasmine and enforce coverage thresholds on newly migrated Angular modules. Maintain parity with existing functionality during migration; deprecate legacy modules only after Angular equivalents meet acceptance criteria and pass regression tests.

Limit new third-party dependencies to AngularJS (and router) to keep the footprint small. Provide developer onboarding guidelines and code style conventions to ensure consistency. Rollback is feasible at the module level by retaining the legacy implementation until the Angular replacement is verified.

Decide to externalize ETL outputs from container-local storage to a durable, shared data layer and expose them via standardized, controlled interfaces. Concretely: the ETL will write its artifacts to a versioned, immutable object store (e.g., S3/Azure Blob/GCS) under run-scoped prefixes, with metadata (schema, lineage, quality metrics) registered in the data catalog. For structured/relational outputs that require query access, a downstream load will publish curated subsets to a managed analytical store (e.g., data warehouse or read-optimized database) with read-only roles.

Consuming applications will access data through:
- Direct object-store access using least-privilege IAM policies or short-lived presigned URLs for bulk file ingestion.
- A read-only SQL endpoint (warehouse) for ad hoc and operational queries.
- An internal data-access API for small, latency-sensitive lookups.

Container-local writes are prohibited for inter-service data exchange. In container orchestration (e.g., Kubernetes), ephemeral volumes may be used only as staging; successful runs must atomically commit to the object store. Retention, lifecycle policies, and partitioning will be enforced at the bucket/table level; schema evolution is managed via a schema registry with backward-compatible changes. Access is audited; PII is segregated and encrypted with KMS-managed keys. SLAs: object-store availability within minutes of job completion; warehouse/API availability within agreed replication windows. This decision ensures durability, scalability, and secure, consistent consumption across services.

Adopt DfE Sign-in (DSI) as the sole authentication provider for trusted school buying professionals, integrating via OpenID Connect (OIDC) using the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. Public pages remain unauthenticated; all privileged routes require a valid DSI session.

Implement an OIDC client in the service that:
- Redirects users to DSI for sign-in and consent.
- Receives ID tokens and minimal claims required for authorization decisions (no local replication of DSI user or school datasets).
- Validates tokens using DSI’s JWKS and enforces short-lived sessions with secure cookies.
- Maps DSI-provided roles/claims to application roles to restrict access appropriately.

Do not build or operate a bespoke passwordless mechanism. This decision aligns with DfE governance, reduces identity assurance risk, and leverages an open, modern standard (OIDC/OAuth 2.0). It also avoids storing credentials, supports SSO, and simplifies future compliance and audits.

Nonfunctional requirements:
- Enforce least-privilege scopes and claim minimization.
- Support step-up or role changes by re-fetching claims at session refresh.
- Provide a secure logout that ends the local session and initiates DSI logout.
- Monitor DSI availability and surface graceful degradation for public pages.

If DSI is deprecated or materially changes its integration model, re-evaluate provider options while maintaining OIDC compatibility.

We will standardize on PostCSS with CSS Custom Properties for centralized design tokens and enhanced authoring, avoiding Sass to reduce toolchain complexity and enable runtime theming.

- Use CSS Custom Properties as the single source of truth for design tokens (colors, spacing, typography, z-index, radii, shadows). Define tokens in a centralized stylesheet (e.g., src/styles/tokens.css) under :root and optional [data-theme] scopes for theming. Example: :root { --color-primary: #...; --space-2: 8px; }.

- Reference tokens across all component CSS Modules via var(--token). Modules may import tokens.css where needed, or we configure bundling to include tokens globally for modules.

- Configure PostCSS with:
  - postcss-import for composable token and utility files
  - postcss-nesting (or postcss-preset-env with nesting-rules) for native-like nesting
  - autoprefixer for vendor prefixing
  - postcss-preset-env to polyfill selected modern CSS features while preserving custom properties

- Do not adopt Sass (dart-sass or node-sass). This avoids duplicate feature overlap, native-interop limitations, and additional dependency surface area. CSS variables provide runtime capabilities (theming, dynamic overrides) that Sass variables cannot.

- Migration: extract duplicated literals into tokens.css; replace usages with var(--...). Co-locate any component-specific variables in the module file and derive from global tokens when appropriate.

- JavaScript access: when needed, read computed CSS Custom Properties at runtime for cross-layer synchronization.

- Governance: changes to tokens require review; document token naming conventions and deprecation process.

This approach aligns with existing CSS Modules, supports theming and runtime overrides, simplifies the build, and future-proofs on native CSS features.

We will reduce the static cell fleet to lower excess capacity while retaining headroom for growth and operational safety, using memory as the primary scaling dimension.

- Target utilization: size the fleet so that steady-state usable memory (free+cached+buffered) is 35–45% of total cell memory (vs. current 77–92%), implying 55–65% memory allocation under normal load.
- Fault tolerance: provision per-AZ capacity such that, after the loss of any single AZ, the remaining two AZs can run current peak load with at least 30% usable memory headroom.
- Immediate change: decrease total cell count by approximately 30–40%, removed evenly across the 3 AZs, validating against the above targets using recent peak metrics.
- Growth buffer without autoscaling: maintain capacity to absorb at least a 60% week-on-week increase in rep-allocated memory (rounded up from the observed 55%) and a 20% surge in container count, without breaching the 30% post-failure headroom.
- CPU/IO guardrail: continue to ignore CPU/disk as primary drivers (given low contention), but cap average CPU at 50% and daily peaks below 85%; if breached, roll back the last reduction.
- Operational thresholds:
  - Add cells (evenly per AZ) if usable memory is <25% for 3 consecutive days or if two consecutive weeks show >40% growth in rep-allocated memory.
  - Remove cells if usable memory is >60% for 2 consecutive weeks and CPU/IO remain within guardrails.
- Review cadence: monthly review of utilization and weekly growth to adjust by ±1 cell per AZ as needed.
- No change to AZ distribution or tenant quotas in this decision.

We will require an explicit exit syscall to terminate execution and remove any implicit termination semantics. The Processor will no longer auto-exit with status 0 when the last instruction is executed.

To enforce this, instruction fetch is bounded by a finite ProgramImage with a declared code size. The Program Counter (PC) becomes a bounded index into this image; fetching at PC >= code_size triggers a MissingExit fault instead of continuing or implicitly exiting. Address remains unbounded for data memory, but instruction addresses are validated against the ProgramImage bounds at fetch time.

The ISA and runtime contract are updated:
- Programs must invoke the exit syscall with an explicit status.
- Reaching the end of the ProgramImage without an exit produces a deterministic fault (MissingExit), not success.
- Loaders/assemblers must produce a ProgramImage with explicit size; optional static validation may warn/error if no exit instruction is present on any path.

Acceptance criteria:
- No path yields implicit success; all successful terminations occur via exit syscall.
- Out-of-bounds instruction fetch is observable as MissingExit.
- Backward compatibility: existing programs lacking exit will fail fast with MissingExit until updated.

Adopt a stable, versioned formatting standard for all katas and stop retroactive cosmetic rewrites. Establish “Kata Style v1.x” as the canonical style guide, with a style-version header included in each kata. Existing katas retain their current formatting and get tagged with the appropriate style version; they are not reformatted unless a substantive change requires touching the file, in which case the formatter may be applied opportunistically. All new katas must use the latest style version. Publish and maintain formatter configurations and linting rules in the repository, and enforce them in CI for newly added or modified files only. Style updates will be introduced via minor/major version increments of the style guide; migration of existing katas is optional and only undertaken when coupled with meaningful content or structural changes. Document exceptions for legacy edge cases where applying the formatter would harm readability or semantics. This approach freezes historical work to prevent churn, ensures consistency moving forward, and provides a clear, low-friction path for incremental adoption of improved formatting without obligating wholesale rewrites.

Decision:
Adopt a monorepo, multi-module layout that “screams” use-cases at the application layer while keeping domain and infrastructure independent and reusable across features and applications.

- Top-level structure:
  - apps/<app-name>: composition roots wiring DI, selecting plugins, and assembling executable applications. No business logic.
  - features/<feature-name>: application layer per feature (use cases, input/output ports, request/response models, orchestrations, policies). No cross-feature dependencies. May depend on domain modules and domain-defined secondary ports.
  - domain/<bounded-context-or-module>: pure domain (entities, value objects, domain services, domain events, invariants) and secondary port abstractions that belong to the domain (e.g., repositories, domain-facing gateways). No dependency on features or adapters.
  - adapters/<technology-or-system>/(<context>): infrastructure implementing primary ports (driving adapters like Web/CLI/UI) and secondary ports (driven adapters like DB, MQ, external APIs). May target multiple features/domains. Depends only on domain and port interfaces.
  - plugins/<plugin-name>: distributable sets that package features and optional adapters/config, exposing a manifest for assembly by apps.
  - shared/: cross-cutting technical utilities (logging, metrics, serialization), never business rules.

- Dependency rules (enforced via build and static analysis):
  - domain → no internal dependencies
  - features → domain (and domain ports), shared
  - adapters → domain (and domain ports), shared
  - features ↛ features; adapters ↛ features
  - apps → features, adapters, plugins
  - plugins → features/adapters they bundle; apps select plugins

- Ports placement:
  - Primary (input) ports in features/<feature-name> (use-case interfaces, DTOs).
  - Secondary (output) ports owned by domain modules where the abstraction is a domain concern (e.g., repositories); otherwise define technology-agnostic gateways in domain/<module> to keep features decoupled from infrastructure.

- Assembly:
  - Each app composes selected plugins, features, and adapters in its composition root (apps/*), binding adapters to ports via DI.
  - Multiple applications can be built from shared domain, features, and adapters without code movement.

This structure preserves screaming architecture at the feature level, avoids cross-feature leakage of domain and adapters, and supports plugin-based assembly within a single evolving repository.

## Decision

Standardize on Ruby on Rails as the default framework for all new user‑facing web applications that adopt GOV.UK styling and components.

- Use Rails for its opinionated, secure-by-default stack (e.g., automatic HTML escaping, CSRF protection, secure headers, and configurable Content Security Policy), reducing the risk of XSS and similar vulnerabilities encountered with Sinatra defaults.
- Adopt the official GOV.UK frontend assets via the supported Rails integrations:
  - govuk_template and govuk_frontend_toolkit gems for existing projects where required.
  - Prefer the govuk-frontend design system as it becomes the primary source of components, using the recommended Rails/asset pipeline or JS build tooling per GDS guidance.
- Target current stable/LTS versions of Ruby and Rails and enable default security middleware and configurations. Security hardening (CSP, secure cookies, session storage, headers) must remain enabled unless explicitly justified.
- Do not create new Sinatra applications for this class of services. Existing Sinatra apps may be maintained but should be migrated to Rails when undergoing significant changes or security work.
- Exceptions (e.g., specialized services where Rails is unsuitable) require architecture review and sign-off, with a documented security plan and integration approach for GOV.UK frontend.
- Leverage team and wider GDS community expertise in Rails for support, peer review, and consistency across projects.

Adopt CSS-in-JS with Emotion v11 as the standard styling approach, using tagged template literals as the primary authoring style and the Emotion Babel plugin/compiled mode to minimize runtime overhead. This choice provides co-located styles with components, strong theming support, SSR/critical CSS extraction, robust TypeScript integration, and a mature ecosystem, while avoiding lock‑in to a custom Webpack loader.

Key directives:
- Author styles via tagged template literals; object syntax is allowed for dynamic fragments only.
- Enable the Emotion Babel plugin in all environments; extract critical CSS on the server; enable source maps and component labels in development; minify in production.
- Centralize design tokens and scales in a typed theme; access via Emotion’s ThemeProvider. No hard-coded colors/spacing in components.
- Restrict global styles to a small, vetted layer (normalization, typography, root layout) using Global; all other styles must be component-scoped.
- Support responsive and stateful styles with standard CSS/media queries and pseudo selectors inside TTL; prefer variants via component props over ad‑hoc class juggling.
- Maintain deterministic class name hashing for stable tests and cacheability; prohibit ad‑hoc class name generation.
- Do not introduce custom CSS loaders or CSS Blocks/Stylable; reusability and performance requirements are met by Emotion’s compiled mode without specialized DSLs or build lock‑in.
- Migration: legacy .css may remain as global imports temporarily; new or touched components should be converted to Emotion. Provide codemods/lint rules to enforce conventions.

Expected outcomes:
- Improved developer experience through co-location, theming, and type safety.
- Production performance comparable to preprocessed CSS via compiled extraction and critical CSS.
- Reduced tooling complexity and vendor lock compared to custom loaders or niche preprocessors.

Decision:
We will update document popularity in-place on the live Rummager index using incremental, throttled bulk partial updates, eliminating the need for index-level locks or index rebuild/swap.

- Nightly popularity refresh runs a streaming process that issues Bulk API partial updates (doc/upsert or scripted update) to only the popularity fields of existing documents.
- Processing is batched and parallelized with bounded concurrency and adaptive throttling to protect cluster health and query latency SLOs.
- The job is idempotent and order-independent; missing documents are safely skipped or upserted based on configuration, and retries are enabled for transient failures.
- Progress is checkpointed (by scroll/batch cursor or ID ranges) to allow safe resume without reprocessing the entire corpus.
- Optimistic concurrency (e.g., if_seq_no/if_primary_term) prevents stale writes during concurrent document updates from other pipelines; conflicts are retried with backoff.
- Real-time search remains fully available throughout; no alias swaps or index locks are used.
- Operational safeguards include health-based pausing, rate limiting, and alerting on error rate, latency, and cluster resource saturation.
- In case of systemic issues, the job can be safely paused or rolled back by rerunning with the previous popularity dataset; data convergence is ensured by the next successful run.

This decision maintains availability, reduces operational risk and rebuild time, and confines nightly work to targeted popularity updates on the live index.

Adopt OpenID Connect using the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow with PKCE for the frontend as a public client. Integrate with a managed identity provider (e.g., Auth0/Okta/Entra ID/Cognito) configured without a client secret for the frontend. The frontend will initiate authentication via redirect to the IdP and will not handle user credentials directly.

Expose the following publicly accessible endpoints on the frontend domain:
- /auth/login: initiates the OIDC authorization request with PKCE, state, and nonce
- /auth/callback: handles the authorization code response and exchanges it for tokens via PKCE
- /auth/logout: performs RP-initiated logout with the IdP and local session cleanup

Token handling:
- Use short-lived access tokens (<= 10 minutes) scoped to required APIs.
- Enable refresh token rotation with revocation on reuse and a bounded lifetime, only if supported with sender-constrained tokens (e.g., DPoP) or secure same-site delivery; otherwise require re-authentication.
- Store tokens in memory (not localStorage) to reduce exfiltration risk; prefer cookie-based session via a lightweight BFF if later required, without changing the public nature of the auth endpoints.

Security controls:
- Enforce HTTPS, strict redirect URI allow-list, CORS only to required origins, and CSP.
- Use PKCE, state, and nonce to mitigate CSRF and replay.
- Validate ID token (issuer, audience, signature, exp) and enforce minimal scopes/claims.

Operational aspects:
- Centralize configuration for IdP metadata (discovery URL), client ID, and allowed redirect URIs per environment.
- Implement rate limiting and monitoring on public auth endpoints.
- Provide a logout redirect allow-list and session timeout aligned with compliance requirements.

Adopt Cypress as the primary end-to-end testing framework for automating user journeys in the application.

- Rationale: Cypress provides reliable, browser-native execution, faster feedback, and a developer-friendly API with rich debugging (time-travel, screenshots, videos). It aligns with MOJ standards and shared practices, enabling reuse of knowledge, examples, and tooling.
- Scope: Use Cypress for critical path user journeys, regression suites, accessibility smoke checks (via plugins), and minimal component-level UI checks where valuable. Unit and integration tests remain in their respective frameworks to preserve the testing pyramid.
- Non-goals: Do not pursue Selenium/WebDriver for new E2E tests unless a documented gap requires it (e.g., specific cross-browser or multi-tab scenarios not supported by Cypress).
- Cross-browser: Default to Chromium in CI; run periodic compatibility checks in Firefox (and WebKit if/when supported and needed). Document any unsupported flows and fall back selectively to Selenium only when justified.
- Environment and data: Execute against ephemeral test environments seeded with predictable data. Use API/setup hooks and fixtures to create and clean test data. Network stubbing is allowed for non-critical dependencies; end-to-end flows to core services must remain fully integrated.
- CI/CD: Run headless in CI on every PR with parallelization and retries for flake mitigation. Publish artifacts (videos, screenshots, JUnit) and fail builds on critical path regressions.
- Stability: Use resilient selectors via data-test attributes. Enforce coding standards, linting, and test review ownership per team.
- Governance: Version-lock Cypress and approved plugins, maintain a shared MOJ template, and periodically review test coverage, runtime, and flake rates to keep suites fast and reliable.

Decision:
- Replace the “Services” link on the results page with a single navigational target: clicking the Organisation name navigates to the organisation’s PIMS Profile Overview page (/organisations/:id/overview).
- Remove rendering of the “Services” link from the results list UI; retain services functionality elsewhere in the application where explicitly needed.
- Update routing so the Organisation name anchor uses client-side navigation (preserving SPA behavior) and opens in the same tab. Include appropriate aria-labels (e.g., “View [Organisation] overview”) to maintain accessibility.
- Preserve search context: pass necessary state (e.g., originating query, filters, pagination) to enable consistent back-navigation and analytics attribution without polluting the Overview URL.
- Add analytics: fire a SearchResultClicked event with destination=Overview and include organisationId and search context metadata.
- Ensure backward compatibility by adding a server-side 301/302 from any legacy results-page “services” URLs (if still referenced/bookmarked) to the corresponding Overview URL. Do not alter deep links to specific Services pages used from other entry points.
- Roll out behind a feature flag; enable progressively and monitor click-through rates, bounce, and error metrics. Provide a quick rollback switch.
- Update automated tests: unit tests for link rendering and routing; integration/e2e tests for navigation, accessibility (tab order, screen reader labels), and back-navigation behavior.
- Update documentation and user guidance to reflect the Overview as the primary entry from search results.

Adopt a single, human-readable “action slug” URL style for all public-facing pages and flows. Canonical paths will be short, lowercase, hyphen-separated, verb-first commands at the root, e.g., /donate, /apply-for-membership, /contact, /start-campaign. Avoid pseudo-REST patterns (/resource/action) and mixed forms (/contact/get-in-touch). Do not localize URLs; English-only slugs are the canonical identifiers. No trailing slashes, no file extensions.

For multi-step flows, use shallow subpaths under the action slug with noun step names, e.g., /donate/payment, /donate/confirmation. Prefer state encoded in server/session over query strings; if needed, use query parameters only for non-canonical filter/sort state. Each user-facing page has exactly one canonical URL.

Migrate existing routes to the new scheme and configure permanent (301) redirects from all legacy paths to preserve inbound links and tracking. Update internal links to use canonical paths only. Reject new routes that do not conform.

Scope exceptions:
- API endpoints remain under /api/... and follow RESTful conventions.
- Administrative tooling may live under /admin/... with nested paths as needed.
- Static legal/info pages may use noun slugs at root (e.g., /privacy, /imprint), but must still follow lowercase, hyphen, no trailing slash rules.

Conventions:
- Slugs use only a–z, 0–9, and hyphens.
- Use singular, concise verbs (donate, apply, contact, start, manage).
- Avoid synonyms for the same action; reuse existing slugs.
- Reserve and document slugs to prevent collisions.

This decision prioritizes consistency, usability, and maintainability over SEO concerns and will be enforced via routing middleware and linting in route definitions.

We will rebuild the PaaS product pages using Next.js with static generation and export (pre-rendered HTML), author content in MDX, and compose pages with shared React components aligned to the GOV.UK Design System. This replaces the current Ruby implementation and aligns with ADR024 (Node for user-facing apps), improving developer experience and enabling shared web component libraries across products.

Key elements:
- Framework: Next.js (with static export) over Gatsby, to support easier setup on non-developer machines and consistent Node-based tooling.
- Content: MDX for Markdown-first authoring with the ability to embed React components; stored in version control to allow any team member to update via simple workflows.
- Design system: Adopt GOV.UK Design System via a shared React component library (wrapping govuk-frontend), easing future upgrades and ensuring accessibility compliance.
- Rendering/performance: Pre-rendered pages served from a static host/CDN for fast, reliable delivery and server-rendered HTML output.
- Operations: CI pipeline to lint, build, test accessibility, and publish on merge; deprecate and retire Ruby pages after migration and redirect mapping.

We retain the option to introduce Next.js SSR/ISR later if use cases expand beyond static content, without changing the chosen stack.

## Decision
Adopt CoreTrackable as the single, canonical interface for event tracking and deprecate LegacyTrackable across all services, SDKs, and libraries.

- Effective immediately, no new code may reference LegacyTrackable; all new implementations must implement CoreTrackable.
- Mark LegacyTrackable as @Deprecated (or equivalent) and provide IDE/lint rules to block new usage and surface migration warnings.
- Provide a lightweight adapter (LegacyTrackableAdapter) to wrap LegacyTrackable implementations into CoreTrackable for a transitional period, ensuring backward compatibility while consumers migrate.
- Supply automated migration aids (codemods/refactors/templates) to convert common patterns and enforce naming/parameter parity with CoreTrackable.
- Update the Core Tracker runtime to accept only CoreTrackable; the adapter will be the sole sanctioned bridge layer.
- Deliver comprehensive documentation and examples for CoreTrackable, including event schema guidelines, lifecycle semantics, and error handling.
- Verification: establish contract tests to assert behavioral parity of migrated components; add metrics to detect any drop or duplication in event volume during rollout.
- Release plan:
  - Minor release: introduce CoreTrackable, deprecate LegacyTrackable, ship adapter and lint rules (default-on warnings).
  - Subsequent minor: escalate to build errors for new LegacyTrackable usages; telemetry dashboards to monitor adoption.
  - Next major release: remove LegacyTrackable and the adapter.
- Ownership: Tracking Platform team owns the interface, adapter, migration tooling, and documentation; feature teams own migration of their components by the published deadline.
- Success criteria: 100% of production event sources on CoreTrackable, zero references to LegacyTrackable, and no net negative change in event fidelity or latency.

Split Content Performance Manager (CPM) and Content Audit Tool (CAT) into independently owned, built, and deployed applications.

- Repositories and ownership: Create two separate repositories (cpm and cat) with clear code ownership and review responsibilities. Establish independent roadmaps and SLAs.
- Build and deploy: Provision distinct CI/CD pipelines, environments, and release schedules to enable independent iteration and rollback. Maintain separate runbooks and on-call rotation.
- Architecture boundaries: Define and document explicit API contracts between CPM and CAT where interaction is required. Prohibit direct code references across apps.
- Data and persistence: Decouple any shared databases. Each app owns its schema and migrations. Inter-app data access occurs solely via APIs or asynchronous events.
- Shared components: Extract common UI components, auth, telemetry, and utility code into a versioned shared library (e.g., internal npm/py package), with clear semantic versioning and changelog.
- Authentication/authorization: Centralize SSO and RBAC in the shared library/service to avoid duplication while preserving independent app policies.
- Observability: Implement per-app logging, metrics, tracing, and dashboards; maintain cross-app correlation IDs for end-to-end traces.
- Migration and compatibility: Maintain temporary compatibility layer (redirects, API gateway routes) and feature flags to ensure a seamless user transition. Freeze cross-cutting changes during the split. Provide URL redirects and preserve bookmarks.
- Backwards compatibility window: Minimum 1 release cycle with dual-operation support; deprecate interdependent endpoints and remove after agreed sunset date.
- Success criteria: Independent releases without cross-app coupling, no shared DB tables, stable shared library adoption, zero critical user-impact incidents during cutover.

We will move Evidence API access from the browser to a server-side Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) and deprecate the client-side proxy middleware. All read and write operations to the Evidence API will be executed on the server during server-side rendering, server actions, or via internal BFF endpoints. The browser will no longer call the Evidence API (or proxy) directly.

The BFF will:
- Authenticate using our server credentials and user identity derived from the incoming session/Google token.
- Derive the user’s allowed services from the Google token on the server and enforce them by constructing the Evidence API request. Client-supplied service filters will be ignored/overridden. Non-whitelisted query parameters will be dropped and requests violating authorization constraints will be rejected.
- Validate and sanitize request payloads and responses (schema validation) and expose only the minimal data required by the UI.
- Provide structured error handling and telemetry for observability.

UX improvements:
- Prefer server-side data fetching to render initial content without loading placeholders; progressively stream content where supported.
- Apply server-side caching with short TTLs and ETags where safe to reduce latency; invalidate on mutations.

Security/architecture changes:
- Remove the client proxy middleware and block any direct browser access to the Evidence API (network policy/CORS).
- Centralize authorization logic in the BFF; treat the client as untrusted.
- Log authorization decisions and attach request IDs for auditability.

Migration plan:
- Page-by-page migration to server-side data fetching/BFF endpoints.
- Feature-flagged rollout, parity tests, then removal of the proxy path.
- Update client components to call only internal BFF/server actions.

We will not honor HTML meta refresh/redirect tags in our runtime. Any <meta http-equiv="refresh"> will be treated as non-executable content: on ingest/sanitization we will strip the directive or neutralize it (e.g., render as text), and during rendering we will ignore auto-refresh intervals and location redirects.

For first‑party content we control, page refresh and navigation must use explicit mechanisms:
- Redirects: server-side HTTP 3xx or framework/router navigation.
- Refresh/polling: application timers and API calls with backoff and cancellation.

For third‑party or user-generated HTML, the sanitizer will remove meta refresh/redirects by default. A guarded, opt‑in configuration is available for legacy compatibility:
- Allowlist per tenant/origin.
- Minimum delay threshold (>= 5 seconds).
- Same-origin only; cross-origin targets are blocked.
- Telemetry and console warnings on use.
- Disabled in embedded/sandboxed contexts and when CSP sandbox is active.

Documentation and linting will flag meta refresh usage in repositories we maintain. This decision centralizes navigation logic, prevents unexpected or hostile redirects/refresh loops, improves accessibility and user control, and aligns with our security posture without blocking legitimate redirect/refresh needs through supported alternatives.

## Decision
Adopt OpenShift’s built-in OAuth server as the single source of identity and authentication for all Operate First applications, implementing Single Sign-On via OpenID Connect (OIDC). All applications must delegate authentication to OpenShift and must not maintain local user credentials.

Integration patterns:
- Preferred: Use the OpenShift OAuth Proxy (or oauth2-proxy) as a sidecar/ingress to enforce login and inject authenticated user identity (and groups) via headers.
- Alternative: Implement native OIDC Relying Party integration against the OpenShift OAuth endpoints using well-supported libraries.

Identity model:
- Canonical username: OpenShift User metadata.name, unique cluster-wide and reused across all applications.
- Stable identifier: OpenShift user UID/OIDC sub. Applications must persist and authorize by UID/sub and treat username as displayable/alias to avoid ambiguity on renames.
- Group membership: Source from OpenShift (IdP-synced groups) and propagate via OIDC claims/headers for consistent RBAC.

Authorization and auditing:
- Applications perform RBAC using OpenShift-provided groups/claims; avoid app-local role stores when feasible.
- All audit events must record both username and UID/sub to ensure traceability.
- Quotas and sandboxing align with the authenticated user identity and groups.

Security and lifecycle:
- Use short-lived ID/access tokens; enable refresh tokens where needed via OIDC flows.
- No long-lived static tokens or app-specific passwords.
- Support centralized logout via OpenShift endpoints; session revocation relies on OpenShift token revocation/expiry.

This decision unifies user management, enforces SSO across applications, and anchors identity and authentication to OpenShift.

We will incorporate DynamoDB access into the benchmark to reflect common real-world Lambda behavior. Each benchmarked Lambda invocation will execute representative DynamoDB read patterns (GetItem and Query) using the AWS SDK v3 with default retry/backoff, JSON marshalling, and client reuse initialized outside the handler. We will use a dedicated DynamoDB table per benchmark suite in the same region as the Lambdas, configured with on-demand capacity and pre-warmed/readily scaled RCUs to avoid throttling. The dataset will be seeded with deterministic schemas and item sizes (e.g., 1 KB and 10 KB), and controlled access distributions (uniform and moderately hot partitions) to model typical workloads while minimizing partition hot-spotting. No VPC attachment will be used (DynamoDB is public); DAX and caching will be excluded from the baseline, but may be added as optional variants.

Two modes will be provided: baseline (no I/O) and integrated (with DynamoDB), enabling separation of compute-only and end-to-end effects. Metrics will capture cold/warm start times, end-to-end latency (p50/p95/p99), and DynamoDB API latency via X-Ray/embedded metrics. IAM will follow least privilege with scoped table access. Test runs will include warm-up phases and consistent load patterns to reduce variability, with reproducible seeds and fixed request mixes checked into the benchmark configuration.

We will accept and preserve unrecognized metadata fields end-to-end to ensure forward compatibility and lossless round-tripping.

- On load: Parsers MUST accept unrecognized fields defined outside the current specification. These fields MUST be retained verbatim in an extensions/unknown-fields map associated with the parsed object. They MUST NOT influence client decision-making or validation logic beyond preservation.
- On validation: Presence of unrecognized fields MUST NOT cause validation failure. Validation applies only to recognized fields as per the current spec. Unknown fields are ignored for semantic checks.
- On write: Serializers MUST emit preserved unrecognized fields back into the serialized metadata alongside recognized fields. Field values must be emitted unchanged; ordering and whitespace are not guaranteed.
- On signatures: Signature verification operates on the canonical representation of the loaded metadata. Unknown fields are part of the signed payload if present in the input and MUST be preserved on re-serialization to avoid signature-invalidating modifications. When generating new signatures, the full set of fields (recognized + preserved unknown) MUST be used.
- API: Provide read-only access to unknown fields via a generic extension map. Provide an optional “strict mode” that rejects unknown fields for testing/hardening; default mode preserves them.
- Backward compatibility: This supersedes the prior behavior that dropped unknown fields on write. Existing code paths remain compatible; only persistence behavior changes to be non-destructive and aligned with TAP 6/10/14/15/16.

## Decision
Adopt Microsoft Azure as the primary cloud provider, deploying exclusively within EU regions to ensure data never leaves EU borders. Select the following fully managed PaaS components:

- Structured data store: Azure Cosmos DB (multi-region, multi-master, automatic sharding, global distribution restricted to EU regions only).
- Message bus: Azure Service Bus (for queues/topics with transactions and peek-lock semantics) and Azure Event Hubs (for high-throughput partitioned event ingestion).
- Serverless framework: Azure Functions with Consumption/Premium plans, integrated with API Management for external APIs.
- Push notifications: Azure Notification Hubs for iOS, Android, and browser push.
- Email/SMS: SendGrid and Twilio via Azure Marketplace.
- Logging/telemetry: Azure Monitor (Metrics/Logs), Application Insights, and Log Analytics for aggregation, tracing, and alerting.

Operational directives:
- Constrain all resources to EU regions (e.g., West Europe, North Europe, France Central, Germany West Central) and enforce EU-only replication policies.
- Use private endpoints, regional VNets, and Azure Firewall to keep data flows within the EU; disable any cross-geo features that traverse non-EU infrastructure.
- Target service SLAs of 99.99% or higher via multi-AZ and active-active multi-region configurations for Cosmos DB, Functions, and messaging.
- Establish IaC (Bicep/Terraform) guardrails and Azure Policy to enforce data residency, region allow-lists, and diagnostic baseline.
- Monitor TCO via Azure Cost Management; enable autoscale for elastic capacity.

We will revisit this decision if competing providers can simultaneously guarantee EU-only data transit and offer a fully managed, geo-distributed, multi-master database with equivalent SLAs and capabilities.

We will deprecate and remove PostgreSQL from all environments (dev, staging, production) since it is not used by any runtime workloads. Effective immediately, new deployments will not provision or configure PostgreSQL. Over the next two sprints we will:

- Remove PostgreSQL resources from IaC (modules, Helm charts, Terraform state), pipelines, and environment configuration.
- Eliminate related secrets, connection strings, security groups, firewall rules, and monitoring/alerting integrations.
- Disable backups, snapshots, and replication jobs tied to PostgreSQL.
- Update documentation, runbooks, and onboarding materials to reflect the absence of PostgreSQL.

To mitigate risk of undiscovered dependencies, we will first disable connectivity in non-production, observe for 1–2 weeks, then deprovision. We will instrument error monitoring to detect latent references. If any team requires PostgreSQL in the future, it must be explicitly requested and provisioned as a new, isolated instance with ownership and cost center identified.

Success criteria: no runtime errors or pipeline failures due to PostgreSQL removal; reduced infrastructure cost; reduced operational overhead and attack surface. Rollback plan: re-enable the previous PostgreSQL module and secrets from version-controlled IaC if a blocking dependency is discovered during the observation window.

Adopt a flat output layout by default for single-client generation. The generate-X-client command will write files directly to <outputDir> instead of nesting them under <outputDir>/<serviceDir> when invoked with a single spec/default generator. This aligns the output with user expectations implied by the command name and the common single-client use case.

Maintain the nested layout for multi-client scenarios. When multiple specs/generators are provided (e.g., via --spec multiple times or a config listing multiple services), the output will be <outputDir>/<serviceDir>/..., where <serviceDir> is derived from the spec/service name.

Provide explicit overrides:
- --service-dir <name>: always place output under <outputDir>/<name>.
- --flat-output: force flat layout regardless of count.
- --legacy-layout: opt into previous behavior for single-client runs.

Backward compatibility and migration:
- Default switches to flat in the next minor version, with deprecation warnings emitted when the legacy nested single-client layout is detected.
- Collision safeguards: if flat output would overwrite existing non-generated files, abort with a clear error unless --force is provided.
- Update documentation, examples, and CI templates to reflect the new default and flags.

Adopt a managed NoSQL document store—Azure Cosmos DB (Core/SQL API) in Serverless mode—as the primary persistence mechanism. Model each aggregate as a JSON document, denormalizing where appropriate to minimize cross-document transactions. Define clear partition keys per container based on high-cardinality, access-path-aligned fields (e.g., tenantId or accountId) to ensure predictable performance and cost. Use eventual consistency for read-heavy paths and override to session/strong consistency only on critical write-read flows. Enable TTL where applicable to control storage growth and costs. Leverage the change feed for downstream processing and integration events.

Introduce a thin persistence abstraction (repository/DAO) to encapsulate data access and query patterns, enabling future migration to a relational store if complexity grows. Enforce schema and invariants at the application boundary (JSON schema validation and versioned payloads) to manage evolution. Implement autoscaled indexing policy per container: include only required properties and set composite indexes for common query predicates/sorts to reduce RU charges.

Start with one write-optimized container per aggregate type; avoid multi-document transactions except where necessary, using Cosmos transactional batch within a partition key. Configure periodic backups and define cost guardrails (budget alerts, RU diagnostics). If data relationships or reporting needs outgrow document modeling, plan a read-optimized projection (e.g., Azure Synapse Link or export to Azure Storage/ADLS) and keep the abstraction layer to allow a future pivot to Azure SQL/PostgreSQL if warranted.

We will decouple platform apps (paas-admin, paas-billing, paas-accounts) from the paas-cf release cycle and deploy them via independent continuous delivery pipelines. We will remove version pinning from paas-cf as the default and stop coupling app deployments to platform-wide pipelines (terraform, bosh, cf acceptance tests).

Each app will have its own pipeline that:
- Builds, tests, and on success deploys directly to staging, with automated smoke/health checks and canary routing.
- Promotes to production via a manual approval gate.
- Is triggered by merges to the protected default branch or by signed, annotated release tags.
- Produces immutable artifacts (container image or buildpack droplet) and captures provenance (commit SHA, build metadata) for auditability and rollback.

Deployment authorization and auditability will be enforced by:
- Requiring GPG-signed commits/tags on protected branches and releases.
- Restricting approvals to designated teams via repository and CI access controls.
- Emitting deployment records (who/what/when/where) to a central audit log.

Compatibility tracking will move from paas-cf pinning to:
- Semantic versioning and release notes that declare required platform capabilities.
- An automated compatibility matrix artifact (generated on release) stored in a shared registry/repo, mapping app versions to minimum platform versions.
- Contract tests in CI to validate compatibility against current platform APIs.

Operational safeguards:
- Blue/green (or rolling) deploys with automatic rollback on failed health checks.
- Feature flags for config-driven toggles without redeploys.
- The ability to temporarily “freeze” or pin a specific app version via an override in paas-cf or a deployment lock in the app pipeline, for incident response.

This decision enables independent, faster app delivery, removes waits on unrelated platform steps, preserves explicit control over who can deploy through signed artifacts and approvals, and maintains a clear, auditable record of app-platform compatibility without relying on global version pinning.

We will log the outbound request URL used by each fetcher via structured, centralized request-logging middleware/interceptors at the point of dispatch and on completion/error. The logger will emit a single event per attempt with fields: fetcher_name, request_id/correlation_id, attempt, method, scheme, host, port, path, query_redacted, status_code, duration_ms, error_class/message, and retry/backoff metadata. Logging occurs at DEBUG on success, and at INFO (or WARN if retried) on failures; additional ERROR logs only for terminal failures. Sampling is supported to reduce noise on success paths.

Security and privacy are enforced by default redaction:
- Query parameters are logged as a key list with values masked, except for an allowlist of non-sensitive keys (e.g., page, limit). Disallowed keys are replaced with “***”.
- Authorization and sensitive headers are never logged; a minimal header allowlist (e.g., Accept, Content-Type) may be included.
- Request bodies are not logged.
- Long fields are truncated to a safe length with an indicator.

The logged URL is reconstructed from components to ensure proper encoding and avoid leaking credentials from raw strings. A utility shared library provides: canonicalization, redaction, truncation, and correlation context propagation.

Configuration toggles permit runtime control of log levels, allowlists, and sampling rates per environment. All logs include a stable request_id to enable end-to-end tracing across services. This decision ensures debuggability while meeting compliance and minimizing sensitive-data exposure.

We will describe core application use cases using structured Use Case Specifications (user-goal level) following Alistair Cockburn’s template, complemented by BDD-style acceptance criteria.

- Format: Markdown, one file per use case, named UC-XXX-ShortTitle.md.
- Template fields: Purpose; Scope/Level; Primary Actor; Stakeholders and Interests; Trigger; Preconditions; Minimal Guarantees; Success Guarantees; Main Success Scenario (numbered steps); Extensions/Alternates (by step); Postconditions; Non‑functional Constraints; Open Questions; Links/Traceability (epic/story IDs, APIs, data models, tests).
- Visuals: One lightweight UML Use Case Diagram per domain area; optional Sequence or Activity Diagram only for complex or highly concurrent flows.
- Acceptance criteria: Gherkin (Given/When/Then) scenarios embedded in each use case and linked to automated tests where applicable.
- Granularity: Core use cases at user-goal level; subfunctions captured as supporting use cases or alternate flows; avoid task-level fragmentation.
- Versioning and location: Stored in /docs/use-cases within the repo, version-controlled with code; changes require PR review from product and engineering.
- Traceability: Each use case links to epics/stories, API contracts, and test suites; IDs referenced in commits and CI reports.
- Currency: Updated as part of Definition of Done for impacted features; deprecated use cases marked and archived with rationale.
- Accessibility: Summary index (catalog) with status (draft/approved/deprecated), actors, and last updated date.

This approach ensures clarity for stakeholders, executable acceptance criteria for teams, and stable traceability across design, implementation, and verification.

Adopt Flannel as the Kubernetes CNI for cluster pod and service networking. We will deploy Flannel’s L3 IPv4 overlay with per-node subnets to provide stable, simple, and widely compatible networking across all nodes. This choice prioritizes operational simplicity, proven reliability, and minimal ongoing maintenance overhead over advanced routing or in-cluster encryption features. Flannel’s maturity and low-friction setup align with our current requirements and team expertise, reducing risk during cluster provisioning and upgrades.

We will not implement Calico, Weave, or a Canal-style combination at this time. Calico’s BGP-based routing and richer feature set (e.g., advanced policy) introduce additional complexity we do not currently need; Weave’s mesh and built-in encryption capabilities incur overhead and operational considerations that are out of scope for our present priorities. Should requirements evolve to mandate granular network policy enforcement, higher-throughput routing without overlays, or in-cluster traffic encryption, we will revisit this decision and evaluate adopting Calico (or integrating complementary capabilities) accordingly.

We will replace the legacy NTA webfonts with a single, optimised build of GDS Transport delivered in modern formats and with corrected metrics:

- Adopt GDS Transport with corrected vertical metrics to align glyphs within the bounding box, eliminating CSS baseline adjustments.
- Consolidate numeral styles: provide tabular numbers via OpenType features (tnum/lnum as appropriate) within the same font files, removing the need for a separate tabular-numbers font.
- Ship only WOFF2 (primary) and WOFF (fallback) to significantly reduce file size and network cost; remove EOT/TTF/SVG and drop old IE support.
- Optimise files via subsetting (required glyph ranges only), modern compression, and removal of legacy hinting.
- Expose numerals and feature toggles through CSS font-feature-settings and font-variant-numeric in the design system, with sensible defaults and utility classes.
- Update GOV.UK Frontend to reference the new font family name, weights, and metrics; remove any compensating CSS for baseline alignment; document migration guidance for downstream services.
- Provide robust system font fallbacks and ensure WCAG-compliant text rendering across supported browsers.
- Version and release as a breaking change with a deprecation window for NTA; include build-time checks to prevent accidental inclusion of legacy formats.

This decision reduces payload size, simplifies typography usage, removes CSS hacks, and aligns browser support with our current policy.

We will extract all testing utilities from the dogma module into a separate dogmatest module.

- Scope: dogma will contain only runtime/public contracts and production APIs. All testing helpers, fixtures, matchers, harnesses, and scenario utilities will live in dogmatest.
- Versioning: dogmatest will follow its own SemVer, decoupled from dogma. We will publish and maintain a clear compatibility matrix (e.g., dogmatest vX supports dogma vY.Z) in both READMEs and release notes.
- Backward compatibility and migration: existing testing APIs in dogma will be deprecated immediately and removed in the next major dogma release. For one minor release cycle, dogma will include thin shims that forward to dogmatest with deprecation notices to ease migration.
- Release process: test tooling evolution (including breaking changes) can proceed without forcing a new dogma major version. dogma releases are unaffected by dogmatest cadence.
- Consumption: users who test with our utilities will add an explicit dependency on dogmatest; users who do not test or use other tools avoid the extra dependency.
- Documentation and discoverability: update guides, examples, and templates to import dogmatest explicitly; provide a quick-start section mapping dogma versions to compatible dogmatest versions.
- Tooling/CI: add compatibility checks in CI to validate dogmatest against supported dogma versions before releases.

This separation maximizes flexibility for evolving testing tools while keeping the core stable and minimizes friction via clear compatibility policy and deprecation shims.

Adopt a dual-read model with session read-your-writes consistency and global eventual consistency:

- Persist purchases synchronously to the transactional OLTP store with ACID guarantees. Use idempotency keys and retries to ensure write success and avoid duplicates.
- On successful write, return the created purchase and emit a domain event to a stream for downstream analytics updates.
- Serve purchase summary/analytics from a precomputed analytics/read-model store for performance, but overlay it with a per-user “delta” computed on-the-fly from the OLTP store for purchases made since the last analytics snapshot. This guarantees accurate, up-to-date totals without waiting for the analytics pipeline.
- Maintain a short-lived cache of base aggregates per user (e.g., Redis) and compute/merge the delta at request time; keep the delta bounded (by timestamp or last snapshot marker) and indexed for fast access.
- In the UI, update the session view only after the server confirms persistence; apply optimistic UI updates post-200 OK and reconcile with server-pushed updates (WebSocket/SSE) that can deliver both new purchases and refreshed aggregates.
- If the analytics store is stale or unavailable, fall back to OLTP+delta-only computation to preserve correctness at acceptable performance for typical user scopes.
- Provide monotonic session semantics (read-your-writes) while accepting eventual consistency across devices/sessions.
- Implement observability around write latency, overlay/merge timing, and reconciliation errors; fail closed (do not display unpersisted purchases).

## Decision
- Place all feed-specific parsing, mapping, conditional validations, derivations, and file-handling idiosyncrasies in ETL services. These items are specialized per feed and are expected to evolve during onboarding and ongoing operations; they will be implemented as configuration-driven, versioned ETL pipelines with plugin/rules-engine support for rapid change.
- Keep CDH focused on stable, cross-cutting, canonical concerns: ingestion contracts, canonical schema exposure, idempotency, deduplication, referential checks against mastered data, enrichment using authoritative sources, metadata lineage, orchestration, and policy/guardrails that are invariant across feeds.
- Promote generic logic to CDH only when it is demonstrably reusable across multiple feeds, stable over time, and central to platform guarantees. Otherwise, default to ETL.
- ETL will own feed onboarding accelerators (templates, mappers, validation rule sets), error handling and quarantine specific to feed rules, and transformation to the CDH canonical model. CDH will accept only normalized, validated payloads that meet canonical contracts.
- Changes to feed behavior will be delivered by evolving ETL configurations/plugins without requiring CDH releases, reducing coupling and deployment risk.
- Governance: CDH contracts (APIs, schemas, SLAs) are versioned with strict compatibility rules; ETL mappings/validations are versioned per feed with lighter-weight change control.
- Benefits realized: faster onboarding, minimized CDH churn, clearer separation of responsibilities, improved scalability and observability, and reduced operational risk from frequent feed-specific changes.

## Decision
Introduce a domain-level lifecycle protocol for aggregates with explicit commands and events, decoupled from persistence semantics and enforceable by the aggregate root.

- Lifecycle states: Nonexistent → Active → Retired (terminal).
- Commands:
  - CreateAggregate: valid only in Nonexistent; establishes initial invariants.
  - RetireAggregate: valid only in Active; closes the aggregate to further mutations.
- Events:
  - AggregateCreated (domain-specific payload).
  - AggregateRetired (metadata: retiredAt, reason, optional actor/correlation).

Semantics and guarantees:
- After AggregateRetired, all mutating commands are rejected with a domain “Gone/Retired” error; queries may still be served subject to engine policy.
- CreateAggregate is not a synthesizing “upsert”; it requires Nonexistent and is concurrency-checked (version = none). RetireAggregate is idempotent.
- Invalid state transitions yield domain errors (e.g., Create on Active/Retired, Retire on Nonexistent).
- Lifecycle handling resides exclusively in the aggregate root to preserve invariants.

Engine mapping (left to implementors):
- CRUD engines may map CreateAggregate/AggregateCreated to insert and RetireAggregate/AggregateRetired to delete or soft-delete; hard vs. soft deletion is an engine policy.
- Event-sourced engines append the corresponding events; “retire” is a terminal event that blocks further appends. Engines may implement tombstones, snapshots, stream deletion, and compaction per their capabilities.

Discovery and GC:
- Existence checks are driven by lifecycle state (Nonexistent vs. Active vs. Retired) rather than storage presence.
- Engines may garbage-collect retired aggregates according to policy; the domain only expresses retirement, not deletion mechanics.

Adopt a distributed, queue-based background job architecture with the following components and conventions:

- A Job Orchestrator service exposing an API/SDK to enqueue jobs as typed, versioned commands with validated payloads. Enqueueing supports priorities, delays, schedules, and per-tenant scoping.
- Redis-backed queues for fast dispatch and leasing; PostgreSQL for durable job metadata, audit trail, and long-lived state. Use separate queues per priority and per domain/tenant where needed.
- Stateless worker processes running in containers, horizontally scalable, each registering handlers for specific job types. Concurrency is controlled per-queue and per-handler. Workers implement at-least-once semantics with idempotent handlers keyed by idempotency tokens.
- Reliability features: exponential backoff retries with jitter, max attempts, circuit breaking for systemic failures, heartbeat/lease renewal, timeouts, and cooperative cancellation. Failed jobs are moved to a Dead Letter Queue with retention policies and requeue tooling.
- Scheduling: use a scheduler component (Kubernetes CronJobs or internal scheduler) that enqueues jobs, not runs logic directly. Delayed jobs leverage queue-native delay.
- Consistency: when enqueueing from within write transactions, use the outbox pattern to ensure atomicity between DB changes and job publication.
- Security and isolation: enqueue APIs enforce authZ; sensitive payloads are encrypted at rest/in-transit; per-tenant limits/quotas; optional dedicated queues for noisy tenants. Untrusted/extension jobs run in isolated containers/VM sandboxes with resource limits.
- Observability: structured logs (job_id, type, tenant), metrics (queue depth, latency, success rate, retries), traces for job lifecycle, and an operations dashboard for inspection, replay, and cancellation.
- Versioning and rollout: handlers are semantically versioned; jobs carry handler version; support dual-run and phased deprecation. Schema evolution is backward compatible.
- Operations: deploy workers with autoscaling based on queue depth and processing latency; blue/green or canary worker rollouts; configuration via environment and feature flags.

We will standardize on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate as the default compute runtime for containerized workloads, and selectively use ECS on EC2 instances for specialized or cost-optimized scenarios. Fargate will host all stateless, horizontally scalable services, scheduled jobs, and bursty/variable workloads to maximize operational simplicity, security isolation, and elasticity without managing server fleets. ECS on EC2 will be employed only when one or more of the following apply: host-level customization (custom AMIs, kernel modules, eBPF), privileged/daemon workloads, GPU/accelerator needs, high-throughput networking or advanced NIC features, persistent local storage constraints, specialized architectures, or when steady-state utilization with Reservations/Savings Plans yields material cost advantage over Fargate.

Implementation details:
- Single ECS cluster with two capacity providers (FARGATE/FARGATE_SPOT and EC2/EC2 Spot); per-service capacity provider strategies define placement.
- awsvpc networking mode across both, with service-to-service communication via VPC constructs and security groups.
- Secrets via AWS Secrets Manager and task IAM roles; no SSH on Fargate. EC2 access via SSM Session Manager only.
- Autoscaling: ECS Service Auto Scaling on metrics; EC2 Auto Scaling Groups with mixed instances and Spot where applicable.
- Observability: CloudWatch metrics/logs, X-Ray tracing; unified logging sidecars allowed on EC2; Fargate uses FireLens where needed.
- CI/CD: immutable image deploys via blue/green (CodeDeploy) or rolling; image provenance enforced via ECR scanning and signing.

This decision balances speed and security by defaulting to Fargate, while retaining EC2 for advanced capabilities and optimized unit economics under predictable load. Periodic cost/perf reviews may reclassify services between Fargate and EC2.

## Decision
- Assets directory:
  - Use docs/adr/assets as the root assets folder for all ADR-related media (images, diagrams, attachments).
  - Each ADR must store its assets in a dedicated subfolder named after the ADR’s file stem: docs/adr/assets/ADR-0001-use-postgresql/.
  - Refer to assets with relative paths from the ADR file to ensure portability.

- ADR filename pattern:
  - Store ADRs in docs/adr/.
  - Use zero-padded sequential numbering, the “ADR-” prefix, and a kebab-case slug: ADR-0001-use-postgresql.md.
  - The slug should be a concise, descriptive summary of the decision in 3–7 words.
  - Numbers are immutable once merged; superseded ADRs retain their original number and filename.

- Titles in ADR documents:
  - The H1 at the top of the file must include the ADR number and a clear, concise title in Title Case, separated by a colon.
  - Format: “# ADR-0001: Use PostgreSQL for Primary Database”.
  - Titles should be imperative or declarative, avoid punctuation at the end, and exclude redundant words (keep to ~50 characters where feasible).

Adopt an in-repository, branch-scoped release notes process aligned with WMF’s model.

- Maintain a RELEASE_NOTES-X.Y file in each release branch that documents all user-visible changes included up to the branch cut, and any subsequent backports. Every backport PR/MR must include an update to that branch’s release notes.
- On main, keep a living RELEASE_NOTES-next template that accumulates changes targeted for the next release. When cutting a new X.Y branch, copy and freeze the relevant sections into RELEASE_NOTES-X.Y on that branch, then reset/refresh RELEASE_NOTES-next on main from the template.
- After a successful release, merge the finalized RELEASE_NOTES-X.Y into a HISTORY.md (or CHANGELOG-HISTORY.md) on main to preserve a complete, chronological archive of past releases; keep HISTORY immutable except for archival merges and formatting fixes.
- Require release-note entries in the same change that introduces a user-visible impact (features, fixes, deprecations, removals, migrations, perf, security). Exempt purely internal refactors/tests/docs unless they affect users.
- Standardize format: categorized sections (Added, Changed, Fixed, Deprecated, Removed, Security, Performance, Upgrade Notes), concise bullets with links to PRs/issues, and attribution where needed.
- Enforce via CI: changes labeled user-visible must touch the appropriate RELEASE_NOTES file; provide an override label for justified exceptions.
- Publish: external release artifacts (e.g., GitHub/GitLab Releases, website) are generated from the branch’s RELEASE_NOTES-X.Y; the repository remains the single source of truth.
- Ownership: the change author writes the note; reviewers ensure quality and placement; release engineers execute the branch cut, template reset, and HISTORY merge.

## Decision
Decouple build and deploy into separate pipelines with artifact promotion and configuration applied at deploy time. The Build pipeline will produce immutable, versioned artifacts (e.g., container images) once per source change, run tests, and publish to a registry. The Deploy pipeline will consume a selected artifact version and apply environment-specific configuration (via environment variables, Helm/Kustomize overlays, or similar) without rebuilding.

Configuration will be stored as code in a separate repo/path and managed independently of the application build. Secrets will be injected at deploy time via a secure secrets manager. Deployment will be parameterized by artifact version and environment, with approvals and quality gates for promotion (dev → test → prod). Rollbacks will be performed by redeploying a previously known-good artifact version with the corresponding configuration.

This approach prevents rebuilds for configuration-only changes, shortens cycle time for long-running builds, enforces “build once, deploy many,” and improves auditability by versioning artifacts and configuration separately. We will standardize on semantic version tags/digests for artifacts, implement retention policies, and enable GitOps-driven or pipeline-triggered deployments to ensure reproducible, traceable releases.

We will make base_path the primary aggregation key for performance and quality metrics for Guides and Travel Advice.

- For Guides and Travel Advice content types, all new metrics ingestion, storage, and reporting will aggregate by canonical base_path; content_id will be retained as a secondary dimension for drill‑down only.
- A canonicalization layer will resolve redirects and renames: when base_path changes, metrics will be merged under the current canonical base_path to preserve continuity over time.
- Historical data for the past three months will be reprocessed to backfill base_path aggregations; where event-time base_path is unavailable, we will map content_id-to-base_path using the closest publish timestamp and redirect history.
- Dashboards and alerts will switch to base_path views for Guides and Travel Advice; content_id views will be deprecated after a 60-day dual-run period.
- The warehouse schema will add base_path (and canonical_base_path) columns to facts and dimensions; content_id remains but will not be used for aggregation in these domains.
- Pipelines will validate one-to-one mapping per event to a canonical base_path; conflicts (e.g., transient duplicates) will be resolved by latest valid routing rules from Publishing API.
