- Other formats continue to use content_id as the primary key; no change outside Guides and Travel Advice.
- API and export contracts that expose identifiers will include base_path for these domains and mark content_id as auxiliary.
- Operational runbooks will be updated to reflect the new primary key and rename/redirect handling.

We will adopt a single, authoritative README at the repository root as the canonical entry point for onboarding, build/run instructions, and system orientation. The README will be concise, action-oriented, and consistently structured across repositories using a shared template. It will include, in order:
- Purpose and high-level overview (what the system does and for whom)
- Quick start (prereqs, one-command setup, build, run, test)
- Architecture at a glance (diagram link and key components)
- Local development (env setup, configuration, data/secrets handling)
- Operational workflows (common tasks, scripts, Make/Task targets)
- Troubleshooting and FAQs
- Contribution guidelines and coding standards
- Links to deeper documentation (docs site, ADRs, runbooks, service-specific READMEs)

For multi-service or monorepo structures, each service/package will include its own README following the same template, with the root README providing a navigation map and cross-links. The README is versioned with code and treated as part of the product: any code change that alters usage, interfaces, or setup must update the README in the same PR.

Quality gates:
- PR template requires confirmation of README impact and updates
- CI enforces markdown linting and link checking
- Diagrams-as-code and command examples are tested or auto-validated where feasible
- Badges surface build/test/coverage status

Ownership: each code area’s maintainers own its README; the architecture/docs guild curates the template and reviews cross-cutting changes. Currency is monitored via a quarterly docs audit and automated staleness checks.

Adopt dotcom-rendering as the shared platform for building Guardian web sites. New frontend sites will be created as applications within the dotcom-rendering repository and use its tooling, conventions, and shared libraries. Existing sites may migrate opportunistically when benefits outweigh costs.

Key elements:
- Shared platform: one repo with common toolchain (build, lint, test, type-check, bundling), code style, release and CI/CD pipelines, observability, security scanning, and performance budgets.
- App isolation: each site is an isolated app/package with clear boundaries; shared functionality lives in versioned libraries; site-specific differences are handled via configuration and extension points, not forks.
- Governance: a platform working group (CodeOwners) stewards shared tooling and libraries, reviews cross-cutting changes, maintains docs and templates, and enforces compatibility policies. Changes to shared contracts follow an RFC process with deprecation periods.
- Defaults and guardrails: new web frontends default to this platform. Exceptions require an ADR documenting why platform needs cannot be met and a plan to upstream missing capabilities. CI enforces standards and prevents divergence.
- Extensibility: platform provides well-defined hooks and APIs to accommodate product-specific requirements. Where capabilities are missing, teams contribute upstream rather than duplicating.
- Migration approach: prioritize high-impact, low-risk candidates. Provide scaffolds, codemods, and strangler patterns to incrementally adopt shared libraries and build pipelines before full app migration.
- Operational model: unified deployment workflows with per-app ownership, monitoring, and alerts. Performance, accessibility, and security baselines are measured consistently across apps.
- Scope: applies to web frontends aligned with dotcom-rendering’s stack (e.g., React/SSR). Non-web services or fundamentally different stacks are out of scope unless the platform is extended via RFC.
- Exit strategy: if platform constraints block delivery and cannot be resolved in time, teams may request time-boxed exceptions with a remediation plan to return to the platform.

This decision reduces duplication, preserves consistency and best practices, and concentrates investment in a single, high-quality developer experience while allowing controlled flexibility.

We will enable full local execution and debugging of all AWS Lambda functions by standardizing on AWS SAM CLI with Docker and LocalStack.

- Tooling:
  - AWS SAM CLI for building, invoking, and hot-reloading Lambdas locally (sam build, sam local start-lambda, sam local start-api).
  - LocalStack (via Docker Compose) to emulate AWS services used by the Lambdas (API Gateway, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, S3, EventBridge, Secrets Manager, Step Functions as needed).

- Configuration:
  - Provide a docker-compose.yml to start LocalStack and any auxiliary containers.
  - Define event sources and resources in template.yaml so sam local mirrors production wiring.
  - Route all AWS SDK clients to LocalStack via environment variables (e.g., AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, region, credentials).
  - Maintain a .env.local with non-secret defaults; secrets stored in a local Secrets Manager namespace seeded at startup.

- Developer workflow:
  - make local spins up LocalStack, builds the stack, seeds resources (queues, topics, tables, buckets), and starts sam local (API and/or Lambda).
  - Language-specific debugger configurations (e.g., VS Code launch.json) attach to local Lambda containers for breakpoints and step-through debugging.
  - HTTP Lambdas run behind sam local start-api; asynchronous/event-driven Lambdas triggered via AWS CLI against LocalStack (e.g., sqs send-message, events put-events).

- Data and provisioning:
  - Seed scripts (Terraform/AWS CLI against LocalStack endpoints) provision schemas, IAM stubs, and test data.
  - Deterministic fixtures checked into repo; idempotent seeding on startup.

- Parity and guardrails:
  - Aim for API-level parity; acknowledge known gaps where LocalStack diverges. For such cases, provide mocks or feature flags.
  - CI runs the same local stack for fast feedback; nightly/integration pipeline still deploys to a shared dev account for final verification.

- Standards:
  - All new Lambdas must be SAM-templated with local debugging targets and adhere to environment/config conventions.
  - Document service endpoints, seeding, and debug steps in /docs/local-dev.md; provide sample events per function under /events for quick invocation.

This decision allows developers to run and debug all Lambdas locally without deployment, with consistent tooling and reproducible environments.

Adopt wrapper scripts selectively as thin, transparent orchestration around existing tools to codify domain knowledge and enforce best practices, with explicit escape hatches and standards to limit opacity and lock‑in.

- Scope: Write wrappers only when they (a) compose multiple tools, (b) encode repeatable SOPs, or (c) enforce security/compliance. Prefer documentation or templates over wrappers for trivial single‑tool invocations.
- Transparency: All wrappers must support: --dry-run (print underlying commands), --verbose (echo each step), --explain (link to docs/SOP), and --show-config (paths, context). Default outputs should clearly indicate which tools are called and with what inputs.
- Escape hatches: Provide --passthrough/-- and env flags to forward arbitrary args to underlying tools; support --no-wrap modes that execute a documented canonical command; never block direct use of underlying tools.
- UX consistency: Follow a standard CLI contract (help, subcommands, exit codes, idempotency, composable stdout/stderr). Prefer shell-agnostic scripts (Python/Go) when complexity, portability, or testing needs exceed simple bash.
- Security by default: Enforce guardrails (e.g., secret encryption with sops, policy checks) with opt-out requiring explicit acknowledgement flags.
- Maintainability: Each wrapper has an owner, versioning, changelog, usage examples, and automated tests (unit + golden + e2e in CI). Instrument with structured logs and metrics for adoption/latency/error rates.
- Discoverability: Central catalog with purpose, underlying tools, supported scenarios, and “equivalent raw commands” section.
- Evolution: Start minimal; extend via plugins/subcommands rather than ad‑hoc flags. Provide deprecation notices and migration guides when changing behavior; remove abandoned wrappers.

This balances productivity and guardrails while preserving flexibility and learnability.

We will continue to use Terraform and standardize on running all infrastructure changes from a centrally managed Jenkins in a dedicated “Operations” AWS account. Jenkins will assume cross-account IAM roles to apply Terraform in each target account (dev, test, staging, prod), using a remote backend (per-account S3 bucket + DynamoDB lock table) to store state. We will not use Terraform workspaces; each environment will have isolated state, roles, and pipelines.

To resolve the bootstrap problem, we will provision the initial CI/CD foundation via a one-time, minimal bootstrap stack executed by the platform team outside Jenkins. This bootstrap will create:
- The Operations account primitives: VPC/networking, Jenkins compute, Jenkins IAM instance profile, artifact/state buckets, lock tables, KMS keys, and secrets stores.
- Cross-account IAM roles and trust policies permitting Jenkins to assume roles into each environment account with least privilege for Terraform plans/applies.

After bootstrap, Jenkins pipelines become the single mechanism to apply Terraform for:
- All environment infrastructure changes.
- Ongoing Jenkins infrastructure and configuration changes (excluding immutable bootstrap primitives such as state buckets/lock tables and KMS roots).

Pipelines will be Git-driven, peer-reviewed, and auditable, promoting changes through environments in order (e.g., dev → test → staging → prod). Each environment will have a dedicated Terraform root (separate directories or repos), explicit backends, and explicit providers bound to the assumed role for that account.

Access control will be enforced by IAM and Jenkins RBAC: developers receive permission to trigger pipelines without direct credentials to production accounts. Auditability is provided by Jenkins build history, CloudTrail, and Terraform state/version control.

A documented “break-glass” procedure will allow controlled, time-bound manual runs (from an admin workstation) only to repair CI itself or bootstrap components, with post-incident reconciliation through Jenkins.

## Decision

Adopt a federated, service-oriented architecture in which:
- Each service owns its domain data and logic, exposing API contracts for its capabilities.
- A dedicated Common Records layer (Master Data Services) provides the authoritative “one source of truth” for cross-cutting entities (e.g., agreements, suppliers, customers, contacts), with globally unique identifiers, canonical schemas, and versioned APIs.
- The consistent web experience (per ADR-002) is the “top bun”; the Common Records layer and shared data platform are the “bottom bun”; individual services are the “filling.”

Key mandates:
- API-first for all services, with mandatory APIs for Common Records and planned APIs for other service data. No direct database coupling; all cross-service access via APIs and events.
- Event-driven data propagation: services publish domain events to a shared event bus; the Common Records layer reconciles and masters common entities; consumers subscribe to changes for eventual consistency.
- Canonical data model for Common Records governed via a schema registry, versioning, and deprecation policy; contract testing required.
- Record identity management with immutable identifiers and provenance metadata; clear ownership and stewardship per entity attribute.
- Read models and caches permitted for performance; source-of-truth remains the Common Records APIs.
- Data quality controls (validation, deduplication, survivorship rules) centralized in the Common Records layer; lineage and audit retained.
- Backward-compatible evolution prioritized; breaking changes gated and scheduled.
- Security and access via centralized authZ/authN, with scoped tokens per API; PII handling aligned to compliance.

This enables multiple services to collaborate while ensuring a consistent user journey and a single, shareable truth for common data.

We will standardize component prop APIs under Prop API Guidelines v1 and apply them across all components.

- Styling:
  - Adopt sx as the sole styling escape hatch. Type: Sx | (theme) => Sx; no string shorthands.
  - User-provided sx merges last and wins over defaults/variants.
  - Continue to accept className and style; both are applied with user values taking precedence on conflicts.
  - Deprecate all Styled System props. Introduce dev-time warnings now, codemods in the next minor, remove in the next major.

- Refs:
  - All components that render a single primary DOM node must forward refs to that node via forwardRef.
  - Components with multiple nodes expose a stable imperative handle (focus(), scrollIntoView(), etc.) and document it.
  - No component accepts ref without honoring it.

- Polymorphism:
  - Support an as prop for designated primitives only. When as is used, merge props of the target element type, omitting conflicts; user props take precedence.
  - Remove/alias any component or componentProp polymorphism to as.

- Prop pass-through and naming:
  - Pass through standard DOM props, data-* and aria-* attributes to the root element.
  - Unknown non-DOM props are stripped with dev warnings.
  - Event handlers use onX naming and are not swallowed unless required; if intercepted, re-dispatch or document.
  - Controlled/uncontrolled conventions:
    - value/onChange with optional defaultValue
    - checked/onChange with optional defaultChecked
    - open/onOpenChange with optional defaultOpen
  - Boolean props default to false. Avoid tri-state booleans; use explicit enums.

- Consistency and compatibility:
  - No implicit magic props; all non-standard props must be documented.
  - Avoid breaking prop renames; when necessary, provide aliases with deprecation warnings for one minor and removal in the next major.
  - Provide codemods for renamed/removed props and Styled System removal.

- Enforcement and rollout:
  - Apply to all new components immediately.
  - Migrate existing components in phases (P1: refs/sx/polymorphism; P2: pass-through/event/controlled patterns).
  - Add lint rules and test helpers to enforce guidelines.
  - Publish a Prop API matrix and migration guide; surface dev-time warnings behind NODE_ENV=development.

Adopt Electron as the primary runtime and distribution mechanism for the application. We will package the existing web app into a cross-platform desktop application (Windows, macOS, Linux) using Electron, bundling all static assets and data required for offline operation. GitHub Pages will no longer be used for hosting runtime builds; it may remain for documentation, marketing pages, or download links.

Build and release strategy:
- Use CI/CD to produce signed installers and portable builds for each target OS via electron-builder.
- Publish artifacts to GitHub Releases; maintain separate channels mapped to branches (e.g., main → stable, develop → beta).
- Enable differential auto-updates where supported to simplify distribution and patching without reinstallation.
- Embed configuration allowing the app to run fully offline; remote calls are optional and feature-gated.

Security and compliance:
- Enable Electron sandboxing, contextIsolation, and a strict CSP; disable nodeIntegration in renderer.
- Code-sign macOS and Windows builds; notarize macOS apps.
- Audit bundled dependencies and lock versions.

Developer workflow:
- Retain a pure web build for local development and testing; Electron shell loads the same production bundle.
- Integrate branch-based versioning to clearly differentiate beta vs. stable builds.
- Decommission PWA packaging for distribution; keep PWA capabilities only if beneficial for browsers, not as the primary channel.

This decision optimizes offline usability and simplifies distribution compared to GitHub Pages and PWA constraints, while providing predictable release management across platforms.

We will adopt a two-tier architecture separating Galaxy integration from the user-facing app:

- Integration layer: Python (3.11) using the official GOG Galaxy 2.0 Integration API (galaxy.api) with asyncio. Packaged with Poetry, structured as a standalone service process managed independently of the UI. This layer owns platform account/auth flows, game/library sync, and event streaming to the UI. Communication to the UI occurs over a localhost WebSocket using JSON messages mirroring Galaxy’s event model.

- Desktop application: Tauri (Rust backend) + SvelteKit (TypeScript) + Tailwind CSS for a performant, modern, cross-platform UI (Windows/macOS). Rust-side commands in Tauri handle secure filesystem/OS access and proxy messages to/from the Python integration. The UI consumes the integration stream, renders rich views, and provides command actions (e.g., resync, link accounts), forwarded to the integration service.

- Data contracts: Versioned JSON schemas for events and commands shared between layers; lightweight codegen to Rust TS types for compile-time safety. Persistent settings stored via Tauri secure store; cached data persisted via SQLite (via Rust) with simple migration strategy.

- Packaging/Distribution: Tauri bundling for native installers; Python integration distributed as an embedded, version-pinned runtime (uv/virtualenv) launched by the app on-demand, with health checks and auto-restart.

- Observability: Structured logging (Python + Rust) with correlation IDs across processes; optional diagnostics panel in the UI. Feature flags toggled via config.

- Security/Privacy: Local-only IPC on 127.0.0.1 with origin checks and token handshake; no external ports. Credentials handled exclusively by the integration layer; UI receives redacted state.

- Testing/CI: Contract tests for the JSON schemas; integration tests spinning up the Python service and UI headless. Cross-platform builds via GitHub Actions.

This stack optimizes ease of GOG Galaxy integration (Python SDK), delivers a modern native-feeling UI (Tauri/Svelte), and introduces new technologies (Rust/Tauri/Svelte) aligned with the learning goal.

We will discontinue writing and maintaining controller specs and standardize on request-level tests for controller behavior, implemented via Rack::Test in this codebase. All new behavior exposed via HTTP must be covered by request specs that exercise the full request/response lifecycle (routing, middleware, filters, params parsing, serialization, and status codes). Unit tests should be reserved for domain logic in models/services/policies, not controllers.

Specifically:
- No new RSpec controller specs will be accepted. Existing controller specs will be deprecated and removed opportunistically as equivalent request coverage is added.
- Request specs will use Rack::Test helpers (get/post/etc.) consistent with current project conventions. Contributors must adhere to Rack::Test argument semantics and not RSpec’s type: :request API.
- Controllers should be kept thin; logic belongs in service objects with isolated unit tests. Controller tests will assert wiring: correct HTTP codes, headers, content type, JSON schema, routing, authorization outcomes, and integration of service results and errors.
- Avoid heavy mocking/stubbing of controller dependencies in request specs. Stub only external network boundaries or non-deterministic/time-dependent concerns. Prefer exercising real app components within the process.
- Deduplicate by removing overlapping controller specs where request specs already verify the same behavior; do not duplicate model/service unit tests at the request layer.
- Test only controller-specific branches not reachable by public routes if absolutely necessary (e.g., rescue_from mappings) via request paths; do not add unit-level controller examples to hit private methods.
- Provide helper factories and shared examples to reduce boilerplate in Rack::Test request specs (auth setup, content negotiation, pagination, error envelopes).
- CI will fail on new files tagged type: :controller; add a linter/check to enforce this rule and update templates/docs accordingly.

This decision increases confidence by testing real behavior at the HTTP boundary while reducing brittleness from implementation-coupled controller mocks, aligns with community guidance, and matches the project’s existing Rack::Test stack.

Adopt DDO-wise expenditure as the primary extraction path from Koshvani and deprecate direct Grant-wise extraction in the ingestion pipeline. Implement a canonical expenditure schema decoupled from source hierarchy and add a deterministic aggregation/mapping layer to derive Grant-wise views from DDO-wise records. Disable Grant-wise crawlers/jobs by default; retain them only as a manual fallback behind a feature flag. Update ETL to include pagination, rate limiting, and idempotent retries for DDO-wise endpoints to minimize site load and avoid crashes. Enforce parity checks by reconciling derived Grant-wise aggregates against historical Grant-wise totals (where available) within acceptable variance thresholds, with alerts on drift. Document the lineage showing DDO-wise as source of truth and Grant-wise as a derived product. Schedule a quarterly review to reassess the stability of Grant-wise endpoints and reconsider direct extraction if reliability improves without compromising system stability.

We will keep the starter seed unopinionated regarding state management. No third‑party state-management library will be included by default. Instead, the seed will:

- Provide minimal, framework-native primitives for simple local state and context (e.g., a lightweight app context pattern) to cover trivial use cases without imposing a stack.
- Define clear extension points (folder structure, interfaces/adapters, and DI-ready boundaries) so teams can plug in Redux, Zustand, MobX, XState, or others without rewiring the app.
- Supply “recipes” and optional presets/generators that install and scaffold popular libraries with consistent patterns (naming, side-effect handling, test setup).
- Keep tooling, linting, and testing agnostic (no rules tied to a specific state library), with example tests demonstrating both native context and a pluggable store.
- Document selection guidelines (scale, concurrency, SSR/ISR needs, devtools, ecosystem maturity) to help teams choose per-product requirements.
- Ensure SSR/edge compatibility and code-splitting friendly boundaries for any chosen library.
- Maintain a small core dependency footprint and faster CI by avoiding bundled state libs.
- Revisit this stance quarterly; if one approach becomes a clear standard for our org, we may provide a default preset (still removable).

This decision preserves flexibility for diverse team preferences and evolving trends while offering a clear, low-friction path to adopt a state solution aligned with project complexity and constraints.

## Decision
Adopt a precomputed, monotonic lookup-table approach to approximate the gamma curve and derive category thresholds from its discretization.

- Represent the gamma function y = x^(1/γ) (or equivalent form per domain) over normalized input [0, 1].
- Precompute a lookup table (LUT) of size N (default N=1024, configurable) sampling the gamma curve uniformly in input space to ensure monotonicity and stable performance.
- Use piecewise-linear interpolation between LUT points at runtime to achieve smoothness without incurring the cost of evaluating the gamma function repeatedly. Monotone cubic interpolation may be enabled optionally if higher fidelity is required.
- Derive category thresholds by discretizing the gamma-transformed output domain into C ordered categories (default C configurable). Two supported schemes:
  - Uniform-output binning (equal-width in gamma space) for predictable perceptual steps.
  - Quantile-based binning (based on input distribution) when balanced category counts are desired.
- Assign categories by binary searching the threshold array computed from the LUT; ties and boundary values snap upward (ceil) to preserve monotonicity and avoid category gaps.
- Make γ, N, C, binning scheme, and interpolation mode configurable; precompute LUT and thresholds at startup and regenerate on configuration change.
- Validate monotonicity and maximum approximation error against analytic gamma at build time; enforce unit tests on boundary conditions [0,1] and category transitions.

Adopt MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records) v3.x as the standard format for all architectural decisions. Each ADR will be a standalone Markdown file stored in the repository at docs/adr/. Files will use a zero-padded sequential prefix and kebab-case title (e.g., 0001-record-adr-format.md). Numbers are never renumbered; later ADRs may supersede earlier ones via explicit links.

Each ADR will follow the MADR structure: Title, Status, Date, Scope, Context and Problem Statement, Decision Drivers, Considered Options, Decision Outcome (including Positive/Negative Consequences), Pros and Cons of the Options, Links. Status values: Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Deprecated, Superseded. Superseding ADRs must include “Supersedes: #NNNN” and superseded ADRs must be updated to “Status: Superseded by #NNNN.”

Process:
- Every significant architectural choice or change requires an ADR PR before implementation.
- Keep ADRs concise (1–2 pages), reference external documents as needed.
- Reviewers: at least one architect and one domain owner must approve.
- Minor clarifications may be amended; substantive changes require a new ADR that supersedes the old one.
- Index is maintained by directory listing; optional README.md provides a curated overview.

Tooling:
- Author in Markdown; optionally use adr-tools or templates provided in docs/adr/0000-template.md.
- Enforce presence and status via CI linting where feasible.

We will centralize ingestion of all platform security/audit events into the Central Security Logging Service (CSLS) via Amazon CloudWatch Logs and CSLS-managed subscription filters.

- Scope: Audit/security events from BOSH Director (kernel audit, CredHub, UAA) and Cloud Foundry (UAA, Cloud Controller security) located under /var/vcap/sys/log on the Director and BOSH-managed instances.
- Collection: Deploy a BOSH-managed log forwarder (Fluent Bit/Vector) to tail the audited files, normalize to JSON, add metadata (environment, deployment, job, instance_id, az, region, ip, bosh_task, cf org/space/app where available), and emit to CloudWatch Logs over TLS.
- Log groups: Create per-environment, per-component CloudWatch log groups with consistent naming and tags. Set retention to comply with security policy (e.g., 400 days) and enforce via IaC.
- Delivery: Configure CSLS-owned cross-account CloudWatch Logs subscription filters to stream these groups to CSLS (Kinesis/Firehose) for onward delivery to Splunk. No direct Splunk forwarding from platform VMs.
- Security: Use instance profiles/IRSA with least-privilege IAM policies limited to PutLogEvents/CreateLogStream on designated groups; encrypt logs at rest with KMS and in transit with TLS; restrict log group access to CSLS and platform ops. Exclude secrets; apply source-side redaction where feasible.
- Reliability: Enable on-disk buffering and backoff/retry in the forwarder; monitor delivery lag, dropped events, and subscription health; alert on failures. Ensure logrotate settings prevent disk exhaustion while retaining sufficient local backlog for retries.
- Time/format: Use RFC3339/UTC timestamps and map fields to Splunk/CIM where practical to aid detection rules. Preserve original message where structure is unknown.
- Out of scope: Application logs and non-security platform logs remain on existing pipelines unless explicitly onboarded to CSLS.

This decision standardizes, secures, and automates audit event delivery to CSLS without bespoke pipelines, enabling central detection and incident response.

Set the minimum supported PHP version to 8.2 and officially support 8.2, 8.3, and 8.4. This balances adoption with maintainability by excluding EOL versions (<=8.1) while retaining a broad, still-secure user base.

- Composer constraint: "php": "^8.2"
- CI matrix: 8.2, 8.3, 8.4 (lowest-deps on 8.2; latest-deps on 8.4)
- Coding guidelines: Leverage PHP 8.2 features (readonly classes, true types for constants, intersection/union improvements, improved enums), and standard library APIs available since 8.2; avoid polyfills for <8.2.
- Dependency policy: Only depend on libraries that also support >=8.2.
- Release policy: Raising the minimum PHP version will be treated as a breaking change and only occur in a new major release, aligned with upstream PHP security timelines.
- Documentation: Clearly state requirements and migration guidance for users on 8.1 or earlier.
- Security posture: Align with supported PHP branches to minimize risk and reduce maintenance of version-specific code paths.
- Rationale trade-off: Choosing 8.2 preserves a large user base still on a security-supported branch while enabling modern language features and simplifying the test matrix.

## Decision
We will adopt a release strategy centered on small, frequent, incremental deployments to reduce risk, accelerate feedback, and deliver user value continuously.

- Implement trunk-based development with short-lived branches and small pull requests to minimize merge risk and cycle time.
- Establish a fully automated CI/CD pipeline with mandatory unit, integration, security, and regression tests to gate every change.
- Decouple deployment from release using feature flags, dark launches, and configuration toggles to enable safe, progressive exposure.
- Use progressive delivery techniques (canary releases, blue/green, phased rollouts) and instant rollback capabilities to mitigate production risk.
- Maintain strict backward compatibility for public interfaces; apply schema/data migrations via expand-and-contract patterns.
- Target a default cadence of daily deploys (or more frequent where feasible), with the capacity for on-demand hotfixes.
- Enforce release readiness criteria (green pipeline, observability coverage, runbooks) and post-deploy monitoring with SLO-aligned alerting.
- Version services and artifacts clearly (semantic versioning where applicable) and document change logs for transparency.
- Limit batch size by prioritizing work to keep changes small, independently releasable, and user-focused.

This approach becomes the default for all services; exceptions require explicit approval with a documented risk and rollback plan.

Adopt Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 across all public deliverables to provide clear upgrade expectations and avoid surprise breaking changes.

- Version format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 2.3.5).
- MAJOR: Introduces backward-incompatible changes to public APIs, CLIs, configuration, on-disk formats, or network protocols. Requires explicit migration notes.
- MINOR: Adds backward-compatible functionality and deprecations; no removals. Deprecations must be documented and warned at runtime/compile-time where applicable.
- PATCH: Backward-compatible bug fixes and security updates; no new features.

Pre-releases and metadata:
- Use pre-release tags: -alpha.N, -beta.N, -rc.N (stability increases from alpha→rc).
- Build metadata (+meta) is internal-only and not used for distribution channels.
- No breaking changes allowed between RC and the final release.

Deprecation policy:
- Features slated for removal must be deprecated for at least one subsequent MINOR release before removal in a MAJOR release.
- Provide clear migration guides and automated tooling where feasible.

APIs and services:
- Client libraries and SDKs follow SemVer strictly.
- HTTP/GRPC APIs expose stable major versions (e.g., /v1); changes within a major must be backward-compatible. Breaking API changes require a new major API version and a deprecation window for the previous major.

Release and distribution:
- Tag source control with vX.Y.Z; publish signed release artifacts and CHANGELOG entries per release.
- Container images and packages are tagged with full versions; latest moves only on stable releases (no pre-releases).
- Maintain an LTS line per designated major; security patches may be backported as PATCH releases.

Dependency constraints:
- Use caret/tilde ranges aligned to SemVer; avoid pinning except for known incompatibilities.

Compliance:
- Changes must include compatibility impact assessment; CI enforces version bump correctness and changelog updates.

Adopt the Parameter Object pattern and constructor injection using a single, cohesive PresenterDependencies object per presenter. Group related collaborators and configuration into immutable value objects (e.g., ViewPorts, DataSources, Formatters, FeatureFlags, Tracing) to replace long primitive/instance parameter lists. Each presenter will expose a single initializer that accepts its PresenterDependencies and an optional PresenterConfig (for feature toggles and non-essential behavior), both with sensible defaults.

Provide factories (PresenterFactory) that assemble PresenterDependencies from the application’s DI container/composition root. Factories shield callers from dependency composition details and enable per-context overrides (e.g., tests, previews). For optional or environment-specific values, use builder methods on the factory (not on the presenter) to maintain presenter immutability. Do not use a Service Locator inside presenters.

Set a soft cap of 5 direct fields inside PresenterDependencies; when nearing the cap, refactor into nested cohesive value objects to maintain readability and intent. Enforce compile-time safety with non-nullable required fields and explicit Optional types for truly optional collaborators.

Migration: deprecate current multi-parameter initializers; introduce new initializers with PresenterDependencies/PresenterConfig; provide adapter factories that map old call sites to the new objects. Tests should construct minimal PresenterDependencies with test doubles via factory helpers.

Outcomes: reduced initializer churn, clearer dependency semantics, improved testability, and a stable API surface as presenters evolve without proliferating initializer parameters.

Adopt an in-repo Infrastructure-as-Code model: co-locate Terraform with each service/application in the same repository and deprecate the separate nulterra repo.

- Repository layout: add an /infra directory per service with /modules (service-local), /envs/{dev,staging,prod}, and environment-specific variable files. Shared, cross-service modules will be published to our internal Terraform Registry (or a dedicated modules repo) and consumed via versioned sources.
- State and execution: maintain remote state per environment (e.g., Terraform Cloud/S3+DynamoDB) with strict workspace/state separation. Continue using PR-driven plans and protected applies via CI/CD with OIDC-based credentials.
- Workflow: all infra changes follow the same branch/PR/review policy as app code. CI runs terraform fmt/validate/tflint, plan on PR, and gated apply on merge to main for targeted environments. Hotfixes follow established release procedures.
- Governance: use CODEOWNERS to require infra reviewers; enforce policy-as-code (Sentinel/OPA) in CI and/or Terraform Cloud. Apply drift detection on a schedule and block manual changes outside Terraform.
- Security: manage secrets via managed secret stores; no plaintext secrets in code or state. Limit CI permissions to least-privilege and environment-specific roles.
- Versioning and traceability: tag releases that include infra changes; include change logs in PRs. Module versions are pinned and updated via dependabot/renovate.
- Migration: freeze nulterra to read-only, migrate active stacks into service repos incrementally, preserve state backends, and archive nulterra after completion.

This decision reduces coordination overhead, keeps infra changes close to code, improves review fidelity, and shortens delivery cycles while retaining modularity and governance through a shared module registry and CI policies.

We will migrate the Pact Broker from Heroku to our AWS platform to remove free-tier database limits, consolidate operational ownership, and meet security/compliance requirements. The Broker will run on ECS Fargate behind an ALB within our VPC; PostgreSQL will be provided by Amazon RDS (multi-AZ, automated backups). Secrets will be managed via AWS Secrets Manager; observability via CloudWatch metrics/logs and alarms; TLS via ACM on the ALB; access restricted via security groups and private subnets, with public access through Route53-managed DNS.

Migration approach:
- Provision AWS infrastructure (VPC, ECS service, ALB, RDS, Secrets, IAM roles, backups, monitoring).
- Stand up a staging Broker and validate compatibility (pactflow/pact-broker image, plugins, webhooks).
- Plan a short maintenance window; freeze Pact publication on Heroku.
- Snapshot/export Heroku Postgres; import to RDS; verify integrity (counts, checksum of critical tables).
- Cut over DNS to AWS ALB; monitor error rates and performance; keep Heroku in read-only as rollback for 48 hours.
- Decommission Heroku after stabilization.

Non-functional targets:
- Availability: ≥99.9% (RDS Multi-AZ, ECS min tasks=2 across AZs).
- Backups: daily RDS snapshots with 30-day retention; point-in-time recovery enabled.
- Cost control: right-size Fargate task and RDS instance; apply scheduled scaling and budgets/alerts.

Risks/mitigations:
- Migration data drift: enforce write freeze; validate post-import.
- Latency for CI/CD publishers: place ALB publicly; consider WAF and IP allowlists if needed.
- Operational burden: codify infra in Terraform and add runbooks.

This decision replaces the Heroku deployment; paid Heroku plans will not be pursued.

We will deploy OPG Metrics as an isolated workload within the opg-management AWS account using strong intra-account boundaries to maximize portability and prevent blast-radius overlap with other products.

- Provision a dedicated VPC (subnets, route tables, gateways) with no implicit peering; allow only explicitly approved connectivity via VPC endpoints/peering/TGW as needed.
- Use fully separate IAM roles, policies, instance profiles, and KMS keys scoped to OPG Metrics resources; deny access from other product roles by default.
- Maintain independent IaC (separate repository, Terraform/AWS CDK stacks, and remote state backends) with environment/account parameterization to enable one-click redeploy to a new account.
- Use distinct resource namespaces and isolation boundaries: unique S3 buckets, CloudWatch log groups and metric namespaces, EventBridge buses, SNS/SQS queues, and DynamoDB tables. Apply strict tagging to all resources for governance and cost allocation.
- Expose integrations through well-defined, network- and auth-boundary interfaces (e.g., API Gateway/ALB with IAM/OIDC, SQS/SNS, EventBridge) rather than shared internal resources.
- Maintain separate CI/CD pipelines, artifact stores, and runtime configurations (SSM Parameter Store/Secrets Manager) to eliminate coupling with other workloads.
- Isolate observability and operations: dedicated dashboards, alarms, traces, budgets, and quotas; no shared alarm actions or dashboards.
- Prepare for future account portability by avoiding account-specific hardcoding (ARNs/domains), using variables and service discovery, and supporting cross-account roles for migration and data egress.

This approach keeps OPG Metrics operationally and performance-isolated while enabling straightforward replication to a new account if required.

Adopt a paired, hypothesis-driven evaluation comparing the base and gamma models on the same holdout dataset, using McNemar’s chi-squared test as the primary statistical test.

- Test: Construct a 2x2 contingency table of per-example outcomes (base correct/incorrect vs. gamma correct/incorrect). Use McNemar’s test with continuity correction; if discordant counts are small (n<25), use the exact McNemar test.
- Metrics and thresholds: Primary metric is accuracy (or task-specific 0/1 success). Significance level α=0.05. Require both statistical significance and a minimum practical improvement (e.g., ≥1.5% absolute). Report 95% CIs via bootstrap on paired outcomes.
- Dataset and pairing: Evaluate on a fixed, stratified, and representative holdout; identical preprocessing and prompts for both models. Ensure pairing at the example level; if pairing is impossible, fall back to a chi-squared test of independence on matched cohorts with propensity controls.
- Multiple comparisons: If evaluating across multiple strata or secondary metrics, control family-wise error via Holm–Bonferroni; require no significant regressions in critical strata.
- Power and size: Perform a priori power analysis to target ≥80% power for the chosen MDE; expand sample if underpowered.
- Decision rule: Promote gamma for the targeted scope if criteria are met and no critical regressions are observed; otherwise retain base. Log all per-example outputs, seeds, and configuration for auditability and reproducibility.

Decision: Implement a unified authorization policy that computes effective permissions by evaluating both authorship and ACL sources through a single authorization service.

- Sources: Two pluggable policy providers feed the engine: OwnershipPolicy (depositor/proxy authorship) and ACLPolicy (user/group ACLs). Both are always consulted.
- Precedence: Explicit Deny entries take precedence over all Allows, including OwnershipPolicy grants. Platform administrators are the sole bypass.
- Ownership baseline: OwnershipPolicy grants a baseline capability set (e.g., view, edit, manage) to the depositor and designated proxy depositors. These are first-class grants but remain subject to explicit Deny.
- ACL evaluation: ACLs may target users or groups. Group membership resolution supports nested groups and dynamic groups where applicable. ACLs can be attached at the resource level and inherited from parent collections.
- Inheritance: Works inherit ACLs from their containing collections. Resource-level ACLs augment the inherited set. Because Deny has global precedence, inherited Deny cannot be overridden by a child Allow.
- Conflict resolution: Effective permission for a user/action is determined by:
  1) If user is platform admin → Allow.
  2) Else if any applicable ACL Deny → Deny.
  3) Else if OwnershipPolicy allows → Allow.
  4) Else if any applicable ACL Allow → Allow.
  5) Else → Deny.
- Performance: The authorization service caches effective permissions per (user, resource) with invalidation on ACL change, ownership change, membership change, or hierarchy changes. Batch evaluation is supported for listings.
- Auditability: All authorization decisions are explainable with a trace of contributing grants/denies, including inheritance origin, to support troubleshooting and compliance.
- Extensibility: Additional policy providers may be added without changing the decision logic, provided they emit Allow/Deny facts that participate in the same precedence rules.

Adopt a dual state-management strategy to control complexity:
- Use Redux Toolkit as the single source of truth for client (UI and domain) state that is shared across multiple features, influences rendering broadly, or requires cross-cutting coordination. Structure state by feature-based slices, normalize collections with createEntityAdapter, and access data via memoized selectors. Co-locate reducers/effects with features and expose a typed facade (hooks/selectors) per slice.
- Use TanStack Query (React Query) exclusively for server state (data fetched from/backed by APIs). Delegate caching, background refetching, synchronization, and request lifecycle to React Query; avoid duplicating server data in Redux.
- Keep ephemeral, strictly local UI state (transient inputs, toggles) in components via useState/useReducer. Use Context only for stable, low-frequency configuration (e.g., theme, i18n), not for rapidly changing data.

Implementation directives:
- Type everything with TypeScript; enforce selector-based access to Redux state.
- Isolate side effects: API interaction in React Query; non-API side effects in Redux middleware only if required.
- Establish clear promotion rules: promote state to Redux only when multiple distant consumers or persistence/undo/coordination is needed; otherwise keep local.
- Provide testing utilities for slices/selectors and Query hooks; add lint rules to prevent direct store access outside feature boundaries.

This decision reduces prop drilling, avoids duplicated sources of truth, and keeps state colocated with its lifecycle and performance characteristics.

## Decision
We will support first-class operation aliasing across namespaces to improve discoverability while preserving a single canonical definition per operation.

- Canonical source: Each op has exactly one canonical namespace and name; behavior, schema, ID, and versioning are defined only there.
- Aliases: Additional namespace-qualified names may reference the canonical op as pure aliases (no behavioral or signature divergence).
- Stability and compatibility: Introducing aliases is non-breaking; removing aliases follows standard deprecation policy with telemetry-informed grace periods.
- Resolution rules: Invocation resolves to the canonical op via alias metadata at compile/build time where possible, or at runtime via a lightweight registry. Ambiguities or collisions are disallowed at registration time.
- Introspection and tooling: Reflection, listing, and code generation surface aliases, but clearly indicate the canonical target. Documentation shows aliases and cross-links; search indexes include aliases.
- Error handling: Errors and metrics attribute to the canonical op but include the alias used when available for support diagnostics.
- Versioning: Aliases always point to a specific canonical version/variant; updating an alias target is a semver-minor change only if signatures remain identical.
- Constraints: No alias may alter defaults, validation, auth, rate limits, or side effects. Policy and quota evaluation occur on the canonical op.
- Governance: Alias creation requires API review to prevent namespace pollution; naming guidelines ensure predictable placement in common namespaces.
- Telemetry and lifecycle: We capture usage per alias to inform pruning and documentation. Deprecated aliases emit warnings before removal.
- Implementation: Introduce an alias registry with validation, conflict detection, and generation of forwarding stubs where needed; ensure SDKs/IDLs carry alias annotations.

Adopt a timezone-aware approach centered on “Europe/London” and replace date-fns for event date handling with a library that natively supports IANA time zones (Luxon), or use the Temporal API via @js-temporal/polyfill where runtime support is unavailable.

- Canonical model:
  - Persist event times as a tuple: { localDate: YYYY-MM-DD, localTime: HH:mm, zone: "Europe/London" }.
  - Additionally store the computed UTC instant for indexing and cross-system interoperability.
- Rendering:
  - Always format using the “Europe/London” zone, regardless of viewer device timezone/locale.
  - Prohibit use of JS Date without an explicit zone; avoid relying on implicit device timezone.
- Library choices:
  - Primary: Luxon (DateTime.fromObject({…, zone: 'Europe/London'})) for construction, conversion, and formatting.
  - Alternative/transition: Temporal.ZonedDateTime with zone "Europe/London" via @js-temporal/polyfill, once available natively we can drop the polyfill.
- Data ingress/egress:
  - On input, construct ZonedDateTime/DateTime in “Europe/London” and derive UTC.
  - On output, render strictly in “Europe/London”; if UTC is required by external APIs, provide the stored UTC instant.
- DST correctness:
  - Rely on IANA rules to handle BST/GMT transitions automatically; validate ambiguous or skipped local times (e.g., 01:30 at spring forward) and require explicit disambiguation on creation.
- Testing and safeguards:
  - Add unit tests around DST boundaries and random dates across multiple years.
  - Lint rule/code review check: disallow date-fns and Date without zone for event logic.
  - Migrate existing usages to Luxon/Temporal; add regression tests to ensure no device-local reformatting occurs.

This ensures all users see the event as it occurs in London time, independent of their device timezone, and removes date-fns-induced ambiguities.

## Decision
Adopt an offline-first content strategy: embed all medically relevant content in the app bundle to ensure full operability without network connectivity. For the initial release, all updates to content will be delivered via app releases. In subsequent phases, introduce an optional, signed, versioned content update mechanism that downloads and caches incremental content packs from a remote source (CMS/S3) when connectivity is available, without creating a runtime dependency on the network. The embedded content will always serve as the authoritative baseline and fallback. Content will be structured and versioned to allow safe diffs, integrity verification, and rollback. This approach prioritizes reliability in crisis scenarios while enabling faster iteration on content in the future, with clear separation between core embedded content and optional remotely updated content.

We will deprecate and remove “sites” from the codebase and converge on a single, core application focused on the article page, while retaining shared tooling via non-site packages.

- Effective immediately, we freeze creation of new sites and stop investing in sites-related functionality.
- Within the next release cycle, we will:
  - Identify and remove sites-specific code paths, configuration, and CI/CD logic.
  - Extract any generally useful tooling (linting configs, build scripts, type-checking, artifact-building) into shared, versioned packages and/or repo-level tasks.
  - Consolidate build and deployment pipelines to a single app target.
  - Archive or remove dormant/experimental site folders; if any contain reusable code, migrate that into non-site packages.
- We will provide a minimal project template (or template repo) for external teams, pointing to our shared packages and standards, rather than hosting additional sites in this repo.
- Documentation will be updated to reflect the single-app architecture, how to consume shared tooling, and how external teams can bootstrap independent projects.
- Success criteria:
  - Reduced build/CI time and complexity (fewer jobs/steps, faster runs).
  - Elimination of sites-related conditionals and code paths.
  - No feature work blocked by sites considerations.
- If a future, validated need arises for multiple projects, we will prefer modularization via shared packages and separate repositories over reintroducing in-repo “sites.” Any reintroduction would require a fresh ADR, explicit ownership, and resourcing.

Adopt a sharded ingress architecture by deploying multiple, independent NGINX ingress controller instances, each fronted by its own AWS load balancer, and partition application ingresses across these controllers using distinct IngressClasses. Decommission the single, cluster-wide ingress controller once migration is complete.

Key elements:
- Create a standard “ingress shard” profile (controller Deployment, Service, AWS LB, dashboards/alerts) with sane default resources and tuning.
- Route ingresses to a shard via ingressClassName; enforce selection via policy/OPA admission.
- Cap the number/complexity of ingresses per shard to keep NGINX configs well below the failure threshold (e.g., target <25K lines or similar measured limit); add new shards as needed.
- Prefer sharding by namespace or product domain to simplify ownership and blast-radius isolation.
- Automate shard provisioning and migration (IaC + pipeline), including health checks and rollback paths.
- Implement monitoring for config size, reload duration, worker SHM usage, and crash loops; auto-scale within shard bounds but avoid unbounded pod counts.
- Accept increased AWS LB cost as a trade-off for stability, isolation, and operability; track cost per shard and optimize where safe.
- Freeze creation of new ingresses on the legacy controller and migrate existing ingresses incrementally, validating each cutover with synthetic checks.
- Document SLOs per shard and establish runbooks for reload failures and shard saturation.

This decision reduces config size per controller, eliminates SHM-related crash loops, limits blast radius, and improves reliability at a manageable increase in cost.

Adopt Service Manager as the orchestrator for CI builds of contact-frontend so that the existing filtering logic for assets-frontend is applied. Specifically:
- Start contact-frontend via Service Manager in Jenkins (PR builder and post-merge builds), instead of running the service directly.
- Provide a curated application.conf to Service Manager that pins only the required assets-frontend version(s) for the acceptance tests (typically the latest), preventing multi-version startup.
- Update build-jobs configuration to include ASSETS_FRONTEND in withServiceManager and pass the application.conf explicitly to ensure only the targeted assets-frontend instance starts.
- Remove any direct start logic for contact-frontend in the pipeline that bypasses Service Manager, to avoid reintroducing the multi-version behavior.
- Add a guard in the pipeline to fail the build if multiple assets-frontend instances are detected.

We will adopt explicit, major-versioned URI path versioning for all HTTP APIs.

- All public endpoints will be rooted under a stable prefix and major version: /api/v{major}/{resource} (e.g., /api/v1/orders). The /new-api prefix is deprecated immediately and replaced by /api/v1.
- Within a major version, only backward-compatible, additive changes are allowed (e.g., new optional fields, new endpoints, new query params with safe defaults). No breaking changes in request/response shapes, semantics, or error codes.
- Any breaking change requires a new major version (v2, v3, …) with a distinct base path. There is no runtime version negotiation; the path determines the contract.
- Deprecation and sunset policy:
  - When releasing v{n+1}, v{n} remains supported for a defined overlap period (default 12 months; configurable per product).
  - Deprecations are communicated via Deprecation and Sunset HTTP headers, changelog, and release notes. Provide a migration guide for each new major version.
  - After the sunset date, v{n} is removed.
- Transition from /new-api:
  - /new-api will be aliased to /api/v1 for a short grace period (max 6 months), announced as deprecated, then removed.
  - No new functionality will be added under /new-api.
- Version discovery and documentation:
  - OpenAPI specs are published per major version at /api/v{major}/openapi.(json|yaml) and in docs with clear change logs.
  - Error formats, pagination, and conventions are fixed per major version and documented.
- Experimental features may be exposed as clearly labeled preview endpoints or fields within a major version only if they are opt-in and explicitly marked as non-stable; they can be removed before GA without breaking-contract guarantees. Previews must not be defaulted on.
- Internal services should follow the same scheme for consistency; gRPC or event schemas mirror this policy using major versioned packages/topics.
- Version identifiers follow semantic major semantics, but only the major appears in the URI. Minor/patch changes do not affect the path.

This decision ensures clarity, cacheability, and long-term evolution without ambiguity or reliance on “new” vs “old” labels.

We will adopt an HTTP-first client API that models all HTTP outcomes as first-class values instead of squeezing them into single-return/exception semantics.

- Responses are not thrown as exceptions for 4xx/5xx; they are returned as values. Exceptions are reserved only for transport-level failures (I/O, DNS, TLS, timeouts, circuit breaks).
- Use Java 17+ sealed interfaces (or a Result/Either-style sum type) to represent endpoint outcomes as a closed set of variants keyed by status codes (or ranges). Example: GetUserResponse = { Ok200(User), Accepted202(JobRef), NotFound404(Error), Conflict409(Error), ... }.
- Provide a general HttpResponse<T> value type (status, headers, body, trailers, request info) plus endpoint-specific mappers that lift HttpResponse into typed variants. Unexpected statuses are represented as UnexpectedStatus(HttpResponse<byte[]>).
- Error responses are decoded into typed error models based on Content-Type with access to raw payload for diagnostics. Headers and body are always preserved.
- Pluggable codecs (JSON, XML, protobuf, text, custom) via a Codec registry negotiated by Content-Type/Accept; supports streaming bodies where applicable.
- Encourage exhaustive handling with compiler-enforced pattern matching over sealed variants. Provide ergonomic helpers for common branches (is2xx(), on4xx(), etc.).
- Provide an endpoint DSL (or codegen from OpenAPI/JSON Schema) to declare expected variants and bind decoders, enabling compile-time safety and documentation generation.
- Observability (logging, metrics, tracing) attaches to the value-level responses; redaction rules apply to headers/body as configured.
- Policy concerns (retry, backoff, idempotency, deadlines) are configured externally and operate on response values and transport exceptions without conflating them with application errors.
- Offer adapters for common clients (RestTemplate, Feign, Retrofit, JAX-RS) to ease migration while preserving the value-based response model.

We will automate RC artifact creation and publication upon cutting or updating a release branch, removing the need for manual intervention or disabling diffcheck.

- Trigger: On release branch creation (and subsequent commits), the CI pipeline will run an RC build workflow.
- Behavior: RC builds run with diffcheck automatically bypassed for release branches to ensure artifacts are always produced, regardless of detected changes.
- Source of truth: Artifacts are built from the release branch commit; if the last dev build is the desired source, the workflow will fetch and promote the last green dev artifacts as a configurable option.
- Publication:
  - Multi-registry: Publish to the dedicated rc feed(s) with immutable, incrementing rc versions (e.g., 1.2.0-rc.N).
  - Single registry: Update rc tags (e.g., :1.2-rc, :rc-latest) atomically; avoid overwriting immutable digests.
- Idempotency: Re-running the workflow produces the same artifact for the same commit digest; rc.N increments only on content change or explicit force-republish.
- Governance: Introduce a release-rc-publish permission set and environment protection rules for rc feeds/registries.
- Configuration: Provide a project-level flag to opt out or enforce “promote dev artifacts” vs “rebuild from source.”
- Observability: Emit metrics and notifications on success/failure; include links to artifacts and tags. Failures do not block release branch creation but block downstream promotion gates.
- Backfill: Allow manual re-run to regenerate/publish RC artifacts for a given release branch commit without local scripting.
- Rollout: Enable by default for all services using the standard release workflow; legacy/custom pipelines may opt in via a shared reusable workflow.

## Decision
Adopt IAM roles and EC2 instance profiles as the default and mandatory mechanism for all AWS API access from workloads running on AWS. Prohibit the creation and use of long-lived IAM user access keys for CI/CD, Cloud Foundry components, and platform automation when those processes run on EC2. All platform components (e.g., Cloud Controller, RDS broker, blobstore clients), Concourse workers, BOSH directors/agents, and Terraform runners on EC2 must assume permissions via attached instance profiles and retrieve short-lived credentials from the instance metadata service (IMDSv2 required).

For processes not running on EC2 (e.g., developer laptops, ephemeral build runners off-cloud), use short-lived, federated role sessions via AWS SSO/IAM Identity Center or SAML/OIDC federation with STS AssumeRole. Configure tools to obtain credentials through credential_process (e.g., aws sso, aws-vault) rather than environment variables. Where environment variables are unavoidable, they must reference short-lived session credentials only.

Operational safeguards:
- Disable creation of new IAM user access keys in the account(s); migrate existing users to roles or SSO. Enforce via SCPs and IAM Access Analyzer.
- Rotate and decommission all existing static keys used by tooling; replace with roles and documented assume-role flows.
- Enforce IMDSv2 and least-privilege role policies; tag roles to specific services and workloads.
- Standardize SDK/CLI configuration to use the default credential provider chain so tools auto-discover instance profile/federated credentials without custom code.
- Implement automated secret scanning in repos/CI and detections for exposed keys; define immediate revocation/runbook for any detected leak.

This decision immediately applies to all new deployments. Existing systems must be remediated to roles/federation on a prioritized schedule, with break-glass static keys disallowed except by explicit, time-bound approval and monitoring.

Adopt a single, canonical hosting location for release artifacts in a dedicated, versioned object storage bucket fronted by a CDN (e.g., S3 or Swift behind CloudFront/Fastly) at releases.example.org. Artifacts (tarballs) will be immutable, content-addressable (include version and commit hash), and accompanied by signed checksums (SHA256 and GPG). Publication will be automated via CI/CD on tagged releases, with retention, lifecycle policies, and provenance metadata (build manifest) emitted at publish time.

The Extension Distributor will be reconfigured to reference and proxy/cache artifacts from this bucket rather than building/serving them itself. Serving tarballs directly from git release branches will be deprecated; existing URLs will receive 301 redirects to the canonical CDN URLs for backward compatibility. A grace period will be communicated before disabling legacy endpoints.

Operational controls:
- Bucket is write-restricted to CI release jobs; read is public via CDN with TLS.
- Lifecycle rules enforce long-term retention for GA releases and shorter retention for pre-releases; automatic Glacier/Cold storage for older artifacts.
- Multi-region replication enables disaster recovery; nightly integrity verification compares stored checksums.
- Naming scheme: /project/{name}/v{semver}/{name}-v{semver}-{commit|build}.tar.gz with corresponding .sha256 and .asc.
- Index and API endpoint provide machine-readable release metadata (JSON) for tooling.

This consolidates distribution, improves performance and reliability, enables auditability/signing, and reduces coupling to VCS infrastructure.

We will adopt a pragmatic, time-boxed decision-making approach that prioritizes reasonable, mainstream solutions over exhaustive analysis. Concretely:
- Use the Node.js ecosystem by default and prefer well-adopted, maintained libraries with permissive licenses (MIT/Apache-2.0), clear SemVer, active issue response, and recent releases.
- Apply the 80/20 rule: choose the simplest option that meets current requirements; avoid premature optimization and over-customization.
- Limit evaluation to the top 1–3 viable options with a strict research/prototyping timebox (60–120 minutes) and decide based on fit, maturity, and risk.
- Treat most choices as two-way doors: implement quickly and iterate. Escalate one-way door decisions (e.g., datastore selection, protocol commitments) via a lightweight RFC, still time-boxed.
- Prefer convention over configuration: adopt sane defaults (e.g., Node.js + TypeScript, Fastify/Express, PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker) unless a clear constraint requires deviation.
- Document assumptions, constraints, and rationale succinctly; set explicit revisit triggers (e.g., performance, maintainability, cost thresholds) to re-evaluate if expectations are not met.
This decision ensures timely, reasonable choices aligned with delivery goals while preserving the ability to change course when evidence warrants it.

We will make the unit-e project public with the 0.1 (testnet) milestone by opening all repositories necessary for external users to build, run, and contribute to the client and its ecosystem. Scope to be made public in this first step:
- Core client/source repository for unit-e (including build scripts)
- Protocol/specs and documentation repositories
- SDKs/examples/devtools required to interact with the testnet
- Website and user/developer documentation

Out of scope (remain private for now):
- Infrastructure/operations (deployment, CI/CD config with secrets, internal monitoring)
- Internal planning/notes, experimental/prototype repos not required for testnet
- Security reports and any repo containing credentials or third‑party licensed artifacts without redistribution rights

Preconditions before flipping visibility:
- Final content review and approval from all code owners
- Repository hygiene: remove or rotate any secrets; history scan completed
- Add/verify LICENSE, README, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY.md
- Set public repo settings: required reviews, protected branches, CI with secret masking, issue/PR templates, labels, CODEOWNERS
- Establish contribution policy (DCO or CLA) and release/tagging conventions

Process and timing:
- 5 business days of team-wide review of the repos in scope
- On approval, change visibility to public and announce testnet availability and contribution guidelines
- Track future candidates for opening in a follow-up ADR and milestones

Ongoing governance:
- Triage and respond publicly to issues/PRs; use milestones/labels for roadmap
- Publish security disclosure process in SECURITY.md with private reporting channel
- Periodically reassess remaining private repositories for openness as the project matures

## Decision
Adopt the GitLab Wiki as the canonical documentation source to comply with project guidelines, and integrate it into the repository checkout to avoid developer disconnect.

- Add the project’s GitLab Wiki repository as a Git submodule under /docs (or /wiki) in the main repository, using a relative URL to support forks and local clones.
- Treat the wiki submodule as read-only from the main repo; documentation changes are made via the wiki repository (through MRs or the wiki UI), preserving a single source of truth.
- Provide standard developer commands (e.g., make docs-init, make docs-update) to clone and update the submodule, ensuring the documentation is present in local checkouts by default.
- Configure CI to:
  - Verify the submodule is initialized and up to date on every pipeline.
  - Fail the build if the submodule commit is behind the wiki default branch, prompting a docs-update.
  - Publish built documentation artifacts if needed.
- Reference and deep-link the wiki prominently from README and CONTRIBUTING, with clear contribution guidelines and editorial ownership.
- For releases, record release notes and version-specific documentation in the wiki; when tagging code releases, also update the submodule pointer to the corresponding wiki commit to maintain traceability across time.
- Establish backup/retention by mirroring the wiki repository to the same backup policy as the code repo.

This decision satisfies the mandate to use the Wiki while keeping documentation accessible in local checkouts, ensuring coherence, discoverability, and CI-enforced synchronization.

We will standardize exports using explicit, layered “barrel” files with clear boundaries and no deep or wildcard re-exports.

- Public API surface: Only the package root index.ts defines the public API. It must contain explicit named exports and re-export only from immediate top-level directories/modules. No export *.
- Directory barrels: Each directory must contain an index.ts that explicitly re-exports only symbols from files within the same directory or its immediate children. No cross-directory or deep chain re-exports.
- No deep re-exports: A file may only be exported by its own directory index.ts; directory index.ts may only be exported by its parent’s index.ts, up to the package root. This enforces a single, predictable path to any exported symbol.
- Explicit over wildcard: All re-exports must be explicit named lists to make the surface grep-able and reviewable. No export * at any level.
- Visibility conventions: Files and directories not intended for export must be marked internal (e.g., filename suffix .internal.ts or directory _internal) and never re-exported.
- Tooling and policy: Add ESLint rules and CI checks to forbid export * and deep re-exports, and to require explicit exports in index.ts barrels. Require API snapshot or doc generation from the package root to verify the public surface.
- Migration: Incrementally refactor to the layered structure, starting at the package root; breaking changes to the public API require normal versioning procedures.

Implement the Privacy Policy and About Me as dedicated static routes (e.g., /privacy-policy and /about) that are accessible via global navigation (footer links and the app menu) but excluded from the map/spiral experience and any progression flows.

- Add a content metadata flag (excludeFromMap=true, excludeFromProgress=true) and update the map/spiral generation to filter out any node with this flag. These pages must never appear as nodes, steps, or checkpoints in the spiral scan.
- Ensure deep-linkability and direct access without gating; they must not block, pause, or reset the user’s spiral scanning session.
- Place persistent links in the footer and secondary navigation; do not include in primary pathfinding UI.
- Include the pages in the XML sitemap for SEO and legal discoverability, but exclude from internal “map” indices and any “start here/continue” logic. Allow search engine indexing; no noindex unless policy requires otherwise.
- Exclude these routes from engagement/progression analytics; track visits separately under “legal/system pages.”
- Ensure consistent theming but visually differentiate them as system pages (no progress controls, no map breadcrumbs).
- Add automated tests verifying the pages never render in map data structures, spiral traversal, recommendations, or “next up” queues, and that direct navigation works from global links.
- Document the metadata contract and map-builder filter so future system pages can be added without risking inclusion in the map.

Adopt ISO 8601 as the default date format. Specifically:
- Use the unambiguous, culture-neutral format YYYY-MM-DD for all dates generated by adr-tools (default strftime format: %F).
- Apply this default in all templates, filenames, and generated content where a date is included.
- Continue to support user overrides via ADR_DATE in config.sh. ADR_DATE remains a strftime-compatible pattern; if set, its value will be used verbatim without transformation.
- Do not alter or migrate existing ADRs; only newly generated entries adopt the new default.
- Preserve backwards compatibility in behavior and interfaces other than the default value change.

## Decision
Adopt a cloud-native, serverless-first architecture on a major public cloud (AWS or Azure) to minimize fixed infrastructure, operational overhead, and scaling costs. Primary execution will use pay-per-use compute (AWS Lambda or Azure Functions), managed API ingress (API Gateway or Azure API Management), managed messaging/queueing (SNS/SQS or Service Bus), and managed data services (DynamoDB/RDS or Cosmos DB/Azure SQL) to leverage auto-scaling and reduce maintenance.

For workloads not well-suited to serverless (e.g., long-running processes, specialized runtimes, or predictable high-throughput batch), deploy containers on fully managed container runtimes without cluster management (AWS Fargate or Azure Container Apps/Container Instances). Avoid self-managed Kubernetes, OpenShift, or on-premises deployments due to higher capital expenditure, licensing, and operational complexity. Managed Kubernetes (EKS/AKS) will be considered only if clear needs arise (e.g., complex service mesh, advanced scheduling) that cannot be met by serverless/managed containers at acceptable cost.

All infrastructure will be provisioned via Infrastructure as Code (e.g., Terraform) with automated CI/CD, cost guardrails (budgets, alerts, tags), and observability baked in. Multi-AZ/high-availability configurations will be used by default. This decision will be revisited if regulatory constraints mandate on-premises, if sustained workloads make reserved capacity cheaper than serverless/managed containers, or if portability requirements materially outweigh operational cost benefits.

Adopt a client-side BookmarkFactory backed by a hydrated, per-page ContentIndex to construct complete Bookmark objects from an item id without remote lookups or encoding full metadata in the link.

- Render a single JSON payload (e.g., in a script[type="application/json"] tag or initial state) containing the minimal bookmarkable metadata for items present on the page (id, canonical URL, source, title, etc.). Hydrate a ContentIndex keyed by id at page load.
- Replace javascript: links with a semantic control (e.g., <button class="bookmark" data-id="gbj1jf">) and delegate clicks to a handler that resolves the id via BookmarkFactory to a Bookmark object sourced from ContentIndex.
- Call the existing application.bookmarks.add(bookmark) unchanged. No additional parameters are added to add(), and no per-click network lookups are performed.
- If an id is absent in ContentIndex, fail fast with a user-visible error or a no-op, and optionally log for diagnostics; do not attempt on-demand fetching.
- For pages that cannot be hydrated (e.g., legacy surfaces), provide an optional, separately versioned initializer to inject the necessary metadata into ContentIndex before user interaction.
- Deprecate javascript: href usage for security and accessibility; rely on unobtrusive JS and progressive enhancement.

This keeps the add API stable, avoids baking all metadata into DOM links, prevents runtime lookups, and ensures bookmarks remain self-contained snapshots derived from the page’s already-available data.

Adopt a CI-generated, versioned flist as the canonical delivery artifact for hosted 3Bot, replacing runtime cloning/build steps with direct runtime boot from the flist. The deployment system will:

- Pull a signed, immutable flist by content digest (default “stable”), with optional “canary” channel for progressive rollout.
- Treat the flist as a fully built, ready-to-run image containing all runtime dependencies, eliminating git clone and install phases.
- Externalize configuration and secrets via environment variables and mounted overlays; persist state on dedicated volumes to keep the flist stateless and replaceable.
- Enforce supply-chain integrity: CI produces SBOMs, runs vulnerability scans, and signs flists; deployment verifies signatures and digests before activation.
- Enable zero-downtime upgrades and fast rollback by switching digests and restarting; keep the last N digests cached for rapid fallback.
- Provide architecture-specific flists and minimum OS/runtime requirements; maintain compatibility tests against dependent services.
- Integrate health checks and post-start validation; promote canary to stable automatically upon SLO-compliant telemetry, otherwise auto-rollback.
- Maintain deterministic releases via semantic version tags mapped to digests; “latest” only for non-production.
- Update documentation, tooling, and observability to reflect flist-first operations; deprecate legacy clone/install paths with a time-boxed sunset period.

This decision reduces deployment time, standardizes artifacts, improves reliability and security, and ensures that hosted 3Bot instances are always up to date through controlled, verifiable rollouts.

We will implement versioned, structured, and immutable documentation per project using a docs-as-code approach.

- Structure: Each project will have its own top-level directory and documentation source co-located with its code repository (e.g., /docs). Published URLs will follow /docs/{project}/{version}/ with /docs/{project}/latest/ aliasing the default branch.
- Versioning: Documentation will be versioned by release tags (e.g., v1.2.0) and long-lived support branches (e.g., 1.x). Past versions are immutable; only “latest” updates with main. Semantic versioning will be used for labels. Each release produces a frozen doc build.
- Tooling: Adopt a static site generator with native versioning support (e.g., MkDocs + mike or Docusaurus). A central docs site will aggregate projects while preserving per-project/version boundaries and navigation.
- Publishing: CI/CD will build and publish docs on every tagged release and on main merges. Artifacts are deployed to versioned paths on object storage/CDN. Indexes and search are scoped to the active project/version.
- Governance: Owners must update docs within the code PRs. No force-push or deletion of published versions; deprecations are marked, not removed. A retention policy keeps all GA versions and the last two minors of EOL lines.
- Migration: Freeze the current flat directory, add redirects to the new structure, and backfill at least the last two released versions per project from Git history. New contributions must follow the structured, versioned model.

Adopt ECMAScript Modules (ESM) as the application’s sole module system and migrate all source code from CommonJS (require/module.exports) to ESM (import/export).

- Set package.json: "type": "module" for the application. All source files remain .js; use .cjs only where CommonJS is unavoidable (e.g., legacy configs).
- Update all imports/exports to ESM syntax and require explicit file extensions in relative imports (e.g., ./util.js).
- Replace __filename and __dirname with fileURLToPath(import.meta.url) and dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)).
- For consuming CommonJS dependencies or JSON where needed, use Node’s ESM interop:
  - Prefer native ESM-compatible imports; otherwise rely on default import semantics for CJS.
  - Where necessary (e.g., JSON, dynamic module resolution), use createRequire(import.meta.url).
- Enable top-level await where appropriate; avoid mixing ESM and CJS within the same module.
- Enforce the change via lint rules (e.g., no-commonjs) and CI checks.
- Baseline runtime: Node.js ≥ 18 LTS. Tooling (test runner, bundler, linters) will be configured for ESM mode; any tools lacking ESM support will be replaced or isolated behind .cjs shims.
- Deprecate and remove require() usage from the application codebase; any remaining third-party CJS usage is isolated at module boundaries with explicit interop.
- Documentation and coding standards are updated to reflect ESM-only practices, and migration changes are applied in a single coordinated refactor to avoid mixed module graphs.

Adopt a variant resolution model with base-overlays and explicit alias-to-variant mapping to eliminate duplication and enable controlled scratch org behavior.
