- Plan for growth with features available in PostgreSQL/managed offerings: read replicas for scale-out reads, partitioning for large tables, and indexing strategies guided by query observability. Defer sharding or polyglot persistence until justified by measured needs.
- Expose data via the API service; no direct client access to the database.
- Reassess in the future if workload characteristics change substantially (e.g., high-throughput time-series, full-text/search-heavy, or analytics), at which point specialized datastores may be introduced alongside PostgreSQL.

We will store ADRs under the repository root at docs/adr using the filename pattern NNNN-title-with-dashes.md.

- Directory: docs/adr
- Filename pattern: 4-digit, zero-padded sequential ID, a hyphen, then a lowercase kebab-case title; e.g., 0001-record-architecture-decisions.md
- Title normalization: lowercase ASCII, spaces to dashes, non-alphanumeric removed, multiple dashes collapsed
- ID policy: monotonically increasing, unique, and immutable once created; new ADRs always take the next available ID
- Index/discovery: adr-cli will list ADRs by scanning docs/adr for files matching ^\d{4}-.*\.md$
- Supersession: handled via ADR content (Status/Supersedes/Superseded by), no renames of existing files
- Configurability: adr-cli allows overriding the base directory and padding width, but the default remains docs/adr with 4-digit IDs for compatibility with adr-tools

Adopt Domain-Driven Design to define domains and bounded contexts as the primary organizing principle for all microservices. Establish and maintain a canonical Context Map, versioned in the architecture repo, as the single source of truth for domain boundaries, upstream/downstream relationships, and integration patterns.

Introduce a centralized service catalog (e.g., Backstage) as the authoritative inventory for all services, capturing owner, domain, lifecycle state, SLOs, APIs (OpenAPI), events (AsyncAPI), dependencies, data ownership, and compliance tags. Make registration in the catalog and linking to the Context Map mandatory for deployment.

Standardize architectural documentation per service: C4 diagrams (C1–C3), ADRs, API contracts, data contracts, and dependency manifests. Require change proposals via lightweight RFCs for boundary or domain changes and update the Context Map accordingly.

Enforce boundaries via automated governance: CI rules and architectural fitness functions that block forbidden cross-context dependencies, unowned data access, and undocumented integrations. Provide service templates and paved paths that encode these rules.

Instrument runtime visibility with tracing, service discovery, and dependency graphs to continuously validate the modeled architecture against reality; trigger alerts on drift. Conduct periodic (e.g., quarterly) architecture reviews per domain to assess cohesion, coupling, and redundancy; apply a consolidation/sunsetting policy when misalignment is detected.

Make product teams domain stewards with clear ownership and accountability for their bounded contexts and interfaces.

We will implement the client as a Progressive Web App (PWA) to run uniformly on mobile and desktop, leveraging installability and native-like UX. Offline capability will be provided via a Service Worker (generated with Workbox) for asset caching and Firebase Cloud Firestore’s built-in offline persistence (IndexedDB-backed) for data caching and queueing of writes while offline. Data access will use the Firebase Web SDK (Firestore + Auth) to minimize setup and fetching code via real-time listeners and straightforward CRUD APIs. Authentication will use Firebase Authentication to avoid custom auth flows and enable seamless multi-device usage.

The PWA will be the primary distribution; on desktop and mobile it will be installable directly from the browser. If a native wrapper is required, we will optionally package the same codebase with Tauri/Electron (desktop) and TWA/Capacitor (mobile) without altering data/access layers.

Key constraints:
- Single codebase for all platforms.
- Service Worker + Workbox for offline asset caching.
- Firestore offline persistence enabled by default; IndexedDB as storage.
- Firebase Security Rules govern access; no custom backend required initially.
- Minimal integration code: Firebase SDK initialization, Auth provider, Firestore collection/document listeners.

We will standardize all API resource identifiers to a single, consistent convention:

- Each resource representation MUST include an id field (lowercase) as the primary identifier.
- The id value MUST be a string UUID (RFC 4122), lowercase hex with hyphens (canonical textual format). Internally generated numeric or composite keys MUST NOT be exposed as primary identifiers.
- References to other resources MUST use camelCase foreign key fields in the form <resourceName>Id (e.g., userId, orderId), using the same UUID format.
- JSON field names across responses MUST use camelCase; id and <resourceName>Id fields MUST NOT appear as ID, Id, identifier, or other variants.
- Error payloads, webhooks, and event messages MUST follow the same identifier naming and format.
- Query parameters for filtering, sorting, and path parameters MUST mirror these names (e.g., ?userId=..., /users/{id}).

Backward compatibility and rollout:

- In current API version(s), we will add the standardized id and <resourceName>Id fields while continuing to emit existing legacy identifier fields. Legacy fields are deprecated immediately.
- We will maintain legacy fields for two minor release cycles (or 6 months, whichever is longer), then remove them in the next major version.
- OpenAPI/JSON Schema will be updated to reflect the new fields and deprecate legacy ones. Changelogs and migration guides will be published.
- A static analysis/linting rule and contract tests will enforce the convention for all new and modified endpoints.

Special cases:

- For resources with composite or natural keys, expose a stable synthetic id and, if needed, include components under a key object without using them as primary identifiers.

Adopt per-request API versioning via an explicit HTTP request header and opaque pass-through in the client library. The library will support a client-level defaultApiVersion and a per-request override; when neither is set, no version header is sent and the server’s default is used. The version value is not validated or transformed by the library (opaque string), ensuring forward compatibility with server versions unknown to the library and backward compatibility by deferring to server defaults.

Details:
- Header: send API-Version: <string> on each request when specified. Do not encode version in URL paths or query parameters to avoid breaking links and allow resource-specific evolution.
- Client API: expose configuration for defaultApiVersion and allow request-scoped apiVersion to override. Environment variable support (e.g., API_VERSION) can set the default non-invasively.
- Response handling: capture and expose the server’s API-Version response header. If the server returns a different version than requested, surface this in the response metadata and optionally emit a warning hook/callback without failing the request.
- Error handling: propagate server errors (e.g., 400/406 for unsupported version) without client-side retries or coercion. Do not attempt automatic downgrades/upgrades.
- Compatibility: unchanged clients continue working (no header sent → server default). New clients can target newer versions immediately by setting the header, even if the library is not updated.
- Documentation: specify supported header semantics, examples, and guidance for setting global vs per-request versions.

Axiomatic will grant dir2consul access to GitHub configuration repositories via short‑lived, runtime-scoped GitHub App installation tokens delivered through Nomad/Vault integration.

- Register a fine‑grained GitHub App scoped to the required org/repos with read-only contents permission.
- Store the App’s private key, App ID, and installation IDs in Vault; do not use long‑lived PATs or static SSH keys.
- Enable Vault’s GitHub App secrets engine (or approved internal signer) to mint short‑lived installation tokens (TTL ≤ 1h) on demand.
- Configure the Nomad job with Vault integration and a Vault Agent sidecar to authenticate and template the token into the task as an environment variable or file with strict permissions; disable token persistence in logs and artifacts.
- dir2consul will clone/pull over HTTPS using the ephemeral token (no SSH), limited to the required repos.
- Enforce network egress policy to allow only github.com over HTTPS from the job allocation.
- Scope and rotate credentials by repository/org as needed; each job run obtains a fresh token. Revoke on job completion and rely on TTL expiry for cleanup.
- Implement log redaction for token patterns and fail the job if token retrieval or scope validation fails.
- As an exception path where HTTPS tokens are disallowed, provision per-repo read-only deploy keys managed in Vault and injected per job, but prefer the GitHub App flow for centralized control and auditability.

## Decision
- Adopt Java 17 LTS with Spring Boot 3.x as the primary backend platform to build RESTful services and background jobs, leveraging Spring Web, Spring Data, Spring Security, and Actuator for observability.
- Use Gradle as the build tool with dependency locking and version catalogs; package and run as container images via Buildpacks (Paketo) for consistent, reproducible builds.
- Standardize on JUnit 5 (JUnit Jupiter) as the unit testing framework, with Mockito for mocking, AssertJ for fluent assertions, and Spring’s Test slices (e.g., @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) for focused tests.
- Use Testcontainers to run integration tests against real dependencies (e.g., PostgreSQL, Kafka/Redis) in ephemeral containers as part of CI.
- Establish test quality gates: minimum 80% line and branch coverage for business logic modules measured with JaCoCo; enforce mutation testing (Pitest) on critical domains.
- Apply the testing pyramid: fast deterministic unit tests as the foundation, component and slice tests in the middle, and limited end-to-end tests on critical paths.
- Enforce static analysis and code style via SpotBugs, Checkstyle (or Google Java Format), and Error Prone; integrate all checks and tests into CI required gates.
- Provide a project template (archetype) with the chosen stack, testing libraries, example tests, and preconfigured CI to accelerate onboarding and ensure consistency across services.

All repositories in the Libero GitHub organization must follow a product-qualified naming convention to ensure attribution and avoid clashes:

- Repository naming: <product>-<component> (lowercase, hyphen-separated). Examples: journal-article-store, reviewer-article-store, publisher-api-gateway.
- Cross-product/shared assets use the libero- prefix (or a neutral domain name) without a product prefix. Examples: libero-schema, libero-tooling.
- Package, module, Docker image, Helm chart, and service names must mirror the repository naming to prevent collisions in build and runtime ecosystems.
- Repository description must begin with the owning product name in brackets, e.g., [Journal] Article storage service.
- GitHub Topics must include product:<product> and domain:<domain> (e.g., product:journal, domain:content), plus shared when applicable.
- README must include a Product section linking to the originating product and a Scope section clarifying whether it is product-specific or shared.
- When a project becomes shared or changes ownership, the repository MUST be renamed to reflect its new scope and topics/descriptions updated accordingly.
- New repositories must be approved against this convention in the creation checklist; CI should validate naming and topic presence.

This convention applies immediately to new projects and will be retrofitted to existing ones through a scheduled rename and migration plan.

Adopt the existing target as the default solution, pending a short, timeboxed evaluation. We will integrate and test the existing target against our functional requirements and baseline acceptance criteria (correctness, performance, stability, extensibility, and minimal configuration). If it meets these needs, we will standardize on it and deprecate our custom target, retaining it only for niche use cases requiring advanced or “fancy” formatting not supported upstream.

Actions:
- Run a 1–2 sprint spike to prototype the existing target in our pipeline/environment.
- Define and execute a compatibility matrix covering our key scenarios and formats.
- Compare output fidelity with our current custom target; allow minor cosmetic differences.
- Assess extension points and theming options to cover foreseeable formatting needs.
- Establish rollout and rollback plans; keep the custom target behind a feature toggle during transition.

Outcomes:
- If the existing target satisfies requirements, switch to it by default, document configuration, and archive our custom target with a clear reactivation path for exceptional formatting needs.
- If gaps are discovered that materially impact outcomes and cannot be reasonably extended, revert to our custom target and document the deltas as future contributions or plugins.

Rationale:
- Favor reducing maintenance burden and leveraging upstream/community support while preserving an escape hatch for specialized formatting demands.

Adopt an automated execution model for the Diamond-Square algorithm with optional observability hooks, replacing manual step-through as the default interaction. Provide a high-level API (and CLI entry point) that runs the full algorithm to completion given size, seed, and roughness parameters, returning the final heightmap. Expose optional callbacks/events (e.g., onSquare, onDiamond, onIterationComplete) and a configurable snapshot interval to support debugging, visualization, and educational tooling without imposing step-by-step control on typical users.

Retain step-through mode only as a non-default debugging feature, gated via a flag, to avoid UI/UX complexity and performance penalties in standard workflows. Ensure deterministic runs via explicit RNG seeding and include structured logging and metrics (iteration count, extrema, variance) to aid diagnosis when step mode is disabled. Provide a lightweight preview renderer and the ability to export intermediate states when observability is enabled.

This decision prioritizes usability and performance for common use cases while preserving sufficient introspection for development and learning. It simplifies the public surface to “run to completion” with tunable parameters, supports reproducibility, and keeps advanced step-level control available without burdening the default experience.

Adopt trunk-based development with Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and immutable, annotated Git tags to represent releases (e.g., v2.3.1). The release name is the Git tag; the commit SHA is resolved directly from the tag. All releases are built from the main branch at the tagged commit. For supported majors, create maintenance branches (release/vX) exclusively for backports and patch/minor releases, tagged likewise.

Establish per-network deployments that track an explicitly configured release tag. Deployment URLs include the network identifier and the major version only, ensuring stability across non-breaking updates and intentional change on breaking updates. Example:
- https://{network}.trubudget.example.com/v{MAJOR}/ → always points to the latest v{MAJOR} tag selected for that network.
- Minor and patch upgrades within the same major do not change the URL.
- When a breaking change is introduced (MAJOR increment), the URL changes to …/v{NEW_MAJOR}/.

CI/CD publishes artifacts for each tag and maintains per-major “channel” aliases (e.g., latest-v2) for convenience. Each network’s environment configuration selects either a specific tag (vX.Y.Z) or the per-major channel, enabling networks to run different versions independently. Hotfixes for older majors are produced from the corresponding release/vX branch and tagged (vX.Y.Z+1), without affecting other networks.

Summary of guarantees:
- Tag-to-commit is one-to-one and immutable.
- Multiple networks can run different versions concurrently.
- Deployment URLs remain stable for non-breaking changes and change only on MAJOR increments.

Decision: Octagon components are stateless, pure view primitives that render solely from props. All application, session, and view state (e.g., active/open/selected/value) must be owned and managed by the consuming application and passed into Octagon via explicit, controlled props (e.g., <OctoNavItem active />). Octagon must not embed internal state that affects visible or semantic output, routing, persistence, or business logic. Components may expose callbacks (e.g., onSelect, onOpenChange) to notify the host app of user intent; the app then updates its own state and re-renders with new props.

Uncontrolled or stateful variants are not provided. Defaults influence appearance only and must not imply internal source-of-truth state. Naming and API conventions must make controllable state explicit (active, open, selected, checked, value), with corresponding aria attributes derived from props.

Exceptions are limited to ephemeral, non-authoritative concerns that do not outlive a render cycle or alter the declared UI state: internal refs, layout measurements, transient animation bookkeeping, memoization, and focus management where required for accessibility—but these must not serve as the state of record and must be resettable on re-mount.

This decision ensures deterministic, reload-safe, SSR-friendly, testable components, preserves top-down “config via props” React patterns, and keeps Octagon a portable, declarative view layer.

We will introduce two new environment variables, ADR_EDITOR and ADR_VISUAL, to allow users to choose dedicated editors for ADR authoring without changing their system defaults. The tool will resolve the editor to launch using the following precedence:

- When a visual editor is explicitly requested (e.g., via a future --visual flag or when the environment signals a GUI context): ADR_VISUAL → VISUAL → ADR_EDITOR → EDITOR → built-in fallback.
- In all other cases: ADR_EDITOR → EDITOR → ADR_VISUAL → VISUAL → built-in fallback.

If a command-line flag or configuration value specifying an editor is provided, it will take precedence over all environment variables. This preserves backward compatibility while enabling fine-grained control for ADR workflows.

Both ADR_EDITOR and ADR_VISUAL accept:
- Executable names discoverable via PATH or absolute paths.
- Optional arguments (e.g., “code -w”, “vim -f”).
- Quoted paths with spaces.

No behavior changes will occur for users who do not set these variables. Documentation and help text will be updated to clearly describe precedence, examples, and cross-platform usage notes (including waiting-for-editor semantics). Automated tests will cover resolution logic, argument handling, and fallbacks on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Adopt a criteria-driven, token-aligned policy for introducing utility classes. We add a new utility only when all of the following are satisfied:
- Reusability: The property/value is needed across multiple components or features (current or forecast), with a threshold of ≥3 distinct components or recurring patterns across surfaces.
- Composability: The utility is orthogonal, side‑effect‑free, and combines predictably with existing utilities (no hidden resets or shorthands).
- Token alignment: Values come from our design tokens or curated scales; no ad‑hoc values embedded in class names.
- Clarity over custom CSS: The utility meaningfully reduces bespoke CSS and cognitive load versus writing component‑local rules.
- Theming/RTL/accessibility: The utility does not undermine contrast, focus, reading order, or motion preferences and can participate in theming and RTL as applicable.
- Performance: Addition fits within bundle budgets with purge/tree‑shaking; we measure impact and avoid explosive combinatorics.
- Consistency: Naming and variant generation (responsive/state) follow our conventions, and docs/examples are provided.

We exclude utilities that are context‑dependent (e.g., shorthands with unclear side effects), behavioral, or better expressed as component APIs. Properties requiring governance (e.g., z-index) must map to tokenized tiers.

Process: proposals land via a lightweight RFC, ship behind a flag, and are promoted when usage and DX benefits are demonstrated; utilities with <1% adoption after two releases are candidates for deprecation.

Applied to positioning, we permit position utilities (e.g., relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) because they are foundational layout primitives, composable, frequently required, and safe when tokenized for related tiers (e.g., z-index).

Decision: Defer shipping a full “examples” feature and run a focused validation pilot before any major investment.

- Priority: Proceed with clojure.spec integration as the next main feature; examples are not on the critical path.
- Scope now: Implement a minimal, opt-in examples “hook” (schema + parser) that can render examples if present, without building a dedicated UI, workflows, or a community repository.
- No community repository: Do not create or maintain a community examples repo at this stage. Reassess only if core/stdlib coverage becomes a validated need.
- Validation plan: 
  - Recruit 5–10 diverse library authors to trial the minimal hook for one release cycle.
  - Accept co-located examples (e.g., EDN/markdown next to sources or docstrings) in one simple, documented format.
  - Collect qualitative feedback (author effort, friction) and quantitative signals (adoption, render rate, usage analytics).
- Success criteria to proceed to a full feature:
  - At least 30% of pilot libraries provide and maintain examples across two releases.
  - Demonstrable end-user engagement (e.g., ≥10% of doc page views interact with examples).
  - Author-reported maintenance cost is low and examples materially improve comprehension of non-trivial APIs.
- If criteria are not met: Sunset the hook as “experimental,” keep format stable but undocumented, and avoid further investment.
- Timeline: 6–8 weeks pilot; formal go/no-go decision immediately afterward.

We will externalize product configuration from Stripe metadata into a first-class, versioned “Product Config” service and store only stable, minimal pointers in Stripe metadata.

- For each Product/Price, Stripe metadata will contain a small, fixed set of keys: config_id (UUID), config_version (int), and config_checksum (short hash) pointing to a canonical JSON document stored in our service (backed by our database and/or S3).
- The Subscription Platform will resolve metadata at runtime by fetching the referenced config document, with caching and signature verification via checksum to ensure integrity and detect drift.
- Product managers will manage all product configuration (checkout content, legal document URLs, support options, etc.) via an internal admin UI that validates against JSON Schemas, enforces RBAC, and provides preview and audit history. Publishing creates a new immutable config_version; rollback is supported by re-pointing to a prior version.
- Stripe metadata usage will be limited to the pointer keys and any legally required or operationally critical leaf values that must remain directly in Stripe (budget: ≤10 keys), preventing future limit exhaustion.
- We will provide a one-time migration: ingest existing Stripe metadata into the Config service, generate config documents, write config_id/version back to Stripe, and keep legacy readers functioning during a deprecation window. A feature flag will control read path cutover.
- Operational safeguards: schema validation on publish, soft limits and alerts for document size, observability around cache misses and resolve latency, and background consistency checks to confirm Stripe pointers reference valid configs.
- Security and availability: configs stored encrypted at rest, served via authenticated API with read-only tokens for runtime services; multi-AZ storage and CDN-backed cache for low-latency reads.
- This approach removes dependence on Stripe metadata capacity while preserving metadata-driven behavior, improves governance and auditability, and provides a scalable foundation for future product configuration.

We will adopt Testify (github.com/stretchr/testify) as the primary testing helper library for the Go codebase.

- Scope
  - Use testify/assert and testify/require for expressive assertions.
  - Use testify/suite for tests that benefit from grouped setup/teardown.
  - Optionally use testify/mock where interface-based mocking is warranted; prefer fakes for simple cases.

- Usage guidelines
  - Keep “go test” as the sole runner; no custom runners.
  - Prefer table-driven tests; use suite only when shared setup/teardown meaningfully reduces duplication.
  - Use require for preconditions and fatal checks; use assert for subsequent validations to maximize signal per test.
  - Keep assertions readable and deterministic; avoid asserting on time-sensitive or flaky conditions.
  - Do not import Testify from non-test code.
  - Keep tests isolated; no reliance on global mutable state in suites.

- Dependency management
  - Pin Testify to a stable, semver-tagged release via Go modules and update intentionally.
  - Vendor as needed per repository policy and include in license/attribution tracking.

- Migration strategy
  - No mass rewrite required; existing stdlib tests remain valid.
  - Adopt Testify incrementally in new and touched tests.
  - Convert high-churn or low-clarity tests first to realize readability benefits.

- Quality and CI
  - Maintain current coverage, race detector, and -count=1 determinism in CI.
  - Lint rules may flag import of deprecated Testify helpers; stick to assert, require, suite, and mock.

This decision balances maintainability and developer productivity while avoiding the cost and risk of building or maintaining a bespoke test framework.

Replace the single-key caching strategy with a sharded, per-property caching model to eliminate the memcached hotspot and deploy-induced key churn. Introduce a new PropertyInfoStore implementation that:

- Caches each property’s info under its own stable WANObjectCache key (e.g., property-info:v1:{propertyId}), avoiding whole-table serialization and ensuring keys remain stable across deploys.
- Uses WANObjectCache with consistent hashing (no deploy-based key prefixing), short TTLs, and a versioned namespace to support controlled invalidation without full-cache churn.
- Adds a small in-process local cache (e.g., APCu) for the most recent lookups in each request/context to reduce memcached read amplification.
- Supports efficient bulk reads by batching misses and issuing a single DB query for the requested set, then populating individual cache entries to prevent thundering herds.
- Performs fine-grained invalidation on writes/updates (purge only affected property keys) instead of invalidating the entire table.
- Optionally groups very cold properties into coarse shards (e.g., buckets of 50–100) behind a feature flag if operational metrics suggest too many tiny keys; default is per-property keys for maximal hotspot reduction.
- Ships with monitoring for cache hit ratio, hot-key distribution, and DB fallback volume, and rolls out gradually with the ability to revert.

Deprecate CacheAwarePropertyInfoStore and its single-key cache. Migrate transparently by reading from the legacy key during rollout and writing to the new keys, then remove legacy reads once hit ratios stabilize.

Decision:

Adopt Algolia as the primary search platform for UI vacancy search and job-alert generation, replacing Elasticsearch-backed query logic for these use cases. Implement a phased migration that introduces an internal search adapter interface; provide an Algolia-backed implementation for search and alerts while keeping the existing Elasticsearch implementation as a fallback during transition.

Key elements:
- Indexing: Build an idempotent indexing pipeline to publish vacancies to Algolia indices, with incremental updates and deletions. Use environment-specific indices and replicas for alternative sort orders (e.g., recency vs. relevance).
- Relevance & configuration: Manage ranking, synonyms, typo tolerance, query rules, and boosts via Algolia’s dashboard, enabling product/ops to tune results without engineering changes. Enable Rules and Dynamic Re-Ranking where applicable. Establish change governance and versioned configurations.
- Search API: Replace the Ruby ES client usage with a thin adapter around Algolia’s Ruby client. Maintain the existing base client abstraction so search and job alerts extend from the new adapter with minimal code changes.
- Job alerts: Represent alerts as saved Algolia filters/queries; leverage facet filters, numeric filters, and synonyms for broader match. Use Algolia Analytics to refine alert criteria and reduce low-signal alerts.
- Observability: Use Algolia’s analytics, click/conversion events, and A/B testing to iteratively improve relevance. Log adapter-level metrics, errors, and rate-limit handling.
- Reliability & performance: Enable multiple replicas for HA; configure timeouts and retries in the adapter. Implement backfill and reindex procedures. Keep ES read path available as a feature-flagged fallback until parity and SLAs are met.
- Security & compliance: Restrict data to necessary fields; use secured API keys for per-user query constraints where needed.
- Cost & vendor management: Track usage against plan limits; add budget alerts. Document a rollback path to Elasticsearch or an alternative (e.g., Typesense/Meilisearch) via the adapter.

Outcome:
- Non-engineering teams can configure and iterate on search relevance and alert rules via Algolia’s UI.
- Improved search quality and alert matching with faster iteration, reduced engineering overhead, and measurable outcomes through analytics and A/B testing.

Decision: Adopt a single master workflow with organization-specific permission filtering

- Maintain one master workflow in application-permissions-view that exposes the full command set and role mappings (superset of capabilities).
- Derive organization-specific workflows purely through configuration by whitelisting/blacklisting permissions per role, per application state, and optionally per application type.
- Prefer role-based permission exposure plus filtering over creating command variations. Only introduce command variants if a behavior difference cannot be expressed by permission policy, and isolate such variants behind explicit feature flags.
- Store workflow policies (permission filters) as data in configuration (e.g., organization-scoped policy documents) with versioning, enabling safe rollout, auditability, and rollback.
- Provide a policy validation step that detects contradictory or incomplete filters (e.g., no actor can ever move an application forward; decisions unreachable), and a conformance test suite per organization to ensure intended flows are achievable.
- Expose a policy introspection view (effective permissions per user/role/state) to aid debugging and support.
- Keep a conservative default policy that mirrors the current generalized process; organizations opt in to restrictions via configuration.
- Deprecate and remove multiple calculate-permissions functions; migrate existing consumers to the master workflow plus policy filters.
- Document a stable extension surface: roles, commands, and states are the contract; filters configure their usage without duplicating workflow logic.

We will extend MADR to explicitly support cross-references between decisions. The MADR template will include a “Related Decisions” section (after “Status” and before “Context and Problem Statement”) that lists links to other ADRs using relative paths and standardized relation labels:

- Follows-up on: <ADR-xxx-title>
- Amends: <ADR-yyy-title>
- Supersedes: <ADR-zzz-title>
- Superseded by: <ADR-aaa-title> (optional back-reference)
- Relates to: <ADR-bbb-title>
- Depends on: <ADR-ccc-title>
- Blocks: <ADR-ddd-title>

Authors of new ADRs must add forward references (e.g., “Follows-up on”, “Amends”, “Supersedes”) in the new ADR’s “Related Decisions” section. When applicable, they should also update the referenced ADR to include a back-reference (“Superseded by”, “Amended by”, “Followed-up by”) and adjust its Status (e.g., superseded) to keep the decision graph consistent.

We will document these relation types and examples in MADR’s README and template, recommend using one relation per bullet, and require stable ADR identifiers (e.g., 0001, 0002) for durable links. This approach keeps ADRs self-contained, human-readable, and version-control friendly while enabling decision lineage and traceability.

Adopt Jest as the interim end-to-end test runner, using Playwright as the automation library. Tests will be written against Playwright’s API and kept framework-agnostic to enable a future migration to Playwright Test with minimal churn.

- Use jest + jest-circus with a dedicated jest.config.e2e.(js|ts) and optional jest-playwright preset or thin custom harness around playwright-core.
- Provide npm scripts for common flows: 
  - e2e (headless, CI defaults), 
  - e2e:dev (headed, watch), 
  - e2e:debug (headed, slowMo), 
  - e2e:ci (junit reports, artifacts).
- Global setup/teardown will bootstrap and tear down the application under test (web server, test DB, seeds) and ensure Playwright browsers are installed. Each test file/case will use an isolated browser context.
- Enable parallel execution via Jest workers (configurable via CI env), with CI-level sharding (matrix by project/spec) for scalability.
- Support cross-browser coverage via environment-driven matrix (Chromium, WebKit, Firefox) and mobile emulations.
- Add reliability features: per-test retries (jest.retryTimes), timeouts, and automatic artifacts on failure (screenshots, videos, Playwright traces).
- Provide standard reporters: concise console locally; JUnit/XML and HTML summary in CI.
- Make configuration portable via environment variables (.env) for base URL, credentials, and feature flags; provide a Docker image (Node + Playwright browsers) for hermetic CI/local runs.
- Establish coding conventions to avoid Jest-specific assertions or lifecycle hooks in page object/helpers, keeping them Playwright-native.
- Revisit this decision and plan migration to Playwright Test when it is sufficiently stable; target a drop-in change by preserving test semantics and shared helpers.

We will standardize continuous integration across all repositories to automatically build, test, and enforce code coverage for every change.

- All pull requests and pushes to default branches will trigger a CI pipeline that: (1) installs dependencies, (2) compiles/builds, (3) runs unit and integration tests, and (4) publishes coverage reports and artifacts.
- Coverage tooling is standardized per tech stack and must emit LCOV or Cobertura:
  - Java: JaCoCo via Maven/Gradle
  - JavaScript/TypeScript: Jest + Istanbul/nyc (or Vitest + c8)
  - Python: pytest + pytest-cov
  - .NET: Coverlet + test runner
- Minimum thresholds (gating):
  - Global project line coverage ≥ 80%
  - Per-module/package coverage ≥ 70%
  - Changed-code (diff-based) coverage ≥ 90%
  Pipelines will fail if thresholds are not met or if coverage decreases on default branches.
- Coverage and test results will be uploaded to a centralized dashboard (e.g., SonarQube or Codecov) and stored as build artifacts. Repositories must include a coverage badge in their README sourced from the dashboard.
- Integration tests run with ephemeral dependencies (e.g., Testcontainers, service mocks) in CI and are part of the gating build. Long-running or end-to-end suites run nightly and on release branches.
- Performance and reliability:
  - Use dependency caching and parallel test execution where supported.
  - Shard large test suites and collect coverage across shards.
  - Flaky tests are quarantined with owner assignment and tracked via ticket; quarantined tests must be stabilized within one sprint.
- Policy and exceptions:
  - New repositories must implement this pipeline before first release.
  - Temporary exceptions to thresholds require architecture approval, a documented mitigation plan, and a time-bound waiver.
  - Security and license scan steps may be added as additional gates without reducing coverage requirements.
- Governance:
  - Code owners are responsible for maintaining pipelines and thresholds.
  - The architecture team maintains shared CI templates, coverage rules, and reference configurations.
  - Any change to thresholds or tooling requires an ADR and cross-team review.

This decision ensures test automation and coverage enforcement are consistent, visible, and merge-blocking, improving code quality and reducing regressions.

## Decision
Adopt the Arkency-style DDD baseline as the initial architectural approach and learning scaffold. We will structure the system around bounded contexts with a monolith-first deployment, applying CQRS (without mandatory Event Sourcing) and explicit separation of concerns into Application, Domain, and Infrastructure layers. Domain logic will be modeled through aggregates and aggregate roots enforcing invariants; repositories will persist aggregates; application services/command handlers will coordinate use cases; read models will serve queries. Domain events will be first-class for decoupling, with process managers/sagas introduced where cross-aggregate or cross-context workflows are required. Controllers/CLIs/handlers remain thin, delegating to application services.

We will follow Arkency-recommended conventions for naming, folder structure, and testing strategy: domain unit tests as the primary safety net, with integration tests for infrastructure and adapters. We will avoid premature microservices and external integrations unless driven by clear boundaries or non-functional needs. The initial scope will focus on one bounded context to validate the approach, iterating incrementally and refactoring as ubiquitous language and model clarity improve.

This decision will be revisited after implementing the first meaningful slice to evaluate fit, performance, team ergonomics, and necessary adaptations to context-specific constraints.

Adopt the cloud provider’s PaaS to reduce operational overhead, with a security-first deployment posture tailored to sensitive data. Use dedicated or single-tenant PaaS tiers where available and strictly disable public exposure: all services are reachable only via private networking (VPC peering/private service endpoints) with egress restricted through controlled egress gateways. Enforce customer-managed encryption keys (CMK) with HSM-backed key storage and automatic rotation; require TLS 1.2+ in transit and at-rest encryption for all data, backups, and logs. Implement application-layer field-level encryption or tokenization for highly sensitive fields to minimize blast radius.

Adopt least-privilege, short-lived, identity-based access (workload identity/managed identities) and centrally managed secrets via the provider’s secrets manager; prohibit static long-lived credentials. Enable comprehensive audit logging (admin, data access, and network flow) with immutable retention and aggregation into the SIEM. Gate PaaS configuration via policy-as-code (CIS/Benchmarks), continuous compliance scanning, and deployment through CI/CD with mandatory security checks. Configure automated, encrypted backups, point-in-time recovery, cross-zone/high-availability, and regionally bound data residency; define tested RPO/RTO objectives.

Where PaaS controls are insufficient for specific constraints (e.g., required HSM FIPS levels, tenant isolation), use the provider’s dedicated/isolated SKUs or augment with compensating controls. Proceed with PaaS under these guardrails to balance strong data protection with simplified operations.

Adopt a backward-compatible extension of Message.examples to support paired payload/header examples without changing the field name or breaking existing consumers.

- Decision: Treat each element of message.examples as a union:
  - LegacyExample: a single example implicitly targeting the payload (current behavior).
  - PairedExample: an object with optional payload and headers members, each holding an example. At least one must be present; if both are present they are considered a pair.

- Parsing/validation:
  - If an element has payload and/or headers keys, interpret as PairedExample.
  - Otherwise, interpret as LegacyExample targeting payload.
  - Validate that PairedExample has at least one of payload or headers; headers-only is allowed for completeness.
  - Maintain existing validation semantics for LegacyExample.

- Serialization:
  - Emit PairedExample only when a header example is present (or explicitly requested).
  - Default to LegacyExample serialization when only a payload example is present to minimize churn.

- Tooling and codegen:
  - Update models to expose a MessageExample type with optional payloadExample and headerExample.
  - Generators should prefer PairedExample where header examples exist; otherwise continue emitting LegacyExample.
  - Consumers must handle both shapes transparently.

- Documentation:
  - Document LegacyExample as supported but deprecated.
  - Recommend PairedExample for new definitions, with a migration guide.
  - Plan enforcement of PairedExample in a future major version.

Adopt direct JPEG2000 ingestion via libvips built with OpenJPEG support and remove the OpenJPEG opj_decompress intermediate step. We will upgrade and/or rebuild libvips with libopenjp2 enabled on all ingestion hosts and modify the pipeline to pass JP2 inputs straight to vips for pyramid/thumbnail generation. This eliminates creation of temporary TIFFs, reduces peak memory and I/O, and prevents host crashes triggered by concurrent opj_decompress executions.

Operational safeguards will be added:
- Constrain JP2 ingestion concurrency via the worker queue (configurable max parallel JP2 jobs per host).
- Enforce per-process memory and CPU limits (ulimits/cgroup) and job timeouts to contain worst-case files.
- Provide a graceful fallback: if vips fails to decode a JP2, mark the item for manual review and retry with a low-concurrency path rather than auto-running opj_decompress.

Rollout steps: provision libopenjp2, rebuild/deploy libvips with JP2 support, validate on a representative corpus, enable the new code path behind a feature flag, then deprecate and remove opj_decompress usage and temp TIFF handling. This decision centralizes image decoding in vips, simplifies the pipeline, and mitigates memory pressure while preserving JP2 support for scanned maps.

We will adopt a configuration-first architecture that externalizes all tunable behavior into declarative configuration, minimizing code changes for initial and subsequent releases. Specifically:
- Use typed, versioned YAML/JSON configuration files as the primary source of truth, with environment-variable and command-line overrides following a clear precedence (CLI > env vars > file > defaults).
- Provide sensible, documented defaults for all options to enable zero-configuration startup, while allowing granular overrides through profiles (e.g., dev, staging, prod) and per-module sections.
- Employ a mature configuration library with schema validation to enforce types, required fields, and deprecation warnings; fail fast on invalid configs.
- Introduce a lightweight feature-flag mechanism for toggling non-breaking features without redeploys; flags read from config/env initially, with the option to integrate a remote flag service later.
- Support configuration hot-reload where the underlying platform/library safely allows it; otherwise require restart, prioritizing correctness and simplicity in the first draft.
- Centralize configuration access behind an internal Config interface to decouple consumers from the library and enable future evolution (e.g., remote config service, secrets manager).
- Exclude a plugin system or custom DSL in the first draft to reduce complexity; instead, design configuration schemas and module boundaries to be forward-compatible with future extensibility.

This approach maximizes configurability with minimal implementation effort while preserving a clean path for future sophistication.

## Decision
We will remove the Skylight profiler from the codebase and infrastructure at this time. The service has not been actively used, is misconfigured, and provides no current value. Immediate actions:
- Remove the Skylight gem, initializer, middleware, and any conditional hooks.
- Delete related environment variables, secrets, and CI/CD configuration.
- Terminate the Skylight account/subscription and revoke API keys.
- Update documentation and runbooks to reflect removal.
- Monitor application performance and error rates post-removal for two release cycles.

We will revisit application profiling needs when there is a concrete performance investigation or capacity-planning initiative. At that time, we will conduct a short evaluation of options (e.g., OpenTelemetry-based solutions, vendor APMs, or lightweight tools like rack-mini-profiler in non-prod) based on current stack, support, cost, and integration complexity.

Exit criteria for re-introduction of a profiler:
- A defined performance objective and success metrics.
- An owner responsible for configuration, alerts, and ongoing usage.
- Verified configuration in staging with documented setup and dashboards.

This decision can be reversed with minimal effort if a profiling need arises.

Adopt a structured SPA built with Vue 3 (Composition API) and TypeScript, bundled via Vite, with Vue Router for navigation/route guards and Pinia for state management. Avoid jQuery and vanilla DOM manipulation to ensure maintainability, testability, and clear separation of concerns as the UX grows.

Implement the PIN “login” as a guarded flow:
- Store only an authenticated flag and minimal session metadata in Pinia and browser sessionStorage; never persist the PIN.
- Use Vue Router navigation guards to restrict access to protected routes based on session state.
- Include an inactivity timeout and explicit logout that clears state and storage.

Integrate Zenroom (WASM) as an isolated service:
- Load the WASM module asynchronously via dynamic import with Vite asset handling.
- Run Zenroom execution inside a Web Worker to prevent main-thread blocking; expose a typed API (request/response) and initialize lazily on first use.
- Provide fallbacks and clear error UX if WASM/worker initialization fails; feature-detect WASM and workers.

UI architecture:
- Componentize pages and shared controls; keep business logic in composables/services.
- Use strict TypeScript settings, eslint/prettier, and unit tests for stores/composables; add E2E tests for auth guards and Zenroom flows.
- Keep framework footprint minimal (no UI framework by default); add utility-first CSS (e.g., Tailwind) only if needed.

This approach balances simplicity and scalability, enables robust routing and state, ensures responsive UX with WASM, and supports future expansion without rework.

Use Azure Cosmos DB with the MongoDB API for the Digital Citizenship project to satisfy CRUD and query requirements while minimizing vendor lock-in. Implement optimistic concurrency control at the application level using MVCC:

- Add a numeric version field to each document.
- Perform conditional updates using findOneAndUpdate (or equivalent) with a predicate that matches both the document identifier and the current version.
- On successful update, increment the version; on mismatch, treat as a concurrency conflict and apply a retry or surface an error.
- Enforce appropriate indexes for query patterns and the versioned conditional updates.

Adopt the official MongoDB driver and avoid Cosmos DB–specific features that are not part of the MongoDB API surface (e.g., stored procedures, triggers, native ETag semantics) to preserve portability. Encapsulate data access behind a repository/DAO interface to enable future migration to native MongoDB or alternative stores with minimal impact.

Reevaluate this decision only if future requirements mandate features uniquely available via the DocumentDB API (e.g., server-side programmable logic tightly coupled to the database or built-in concurrency via ETags) that cannot be reasonably reproduced in the application layer.

Adopt a layered testing strategy that maximizes automation for #1 and #2, and provides targeted, maintainable assurance for #3:

- Validation and transformation (#1 and #2): Define a strict input schema and implement validation with precise error messages. Make the HTML generation a pure function that returns a deterministic, self-contained document (embedded CSS/JS). Cover with unit tests and snapshot (“golden”) tests for representative inputs and edge cases.

- Interactive behavior (#3): 
  - Factor the client-side logic into testable modules (pure functions and event handlers) with unit tests for state transitions and boundary cases.
  - instrument the generated HTML with stable selectors (data-testid) and accessible roles to support automation.
  - Add a minimal, high-value set of end-to-end browser tests using Playwright in headless mode that load the generated HTML and verify critical user flows and link behaviors (clicks, keyboard navigation, dynamic updates). Keep these tests small in number, focused on the happy path and one failure path per feature, to control brittleness and runtime.
  - Use DOM-level assertions (not visual diffs) for stability; reserve visual regression to a single smoke test if necessary.

- CI/CD: Run unit and snapshot tests on every commit; run the Playwright suite on PRs and nightly. Cache browsers and parallelize to keep build times acceptable.

- Contract: Maintain a contract between the transformer and UI by documenting and testing required data attributes and structure. Breaking changes must update the contract tests.

This balances high confidence in behavior with test maintainability, acknowledging #3’s inherent difficulty while ensuring critical interactivity is verified automatically.

## Decision
Persist all locations, bookables, and bookings in a managed PostgreSQL database (e.g., AWS RDS/Azure Database for PostgreSQL/Cloud SQL) to ensure durability across instances and deployments, strong transactional guarantees, and operational resilience.

- Schema-first relational model with normalized tables (locations, bookables, bookings) and foreign keys. Enforce data integrity with constraints, including:
  - Unique business keys where applicable (e.g., location code).
  - Booking conflict prevention using PostgreSQL range types with an EXCLUDE constraint on (bookable_id WITH =, tsrange WITH &&) via GiST index, or transactional checks with advisory locks if range types are unavailable.
- All write operations wrapped in ACID transactions; use optimistic concurrency (row version column) and idempotency keys for booking creation to handle retries and prevent duplicates.
- Time stored in UTC; clock and time zone handling centralized in the service layer.
- Managed HA setup: multi-AZ/zone deployment, automated backups with point-in-time recovery, regular snapshot retention, and monitored replication. Read replicas may be added for scale; writes remain single-primary.
- Access via an ORM with explicit, versioned migrations (e.g., Flyway/Liquibase) to evolve the schema safely across deployments; migrations are backward-compatible and reversible.
- Secure connectivity via TLS, secret management via the platform’s vault/secret store, and connection pooling (e.g., pgbouncer) for multi-instance scalability.
- Implement data lifecycle policies (retention/archival), soft deletes where needed, and audit trails for booking changes to support compliance and recovery.
- Prepare for future scale with partitioning on time-based booking data and index strategies reviewed regularly.

Adopt runtime alias resolution for TypeScript by standardizing on ts-node with tsconfig-paths. All developer and CI scripts that execute TypeScript directly must preload tsconfig-paths to honor compilerOptions.paths. Concretely:
- Replace any direct ts-node invocations with: ts-node -r tsconfig-paths/register <entry.ts> (or node -r ts-node/register -r tsconfig-paths/register <entry.ts> where applicable).
- Provide npm scripts (e.g., dev, migrate, seed, test:e2e) that wrap the above to prevent alias breakage and ensure consistent bootstrap behavior.
- For production, do not rely on ts-node; emit JavaScript via tsc (or bundle via tsup/esbuild) so aliases are fully resolved at build time. Block or warn on plain ts-node usage in production contexts.

Rationale: This preserves mandatory path-alias bootstrapping without refactoring imports, avoids lock-in to relative paths, and minimizes disruption to existing code. It also keeps test and tooling parity with application runtime.

Acceptance criteria:
- tsconfig-paths is added as a dependency and preloaded wherever ts-node runs.
- CI pipelines execute with the updated scripts.
- Documentation and contributor guidelines reflect the new commands and explicitly prohibit raw ts-node without tsconfig-paths.
- Lint/commit hooks (optional) detect and flag noncompliant scripts.

We will implement LaTiS primarily in Scala, adopting a functional-first architectural style with pragmatic object-oriented boundaries.

- Language and platform: Scala 3.x on JVM 17+ as the default runtime.
- Paradigm: Pure functional core for data modeling, transformation, and streaming, complemented by OO abstractions where domain modeling and interop benefit from classes/traits.
- Libraries and ecosystem: cats-core and cats-effect for type classes and effect management; fs2 for streaming; http4s for HTTP services; circe for JSON; direct Java interop for specialized libraries (e.g., NetCDF, JDBC) when needed.
- Concurrency and scalability: Use structured concurrency via cats-effect fibers and fs2 streams to support parallel, backpressured data pipelines; avoid ad-hoc threading.
- Modularity: Separate functional core (pure, referentially transparent) from integration layers (I/O, persistence, network), enabling testability and substitution.
- Interoperability: Leverage JVM compatibility for integrating existing Java libraries and tools; expose Java-friendly façades where external consumers require them.
- Tooling and quality: sbt as the build tool; scalafmt and scalafix enforced; semantic versioning; comprehensive property-based and law-checking tests for core abstractions.
- Performance posture: Prefer immutable, streaming-first designs; profile hot paths and selectively optimize with specialized collections or Java interop where justified.
- Exceptions: Small operational scripts may use Python/Bash; performance-critical native modules require explicit approval and stable interop boundaries.

This decision standardizes Scala as the foundation for LaTiS core, services, and libraries.

We will implement platform-wide single sign-on with GitHub as the initial authoritative user directory and identity provider. A central identity broker (e.g., Dex or Keycloak) will be deployed and configured with GitHub OAuth/OIDC as the upstream IdP. All user-facing systems (Kubernetes API/CLI, Prometheus/Grafana, ELK, Concourse, and platform portals) will integrate with the broker using OIDC (preferred) or SAML.

Authorization will be derived from GitHub organization and team membership:
- Organization membership required for any access.
- GitHub teams map to platform roles and groups; mappings are defined as code and version-controlled.
- Kubernetes RBAC bindings will be generated/synchronized from team-to-role mappings per namespace/cluster.
- Tooling uses broker-issued claims (groups/roles) for consistent access control.

For AWS, we will use federation only (no long-lived IAM users): the broker will federate users to AWS via SAML to IAM Identity Center (or directly to IAM roles where needed) to issue short-lived credentials based on mapped GitHub teams/roles.

Security and compliance:
- Enforce MFA via GitHub org policies; require short session TTLs and refresh via the broker.
- Centralized auditing using broker logs plus GitHub org audit logs; propagate user identity and groups as claims to downstream services.

Lifecycle management:
- Joiners/leavers/role changes are managed in GitHub teams and automatically reflected platform-wide via synchronization pipelines.

This establishes a single, consistent access model now, while allowing future migration to another IdP without changing service integrations.

We will standardize class structure to keep responsibilities clear and code maintainable beyond default Rails MVC:

- Controllers: Thin orchestration only. No business logic. One controller per resource; actions delegate to service/command/query objects.
- Models (ActiveRecord): Persistence, associations, validations, simple scopes. Avoid business logic and callbacks beyond data integrity. Prefer composition over concerns; use concerns sparingly and only for true cross-cutting behavior.
- Services/Commands (app/services): Encapsulate business use-cases and transaction boundaries. Name with verb-oriented suffix (e.g., CreateOrderService). Services return result objects (success?, value, errors) and are side-effect aware.
- Queries/Repositories (app/queries): Read-only data access beyond simple scopes. Return simple DTOs or relations. Name with Query suffix.
- Value Objects (app/value_objects): Immutable, comparable POROs for domain concepts (e.g., Money, DateRange). No persistence.
- Forms (app/forms): Input aggregation/validation for multi-model or complex forms. Include ActiveModel::Model.
- Presenters/Decorators (app/presenters): View-specific formatting only. No business rules.
- Policies (app/policies): Authorization rules (e.g., Pundit). Controllers/services consult policies.
- Serializers (app/serializers): API representation shaping. Keep deterministic and side-effect free.
- Jobs (app/jobs): Background work units; delegate to services.
- Mailers (app/mailers): Delivery only; content assembled via presenters/serializers.
- Namespacing: Group by domain first, then layer (e.g., app/services/billing/ChargeCustomerService). Avoid top-level dumping grounds.
- Error handling: Domain-specific error types under app/errors; services translate to result objects.
- Transactions: Initiated in services at use-case boundaries; no nested DB work in presenters/serializers.
- Conventions: One class per file, clear suffixes, YARD docstring describing purpose/responsibility. New structural patterns require an ADR update before adoption. RuboCop/linters enforce class size/complexity limits.

Adopt a TypeScript-first, per-component folder structure with Rollup-based builds producing ESM and CJS module distributions by default, plus a single UMD bundle for CDN use.

- Source layout: src/components/<Component>/ with an index.ts(x) per component and a top-level src/index.ts barrel for full-package entry.
- Build outputs:
  - dist/esm preserving module structure for optimal tree-shaking.
  - dist/cjs preserving module structure for Node/CommonJS consumers.
  - dist/umd/<package>.umd.js as a single file for legacy/CDN scenarios.
  - dist/types with .d.ts generated from TypeScript.
  - Source maps for all outputs.
- Bundler: Rollup with appropriate plugins for TS, JSX, and externalization of peer dependencies (react, react-dom). Styles and other assets are handled via Rollup plugins but remain external unless explicitly inlined.
- Package configuration:
  - package.json “exports” with conditional exports for the package root and per-component subpaths:
    - ".": { "import": "./dist/esm/index.js", "require": "./dist/cjs/index.js", "types": "./dist/types/index.d.ts" }
    - "./components/*": { "import": "./dist/esm/components/*/index.js", "require": "./dist/cjs/components/*/index.js", "types": "./dist/types/components/*/index.d.ts" }
  - “module”: "./dist/esm/index.js", “main”: "./dist/cjs/index.js”, “types”: "./dist/types/index.d.ts”.
  - “sideEffects”: false (or narrowly scoped to style side-effect files).
  - “files”: ["dist"] and necessary metadata.
  - Peer dependencies: react, react-dom (version ranges aligned with supported React versions).
- Publishing: ship only compiled artifacts from dist. Ensure semantic versioning and changelog discipline.

This mirrors leading libraries’ multi-format support, enables tree-shaking and deep imports, provides robust TypeScript typings, and keeps legacy UMD consumers supported without penalizing modern bundlers.

## Decision

Adopt a server-side rendered (SSR-first) application with progressive enhancement and selective client-side hydration (“islands architecture”) for interactive features, rather than a full single-page application (SPA) shell.

- Rendering strategy: Render HTML on the server for all routes to optimize first contentful paint, SEO, and resilience. Enhance only necessary components with client-side JavaScript via hydration. Use route-based code splitting and streaming SSR where supported.
- Interactivity: For highly interactive sections (e.g., dashboards, editors), encapsulate them as client-hydrated islands with localized state management and, where needed, opt-in client-side routing confined to that island. Avoid global SPA routing for the entire app.
- Data fetching and caching: Prefer server-driven data fetching to leverage server/cache locality and simplify error handling. Enable CDN/edge caching for public pages; apply HTTP caching (ETag/Cache-Control) and incremental revalidation where applicable.
- Performance: Minimize shipped JavaScript by default; measure and budget per route. Defer non-critical scripts, preload critical assets, and use image optimization on the server/edge.
- Maintainability: Share types/models between server and client where needed, but keep domain logic on the server. Limit client state to UI concerns; persist business state on the server. Establish clear boundaries for when a component becomes an island (thresholds for interactivity/latency).
- Operational considerations: Ensure observability for both server render performance and client hydration costs. Plan capacity for increased server rendering load; mitigate with caching, edge rendering, and background pre-rendering. Provide a fallback static render path for degraded modes.
- Reversibility: If usage patterns shift toward heavy client interactivity, individual routes or sections can be promoted to SPA-like behavior without converting the whole app. Periodically review telemetry (TTFB, LCP, JS payload, error rates) to validate the choice.

Adopt a platform-managed Form Registry as the system of record for form metadata, replacing GitHub as the primary storage and transport between Editor and Publisher. The Form Registry exposes authenticated APIs (REST/GraphQL) for create/read/update/version operations. The Editor writes form artifacts directly to the Registry; the Publisher consumes artifacts from the Registry to generate and deploy forms. The Registry persists immutable, versioned form packages in cloud object storage (e.g., S3/GCS/Azure Blob) with an indexed metadata store (e.g., Postgres) for search, lineage, and permissions. It provides workspace/organization scoping, role-based access control, audit trails, draft/release channels, semantic versioning, and publish approvals as configurable policy. Webhooks and eventing enable CI-style automation without requiring Git. An optional Git integration (import/export/sync) remains for advanced users, preserving transparency and external collaboration when desired but not required. Existing GitHub-based forms can be migrated via a one-time import. This decision removes Git as a prerequisite, reduces friction for self-service users, and standardizes a robust, API-first path from authoring to publishing while retaining an escape hatch for teams that prefer Git workflows.

We will model the Submission domain entity with an explicit, versioned state machine and persist the state as an enum using the canonical identifiers: pending, processing, validation_failed, validation_passed, supplier_rejected, supplier_accepted.

Allowed transitions (v1):
- pending -> processing
- processing -> validation_failed | validation_passed
- validation_failed -> processing (upon supplier resubmission) | pending (if reset/cleared)
- validation_passed -> supplier_accepted | supplier_rejected
- supplier_rejected -> processing (upon amended resubmission) | pending (if reset)
- supplier_accepted -> [terminal in v1]

State changes are only performed via a domain service that enforces transition rules, records timestamps (entered_at), correlates actor/initiator, and captures reason codes/messages for failure or rejection. Each successful transition emits a domain event (e.g., SubmissionStateChanged) for downstream processing and UI updates; events are idempotent and ordered per submission.

We will not overload states with process sub-steps; detailed processing/validation progress is captured as orthogonal metadata. Transient/async work (ingest/validate) is edge-triggered by commands and guarded to prevent illegal or duplicate transitions.

The machine is extensible: new states and transitions may be added in future versions (e.g., approval flows, corrections). Additions must be backward compatible (no semantic change to existing states), accompanied by migration rules, and exposed via a versioned workflow contract. Unknown future states must be tolerated by clients (treat as read-only unless explicitly supported).

Adopt Alpine.js (v3) for client-side templating and reactive data binding and deprecate lit-html in interactive views. We will progressively enhance existing HTML with Alpine directives (x-data, x-bind, x-on, x-model) to achieve one- and two-way binding without introducing custom Web Components or a complex component model. The current polymer.js path remains read-only and is preserved behind the existing ?use-polymer flag.

Scope:
- Replace lit-html usages in pages requiring interaction with Alpine-powered markup embedded in standard HTML templates.
- Introduce a thin data bootstrapper that fetches JSON and hydrates Alpine component state via x-init or a shared store.
- Standardize on fetch-based data feeds and explicit state updates; no implicit magic or decorators.

Constraints/Non-goals:
- Do not adopt lit-element or custom elements.
- Avoid build-time compilation requirements; Alpine is included as a small runtime script.
- Preserve server-rendered markup as the initial HTML; Alpine enhances behavior post-load.

Implementation notes:
- Include alpine@3 from CDN or pinned package; create a tiny helper for API calls and error handling.
- Provide a migration guide to translate current lit-html templates to static HTML + Alpine bindings.
- Keep polymer.js code path read-only; new interactive features go to Alpine-based views.

Success criteria:
- Bi-directional data binding, event handling, and conditional rendering achieved with <10% bundle increase.
- No custom component authoring required; developer onboarding time < 1 day.

Adopt per-locale Elasticsearch indices, each with locale-appropriate analyzers for identically named fields. For each supported locale, provision an index (e.g., search-<locale>) with a shared base mapping and locale-specific analyzer settings applied via index templates. Application queries resolve the active locale through an index alias (e.g., search-active-<locale>) to keep query syntax uniform and minimal. Cross-locale search or analytics will target multiple indices via alias patterns (e.g., search-*), acknowledging that relevance tuning and aggregations remain language-specific.

Content fields that require linguistic processing (e.g., content, title, keywords) are analyzed with the locale’s language analyzer in that locale’s index; language-agnostic fields (IDs, facets, numeric/date fields, sort keys, exact-match keywords) share identical mappings across all indices. This avoids field-name proliferation, mapping bloat, and field-count limits inherent to a single multi-locale index with per-locale field suffixes, while enabling independent scaling, reindexing, and relevance tuning per locale.

Operationally, we will manage lifecycle policies, shard/replica counts, and relevance settings per locale; provide migration/reindex paths per locale; and maintain consistent aliases for zero-downtime rollovers. This structure aligns with Elasticsearch’s post-v7 constraints and preserves high-quality language-specific search behavior.

Adopt encrypted, integrity-protected cookies sealed with the Iron library to store client-side state that may include sensitive user-submitted values. We will encrypt using AES-256 and authenticate with HMAC-SHA-256, employing per-cookie random 256-bit salts for encryption and integrity keys, plus a cryptographically secure random IV. Keys will be derived from a server-held password via Iron’s KDF, producing distinct keyE/keyI; only the sealed, opaque blob (saltE, saltI, iv, ciphertext, mac) is sent to clients.

Cookie handling requirements:
- Set Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Lax (or Strict where possible).
- Enforce a strict TTL and automatic expiration within the sealed payload.
- Limit cookie size (<4KB) and avoid placing large payloads or PII when not necessary.
- Do not rely on this mechanism for transport security; TLS 1.2+ is mandatory.

Key management:
- Store the Iron password/secret in a centralized KMS/secret manager; never in code.
- Support key rotation using a primary/secondary password list to unseal with old, reseal with new.
- Enforce minimum entropy and access controls; audit all access.

Operational controls:
- Use strong RNG for salts and IVs.
- Validate MAC before any decryption; reject on any failure.
- Version the sealed format to allow future migrations.
- Log only high-level seal/unseal outcomes; never log cookie contents or secrets.

This decision protects user data at rest on compromised devices and prevents session tampering by making cookies opaque and tamper-evident, while leaving transport security to TLS.

Expose immutable instance data via accessor methods, not public fields. All instance fields remain private final and are initialized via constructor (or builder), with read access provided through getters/accessors. Prefer Java records for simple immutable aggregates, leveraging their generated accessor methods (without get prefixes). For collections and arrays, return unmodifiable views and/or defensive copies to preserve immutability guarantees. Only expose public static final constants for true, universal constants of primitive or intrinsically immutable types; otherwise use accessors.

Rationale constraints baked into the decision:
- Preserve encapsulation and future flexibility (fields can change without breaking binary/source compatibility).
- Enable validation, lazy computation, and invariants behind accessors without API breakage.
- Maintain thread-safety guarantees with final fields and clear immutability contracts.
- Facilitate testing, mocking, and framework integration (e.g., serialization) via conventional getters/accessors.

Implementation notes:
- Use Collections.unmodifiableX and List.copyOf/Map.copyOf; clone arrays on input/output.
- Avoid leaking internal references.
- Lombok @Getter/@Builder acceptable; ensure generated methods match API conventions.
- Document immutability in Javadoc; mark classes final where appropriate.

Implement resumable ETL via durable checkpointing and idempotent, partitioned processing to eliminate full restarts after interruptions.

- Segment the ETL into independently restartable stages and process data in deterministic chunks (e.g., source partitions, time windows, or primary-key ranges).
- Persist a high-watermark/low-watermark per source entity and per stage in a durable metadata store (e.g., relational DB or orchestration metadata), alongside a write-ahead log of in-flight batches.
- Ensure each stage is idempotent: use upserts/merges with natural/business keys or dedupe hashes, and avoid side effects prior to commit.
- Write results to a staging area and promote via atomic swaps/transactions to guarantee exactly-once semantics for committed chunks.
- On recovery, the orchestrator reads the last committed checkpoint and replays only incomplete or failed chunks; in-flight batches are rolled back or safely reprocessed.
- Enforce single-writer execution via distributed locking to prevent concurrent overlap on the same partitions.
- Support backfills by allowing controlled checkpoint rewinds for selected ranges without resetting the entire pipeline.
- Add retries with exponential backoff per chunk, bounded concurrency, and circuit breaking to contain blast radius.
- Expose operational telemetry (checkpoint positions, lag, retries, promotions) and alerts to detect stuck or regressing pipelines.
- Define SLAs/SLOs around checkpoint frequency and recovery time; default checkpoint granularity ≤15 minutes to cap worst-case rework.

## Decision
Represent each shard as a standalone UTF-8 plain-text file using a minimal, Unix-friendly Markdown subset.

- Encoding: UTF-8, newline-terminated, no binary content or ANSI escape sequences stored.
- Format: Free-form text body; optional minimal Markdown (paragraphs, lists, code fences, inline emphasis). Links may be bare URLs or Markdown [text](URL). Avoid complex or custom markup.
- File-per-shard: Exactly one shard per file to enable simple compose/edit with standard editors and pipelines.
- Naming: Use UTC timestamp-based, sortable, POSIX-safe filenames: YYYYMMDDThhmmssZ-xxxxxx.md (e.g., 20260123T141530Z-k3f9s2.md), where xxxxxx is a short random or monotonic suffix to ensure uniqueness.
- No required in-file metadata: Timestamp and identity are conveyed by filename. Additional organization (e.g., tags) is expressed in content (e.g., #tags) or directory structure. Avoid front matter to keep shards grep/awk/sed friendly.
- Terminal readability: Content should render legibly in standard terminals without specialized viewers; wrapping is left to terminal/editor. Lines should avoid excessive length where practical.
- Tooling compatibility: Creation and manipulation use standard Unix tools (cat, echo, tee, sed, awk, grep). Shards are append-only immutable by convention; edits happen via $EDITOR, preserving plain text.
- Portability: Filenames restricted to [a–z0–9-] and “.md”; no spaces or locale-sensitive characters to simplify scripting and cross-platform handling.

This choice maximizes human readability and shell composability while allowing lightweight formatting and links, without introducing a schema or parser burden.

We will migrate projects to a single-source codebase compatible with Python 2.7 and Python 3.5+ during a defined transition window, then drop 2.7 support on an announced date and remove compatibility shims.

Key elements:
- Conversion approach: use python-modernize (not 2to3/use_2to3) to automate initial refactors and adopt the six library for runtime shims. Avoid per-version branches and avoid install-time translation.
- Language pragmas: add from __future__ imports: absolute_import, division, print_function. Do not enable unicode_literals globally; instead use explicit u"" for text where needed and b"" for bytes, and prefer io.open(..., encoding="utf-8") for file I/O.
- Text/bytes strategy: make text/bytes boundaries explicit, use .encode()/.decode() at edges, use six.text_type/binary_type as needed, and ensure all public APIs specify expected types.
- Dependencies: prefer packages already supporting 3.x; pin compatible versions for 2.7 where needed; use backports (e.g., typing) only if necessary and isolated behind try/except imports.
- Tooling/quality: establish a CI matrix for 2.7, 3.5, and latest LTS 3.x; use tox to run tests; measure coverage across versions. Enforce flake8 and black (run on Python 3) via pre-commit; enable mypy on 3.x code paths with type hints guarded by TYPE_CHECKING or comments for 2.7.
- Packaging: ship universal wheels (bdist_wheel --universal) while 2.7 is supported; update classifiers to reflect dual support; avoid features that are 3-only during the transition.
- Governance: publish a migration guide, code examples, and a checklist; require all new and modified modules to be modernized as they are touched; block new 2.7-only patterns in CI. Set and communicate a firm deprecation date for Python 2.7 and remove compatibility code immediately after.

We will implement the UI library by closely aligning its architecture, API design, and conventions with established, widely adopted UI libraries in our target ecosystem. Specifically:

- Mirror proven component patterns, naming, and prop shapes to minimize invention and learning curve.
- Favor composition over inheritance and ship accessible, unstyled/low-opinion primitives with opt-in theming, following WAI-ARIA best practices and established focus/keyboard patterns.
- Adopt design tokens as the foundation for theming (colors, spacing, typography), with a theming system compatible with the dominant styling approach in our stack.
- Start with a minimal, high-value component set modeled after reference libraries, expanding only based on concrete product needs and usage feedback.
- Prioritize API stability and semantic versioning; when divergence is required, prefer additive changes and deprecation paths consistent with community norms.
- Use open-source exemplars as implementation references and benchmarks for quality, documentation structure, and testing practices.
- Maintain compatibility with ecosystem tooling (icons, form libs, validation, i18n), aligning defaults and interoperability with common patterns.
- Establish a “follow first, differentiate later” rule: new abstractions or departures from reference designs require a compelling, validated use case and ADR approval.

This decision reduces risk, accelerates delivery, and ensures maintainability by leveraging community-proven solutions while allowing controlled evolution as real requirements emerge.

We will introduce a cluster-wide awaitable Task abstraction backed by a central Task Orchestrator and durable state.

- Each submitted task receives a globally unique TaskId and a TaskHandle (opaque) that can be awaited from any node.
- A highly available Task Orchestrator (active/active) backed by a strongly consistent store (e.g., Postgres/etcd) maintains authoritative task state (Queued/Running/Completed/Failed/Cancelled), ownership (node), heartbeats, and metadata.
- Node-local executors pull work, execute tasks, emit heartbeats, and upsert status/results to the orchestrator. On missed heartbeats beyond threshold, the orchestrator marks tasks as lost and re-queues for reassignment.
- Results and errors are persisted durably and retrievably by TaskId. Short-lived results are cached in a distributed cache (e.g., Redis with TTL); large payloads are stored in blob storage with pointers in the orchestrator.
- Await is implemented as a server-side streaming RPC (or WebSocket) to the orchestrator that delivers completion signals and results. If streaming is unavailable, clients fall back to long-polling. Await supports timeout and cancellation tokens propagated to the executor.
