- Semantics: at-least-once execution with idempotency keyed by TaskId; the orchestrator enforces de-duplication on retries. Exactly-once delivery to awaiters is guaranteed by storing once, streaming many.
- API: await(TaskId, timeout, cancelToken) returning Result<T> or throwing on failure/cancel/timeout. Local calls to await automatically route to the orchestrator to unify behavior while retaining fast-path for local-only tasks.
- Backpressure: orchestrator limits concurrent awaits per TaskId and streams fan-out via pub/sub to avoid n× duplication. Result payloads are chunked and size-capped.
- Security: TaskHandle is a capability token scoped to tenant and permissions; all await/inspect operations are authorized at the orchestrator.
- Observability: task events are emitted to telemetry; IDs are trace-propagated; dead-letter queue for permanently failing tasks.
- Migration: wrap existing in-process futures in a compatibility layer that issues TaskIds and registers state; progressively enable remote execution.

This design enables await from any node, resilience to node failure, and consistent behavior across local and distributed execution.

Defer the architectural decision until the motivating problem, scope, constraints, and stakeholders are clearly defined and documented. Establish this ADR as a placeholder with the following mandates: (1) a concise problem statement, functional and non-functional requirements, success metrics, and explicit constraints (technical, regulatory, budgetary, timeline) must be produced; (2) key stakeholders and decision-makers must be identified with RACI assignments; (3) relevant options, risks, and assumptions must be enumerated; and (4) a decision deadline and review cadence must be set. No implementation work dependent on this decision may proceed until the context is complete and approved. Assign an owner to compile the missing context within five business days and schedule a decision workshop immediately thereafter. If the context remains incomplete by the deadline, escalate to the architecture governance board for resolution or formal decision deferral.

We will instantiate a new interactor per request and inject dependencies via scoped factories, avoiding shared interactor instances. Dependencies are classified and provided by a DI container with explicit lifetimes:
- Application-scoped singletons: identity-bearing, configuration-driven, thread-safe services (e.g., loggers, DB clients, caches, metrics) are created once and reused.
- Adapter/request-scoped dependencies: request-specific components whose behavior depends on request parameters (e.g., concrete presenter determined by device adapter and output model) are constructed per request.
- Pure utilities: stateless, immutable helpers may be singletons.

Interactors remain stateless with no mutable shared fields; any unavoidable shared state resides in dedicated services that are explicitly made thread-safe. No interactor instance is reused across requests, eliminating concurrency hazards within interactors.

Routing and concurrency are handled by a dispatcher that:
- Selects the appropriate interactor type based on the use case.
- Uses an InteractorFactory to assemble the interactor with the correct adapter-specific presenter and shared services.
- Executes interactors on a bounded, instrumented executor to control parallelism and provide backpressure.

Presenters are provided by the device adapter per request, enabling correct output models without leaking adapter concerns into core logic. Where adapter-specific mapping is needed, an abstract presenter interface is implemented by per-adapter concrete presenters.

Object pools are avoided for interactors; pooling may be used only for heavy resources (e.g., DB connections) managed by their respective services. This approach ensures correctness under concurrency, minimizes per-request construction cost, and preserves testability and clear separation of concerns.

Adopt NUKE as the repository-wide build orchestrator, with a single build entry point (build.cmd/build.sh) that drives restore, compile, test, pack, publish, and release workflows across multiple solutions and projects. NUKE will host strongly-typed C# targets, support multi-targeting and cross-platform execution via the .NET SDK, and provide first-class IDE/debugger integration, reproducibility, and CI/CD pipeline generation. The build will standardize versioning, artifact staging, cache usage, and dependency graphs across all back-end projects, replacing ad-hoc Makefiles or per-solution scripts.

Frontend projects will be orchestrated from NUKE targets but executed with Node tooling. We will use npm as the default package runner (install, build, test) to minimize tooling surface; yarn may be used only if a specific project mandates it and must be invoked via the same NUKE targets. Bundlers (e.g., Webpack) remain project-local choices and are executed through npm scripts; NUKE will not encode bundler specifics beyond invoking those scripts.

Repository conventions:
- /build hosts the NUKE build project (Build.cs with targets like Clean, Restore, Compile, Test, Pack, Publish, IntegrationTest, E2E, Release).
- All CI pipelines (e.g., GitHub Actions/Azure DevOps) call the same NUKE targets for consistency.
- Artifacts (packages, zips, docker images) are produced via NUKE and stored under a common artifacts directory.
- Configuration is driven by convention plus minimal configuration files (e.g., global.json, Directory.Build.props), allowing per-project overrides when required.

This decision unifies build orchestration while allowing specialized frontend tooling behind a consistent, single-command developer and CI experience.

Decision: Implement the function in TypeScript targeting Node.js 20 (LTS) for the serverless runtime.

Rationale:
- Broad provider support (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions/Run) with mature tooling and SDKs.
- Fast cold starts and small deployment artifacts when bundled with esbuild, suitable for low-latency “Hello World!” and scalable future endpoints.
- Type safety improves maintainability and early error detection while retaining JavaScript’s developer velocity and rich ecosystem.
- Excellent async I/O model aligns with typical serverless integration patterns (APIs, messaging, storage).
- Strong local development, testing, and observability toolchains; widespread team familiarity is likely.

Implementation notes:
- Author in TypeScript; transpile and bundle to a single file with esbuild (or SWC), targeting node20; exclude cloud-native SDKs provided by the runtime.
- Keep dependencies minimal; use native runtimes and standard libraries where possible.
- Use modern module resolution (ESM) or CommonJS consistently per platform guidance.

Trade-offs:
- Adds a build step versus pure Python or JavaScript; requires type tooling and CI setup.
- Not ideal for CPU-bound workloads where Go/Java may outperform.
- If the team is predominantly Python-focused or needs heavy scientific libraries, Python 3.12 may reduce friction.

Scope and revisit:
- Applies to this function and subsequent similar serverless functions unless requirements change.
- Revisit if latency/cost profiles demand Go, workloads become compute-heavy, or platform constraints/team expertise strongly favor another language.

Adopt a centralized Identity and Access Management (IAM) solution using Keycloak (self-hosted) as the primary Identity Provider, exposing OpenID Connect/OAuth 2.0 (and SAML 2.0 where required). The application will integrate via OIDC using Authorization Code + PKCE, validating signed JWT access tokens at the API gateway. Tokens will be short-lived with refresh token rotation and revocation; service-to-service auth will use OAuth 2.0 client credentials with optional mTLS.

Implement MFA via Keycloak’s built-in policies (TOTP and WebAuthn/passkeys), with step-up authentication for sensitive operations and mandatory MFA for administrative roles. Authorization will use RBAC backed by realm/client roles and groups, with optional attribute-based policies via Keycloak authorization services. User provisioning will leverage SCIM where available or IdP federation (e.g., Azure AD, Okta, Google) with just-in-time provisioning and group/role mapping.

Ensure GDPR compliance by minimizing stored PII, enabling user consent and data export/delete flows, encrypting data at rest (PostgreSQL) and in transit (TLS 1.2+), and hosting in EU regions. Enable comprehensive audit logging for authentication, admin actions, and consent events with retention policies. Rate limiting, brute-force protection, and account lockout will be enforced at Keycloak and at the API gateway.

This approach provides a secure, flexible, and extensible foundation with low ongoing license cost (self-managed), supports multi-tenant federation configurations, and allows future extensibility via custom authenticators, identity brokering, and provider plugins without changes to application code. Continuous availability will be achieved via HA Keycloak deployment behind a load balancer with externalized shared storage (PostgreSQL) and backups.

Adopt status-aware ADR header styling in adr-viewer. The viewer will parse each record’s Status field and render a consistent header layout with a prominent, text-first status badge and status-specific accent color. Default mapping:
- Proposed: blue
- Accepted: green
- Rejected: red
- Superseded: gray
- Deprecated: orange
- Draft/Exploring: purple
Unknown or missing status uses a neutral header with no color accent.

Implementation:
- Introduce semantic CSS classes per status (e.g., .adr--status-accepted) and a neutral base header.
- Use a compact status badge with label text and an accessible color token; header background remains neutral to preserve readability, with only accents (badge, left border) colored.
- Provide a configuration file to override status-to-color mappings and to alias custom statuses.
- Ensure WCAG AA contrast for light and dark themes; offer shape/label cues so status is not conveyed by color alone.
- Add a legend in the index view and tooltip titles for badges.
- Gracefully degrade when CSS is unavailable by keeping the text label.

This change differentiates ADR states at a glance without sacrificing accessibility or theming flexibility, and it remains backward compatible with existing ADR content.

Adopt annotation-processor–based code generation with the Immutables library for all new and refactored data/value classes and builders. Concretely:
- Define value types via abstract interfaces/classes annotated with @Value.Immutable and a project-wide @Value.Style to standardize naming, builders, and defaults.
- Generate equals/hashCode/toString, builders, copy-withers, optional handling, and collections via Immutables; do not hand-write these methods.
- Integrate the Immutables processor in the build (Maven/Gradle) and enable it in CI; treat generation warnings as build warnings and compilation as cacheable/incremental.
- For JSON, enable the Immutables Jackson module; generated types must be the wire/DB models where applicable to avoid adapters; otherwise map at boundaries.
- Testing policy: do not unit test generated methods (equals/hashCode/toString/builders). Test only domain behavior and invariants declared in the abstract type (e.g., validation). Rely on the library’s upstream test coverage for generation correctness.
- Coding standards: disallow Lombok and hand-written builders/value boilerplate in main code via static analysis (Checkstyle/Revapi rules) and PR checks. Provide archetypes/templates for new value types.
- Migration: incrementally convert existing boilerplate-heavy classes to Immutables when touched. Maintain binary compatibility using derived immutable types with adapters as needed.
- Tooling: configure IDEs to enable annotation processing and source/generated-sources indexing; commit no generated sources to VCS.

This decision is project-wide for JVM modules to reduce boilerplate, improve consistency, and leverage well-tested generated code.

## Decision
Adopt a design token–driven theming system backed by CSS Custom Properties, enabling per-application and per-subtree theme customization without modifying component code.

- Define a canonical set of semantic design tokens (e.g., color.surface, color.text.primary, color.accent, border.radius, spacing) as the sole inputs to component styling. Components must not reference raw color values.
- Store tokens in a technology-agnostic format (e.g., JSON) and generate platform artifacts (CSS variables, TypeScript typings, SCSS maps) via a token build step. CSS variables are namespaced and emitted per theme.
- Ship a default theme and support additional themes as overlay token sets. Themes are applied by attaching a data-theme attribute or class to a root element, enabling runtime switching and coexisting themes on different subtrees.
- Provide framework bindings (e.g., ThemeProvider for React/Vue) that scope themes, support partial overrides, and allow apps to augment tokens safely. Unspecified tokens fall back to the default theme.
- Ensure SSR compatibility by inlining critical CSS variables and avoiding FOUC; allow prefers-color-scheme to drive dark/light token selection.
- Enforce accessibility by providing token palettes that meet contrast guidelines and by documenting safe combinations.
- Manage versioning: additive token introductions are minor; renames/removals are major with codemods and deprecation windows.
- Optimize performance by using semantic tokens layered over primitive tokens to minimize duplication, and by avoiding per-component CSS duplication.

We will introduce a formal query interface for dashboard filtering by adopting Common Expression Language (CEL) as the canonical query language for search expressions. CEL will be the only supported user-authored expression format for advanced filters in custom dashboards. A dedicated Query Service will parse, type-check, and evaluate CEL expressions against an explicit domain schema and compile them into underlying data-store predicates (e.g., SQL WHERE clauses or search engine filters). The service will run expressions in a sandbox, enforce resource limits, and block disallowed functions to ensure safety and performance.

Key elements of the decision:
- CEL selected for its concise, readable syntax, strong typing, safety, embeddability, and broad operator/function support (logical, comparison, string, list, map, date/time).
- Schema-bound variables and function bindings expose only permitted fields and domain functions; no direct access to system internals.
- Expressions are purely filtering/scoping; aggregations, projections, and ordering remain in the dashboard configuration layer, not in CEL.
- Versioned expression support with server-side validation, linting, and helpful diagnostics; saved queries are stored with language version metadata.
- Backward compatibility: existing filter box inputs continue to work and are translated to CEL where feasible; a migration assistant helps users upgrade.
- Governance and safety: maximum expression size/depth, execution timeouts, rate limiting, and audit logging of evaluated expressions.
- Developer ergonomics: SDKs, examples, and a playground with live schema awareness and test data.

This decision enables flexible, composable, and safe search expressions while keeping execution centralized, observable, and portable across data backends.

Adopt a schema-driven CSV validation service for Archivematica-related manifests prior to ingest, with first-class support for metadata.csv, rights.csv, and Avalon Manifest.csv.

- Define machine-readable, versioned schemas for each manifest type using Frictionless Table Schema (for structure, required fields, types, constraints) and CSV Dialect (for delimiters/quoting), with optional JSON Schema for cross-field rules.
- Publish schemas in a dedicated, versioned repository (SemVer), tagged per Archivematica release and per external profile (e.g., Avalon), with clear aliases (latest, 1.x).
- Implement a stateless validation service:
  - REST API and CLI accepting CSVs (file or URL) and schema/profile id.
  - Deterministic results: pass/fail, normalized warnings, machine-readable error report (JSON) detailing row/column, rule, message, and remediation hint.
  - Support batch validation and streaming for large files.
  - Return non-zero exit codes for failures in CLI; HTTP 200 with structured result payload in API.
- Provide built-in profiles:
  - Archivematica metadata.csv: field presence, repeatability, namespace/predicate validation, value type constraints.
  - Archivematica rights.csv: rights type vocabularies, date formats, required groupings, cardinality.
  - Avalon Manifest.csv: hierarchy integrity (parent/child refs), identifier uniqueness, required descriptive fields, controlled vocab checks.
- Allow custom profiles by supplying external Table Schema/JSON Schema documents; enforce strict-by-default with configurable warning→error promotion.
- Integrate as a pre-ingest gate:
  - Optional hook in Archivematica transfer workflow to invoke validation and block/flag on failure.
  - Standalone use by upstream systems (e.g., Avalon) via API.
- Ensure backward compatibility via schema pinning; deprecate with grace periods and migration notes.
- Ship minimal UI for manual uploads, plus libraries for Python/Go to embed validation.

We will require authentication for all externally accessible NHSUK prototype kit deployments by integrating Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) OIDC authentication and conditional access (including MFA) in front of the prototype runtime. Access will be restricted to an Entra security group containing NHSmail users and explicitly approved, time-bound guest accounts; anonymous access will be disabled. The authentication enforcement will be implemented at the edge/reverse-proxy layer (e.g., Azure Front Door/Application Gateway) or via platform-native capabilities (e.g., App Service “Easy Auth” or Azure Static Web Apps Auth) so that no credentials are embedded in the prototype codebase.

Additional safeguards will be applied:
- Public search indexing will be disabled (robots headers) and the “Prototype – not a live service” banner will be consistently displayed on all pages.
- Access logging and audit trails will be enabled via platform telemetry; alerts will be configured for unusual access patterns.
- Short-lived preview links for external research participants will use time-limited guest access or expiring links protected by Entra ID.
- Local development remains unauthenticated; any shared URLs must use the authenticated environment.
- No prototype will be published to a publicly reachable endpoint without this protection; exceptions require senior approval and documented risk acceptance.

This approach provides low-friction SSO for staff, fine-grained access control, and a clear boundary preventing public confusion with live NHS services.

Adopt vendoring of the citerus library into this repository via Git subtree and include it as a Maven reactor module under a single project root.

- Use git subtree to import citerus into /vendor/citerus, tracking the upstream main repository. Periodically pull upstream changes (git subtree pull) and resolve conflicts locally, enabling close synchronization without requiring separate installs.
- Convert the project to a Maven multi-module build with an aggregator POM at the repository root; include the vendored citerus module and all project modules so everything builds from a single root location.
- Depend on the local citerus module via the reactor; do not publish or install a separate citerus artifact. This removes the need to install citerus into local repositories and keeps the touch on upstream code light.
- Apply local fixes directly within the vendored module. Upstream contributions remain optional and can be submitted as PRs when desired, avoiding debates that could block local progress.
- Maintain subtree hygiene: pin to specific upstream commits, tag sync points, and use a dedicated “upstream-sync” branch for integrating upstream updates before merging to main.
- Avoid Git submodules and non-rooted layouts to align with current comfort and tooling.

Consolidate the current two-stack setup into a single parent CloudFormation stack that orchestrates two nested stacks: (1) Foundation (long‑lived) and (2) Application (mutable). The Foundation nested stack will include CloudFront and any resources it inherently requires (e.g., Route 53 records, ACM certificates, key policies, logging buckets), acknowledging that CloudFront cannot be isolated in practice. The Application nested stack will contain the faster‑changing resources (e.g., compute, APIs, functions, standard buckets, IAM roles specific to runtime).

The parent stack will own all cross‑cutting/shared values and pass them as Parameters to the nested stacks, eliminating direct cross‑stack references and circular dependencies. Shared identifiers (e.g., ARNs, domain names, bucket names) will be surfaced as Outputs from the nested stacks to the parent only. Where late‑binding is required, small dynamic values may be published/read via SSM Parameter Store to decouple deployments.

Deployment will target nested stacks selectively: routine changes update only the Application nested stack, avoiding CloudFront’s long provisioning cycles; Foundation updates occur infrequently and are protected by stack policies and explicit approvals/change sets. Replacement of long‑lived resources is prevented by stack policies and Retain/UpdateReplacePolicy where appropriate.

This structure preserves the intent to minimize slow updates while removing ambiguity and fragile cross‑stack coupling, yielding clearer ownership, simpler dependencies, and predictable pipelines.

We will operate the ordering system with a resilient, cache-first, degraded-mode strategy when the smart fridge is unavailable or stale.

- Maintain a per-fridge, per-SKU local inventory cache with timestamps. Track: last-known stock, pending reservations, fulfilled pickups.
- Define freshness thresholds: soft-stale (e.g., >2 min) and hard-stale (e.g., >10 min). Apply a circuit breaker with exponential backoff when the fridge API is unavailable or throttled.
- In normal/soft-stale mode, accept new orders using: sellable = max(0, cached_stock − pending_reservations − contingency_buffer). The contingency_buffer accounts for occasional cash users and uncertainty; it is dynamic (learned from historical variance) with a nonzero floor.
- In hard-stale mode, pause new orders for affected SKUs/fridges unless stock is physically controlled by us (e.g., locked bay). Pre-paid orders already placed remain valid.
- Support only pre-paid orders in degraded modes; do not allow cash-on-pickup through the ordering system. Communicate “low-confidence availability” in UI when soft-stale.
- Assign idempotent reservation tokens with expiry to all orders; tokens decrement sellable immediately and are reconciled on pickup or expiry.
- On reconnection, reconcile state: pull authoritative stock, apply reservations FIFO; if oversell is detected, prioritize earliest paid orders, proactively notify impacted customers, auto-refund, and mark items out-of-stock.
- Log staleness, buffer hits, and oversell incidents to continuously tune contingency buffers and thresholds per fridge/SKU.
- Expose health signals (API availability, staleness) to operations and block batch promotions when fridges are degraded.

This decision minimizes customer dissatisfaction and oversell risk while allowing continued service with transparent degradation when the external smart fridge is unavailable or delayed.

Adopt CodeClimate as the standard automated code review and code quality platform across all repositories. Integrate CodeClimate Maintainability and Test Coverage into the CI pipeline and VCS to provide pull request annotations, status checks, and quality gates.

- Enforce minimum coverage thresholds: 80% global per repo and 90% on changed lines; block merges on coverage regressions for changed code and when repo-wide coverage drops below threshold.
- Enable code smell and technical debt detection; block merges on critical and high-severity issues; require issue triage for medium severity before merge; allow informational issues to pass with warnings.
- Use a centralized .codeclimate.yml baseline managed by the architecture team with language-specific engines; allow repository-level overrides via approved pull requests.
- Apply a ratcheting policy: new/modified code must meet thresholds; legacy hot spots receive incremental improvement targets defined per team.
- Require all pull requests to pass CodeClimate checks; failed checks must be addressed or explicitly waived via an approved exemption recorded in the repo (time-bound, with a remediation ticket).
- Provide team dashboards for maintainability, coverage trends, and debt backlog; include CodeClimate metrics in release and quarterly quality reports.
- Roll out in phases: pilot on two services, then org-wide adoption; treat any false positives by tuning rules rather than disabling checks.
- Assign ownership: each repo’s tech lead is responsible for configuration, visibility, and continuous improvement of CodeClimate metrics.

Adopt a lightweight, declarative function decorator @model that turns pure computation functions into Model nodes with explicit IO metadata used to synthesize and execute a DAG.

- Each model declares:
  - name (default: function name)
  - effect: add_columns or select_rows
  - inputs: mapping of argument names to sources (Param(name, default?), Col(name), Const(value), Derived(name))
  - outputs: list of column names (for add_columns) or a single boolean mask/row index output (for select_rows)
  - requirements: optional schema/units/shape constraints

- The decorated function remains a pure, side-effect-free callable that:
  - accepts resolved numpy arrays/scalars (and an injected rng if needed)
  - returns a dict {col: array} for add_columns, or a boolean array / index array for select_rows
  - is vectorizable over rows and supports broadcasting

- The decorator records metadata and registers the node; a separate execution engine:
  - composes a global DAG from declared inputs/outputs
  - validates acyclicity and schema compatibility
  - resolves parameters vs. table columns at runtime
  - orchestrates ordered execution, chunking, and memory-aware writing to output tables
  - injects a reproducible RandomState/Generator per node (or per chunk) when requested

- Errors are surfaced early via static validation (missing inputs, output collisions), with runtime guards (shape/units).

- Backward compatibility: existing functions can be wrapped without modification by providing IO declarations to the decorator.

- Example mapping for redshift_gamma: inputs = {shape: Param, scale: Param, size: Col or Param}, effect = add_columns, outputs = [redshift].

We will replace all intra-cluster name resolution via /etc/hosts with AWS Route 53-based DNS.

- Create a Private Hosted Zone per environment (e.g., dlp.internal) and manage all internal service records (SolrCloud nodes, Zookeeper ensemble, Fedora, application endpoints) in Route 53.
- Assign stable, human-readable DNS names to services (e.g., solr-0.dlp.internal, fedora.dlp.internal) and decouple them from ephemeral private IPs.
- Use short TTLs (30–60s) to accommodate instance churn and allow rapid failover.
- For load-balanced services, point records at NLB/ALB aliases; for stateful clusters (Solr/ZK), maintain A records per node and a service-level record for clients when appropriate.
- Remove automation that writes peer addresses into /etc/hosts and enforce a minimal, immutable hosts file baseline via configuration management.
- Update application and infrastructure configuration to resolve peers by DNS names only; remove any IP pinning.
- Implement change control for DNS updates (IaC-managed in version control) and monitoring/alerting for DNS resolution failures.
- Rollout plan: stand up Route 53 records in parallel; update one service/environment at a time to use DNS; verify stability; then purge /etc/hosts population; repeat across environments.
- Rollback plan: retain the previous /etc/hosts automation scripts for emergency reversion during rollout; disable after successful cutover.

This decision centralizes name resolution, eliminates mutable /etc/hosts as a single point of failure, and provides resilient, auditable service discovery across rebuilt instances.

## Decision
Adopt a lightweight, custom validation approach and keep validation concerns within our own layers, avoiding external validation libraries. Validation is split by responsibility:

- Presentation/framework layer: perform only syntactic checks (presence, type/format, basic normalization) and map inputs into explicit request DTOs. This protects controllers from malformed input but does not attempt to enforce business rules.
- Use case layer: performs authoritative business validation and orchestrates creation of domain objects. Use cases return a standardized ValidationResult (success with value, or failure with a collection of error codes/messages/fields), not exceptions, for expected validation failures.
- Domain layer: enforce core invariants in value objects, entities, and factories; invalid domain objects must not be instantiated. Prefer factory methods that return ValidationResult to avoid partially constructed aggregates.

Introduce a minimal, framework-agnostic validation abstraction (e.g., rule interfaces, combinators, and error types) sufficient for readability and reuse without coupling to a third-party API. This preserves testability, isolates validation from framework concerns, and avoids dependency/update risks. We will review this decision if validation complexity significantly increases or if a third-party library can be adopted behind our abstraction without leaking into the domain.

We will implement a static, client-only site with no backend, no build step, and minimal dependencies to ensure simplicity, fast deployment, and easy reuse.

- Stack: Plain HTML and CSS, with optional minimal JavaScript (Alpine.js or vanilla) only if needed for basic interactivity. No SPA framework, no bundler, no package manager required.
- Structure: Single-page layout (index.html) plus a small number of modular partials (e.g., header, footer) and assets. A single config.json will drive text content, basic branding (title, logo, colors), and simple feature toggles to allow reuse without code changes.
- Reusability: Published as a template repository with a clear README, example config.json, and commented HTML. Users create a new site by copying the repo or using “Use this template,” then editing config.json and assets. Naming and structure will remain consistent across uses to reduce relearning.
- Deployment: Static hosting via GitHub Pages, Netlify, or any S3/CloudFront-like host. No server processes; deployment is a push to main or a drag-and-drop of the /dist (root) folder. Optional GitHub Action will validate JSON and run a link check.
- Scope constraints: No embedding support, theming is limited to simple variables in CSS and config, and no plugin system. Accessibility and responsive layout will be addressed with semantic HTML and a lightweight CSS approach (e.g., utility classes or a tiny custom stylesheet).
- Maintenance: Versioned template releases with a changelog; changes aim to remain backward-compatible with existing config.json.

Adopt an automated “email-to-case” integration that captures all inbound and outbound messages from the Procurement Operations shared mailbox in Exchange Online into the case management system.

- Implement a mailbox listener using Microsoft Graph change notifications (webhooks) on the shared mailbox to ingest new messages and replies, including attachments and metadata (sender, recipients, timestamps, Internet-Message-Id, threadId).
- Require a case reference token (e.g., [CASE-12345]) in the subject line; the ingestion service matches messages to cases via this token. Where absent, operators can add the token via reply/forward, or the message is queued for manual triage.
- Enforce use of the shared mailbox for all case communications; configure transport rules to auto-BCC an ingestion address for outbound mail and to prevent sending from personal mailboxes to external SBPs for case topics.
- Deduplicate using Internet-Message-Id and maintain conversation threading; store attachments in the case file and persist immutable email metadata for audit.
- Apply role-based access and retention aligned with DfE policies; log all ingestion and matching actions.
- Provide minimal Outlook add-in/quick-steps to insert case tokens and standard templates to reduce user friction.

This decision ensures a complete, auditable view of case-related email interactions without relying on manual copy/paste.

Adopt cucumber-js with Puppeteer as the primary browser automation stack for BDD scenarios. We will standardize on headless Chromium execution in CI and local developer runs, leveraging Puppeteer’s native Node.js API, faster startup, and lower operational overhead compared to Selenium WebDriver. This choice optimizes for developer productivity, stability, and tighter coupling with our JavaScript toolchain, enabling rapid feedback and easier test authoring for the broader team.

Scope:
- All new UI BDD tests will be implemented using cucumber-js + Puppeteer.
- Tests will run in headless Chromium within containers for reproducible CI builds.
- A thin browser-automation abstraction will be introduced to minimize framework lock-in and ease potential migration.

Non-goals (initial phase):
- Full cross-browser coverage (Firefox/Safari) and mobile automation.

Fallback/Expansion criteria:
- If validated requirements demand cross-browser parity (notably Safari or legacy Firefox), we will revisit adopting Selenium WebDriver (or an equivalent cross-browser runner) behind the same abstraction, or selectively add Playwright/Selenium for specific suites.

Operational considerations:
- Use deterministic selectors and test IDs to reduce flakiness.
- Parallelize scenarios where feasible to maintain acceptable build times.
- Monitor test stability and execution time; establish guardrails for test scope (favor API/service tests for non-UI logic).

This decision will be reviewed upon material cross-browser or device coverage requirements.

Adopt a deliberately flat top-level code layout by removing the src/ directory and reducing directory depth across the codebase. All primary domains will live at the repository root with a target maximum depth of two levels for most artifacts.

- Top-level directories: app/ (routes and server components), components/ (reusable UI), features/ (verticals with co-located UI/hooks/utils), lib/ (cross-cutting utilities), styles/, public/, scripts/, tests/ (for e2e/integration), config/ (tooling), and types/.
- Co-locate unit tests, stories, and fixtures with their subject files (e.g., Button.tsx, Button.test.tsx, Button.stories.tsx).
- Prefer feature-first organization: components used exclusively by a feature live under features/<feature>/. Shared building blocks go in components/ or lib/.
- Limit subfolder nesting within any top-level folder to one additional level where possible. Avoid creating intermediate “glue” folders; collapse single-child folders.
- Use path aliases to avoid brittle relative paths (e.g., @app, @components, @features, @lib) and update tsconfig, eslint-import-resolver, and bundler settings accordingly.
- Discourage barrel files that hide deep structure; allow local index.ts only where it materially improves DX without obscuring ownership.
- Migrate by moving files out of src/ to their new homes, updating imports with codemods, and removing the src/ folder. CI and deployment configs will be updated to reflect new paths.
- Success criteria: simpler navigation, shorter import paths, reduced churn from rename/move operations, and faster onboarding. Reevaluate after two sprints; if pain points emerge (e.g., name collisions or growth hotspots), introduce only the minimal additional grouping needed rather than re-nesting broadly.

We will standardize on “Device” as the user-facing term for any physical or virtual equipment that generates, consumes, or stores energy in Smarthub, replacing “Asset” in all UX copy, documentation, support materials, analytics dashboards, and customer communications. The backend domain will retain “Asset” where it has a broader financial/portfolio meaning; when referring specifically to equipment endpoints, services will use “Device.”

APIs: We will add /devices endpoints equivalent to current /assets equipment endpoints. Existing /assets endpoints remain for backward compatibility, marked deprecated in v1 and removed no earlier than two major versions after general availability of /devices. IDs remain stable; /devices/{id} maps 1:1 to existing asset IDs. SDKs will introduce Device classes with Asset aliases for a deprecation period.

Data model: No immediate database renames. The Asset table persists; a Device view/ORM alias will be introduced for equipment contexts. Services handling financial constructs (e.g., valuation, contracts) may continue using Asset terminology internally but must expose “Device” when addressing equipment in cross-service APIs.

Events/telemetry: Begin dual-publishing Device.* and Asset.* events for two release cycles; then drop Asset.*. Update metrics, logs, and feature flags to “Device.”

UI/Permissions: Rename “Assets,” “Asset Groups,” and related labels to “Devices,” “Device Groups,” etc. RBAC scopes gain device.* aliases; asset.* scopes remain during deprecation.

Governance: Add a glossary entry defining Device (equipment endpoint) and Asset (financial/portfolio construct). Introduce a terminology lint check for new code and copy.

Migration timeline: Ship /devices and UI copy changes in the next minor release; announce deprecation with 6-month overlap; remove Asset terminology from public surfaces in the following major release.

## Decision
Adopt Flutter Beta as the project’s default channel to ensure correct iOS builds, with a pinned, vetted Beta version for reproducibility. All developers and CI pipelines will switch to the specified Beta version, and the version will be explicitly pinned in tooling scripts and CI configuration. We will maintain a CI matrix that also builds on Stable to detect regressions and readiness for reversion.

Acceptance criteria to return to Stable:
- The next Stable release includes the iOS build fixes currently only available on Beta.
- Our app passes the full CI suite (including iOS signing/build, integration tests, and smoke tests) on Stable without workarounds.
- No blocking regressions are observed in platform plugins or core features for at least one week of canary runs on Stable.

Risk mitigation:
- Pin the exact Flutter Beta version and Xcode toolchain; upgrade only via an explicit approval process after a green pre-merge canary.
- Maintain a rollback path by keeping Stable workflows intact and periodically validated.
- Document environment setup for Beta, and enforce via preflight checks in dev scripts.

Scope:
- iOS builds: Must use pinned Flutter Beta.
- Android/Web/Desktop: Use the same pinned Beta unless a platform-specific blocker is identified; in such cases, platform owners may opt into Stable with ADR addenda.

This decision remains in effect until the above criteria are met and we formally migrate back to Stable.

## Decision
CCS will standardise on Amazon Web Services (AWS) as the primary cloud hosting platform for Crown Marketplace (CMp) and all new greenfield digital services, including Facilities Management and the Data Submission Service. We will adopt an AWS multi-account landing zone operated under CCS control, with shared guardrails for security, compliance, networking, observability, and cost management, and deliver all infrastructure via Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) and a standard CI/CD pipeline.

Specifics:
- Migrate the DigiTS (Travel) service from supplier-managed AWS to the CCS AWS landing zone, retaining service continuity while bringing operations, security, and cost control in-house.
- Host Facilities Management and subsequent CMp frameworks on AWS to maximise reuse of Digital Marketplace assets and patterns, minimise integration friction, and consolidate vendor management.
- Use GDS Government-as-a-Platform managed services on AWS where advantageous, aligning with existing DM approaches and common government standards.
- Maintain Microsoft Azure only for services with platform constraints or contractual obligations (e.g., existing Powerbuilder/SQL Server Data Warehouse and supplier-specific platforms). These are treated as exceptions governed by an exceptions process, with a medium-term plan to rationalise where feasible.
- Establish cross-cloud integration patterns (secure APIs, messaging, and data exchange) to interoperate with retained Azure/SaaS systems without dictating further multi-cloud expansion.
- Implement standardised operational controls: central identity and access management, secrets management, logging/monitoring, vulnerability management, backup/DR, and tagging for FinOps across AWS accounts.
- Procure a single strategic AWS partner (where required) for enablement and support under CCS ownership, avoiding project-by-project hosting divergence.

This decision reduces overheads, accelerates delivery via reuse of DM-aligned components, strengthens governance and security, and provides a clear, exception-based path for legacy and supplier-hosted systems.

## Decision
Adopt upstream-conformant Kubernetes as the orchestration primitive for container-based workloads. We will provide a minimal, extensible Kubernetes-based platform that delivers high availability, load balancing, horizontal scalability, declarative configuration, internal networking, and service discovery, with self-healing and logging supported via curated add-ons.

To balance flexibility with operational burden, we will prefer managed Kubernetes control planes from cloud providers (e.g., EKS/AKS/GKE) where appropriate, while strictly adhering to CNCF-conformant APIs and portable cluster add-ons to avoid vendor lock-in. We will avoid “batteries included” PaaS layers (e.g., CloudFoundry, OpenShift) and additional abstraction layers (e.g., DC/OS, Swarm).

The platform team will supply:
- A standard cluster baseline (CNI with network policies, ingress, autoscaling, pod disruption budgets, and storage classes).
- Declarative, GitOps-driven delivery (e.g., Argo CD/Flux) and infrastructure-as-code (e.g., Terraform/Cluster API) for repeatable environments.
- Curated, optional add-ons for logging and monitoring (e.g., OpenTelemetry/Fluent Bit, Prometheus/Grafana) and internal-only networking defaults.
- Service discovery via native Kubernetes Services/DNS; service mesh is optional and team-driven.

Service teams retain control over their workloads and may extend with compatible CNCF projects as needed, within guardrails that preserve security, reliability, and portability. We will avoid provider-specific features unless a clear portability path exists or the benefit outweighs the lock-in risk, in which case usage must be explicitly justified and documented.

We will adopt a docs-as-code approach and store technical documentation in GitHub, colocated with the code it describes.

- Scope: All technical documentation for the new platform (architecture, design, runbooks, operations, investigations, ADRs, RFCs, onboarding, incident postmortems) will live in the repository that implements or owns the subject matter. Non-technical policy, portfolio, or broad organisational content may remain in Confluence.
- Structure: Each repository will contain a README and a docs/ folder for detailed documentation, including ADRs in docs/adr/. Documentation will be written in Markdown and reference code and configuration directly.
- Workflow: All documentation changes will be made via pull requests, reviewed and approved using the same process as code (including CODEOWNERS). Documentation updates are required alongside code changes that impact behaviour, operations, or interfaces.
- Visibility: Repositories should be public by default where appropriate. Sensitive content will be kept in private repos with access controls and secrets excluded.
- Quality and automation: We will add CI checks for link integrity, Markdown linting, and structure conventions; optional GitHub Pages generation is permitted for discoverability. Templates for ADRs, READMEs, and runbooks will be standardised.
- Discoverability: A central “platform-docs” index repository will aggregate and link to per-repo documentation and provide cross-cutting navigation.
- Migration: Existing relevant technical content from Confluence will be migrated into the appropriate repositories and kept in sync; stale Confluence pages will be archived with pointers to GitHub.

Adopt Sidekiq with Redis as the background job platform for sending all notifications (starting with GOV.UK Notify emails, later extending to reminders and approval notifications). We will not use a Postgres-backed queue (e.g., DelayedJob).

Key points:
- Use a dedicated managed Redis instance for Sidekiq (not shared with caching) with appropriate persistence (AOF or RDB), TLS, and access controls.
- Encapsulate notification dispatch behind a Notifications service layer and job interface to keep Notify-specific and Sidekiq-specific code isolated, enabling future provider changes or queue migration with minimal impact.
- Implement job idempotency (dedup keys), structured payloads, and store outbound notification attempts/results for traceability.
- Configure queues with priorities (e.g., critical, mailers, low), bounded concurrency, backoff retries, and circuit-breaking around Notify errors; alert on exhausted retries and monitor the dead set.
- Use sidekiq-cron (or equivalent) for scheduled and recurring jobs (e.g., reminders), keeping schedules in code and version-controlled.
- Provide health checks and metrics (queue latency, retry counts, dead jobs) integrated with application monitoring and alerting.
- Ensure rate limiting and batching compliant with Notify constraints; propagate correlation IDs for observability.
- Secure secrets via environment configuration; follow least privilege for Redis access.
- Document operational procedures (draining, pausing queues, replays) and provide runbooks.

This decision prioritizes reliability, performance, and team familiarity while preserving an abstraction that allows revisiting the queue choice in the future if requirements change.

Adopt an indirection layer for service invocation: replace direct internal URLs in Task “Resource” definitions with stable, logical resource identifiers resolved at runtime via the mdsCloud API Gateway and Service Registry.

- Define canonical resource identifiers (e.g., mds:function:<service>/<function>[:version]) as the only supported “Resource” value for state machine tasks and other orchestration artifacts.
- Route all consumer traffic through the API Gateway, which will resolve logical identifiers via the Service Registry to current backend instances, handling load balancing, retries, and failover.
- Prohibit exposure of internal IPs/ports to consumers; internal topology remains opaque. Operators may reconfigure, scale, or “shuffle” services without consumer impact by updating registry entries and gateway routes.
- Introduce versioning and environment scoping in identifiers (e.g., mds:function:payments/charge:v2@prod) to support evolution, blue/green and canary releases, and safe rollback.
- Update SDK/CLI to accept logical identifiers and default to gateway endpoints; provide client-side validation and helpful errors when resolution fails.
- Enforce authentication/authorization at the gateway; apply TLS termination and centralized observability (metrics, tracing, structured logs) per logical resource.
- Maintain backward compatibility for a deprecation window by supporting existing URL-based “Resource” values through a compatibility resolver; log and alert on usage to drive migration.
- Codify operator workflows: changes to backends occur via registry updates and gateway config, not consumer artifact edits; health checks and readiness gates guard route activation.
- Document SLAs/SLOs at the logical resource level and monitor them via gateway-level telemetry.

This decision decouples consumers from infrastructure details, reduces operational risk during maintenance or topology changes, and establishes a consistent contract and control plane for service invocation across the mdsCloud ecosystem.

We will adopt sparse, layered configuration with deep-merge semantics so that users can set or override a single key without replicating parent structures.

- Format: YAML and TOML are supported; JSON accepted where applicable. Both nested objects and dotted-path keys (e.g., build.output.dir) are allowed for brevity.
- Merge strategy: Config is resolved by recursively merging maps/objects; scalar values are replaced; arrays are replaced wholesale (no element-wise merge) to keep semantics predictable. Optional extensions for array merging may be introduced later with explicit operators.
- Layers and precedence (lowest to highest): built-in defaults < project config < user config < environment variables < CLI flags. Later layers override earlier ones at the leaf key level.
- Unsetting: Setting a key to null (or TOML none) removes the key from the effective config, falling back to the next lower layer or default. An explicit unset operator may be added in future if needed.
- Validation and defaults: After merge, the effective configuration is validated against a schema; missing values receive defaults at validation time. Unknown keys are rejected by default to avoid silent typos (configurable per environment).
- Determinism: Merge order is stable and documented; tie-breaking favors the highest-precedence source encountered last.
- Tooling: The config loader accepts both file-based and in-memory overrides using the same merge rules. Dumping tools will, by default, emit only changed keys to discourage structure copying; a --expand option will render the fully resolved config when needed.

This decision ensures minimal, focused config files while preserving clarity, predictability, and strong validation.

## Decision
Terraform .tf files are the single source of truth for provisioning and changing AWS API Gateway endpoints and Lambda functions. No manual changes will be made in the AWS Console; all resources must be created, modified, and deleted via reviewed Terraform changes.

We will structure the code by logical components:
- Per service/domain: dedicated Terraform module encapsulating API Gateway configuration (stages, deployments, routes, integrations) and associated Lambdas (functions, aliases, permissions, IAM, logs).
- Per environment (dev, stage, prod): separate stacks using environment-specific workspaces or directories that instantiate service modules with environment-specific variables.
- Within each stack: files are organized by concern (api_gateway.tf, lambdas.tf, iam.tf, networking.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, providers.tf) to keep diffs focused and readable.

Remote state is mandatory via S3 backend with DynamoDB table for state locking, one state per environment per stack. Providers and modules will be version-pinned. All resources must include standardized tags (env, service, owner, cost-center, compliance).

CI/CD will run terraform fmt/validate/tflint and generate a plan on pull requests; applies are performed only on protected branches after approval. Drift detection runs on a schedule and on-demand; detected drift must be reconciled by updating Terraform, not by console edits. Artifact packaging for Lambdas is handled by the build pipeline; Terraform references immutable artifacts (e.g., versioned S3 objects or container images) rather than building code.

Common patterns (e.g., Lambda + API route + permissions) will be abstracted into reusable internal modules to enforce consistency. Naming conventions will align resource names with API paths and HTTP methods where feasible and be standardized across environments.

All changes impacting public APIs require explicit review for backward compatibility and security. Breaking changes must be accompanied by staged deployments (aliases/weighted traffic) and rollbacks defined in Terraform.

## Decision
Adopt an API-first approach and publish a contract-driven, RESTful JSON API documented with OpenAPI 3.1 as the single source of truth. The OpenAPI specification will be authored and reviewed before implementation, and will include comprehensive schemas, authentication flows, request/response examples, error formats, pagination, filtering, sorting, rate limiting, and webhooks (if any).

Documentation will be generated from the spec and published to a developer portal with:
- Human-friendly reference via Redoc/Swagger UI and a “Try It” console against a sandbox.
- Downloadable OpenAPI file, Postman collection, and quickstart guides.
- Auto-generated SDKs for key languages (e.g., TypeScript/Java, Python) using the spec.

Standardization decisions:
- Resource-oriented REST over HTTPS; JSON as the canonical media type.
- OAuth2 Client Credentials for server-to-server, with API keys as a limited alternative if required; bearer tokens over TLS only.
- Consistent conventions: cursor-based pagination, sparse fieldsets, filters, and sorting; idempotency keys for unsafe methods; RFC 7807 problem+json error responses; UTC ISO-8601 timestamps; snake_case or camelCase consistently across all fields.
- Versioning via URI (/v1) with semantic versioning and a documented deprecation/sunset policy surfaced via headers.
- Rate limits communicated via standard headers; retry and backoff guidance provided.

Quality and governance:
- Lint and validate the spec (e.g., Spectral) in CI; generate mock servers from the spec for consumer testing.
- Contract tests ensure implementation and documentation remain in sync; breaking changes blocked by CI.
- Changelog and migration guides accompany releases; examples cover common workflows and edge cases.

This decision minimizes integration friction, reduces support queries, and ensures durable, discoverable API behavior for external consumers.

Select Material UI (MUI v5) as the primary front-end component framework for styling the web application.

MUI provides the most comprehensive and actively maintained React component library with strong TypeScript support, robust theming and design tokens, accessibility conformance, responsive utilities, and an extensive ecosystem (X Data Grid, date pickers, charts via community). Its customization system (SX prop, theme overrides, styled API) enables us to implement our product brand without being constrained by the default Material aesthetic. MUI’s documentation, community size, and release cadence reduce risk and onboarding time relative to Semantic UI (slower maintenance) and React-Bootstrap (narrower component surface, Bootstrap-first look-and-feel).

Decision constraints and guidelines:
- Adopt MUI v5 with emotion styling (default). Use SX and theme tokens for all styling; avoid ad-hoc CSS.
- Define a central theme (colors, typography, spacing, breakpoints) and component-override policy to enforce consistency.
- Prefer MUI components over custom implementations where available; allow exceptions for specialized needs with design review.
- Ensure accessibility by using MUI’s a11y patterns and running automated checks.
- Avoid mixing UI kits; phase out any existing Semantic UI or React-Bootstrap usage upon touch and during scheduled refactors.
- Monitor MUI roadmap; reassess if maintenance, licensing, or performance materially change.

Adopt a process-aware Domain Event Dispatcher that provides reliable fan-out to both in-process and cross-process/background components.

- Introduce a single publish API (DomainEventBus) that persists each domain event (ID, type, payload, timestamp, TTL) to a durable store (Room) and immediately fans out.
- In-process delivery: forward to the existing Otto bus for components running in the main process.
- Cross-process/background delivery: emit explicit, permission-guarded broadcast Intents carrying the event envelope to app-internal receivers. Receivers must enqueue handling via WorkManager (or Foreground Service when required) to ensure execution even if the component is not currently running and to respect device constraints.
- Reliability: at-least-once delivery with deduplication by event ID on the consumer side. Publishers do not assume synchronous handling; all handlers must be idempotent.
- Backpressure and cleanup: dispatcher prunes expired/handled events by TTL and retention policy; WorkManager retries transient failures with exponential backoff.
- Security: broadcasts are signature-permission protected; payloads avoid PII where possible and are validated/deserialized defensively.
- Contract: publishers emit only through DomainEventBus (not directly to Otto). Subscribers register via:
  - Otto for in-process listeners.
  - A BroadcastReceiver that enqueues WorkManager jobs for background/off-process listeners.
- State access: consumers should derive UI from repositories; sticky broadcasts are avoided. For “latest state” needs, query the repository rather than relying on event replay.
- Observability: dispatcher logs publication, fan-out results, and delivery metrics (success/failure, latency). Feature flags allow toggling broadcast fan-out during rollout.

This decision ensures all interested components, including background services, receive domain events reliably across processes without coupling publishers to transport or process boundaries.

We will consolidate application Redis usage to a single, shared ElastiCache Redis cluster and decommission redundant instances.

- Standardize on backend-redis as the shared ElastiCache Redis for application workloads (caching, queues, rate limiting), including Rummager. Migrate Rummager off api-redis to backend-redis.
- Freeze logs-redis for legacy logging only; do not add new dependencies. Decommission logs-redis once the logging replacement is live.
- Decommission api-redis after Rummager migration completes and stability is verified.

Configuration and operational guardrails:
- Use key prefixing by application/service and function (e.g., app:feature:*), and enforce TTLs where applicable.
- Right-size backend-redis capacity and I/O headroom for combined workloads; enable Multi-AZ with auto-failover and at least one replica.
- Standardize on Redis 7.x, encryption in transit/at rest, AUTH, parameter group with safe eviction policy (allkeys-lru) for caches; avoid persistence (AOF) unless explicitly justified per use case.
- Prefer cluster mode disabled initially for operational simplicity and atomic operations; reassess enabling cluster mode if vertical scaling limits are approached.
- Define SLOs and alerts for memory, CPU, evictions, latency, failover events; establish a maintenance window and snapshot schedule for disaster recovery.

Execution:
1) Load/perf test backend-redis with projected combined traffic. 2) Migrate Rummager to backend-redis and monitor. 3) Retire api-redis. 4) Migrate off logs-redis per logging replacement plan, then retire it.

We will formalize a Health Module Contract to decouple the app from module implementations and enable independent evolution and potential extraction into a standalone project.

- Define a stable “health-module-contract” artifact exposing interfaces (e.g., HealthModule, Capability providers, Lifecycle hooks, Event handlers) that every health module must implement. The app depends only on this contract.
- Use a shared “health-models” artifact for data models and serialization, consumed by both openchs-android and openchs-health-modules. All inter-component communication (requests, responses, events) occurs strictly via these models.
- Health modules encapsulate common domain logic reusable across modules. Module-specific business rules that influence data shape, validation, and transformations are expressed in and alongside the shared models, preserving a single source of truth for interop.
- Enforce dependency direction: app → contract + models; modules → contract + models; modules must not depend on the app or other modules.
- Provide a discovery/registration mechanism (e.g., ServiceLoader/DI registry) for modules to declare capabilities and be wired at runtime without compile-time coupling.
- Standardize lifecycle callbacks (initialize, warm-up, execute, teardown) and error/health reporting interfaces so modules can be monitored and managed uniformly.
- Adopt semantic versioning:
  - models: MAJOR for breaking schema changes; MINOR for additive fields; PATCH for fixes.
  - contract: MAJOR for breaking interface changes; MINOR for new optional interfaces/capabilities.
  - The app must remain backward compatible across at least one MAJOR version; shims/adapters may be used when necessary.
- Provide contract compliance tests and a TCK that module implementers must pass; publish example reference modules.
- Build and distribute modules as separate artifacts to allow independent release cadence and potential extraction into a dedicated “openchs-health-modules” project.
- Documentation: publish the contract, model schemas, lifecycle, versioning policy, and migration guides to enable third-party module development.

## Decision
Adopt Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) as the authoritative mechanism to capture, communicate, and evolve significant architectural decisions for this project.

- Format and template: Use the MADR template (Markdown Any Decision Records) with the headings Context, Decision, Status, Consequences, and Alternatives.
- Location: Store ADRs in the repository at docs/adr/, committed to version control alongside the code.
- Numbering and naming: Sequential numbering with descriptive slugs (e.g., 0001-use-adr.md). One ADR per decision.
- Scope: Create ADRs for decisions that impact architecture, cross-cutting concerns, security, data model, interfaces, significant dependencies, deployment, or cost. Minor implementation details are excluded.
- Status workflow: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated → Superseded. Superseding ADRs must link bidirectionally.
- Process: New ADRs are introduced via pull request with review by at least one architect and one representative from impacted teams. Acceptance requires consensus or designated architect approval.
- Traceability: Reference relevant tickets, RFCs, diagrams, and code modules. Link ADR IDs in PR descriptions and commit messages where applicable.
- Change control: Changes to Accepted ADRs require a new ADR (do not rewrite history). Minor edits (typos/clarifications) allowed without status changes.
- Tooling: Use adr-tools or log4brains for scaffolding and publishing; optional CI check verifies ADR syntax, unique IDs, and status links.
- Visibility: Publish ADR index at docs/adr/README.md and surface in project wiki/portal. Review ADRs quarterly for relevance.
- Ownership: The Architecture group curates the ADR catalog; all teams are responsible for proposing and adhering to ADRs.

We will use a standard project boilerplate for scaffolding, build tooling, routing, authentication, i18n, form handling, and general layout to accelerate delivery. The map will be treated as a first-class, domain-specific component that we design, implement, and own; we will not adopt generic map UI widgets beyond a proven rendering engine.

We will leverage a battle-tested mapping SDK (Mapbox GL JS as default) solely as the rendering/tiling engine and data source provider. Access to the SDK will be encapsulated behind a MapService adapter interface, enabling future substitution (e.g., MapLibre GL, Leaflet, Google Maps) without rewriting the application. All domain interactions (layers, selections, drawing, clustering, tooltips, controls) will be implemented in a custom Map UI library within the repo as an independent package.

The Map UI library will:
- Expose a stable API and events aligned with our domain model.
- Use app design tokens and theming; avoid external UI kits on-canvas.
- Maintain unidirectional data flow and remain store-agnostic (adapters for Redux/Query/etc.).
- Enforce a performance budget (FPS targets, memory, tile count) and support WebGL fallbacks.
- Include accessibility features (keyboard navigation, ARIA for controls, screen-reader summaries).
- Ship with comprehensive tests (interaction, visual regression, performance) and story-driven docs.

Ownership resides with the core team; semantic versioning and changelog are required. Boilerplate choices elsewhere must not constrain the map’s rendering loop or event model. Non-map screens may use generic components. All new features that touch spatial UX land in the Map UI library first, then integrate into the app.

We will adopt automated testing as the default approach for all testable aspects of the system. All new functionality must include appropriate automated tests following a test pyramid: extensive unit tests, targeted integration and contract tests, and a minimal set of end-to-end tests for critical user journeys. Non-functional tests (security checks, static analysis, linting, dependency scanning, license compliance, performance baselines, and accessibility checks) will be automated where tooling permits.

Automated tests will run in CI on every pull request and on main branch merges. Merges must be blocked by failing tests, static analysis, or policy checks. Baseline code coverage thresholds will be enforced and may ratchet upward over time; new code must not reduce coverage. Nightly and scheduled pipelines will execute extended suites (e.g., longer-running performance, cross-browser, or soak tests).

Test environments will be provisioned as code and ephemeral where possible. Test data management will be automated and repeatable. Flaky tests will be treated as defects and fixed or removed promptly; quarantining is temporary and time-boxed.

Manual testing will be limited to exploratory, usability, and rare scenarios not yet automatable, and must be documented with a plan to automate when feasible. Exceptions require explicit risk acceptance and approval from the product and engineering leads.

Adopt a standardized template for all decision records to ensure consistency, comparability, and auditability. We will use a lightweight variant of MADR, with the following required fields: Title, Status, Date, Context (Decision Drivers), Considered Options, Decision, Consequences, and Links. Optional fields include: Pros/Cons per option, Risks/Mitigations, Decision Makers/Contributors, and Related ADRs. All ADRs are stored under /docs/adr (or /adr) using the naming convention YYYYMMDD-short-title.md. ADRs are immutable once “Accepted,” except for metadata updates (links, status).

When re-deciding an issue, do not modify or delete the original record. Instead:
- Create a new ADR that supersedes the old one, clearly stating the rationale for change and what has changed.
- Update the old ADR’s Status to “Superseded” and add a Superseded-by link to the new ADR.
- In the new ADR, include a Supersedes link back to the prior ADRs and summarize prior decisions for context.
- Preserve the full history to provide traceability for audits, knowledge transfer, and rollback considerations.

For legacy decision documents without the template:
- Do not retroactively rewrite history; instead, add a wrapper ADR (using the template) that references the legacy document and captures missing metadata.
- When revisiting such a decision, create a new templated ADR that supersedes the legacy decision as above.

Tooling such as adr-tools may be used to enforce structure and naming, but the written template takes precedence.

Rename the package utils-demo to origin-deploy to accurately reflect its role as the deployment tool for the Origin system.

- Publish origin-deploy as the successor package, starting at the next minor version of utils-demo to preserve semantic continuity (e.g., utils-demo v2.7.x ➜ origin-deploy v2.8.0).
- Deprecate utils-demo on the registry with a clear deprecation message pointing to origin-deploy; publish a final patch release of utils-demo that prints a runtime notice and forwards CLI commands to origin-deploy when feasible.
- Migrate repository name, documentation, CI/CD pipelines, release automation, and issue tracking to origin-deploy, preserving git history and tags; update package metadata (description, keywords) to emphasize “Origin system deployment.”
- Provide a compatibility shim for one release cycle: a thin utils-demo package that depends on and invokes origin-deploy, then archive utils-demo after the grace period.
- Update all internal references (scripts, Dockerfiles, Helm charts, Terraform, pipelines) and external docs/examples to use origin-deploy; add redirects for docs links where supported.
- Communicate the change via release notes, CHANGELOG, and a migration note; no breaking behavior changes are introduced beyond the name change.
- Ownership and support remain with the current team; SLA and support channels unchanged.

## Decision
Adopt a turn-based, player-directed command system with party-level control to ensure meaningful player choice in combat. Each combat round proceeds by initiative order; when a friendly character’s turn begins, the game pauses and the player selects that character’s actions using a command interface. Each character has a fixed Action Economy (e.g., 1 Main Action, 1 Movement, 1 Bonus/Reaction per round) with clearly previewed outcomes (range, AoE, hit chance, resource costs, cooldowns). No friendly character will perform combat actions without explicit player input or a player-defined tactic.

Allies are controllable on their turns by default; alternatively, the player can assign per-ally Tactical Directives (aggressive, defensive, support, custom priority lists) that the AI executes only when the player does not issue manual commands. If the player fails to choose within a configurable turn timer, a safe default is applied (Defend/Take Cover) rather than a random action.

Resolution uses deterministic rules with bounded RNG only for outcome variability (e.g., hit/miss, crit) but never for action selection. The UI supports mouse/keyboard and controller with a unified radial/menu-based command palette, target cycling, and previews. Actions are queued and can be adjusted before confirmation; once confirmed, execution is final for that turn.

This model guarantees player agency, supports party micromanagement or high-level tactics, and is extensible to new abilities without altering the core interaction loop.

Adopt Sentry as the standard platform for real-time production error discovery and reporting for this application, leveraging the existing DLS Sentry organization. Implement official Sentry SDKs across all application tiers (frontend, backend, background jobs) with release and environment tagging, source maps (frontend), and commit integration for suspect commit identification. Enable Sentry Performance for traces and spans to correlate errors with latency and throughput issues.

Configure alerting and routing via existing DLS channels (Slack, email, PagerDuty) with ownership rules by service/team, severity-based alert policies, and auto-issue grouping. Apply dynamic sampling and rate limits to control cost and noise, while ensuring 100% capture for high-severity exceptions. Enforce PII scrubbing at SDK and server levels, use allow/deny lists for context data, and adhere to DLS data retention and GDPR policies. Use environment separation (dev/stage/prod) and project-per-service where appropriate.

Establish operational practices: release health tracking, deploy marker automation in CI/CD, source map upload in build pipelines, and error triage SLAs integrated with the on-call process. Configure dashboards and queries for error budgets and top regressions. Define escalation workflows to incidents in Sentry (or PagerDuty) for critical error-rate thresholds.

Centralize access via DLS RBAC and SSO; audit logs retained per compliance standards. Export structured events to the observability data lake for long-term analytics if needed. Reevaluate this decision if Sentry ceases to meet SLAs, required compliance, or cost objectives, or if consolidated observability mandates a platform change.

Adopt a multi-layer, deny-by-default execution model that only permits vetted DataSHIELD aggregate methods to run, and prevents arbitrary script execution.

- Enforce an explicit allowlist of approved functions and packages; block dynamic evaluation (e.g., eval/parse, do.call on unapproved symbols), reflection, and native extensions. Disallow user-installed packages; deploy only signed, pinned, reproducible builds of DataSHIELD packages.
- Pre-execution static validation: parse submitted code, resolve symbols, and reject anything outside the allowlist or containing prohibited constructs (system calls, file I/O, network I/O, subprocess, unsafe Rcpp/C). Complement with runtime policy enforcement using a restricted interpreter configuration.
- Execute workloads in ephemeral, non-privileged containers/pods with read-only root, no host mounts, no shell, seccomp/AppArmor profiles, cgroups resource limits, and PID/IPC/user namespace isolation. Disable outbound network egress and inbound access; only broker-mediated control channel is allowed. Secrets are not mounted.
- Remove access to filesystem paths beyond a scratch tmpfs; block fork/exec and LD_PRELOAD; disable loading of shared libraries unless on the signed allowlist.
- Comprehensive auditability: immutable, centralized logs of submitted calls, resolved functions, package versions, and outcomes. Alerts on policy violations; auto-termination of non-compliant sessions.
- Governance: change control for the allowlist via code review and security sign-off; periodic penetration testing and automated conformance tests in CI; routine key/package rotation and image rebuilds.

This decision prioritizes a verifiable, least-privilege sandbox that prevents malicious execution while preserving approved DataSHIELD analyses.

Adopt Terragrunt to centralize and DRY shared Terraform configuration across all projects and stacks. We will:

- Introduce a top-level terragrunt.hcl (per repo or org “live” repo) that defines:
  - Remote state (bucket, key format, DynamoDB/S3 settings) via remote_state.
  - Common provider configuration via generate blocks.
  - Organization-wide locals (e.g., stackname/environment/account/region conventions, tags).
  - Standard input defaults (e.g., stackname) and hooks/policies.

- Structure environments/stacks to inherit from the root via include, overriding only stack-specific inputs. No backend blocks or duplicated provider config are permitted in stack modules.

- Reference modules from a dedicated modules repo (or local path), preserving ADR 10 directory structure while replacing per-stack duplication with terragrunt.hcl files. Module code will not contain backend configuration.

- Standardize state key naming and tagging conventions to ensure consistent state isolation and discoverability.

- Enforce usage via CI/CD: terragrunt run-all plan/apply for orchestrating stacks; block direct terraform init/plan/apply in pipelines. Provide bootstrap/migration scripts to wrap existing stacks, and deprecate repeated configuration.

- Maintain parity with ADR 10 by keeping project boundaries and stack directories; Terragrunt becomes the orchestration layer that supplies shared config and wiring.

This decision reduces repetition, prevents drift in critical settings (remote state, providers, tags), and enables consistent governance, while allowing incremental migration of existing stacks.

Adopt a polyglot persistence approach:

- Use a document database (MongoDB) as the source of truth for aggregates, storing one aggregate root per document and persisting state changes atomically within the aggregate boundary.
- Maintain a separate read model optimized for cross-aggregate queries in a relational database, populated via projections/event handlers (CQRS). Projections will denormalize and join data from multiple aggregates into query-friendly tables/views, enabling efficient reporting and ad-hoc queries without impacting write performance.
- Implement eventual consistency between the write store (MongoDB) and the read store (RDBMS) via an outbox pattern and idempotent consumers to ensure reliability.
- Keep aggregate schemas in MongoDB simple and self-contained; disallow cross-aggregate references beyond immutable identifiers.
- Define clear SLAs and monitoring for projection lag; provide mechanisms for read model rebuilds and backfills.
- Use MongoDB for read scenarios confined to a single aggregate; route multi-aggregate reads to the relational read model.

We will not commit ABCI events into Header.LastResultsHash. LastResultsHash will be the Merkle root over DeliverTx results including only deterministic fields: Code, Data, GasWanted, and GasUsed. ResponseBeginBlock.Events and ResponseEndBlock.Events will not be included in LastResultsHash, and ResponseDeliverTx events will be excluded as well. Log, Info, and Codespace remain excluded.

To preserve provability for applications that require it, we will provide two supported approaches:
- Applications may explicitly commit any event data they need to the application state tree under their own schema.
- We will introduce an opt-in, separately versioned EventsRoot commitment outside of LastResultsHash in a future protocol upgrade, gated by a consensus parameter/feature bit and accompanied by an application-declared schema/version so that event format changes do not necessitate a hard fork.

For existing networks that adopted PR#4845’s event hashing, the event commitment will be disabled via a protocol version bump and/or consensus param at a coordinated upgrade height, after which blocks will use the revised LastResultsHash definition above.

Adopt Helm 3 charts as the primary mechanism to install, configure, and upgrade Kyma, replacing the custom Kyma Installer. Each Kyma component will be packaged as an independent, versioned Helm chart; an umbrella chart will orchestrate dependency management, configuration, and lifecycle across components. Charts will be published to an OCI-backed registry and versioned using semantic versioning to enable reproducible deployments and controlled rollbacks. Configuration will be expressed via values files with opinionated profiles (e.g., evaluation, production) and presets to standardize common scenarios while preserving extensibility. Upgrades will be performed using Helm’s native upgrade/rollback flows with pre/post hooks and health checks; component contracts must define upgrade safety and backward compatibility. CI/CD will validate charts (linting, e2e, conformance), sign artifacts, and attest provenance. The Installer CR and controller are deprecated; a migration path will be provided, including automated translation of Installer CRs to values, data migration hooks, and documentation. Support for the legacy installer will be maintained for a limited period with security-only fixes, followed by removal per the deprecation policy.
