- Use a managed Kafka offering where available to reduce operational burden; otherwise deploy a highly available Kafka cluster with 3+ brokers and ZooKeeper-less (KIP-500) mode.
- Establish a domain-driven topic taxonomy (domain.context.eventName.v1), with partitioning sized to expected throughput and keying by business identity to preserve order per entity.
- Standardize event contracts using Avro with a Schema Registry to enforce compatibility (backward by default) and enable evolution without breaking consumers.
- Implement at-least-once delivery semantics with consumer groups and offset commits; require producer idempotence and keys; consumers must be idempotent and support replay.
- Apply the Transactional Outbox pattern (or Change Data Capture via Debezium) to publish events reliably from transactional stores.
- Define retention policies per topic (time- or size-based) and compaction where appropriate for state-like streams.
- Provide dead-letter topics and retry policies (exponential backoff) for poison messages; prohibit infinite retries on primary topics.
- Enforce secure transport (TLS), authentication (SASL/OAuth), and authorization (ACLs). Isolate environments (dev/test/prod) and use dedicated clusters for critical workloads.
- Instrument producers/consumers with standardized tracing/metrics/logging; enable Kafka metrics and lag monitoring with alerting SLAs.
- Create an Event Catalog documenting topic purposes, schemas, ownership, SLAs, and change processes. Changes require review via ADRs and schema compatibility checks.
- Provide client libraries and templates for common languages with bootstrap configuration, observability, and policy compliance baked in.

This decision enables scalable, resilient, and evolvable inter-service communication while maintaining governance and operational clarity.

We will adopt an online third‑party headless CMS to manage static site content (About, Publications, Team) and deprecate hard‑coded JSON in the front end. The CMS will serve as the single source of truth, exposing content via read‑only APIs consumed by the front end at build time (preferred) or runtime with caching. We will select a SaaS headless CMS with versioning, roles/permissions, editorial workflows, Markdown support, localization, webhooks, and export capabilities.

Scope:
- Migrate existing static content to CMS models (e.g., Pages, People, Publications).
- Update the front end to fetch content via an abstraction layer with schema mapping and graceful fallbacks.
- Configure build hooks to re-deploy on content changes; enable runtime cache invalidation for time‑sensitive updates if needed.
- Establish RBAC for editors, audit logs, and review workflows.

Constraints and quality attributes:
- Reliability and performance via CMS CDN and front‑end caching/ISR; offline fallback to last successful build.
- Security via environment‑scoped read‑only API tokens; no write access from the client.
- Cost controlled by selecting an appropriate tier; monitor usage and storage.

Migration and governance:
- One‑time content migration from current JSON; archive originals.
- Define content schema as code (versioned) and document editorial processes.
- Implement periodic content backup/export to mitigate vendor lock‑in; maintain a thin repository‑agnostic content interface to enable future CMS swaps.

We explicitly reject building a custom CMS and self‑hosting a third‑party CMS due to higher maintenance burden. We reject continuing to hard‑code content due to poor editor experience and fragility.

We will implement A/B tests using a centralized feature flag and experiment registry, isolating variant logic from baseline code and avoiding conditional branches within existing MVC files.

- Introduce an Experiment Service responsible for assignment, exposure, and metrics events, backed by a config-driven registry (with metadata: owner, start/end dates, kill switch, removal checklist).
- Route selection will occur at composition boundaries via dependency injection or controller routing to separate modules/controllers/views per variant; no variant-specific if/else in shared code paths.
- Each variant will live in isolated files/namespaces with explicit wiring, enabling straightforward removal by deleting the variant module and registry entry.
- Baseline behavior remains the default; the experiment flag only adds a new route/module without changing existing code paths.
- Tests for baseline remain unchanged. Variant-specific tests are added in parallel directories, scoped to the variant modules and gated by the feature flag. Contract tests ensure both variants meet the same interfaces.
- Deployment and rollout are controlled via configuration (per-env, per-cohort). Telemetry is mandatory and standardized through the Experiment Service.
- Every experiment requires an expiration date and cleanup task created at inception; CI will fail builds for expired experiments to enforce removal.

Adopt a single, cross‑platform, npm‑driven automation flow for all project tasks. Concretely:
- Standardize on npm scripts as the primary task interface (no additional task runners like Gulp/Grunt/Make).
- Provide a bootstrap script (Node-based) invoked via npm run setup that:
  - Verifies prerequisites (Node version, npm).
  - Executes dependency installation via npm ci.
  - Copies required files from dependencies into the application structure deterministically and idempotently.
  - Writes any generated artifacts to a .generated/ or vendor/ directory tracked by .gitignore.
- Expose discrete, composable scripts:
  - npm run setup: one-shot environment bootstrap (safe to re-run).
  - npm start: launches the application in watch/development mode.
  - npm run build: produces a production-ready build (minified, hashed assets).
  - npm test: executes automated tests and linters.
  - npm run clean: removes generated artifacts/node_modules as needed.
  - npm run postinstall: automatically triggers minimal setup steps on install in CI.
- Implement file movement/copy via a Node CLI (e.g., using fs/promises) to ensure Windows/macOS/Linux compatibility; avoid shell-specific commands.
- Provide a single entrypoint script (scripts/cli.mjs) that orchestrates the above tasks and can be invoked directly (node scripts/cli.mjs <task>) if needed.
- Document tasks and expected outcomes in README and package.json descriptions; errors must be actionable with non-zero exits.
- Default to deterministic, repeatable runs (lockfile required) and avoid mutating source outside designated generated directories.

## Decision
We will discontinue the standalone Advance Passenger Info (API) web service and integrate its functionality directly into the drtv2 codebase as an internal module. The API project will be archived and its code migrated into drtv2 with clear domain boundaries and interfaces to preserve modularity and allow potential future extraction.

Key actions:
- Consolidate repositories by moving API logic into drtv2 under a dedicated module/package (e.g., api/ or services/api/), with well-defined interfaces and dependency boundaries.
- Remove cross-service communication and replace with in-process calls to reduce operational overhead, latency, and failure modes.
- Stop targeting PHP drt as a consumer and officially deprecate any shared or public contracts designed for multi-client consumption.
- Refactor external API contracts to internal data models; retain adapter layers to minimize ripple effects and to keep the option to re-expose as a service if priorities change.
- Update CI/CD to build, test, and deploy as part of drtv2; retire the API service pipeline, infrastructure, and monitoring.
- Migrate configuration, secrets, and observability to drtv2 standards; maintain dedicated tracing/logging contexts for the API module.
- Document the deprecation of the standalone service and communicate the change to stakeholders; provide a short-term compatibility note if any auxiliary tools depended on the old endpoint.

Success criteria:
- Single deployment artifact for drtv2 including API functionality.
- Reduced operational complexity and cost (one service, one pipeline).
- No loss of functionality in drtv2; improved performance from in-process integration.
- Maintained modularity enabling future re-separation with minimal effort.

Decide not to implement tracking or automated resubmission of CaiaSoft-denied holds. Aleph is the system of record for valid holds; circrequests will only track which holds have been submitted to CaiaSoft to prevent duplicate submissions. On each synchronization, the application will submit to CaiaSoft only holds that appear in the current Aleph list and have not been previously submitted. Holds that CaiaSoft denies will not be retried automatically, even if they continue to appear in Aleph; resolution occurs via the CaiaSoft interface and/or library workflows. This avoids repeatedly reintroducing denied entries into CaiaSoft, reduces operational noise, and simplifies application logic. If exceptional resubmission is ever required, it will be handled manually or via a future explicit administrative override, not by default retry logic.

- Adopt named exports exclusively for all first-party ESModules; disallow default exports in authored code.
- When a module conceptually exposes a single primary symbol, export it as a named symbol whose identifier reflects its purpose (preferably matching the file/module name) rather than a default.
- Consumers must import via named imports. Example: import { List } from 'list'; not import List from 'list'.
- Public entry points should aggregate and re-export named symbols to provide a stable, discoverable surface. Example: export { Foo } from './foo.js'; export { Bar } from './bar.js';
- Re-exports must remain named. Avoid export default from ... and avoid mixing default with named in re-export barrels.
- Interop:
  - For third-party modules that only provide a default, create a thin adapter that re-exports a named alias: export { default as ThirdPartyThing } from 'third-party';
  - For CommonJS consumers of our packages, expose named properties on module.exports via build tooling or compatibility layers, avoiding synthetic defaults.
- Tooling and enforcement:
  - Enable lint rules (e.g., import/no-default-export, no-restricted-exports for default) and CI gates to prevent regressions.
  - Configure IDE/code actions and codemods to auto-convert default exports/imports to named equivalents.
- Naming conventions:
  - Use PascalCase for components/classes, camelCase for functions/values; keep exported identifier stable and unique across the codebase.
- Scope:
  - Applies to all new code immediately; existing modules with default exports must be migrated to named exports before major releases or when touched significantly.

We will not publish or maintain official packages for any OS or package manager. Instead, we will:
- Release source and portable archives (e.g., .tar.gz/.zip) via tagged Git releases as the canonical distribution.
- Provide clear manual installation instructions (clone/extract + make/install) that require no specific package manager.
- Adopt semantic versioning, maintain a CHANGELOG, and avoid breaking changes without a major version bump to support downstream packagers.
- Sign releases and publish checksums to enable verification by downstream distributors and users.
- Publish concise packaging guidelines (build steps, runtime dependencies, directory conventions, license info, test invocation, example metadata/specs) to assist downstream maintainers across ecosystems (e.g., apt, yum/dnf, Homebrew, BSD ports).
- Remain neutral by neither endorsing nor prioritizing any packaging ecosystem; where appropriate, we may list community-maintained packages in documentation as “community packages” with provenance, without guarantees.
- Direct packaging-specific issues (e.g., distro policy compliance, repo inclusion, update cadence) to the respective downstream maintainers, while addressing upstream issues (bugs, features, portability) in our repository.
- Automate release artifacts (tagging, build, signing, checksum, GitHub Releases) to provide predictable, timely inputs for downstream packaging workflows.

This decision ensures broad user choice via downstream packaging while keeping upstream responsibilities focused on source quality, portability, and stable, verifiable releases.

We will manage all runtime and build-time dependencies via npm using a checked-in package.json and package-lock.json to guarantee reproducible installs across environments.

- Package manager: npm (LTS), with npm ci used in CI/CD for deterministic builds.
- Node version: pinned via .nvmrc and package.json engines to the project’s supported LTS.
- Server framework: express declared with a semver-compatible major range (e.g., ^4.x or ^5.x when adopted) to accept non-breaking updates automatically.
- NHSUK UI Kit: consume the official npm package (@nhsuk/frontend). No CDN at runtime; assets are built and served locally.
- Frontend assets: copied or bundled from node_modules to the app’s public assets directory during build (e.g., via npm scripts or a lightweight bundler such as esbuild/rollup if needed), ensuring offline capability and theme consistency.
- Versioning policy:
  - Use caret ranges for libraries where minor/patch updates are backwards compatible.
  - Pin exact versions for critical or historically unstable packages as required.
  - Lockfile committed to VCS; any changes occur via PR.
- Updates: automate via Dependabot/Renovate to raise PRs for dependency updates with CI verification before merge.
- Integrity and security: enable npm audit in CI; fail builds on high/critical vulnerabilities unless explicitly waived.
- Caching: enable CI caching of ~/.npm and build artifacts to reduce install times; do not check in node_modules.
- Scaffolding: provide npm scripts (install, build, start, dev, test, audit, update:deps) to standardize local and CI workflows.

This approach ensures consistent, secure, and maintainable dependency consumption for Express and the NHSUK UI Kit across all environments without runtime external dependencies.

We will use flutter_downloader as the single, unified download manager across My Space, Received Shares, and Shared Spaces. All file downloads are initiated by enqueuing individual tasks via enqueue(url, saveDir, header...), ensuring consistent behavior and progress tracking regardless of source. Batch downloads (multi-selection) will be implemented by enqueuing multiple single-file tasks in sequence, relying on the library’s internal queue to manage ordering and execution.

Each enqueued task will be associated with its originating space and persisted with its TaskId to enable status tracking, error handling, retry, and user actions (open, cancel, remove). The saveDir will be selected based on the user’s configured storage location and the logical source (to allow organized file placement), and required headers (e.g., authentication) will be provided per task.

The application will expose clear and cancel controls mapped to flutter_downloader’s clear and cancel capabilities, allowing both per-task cancellation and clearing of pending tasks when appropriate. We will not introduce a custom download stack or parallel queue; flutter_downloader’s queue semantics are the single source of truth for download lifecycle and state, providing a uniform UX and minimizing platform-specific complexity.

## Decision
Vi etablerer kontinuerlig leveranse av Modiapersonoversikt som en selvstendig, uavhengig deploybar frontend. Vi praktiserer trunk-based development med små, hyppige endringer (korte PR-er) som merges til main, der main alltid er produksjonsklar. Deploy til produksjon skjer automatisk ved grønn pipeline, uten manuell godkjenning.

All ny funksjonalitet leveres inkrementelt bak feature toggles (serverstyrt, f.eks. Unleash), slik at vi kan:
- Dark-launche og verifisere i produksjon uten å eksponere for alle.
- Gjennomføre gradvis utrulling (canary/rollout per gruppe/enhet/bruker).
- Rulle tilbake umiddelbart ved avvik ved å slå av toggler.

Kvalitetsporter i CI/CD inkluderer automatiske tester (enhet, integrasjon, e2e på kritiske brukerreiser), statisk analyse, bygg- og bundle-sjekker, samt kontraktstester mot API/BFF for å sikre bakoverkompatibilitet når vi leverer små, hyppige endringer. Observability (metrics, logger, feilmeldingsrater, bruker-/feature-metrikker) fungerer som release-gate og for løpende effektmåling.

Vi versjonerer kontinuerlig via tags i stedet for release-brancher og unngår breaking changes; nødvendige migreringer fases inn via toggler og “strangler”-mønster. Vi sikrer uavhengig utvikling og utrulling fra eksisterende modiabrukerdialog, og opprettholder nødvendig kompatibilitet i overgangsperioden.

Denne arbeidsformen optimaliserer flyt, reduserer risiko per leveranse, og muliggjør rask verdileveranse til saksbehandlere med kontrollert eksponering og rask tilbakestilling ved behov.

Adopt Ubuntu LTS (starting with 22.04 LTS and progressing to subsequent LTS releases within support windows) as the standard Linux distribution for all Prometheus hosts across all environments.

Rationale:
- Aligns with existing operational experience in GDS (Verify, GOV.UK), reducing operational risk and accelerating onboarding/support.
- Strong LTS support lifecycle with predictable security updates and kernel/HWE options.
- Broad ecosystem support for Prometheus and exporters, including well-maintained APT repositories and systemd-native service management.
- Compatibility with existing automation, hardening baselines, monitoring/logging agents, and incident response runbooks used by Reliability Engineering.
- Simplifies cross-team collaboration and reuse of tooling, images, and AMIs.

Scope and implications:
- All new Prometheus deployments will use Ubuntu LTS AMIs/images; existing non-Ubuntu deployments will be migrated opportunistically as part of lifecycle events.
- Standardize on APT-based packaging, systemd unit management, and Ubuntu CIS-aligned hardening profiles.
- Maintain golden images and Packer/Terraform modules targeting Ubuntu; ensure parity in CI/CD pipelines and base OS patching processes.
- Amazon Linux is not adopted; it may be reconsidered only if a clear, demonstrable platform constraint or managed service dependency requires it, with a formal ADR revisit.

Review cadence: reassess on new LTS releases and major Prometheus/runtime changes or if organizational platform standards shift.

## Decision
Implement a multi-perspective health/status capability composed of:
- Machine endpoints:
  - /live: minimal liveness probe indicating the process is running (no dependencies).
  - /ready: readiness probe indicating the portal can serve traffic based on mandatory dependencies.
  - /health: comprehensive, machine-readable JSON with component-level checks, severities, and reasons.
- Admin-facing status page (/status): authenticated UI that visualizes the same component checks with drill-down, remediation hints, and historical trend snapshots.

Define a hierarchical health model:
- Components: configuration syntax/semantics, datasource connectivity (I/O), external services, queues, storage, background jobs, feature flags, licensing/quotas.
- Each check reports: name, status {OK, DEGRADED, FAIL, UNKNOWN}, severity {CRITICAL, IMPORTANT, INFO}, lastChecked, duration, and message.
- Overall state is computed via policy:
  - Green: all CRITICAL pass.
  - Yellow: any IMPORTANT fails but all CRITICAL pass.
  - Red: any CRITICAL fails.
  - UNKNOWN if insufficient data at startup.
Severity is configurable per environment, allowing “good state” to vary by perspective and deployment.

Behavioral guarantees:
- /live always OK if process loop is healthy.
- /ready depends only on CRITICAL checks.
- /health returns full detail; unauthenticated callers see only overall state and redacted messages, authenticated admins see full detail.
- Connectivity checks are isolated from configuration syntax checks to distinguish “valid config” from “unreachable datasource.”

Operational considerations:
- Bounded execution time with timeouts and fallbacks; cache last results with TTL.
- Emit metrics and structured logs per check; integrate with monitoring/alerting.
- Backward-compatible JSON schema with versioning.

Adopt SDL2’s logical rendering feature as the single scaling mechanism. The game will target a fixed internal “logical resolution” derived from the classic 15x13 tile grid plus reserved vertical space for UI. All rendering will be performed in this logical coordinate space; SDL_RenderSetLogicalSize will scale to the actual window or display resolution. We will not introduce a separate “world coordinates” system; game logic will operate in terms of tile indices and/or logical pixels consistent with the base grid, and the renderer will not perform additional coordinate conversions beyond SDL’s logical scaling.

We will enable letterboxing/pillarboxing as needed to maintain aspect ratio and prefer integer scaling when possible to preserve visual fidelity. Texture filtering will be set to nearest-neighbor to maintain crisp pixel art. Input handling will use SDL’s logical coordinate mapping to align with the internal resolution.

This approach minimizes complexity in the current codebase while supporting multiple output resolutions. We will revisit a distinct world coordinate system only if future requirements (e.g., camera zoom/pan, sub-tile physics, parallax) demonstrate clear value that outweighs the added complexity.

Adopt a layered architecture with strict, enforceable boundaries to separate concerns, control dependencies, and prevent unauthorized layer access.

- Layers and responsibilities:
  - Presentation (UI/HTTP/gRPC): input handling, request/response mapping, no business logic.
  - Application/Service: orchestration, use cases, transactions, security checks, no UI/IO concerns.
  - Domain: entities, value objects, domain services, invariants; pure business logic, framework-agnostic.
  - Infrastructure: persistence, messaging, external integrations, framework adapters.

- Dependency rules:
  - Dependencies only downward: Presentation → Application → Domain; Infrastructure may be depended on only via defined ports (interfaces) in Application/Domain.
  - Domain has zero dependencies on Presentation/Infrastructure frameworks.
  - Cross-layer access is forbidden except via approved interfaces/ports and DTOs.
  - No lateral coupling across features within the same layer without explicit contracts.

- Communication patterns:
  - Synchronous calls within process: services exposed via interfaces; data passed as DTOs/commands/events.
  - Asynchronous integration via domain/application events; adapters reside in Infrastructure.
  - Mapping between layers via mappers/assemblers; no entity leakage across layer boundaries.

- Enforcement:
  - Package/module structure mirrors layers; limit visibility (e.g., internal modules).
  - Static analysis rules (e.g., ArchUnit/Deptrac), CI checks, and code review checklists to prevent violations.
  - Dependency injection to invert Infrastructure details behind ports.
  - Testing strategy aligned with layers: domain unit tests, application service tests, contract tests for adapters.

- Exceptions and cross-cutting:
  - Cross-cutting concerns (logging, metrics, auth) applied via middleware/aspects without breaking boundaries.
  - Any justified deviations require an explicit exception record and automated rule updates.

We will implement role-based access control using a centralized OpenID Connect provider (e.g., Keycloak) with institutional identity federation:

- Model each cohort as an OIDC client (application).
- Define per-study client roles on the cohort client using the convention ROLE_<STUDY>_RESEARCHER.
- Gate read access to shared folder <study> on the presence of ROLE_<STUDY>_RESEARCHER in the cohort client’s access token/ID token (or via token introspection).
- Federate user identities to their home institutions (SAML/OIDC identity brokering); no local credentials are managed by Armadillo.
- Delegate user and permission administration to cohort representatives by granting them manage-membership permissions for their cohort client roles; they can assign/revoke ROLE_<STUDY>_RESEARCHER to researchers seeking access to that cohort.
- Grant consortium representatives read-only visibility across all cohort clients to list users and their role mappings (no grant/revoke capabilities).
- Enforce least privilege by scoping roles to the cohort client and limiting admin privileges to the relevant cohort.
- Emit standardized role claims in tokens and maintain audit logs of role assignments/changes for traceability and compliance.

Adopt Locust as the primary framework for HTTP load testing and benchmarking, leveraging its greenthread efficiency, distributed workers, and web UI for orchestration and high-level reporting. To address its limitations, we will augment Locust with custom instrumentation and data export:

- Timing control: Bypass the auto-timed HTTP client path for measured segments. Use either catch_response to set explicit response_time based on our stopwatch, or perform I/O with an external client (e.g., httpx) and emit custom metrics via locust.events.request.fire, ensuring event time covers precisely the code path of interest (not just the HTTP layer).
- Raw data capture: Subscribe to Locust’s request events and stream per-sample measurements to an external sink (e.g., CSV/Parquet or Kafka). In parallel, build HDR histograms in-process using hdrhistogram to persist both raw and histogrammed data for offline analysis.
- Reporting split: Use Locust’s UI and summaries for operational monitoring during runs; use offline analysis notebooks/dashboards for percentiles, tail analysis, and comparative baselines from the exported raw data/HDR files.
- Validation: Implement cross-checks that compare Locust’s summary stats with the offline histograms to detect drift or instrumentation errors.
- Scope guardrail: If a benchmark requires precise non-HTTP timing (e.g., cross-service workflows, client-side processing), encapsulate the measured region explicitly and emit custom metric events; if this proves unworkable for a specific case, fall back to a minimal standalone harness for that case only.

This decision provides rapid authoring, scalable load generation, and an operator-friendly UI while preserving access to raw per-sample data and precise control over what we time.

Adopt AndroidX WorkManager as the primary orchestration mechanism for all background file transfers (uploads/downloads) and related sync tasks in the mobile app.

- Use OneTimeWorkRequest for discrete upload/download operations; use PeriodicWorkRequest for recurring sync.
- Configure constraints to ensure reliable transfer: require network connected (and optionally unmetered for large payloads), battery-not-low for heavy tasks, and device-charging where appropriate.
- Implement resilient execution with WorkManager’s guaranteed delivery, persisted work across app/device restarts, exponential backoff on failures, and automatic retries on network interruptions.
- Model multi-step transfers (e.g., chunked/multipart upload, checksum/commit) as chained work with input/output data passing; tag and uniquely name work to prevent duplication and enable targeted cancellation.
- Surface long-running user-initiated transfers as foreground Work (setForeground with ForegroundInfo) with system notification compliance; use expedited work only when latency is critical and allowed by quotas.
- Provide observable progress and state to the UI via WorkManager’s LiveData/Flow observation, setProgress for incremental updates, and robust cancellation (e.g., on user action, logout, or policy changes).
- Enforce security and governance: persist only minimal metadata in WorkData, avoid placing PII/large blobs there, and ensure encrypted at-rest/at-transit data using the networking stack (e.g., OkHttp) outside WorkManager.
- Standardize retry/backoff policies, concurrency limits, and queue policies (e.g., KEEP/REPLACE for unique work) to control throughput and resource usage; separate queues for uploads vs. downloads when needed.
- Reserve alternatives (e.g., system DownloadManager) only for OS-managed public downloads; otherwise, keep a single scheduling model with WorkManager to maximize consistency and compatibility across Android versions.

This decision ensures background execution aligned with system health best practices, resilience to network changes and restarts, and a unified, observable pipeline for cloud file management.

We will implement two distinct, pluggable comparison strategies for whale observations using the Strategy pattern. An ObservationComparator interface (compare(a, b): int) will define total ordering requirements. Two concrete, domain-defined comparator implementations will be provided to realize the two proposed sorting methods. Each comparator will:
- Be pure and deterministic, producing a total order.
- Handle missing/partial data with explicit rules and consistent tie-breakers (final tie-breaker: observationId).
- Be unit- and timezone-safe, normalizing inputs as needed.
- Avoid locale-sensitive comparisons unless explicitly required.

Sorting will use a stable sort from the standard library to preserve relative order of equal keys. Selection of the comparator will be driven by a SortMode enum exposed in APIs/CLI, mapped via a ComparatorRegistry. Default mode is Chronological unless explicitly overridden. The chosen SortMode will be recorded in dataset/query metadata to ensure reproducibility; comparator versions will be versioned and embedded in outputs (e.g., sortMode=Chronological:v1).

For performance and consistency on large datasets, comparators may precompute immutable sort keys per observation (e.g., normalized timestamps, species rank) and cache them within the sort scope. Memory usage will be bounded and tunable.

This design isolates domain-specific ordering logic, enables straightforward addition of future sorting methods as new comparator implementations, and minimizes regression risk through unit and property-based tests that validate total ordering, stability, null handling, and determinism across platforms.

## Decision

Adopt trunk-based development with short-lived pull requests as the only path to main. The main branch is protected and always releasable.

- All changes are developed on brief-lived branches and merged via PRs within 24–48 hours; long-lived branches are prohibited.
- Keep PRs small and focused; prefer incremental slices behind feature flags/toggles to avoid breaking user-facing behavior while integrating frequently.
- Require at least one peer review (CODEOWNERS where applicable). Encourage asynchronous discussion in the PR; use drafts for early visibility.
- Enforce mandatory status checks before merge: compile/build, unit tests, integration/contract tests where applicable, static analysis/linters, code coverage threshold, dependency/license/security scans, and formatting.
- Enable branch protection rules: required reviews, required status checks, dismiss stale approvals on updates, linear history, and no direct pushes to main.
- Use squash-merge to maintain a clean, comprehensible history per change; avoid merge commits from feature branches.
- Automatically deploy from main via CI/CD when all gates pass; use progressive delivery (e.g., canary/percentage rollouts) controlled by flags to reduce blast radius.
- If main breaks, prioritize immediate fix-forward; if not resolved quickly, revert the offending change via PR.
- Set SLAs: PRs should be reviewed within a business day; CI pipelines should complete within a target duration (e.g., <15 minutes). Optimize pipelines to sustain this.
- Monitor and publish PR and build health metrics (lead time, change failure rate, MTTR) to continuously improve flow and quality.

Adopt an immutable Auto Scaling Group pattern: create a new ASG for every Launch Configuration change and cut over traffic, then decommission the old ASG.

- Each LC update results in a new, uniquely named ASG referencing that LC. The previous ASG remains intact until the new ASG is healthy and serving traffic.
- Terraform will manage this with distinct ASG resources per revision and cutover orchestration:
  - Use ELB/ALB Target Groups to attach both ASGs during transition.
  - Scale the new ASG to desired capacity, wait for health checks, then detach/drain and scale down the old ASG.
  - Destroy the old ASG only after all instances are drained/terminated.
- Enforce create-before-destroy semantics to guarantee capacity and minimize risk.
- All instance-level changes (AMI, user-data, security groups, tags) are guaranteed to propagate immediately to the new fleet, eliminating long-lived drift and manual terminations.
- Avoid embedding CloudFormation and avoid ad-hoc instance termination; rely solely on Terraform to declaratively manage lifecycle and rollouts.
- Naming/versioning conventions (e.g., ASG and LC with timestamp or hash suffix) ensure coexistence during rollout and clear traceability.
- Rollout policy can be tuned (e.g., maxSurge/maxUnavailable equivalents via ASG capacities) to meet SLOs and cost constraints.

This decision ensures predictable, fast propagation of LC changes, safer deployments, and full rollback capability by retaining the previous ASG until the new one is verified.

We will adopt a faceted taxonomy with a canonical, version-agnostic “group” dimension shared across all ES versions. Each kata must reference one or more canonical group IDs (slugs) from a centrally managed registry rather than using free-text group names. Example canonical IDs: array-api, object-api, string-api.

Details:
- Group registry: A version-controlled JSON/YAML file defines all allowed groups with fields: id (slug), displayName, description, aliases (legacy names), i18n labels, and optional parent for hierarchical grouping. New groups require review.
- Kata schema: Katas include fields: version (e.g., ES6), groups (list of canonical group IDs), optional primaryGroup, and tags. Free-text groups are disallowed.
- Aggregation: UIs and APIs aggregate katas by group across versions using canonical IDs, enabling “all Array API katas” views regardless of ES version.
- Backward compatibility: A migration map translates legacy group names to canonical IDs. CI validation enforces canonical usage and flags unmapped names.
- Governance and consistency: PR checks validate that every group referenced by a kata exists in the registry; registry changes require approval from maintainers. Aliases allow gentle deprecation while keeping URLs stable.
- URLs and presentation: Routes use canonical group slugs (e.g., /katas/group/array-api), while display names come from the registry and support localization.
- Extensibility: Hierarchical groups support future refinements (e.g., array-api > iteration), without coupling to ES versions.

This decision ensures consistent grouping across ES1/6/7/10+, enables cross-version aggregation, and provides a single source of truth for group semantics and presentation.

We will use forwarders with bounded, persistent buffering sized to absorb expected database unavailability without data loss, while protecting cluster stability.

- Metrics: Use Prometheus with local TSDB WAL and retention configured to cover the target outage window (default 24 hours of typical ingest). Enable backpressure to scrape targets at normal cadence; if storage nears threshold, prefer dropping oldest local samples over evicting Prometheus. Remote write resumes on recovery.

- Logs: Use fluentd with persistent file buffer on a dedicated StorageClass. Size buffers for the same outage window (default 24 hours), use chunked, at-least-once delivery with exponential backoff and retry. When buffer reaches a high-watermark, start dropping oldest chunks to prevent node or PV exhaustion.

- Storage resilience: Allocate dedicated PVs with quotas and alerts; set filesystem and application-level watermarks; avoid sharing buffers with critical system volumes. Prefer storage classes with good availability; tolerate temporary CSI hiccups via retry/backoff.

- Availability: Run fluentd as a DaemonSet with node-local buffers; run Prometheus in HA (two replicas) to avoid single forwarder outage. Forwarders must be restart-safe (no data loss beyond configured bounds).

- Operations: Continuously monitor buffer utilization, disk usage, and backpressure; alert before saturation; document and review sizing quarterly. Accept bounded loss beyond configured retention to safeguard cluster reliability.

We will standardize system startup around a single, deterministic boot pipeline with explicit phases and extensibility points:

- Adopt a unified boot sequence: Relocate → Zero .bss → Call constructors → Initialize RTOS (optional) → Set default hardware pin states → Create drivers → Configure system.
- Implement a Boot Manager that executes ordered phases via a registry. Each phase exposes pre/post hooks and can be enabled/disabled by build-time flags (e.g., no-RTOS, minimal boot).
- Define strict contracts per phase:
  - Inputs/outputs, allowed side effects, and idempotency requirements.
  - No cross-phase resource access before its owning phase completes (e.g., drivers cannot access pins until pin defaults applied).
  - Fail-fast on unrecoverable errors; return standardized status codes for recoverable failures.
- Provide a board/platform descriptor (compile-time manifest) for pin defaults and driver inventory, plus overridable runtime configuration for system tuning.
- Use a single entry point (Reset_Handler) that delegates to the Boot Manager, replacing ad-hoc initialization in scattered modules.
- Support platform-specific early init hooks (e.g., clock, MPU, caches) before Relocate, guarded by conditional compilation.
- Enforce logging/trace at each phase (with compile-time selectable sinks) and watchdog-friendly timeouts to prevent hangs.
- Require unit and integration tests per phase, plus a simulation harness to validate ordering, timing, and failure paths.
- Establish recovery: on phase failure, attempt rollback/diagnostic mode; if RTOS initialized, switch to a minimal safe task set; otherwise enter a safe loop.
- Version the boot pipeline schema and maintain backward-compatible defaults; additions must be appended as new phases or hooks to avoid breaking existing boards.

## Decision
- Minimize the number and criticality of runtime third-party dependencies to maximize availability. For user-facing, revenue- or safety-critical paths, prefer in-house implementations or deploy vendor-neutral abstractions. Adopt external services at runtime only when they deliver clear strategic value with strong SLAs and multi-region resilience, and when graceful degradation is achievable.

- Encapsulate all external services behind an internal anti-corruption layer with strict timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and idempotency. Pin API versions and contracts; changes must be opt-in and tested via canary releases.

- Where third-party outputs are stable during run, implement caching or replication: prefetch/warm caches, define TTLs and staleness policies, and provide local fallbacks to sustain service during vendor outages. For reference data or deterministic computations, prefer periodic syncs or precomputation to eliminate live calls on the critical path.

- In build and development environments, prioritize speed and cost efficiency by leveraging managed third-party services and hosted tooling. Do not invest heavily in independence here beyond basic resiliency (e.g., retrying artifact fetches); accept higher dependency churn.

- Classify dependencies by impact (Tier 1: critical path, Tier 2: non-critical runtime, Tier 3: build/dev) and apply controls accordingly. Maintain an exit strategy for each Tier 1/2 vendor, review dependency posture semi-annually, and track compliance/security posture continuously.

Adopt explicit, instance-based logging configured at application bootstrap; avoid all global/singleton logger configuration and mutable global state.

- Introduce a LoggerProvider (factory) initialized from an application Config at startup. Components obtain a logger via dependency injection from this provider; no global accessors or module-level state.
- Logger instances are immutable and contextual. Support child/context loggers (e.g., with_fields/request_id) without mutating shared state.
- Configuration is explicit and versioned, sourced from environment variables and config files. Supported options: level per namespace, appenders/sinks, formatter, sampling, and redaction rules.
- Defaults: STDOUT sink, INFO level, UTC timestamps. Development formatter: human-readable/colorized. Production formatter: structured JSON with stable keys.
- Sinks support fan-out (e.g., console, file, syslog/HTTP), are thread-safe, and non-blocking with bounded queues and backpressure/drop policies configurable per sink.
- Provide an adapter that implements Ruby’s Logger-compatible interface for third-party libraries, scoped to the provider; do not mutate third-party globals. Disallow direct use of global loggers (e.g., SomeLogger[...] or global constants).
- Namespacing: each component/class receives a namespaced logger (e.g., logger.with_namespace("MyClass")); levels can be overridden per namespace via config.
- Correlation: include request/trace IDs and other context via scoped loggers rather than thread-local/global variables.
- Testing: supply a TestLogger and in-memory sink for assertions; tests inject loggers explicitly. No test relies on or mutates global logging state.
- Operational controls: allow runtime reconfiguration through hot-reload of the provider’s config (opt-in), applied atomically by replacing the provider; existing logger instances continue functioning with previous settings until replaced.

This decision ensures deterministic, testable, and composable logging without unintended global side effects while supporting structured, multi-sink, and contextual logging needs.

Decision

Adopt a monorepo with one npm package per component, supplemented by an optional “umbrella” package that re-exports all components.

- Repository structure: pnpm workspaces (or Yarn/NPM workspaces) with one package per component (independent semver), plus:
  - @org/design-system (umbrella) that depends on and re-exports all components for one-line install and DX.
  - @org/config/* (build, ESLint/TS config) shared packages to standardize tooling.
- Versioning and publishing: independent versioning per component using Changesets (or Nx release). Conventional commits drive semver. CI publishes changed packages. The umbrella package auto-bumps and republishes when any constituent component changes.
- Dependencies:
  - React and other shared externals as peerDependencies.
  - Internal component inter-dependencies allowed; use caret ranges and Changesets to coordinate bumps.
- Build and tree-shaking:
  - Emit ESM + CJS + type declarations; mark sideEffects: false.
  - Ensure per-entry re-exports in the umbrella package to enable dead-code elimination.
- Consumption patterns:
  - Performance-critical apps import only needed components (@org/button).
  - Simplicity-first apps install @org/design-system and import from it; bundlers tree-shake unused parts.
- Style guide:
  - Lives in the monorepo; consumes workspace packages for local dev.
  - Deployed independently of component releases. For released docs, publish per-tag Storybook (or Storybook composition) to represent multiple versions concurrently (e.g., latest, previous minors).
  - “Next/canary” channel builds from main to preview unreleased changes.
- Release policy:
  - Backward-compatible changes prefer additive APIs; breaking changes require major bumps per component and umbrella.
  - Document migration notes in component CHANGELOGs; umbrella CHANGELOG aggregates.
- Mitigations to cons:
  - Installing many packages manually is optional due to the umbrella package.
  - Interdependencies and publishing complexity handled by Changesets and workspace linking.
  - Avoid unintended app-wide changes by pinning only the specific component versions; umbrella users accept coordinated updates with clear changelogs.

Adopt explicit, stateful modeling of enzyme phosphorylation as a first-class regulatory mechanism in the metabolic simulation. Each enzyme will exist in at least two discrete states: active (unphosphorylated) and inactive (phosphorylated), with phosphorylation events deactivating catalytic function and dephosphorylation restoring activity. Kinases and phosphatases will be represented as catalytic reactions that toggle enzyme states, with kinetics parameterized independently from metabolic reactions.

We will:
- Encode phosphorylation/dephosphorylation as separate reactions with their own stoichiometry, catalysts (specific kinases/phosphatases), and kinetic laws (mass-action or Michaelis–Menten as appropriate).
- Represent enzyme states distinctly in the model (e.g., E_active, E_P), ensuring flux through metabolic reactions is conditioned on the active state only.
- Integrate regulatory reactions into the same ODE/SSA simulation engine as metabolic fluxes to capture dynamic coupling between signaling and metabolism.
- Support modular extension for multi-site phosphorylation by expanding state space as needed, defaulting to a single-site binary model for tractability.
- Centralize parameters (kcat, Km, kphos, kdephos) with configuration-driven overrides to enable organism- or context-specific tuning.
- Provide deterministic and stochastic solvers with consistent handling of state transitions and ensure serialization/export compatibility with standard model formats.

This decision ensures accurate, dynamic regulation of metabolic networks via phosphorylation while maintaining model clarity, performance, and extensibility.

Adopt Jest snapshot testing to detect unintended visual output changes in React components.

- Scope: Use snapshots primarily for leaf/presentational components with stable markup. Avoid large or frequently changing containers, logic-heavy components, and dynamic content; prefer explicit assertions for behavior there.
- Tooling: Use Jest with React Testing Library and toMatchSnapshot/inline snapshots. Commit snapshot files to the repository. Add serializers for CSS-in-JS/styled-components and HTML formatting to ensure stable diffs. Mock nondeterminism (dates, timers, random, UUIDs, timezones) and network calls.
- Process: Snapshots must be reviewed like code. Updating snapshots requires intent via --updateSnapshot and clear PR rationale. Cap snapshot size to keep diffs meaningful; break down components or switch to targeted assertions if snapshots become noisy.
- CI: Fail builds on snapshot mismatches. Run Jest in CI with consistent environment/config (node version, locale). Cache node_modules but not snapshot artifacts outside VCS.
- Organization: Co-locate tests with components. One snapshot per significant variant/state; rely on data-driven test cases over sprawling single snapshots. Document when snapshots are added/retired.
- Maintenance: Periodically prune stale snapshots, refactor over brittle snapshots, and prefer inline snapshots for small outputs. Add lint rules/pre-commit checks to prevent accidental mass updates.
- Alternatives: For pixel-level regressions, complement (not replace) with visual regression tooling via Storybook/Playwright if needed.

## Decision
Adopt the Alfresco community benchmark framework as the authoritative benchmark harness for validating REQ production-readiness, implemented with TAS for REST API scenarios. We will not adopt the APS JMeter-based benchmark as the primary solution; it may be used only for ad-hoc smoke comparisons if needed, but will not be a source of record.

Implementation approach:
- Create a dedicated benchmark driver project (cloned from a sample such as Benchmark-claims), defining test-context.xml, EventProcessor, and LoadProcessor to execute APS-specific scenarios.
- Author test scenarios in TAS DSL, reusing REST models for benchmark, data preparation for UI tests, and integration testing to maximize consistency and reduce duplication.
- Register the Test Suite Definition with the Management Server, schedule/runs via the Management UI/API, and execute via scalable Driver Servers.
- Persist results to MongoDB and expose them via the Management Server for analysis and audit.

Operationalization:
- Integrate benchmark runs into CI/CD with environment-specific configuration, secrets management, and parameterized load profiles aligned to REQ targets (throughput, concurrency, latency, error budgets, endurance).
- Define pass/fail SLOs and thresholds per scenario; results will be reproducible, comparable across runs, and retained for reports.
- Enable horizontal scaling by adding Driver Servers to meet peak load requirements; ensure deterministic test data provisioning and cleanup.

De-scoped/constraints:
- No separate APS REST test project exists; TAS models will serve as the single source for REST assertions.
- JMeter artifacts will not be maintained or extended as part of this effort.

Adopt TypeScript as the default language for all client-side development. All new frontend code, including the Vue 3/Vuex rewrite, will be authored in TypeScript. We will not perform a wholesale migration of existing JavaScript; legacy code will be migrated opportunistically when modules are touched or fully rewritten.

Set up and enforce a TypeScript toolchain across the frontend: a shared tsconfig with strict type-checking, integrated linting and formatting, editor support, and CI type checks as gates for merge. Public APIs, domain models, and Vue component props/emit contracts must be fully typed; internal implementation details may use transitional typing (e.g., unknown/any) only with documented follow-up tasks. New packages, components, and utilities must be delivered with types and tests.

Align with Vue 3’s TypeScript-first ecosystem by using idiomatic patterns (Composition API with typed refs/reactive state, typed Vuex/Pinia stores, and typed HTTP/DTO layers). Provide starter templates, coding guidelines, and examples to reduce learning curve and onboarding friction; schedule focused training and code reviews to disseminate best practices.

Deprecate plain JavaScript for new client-side code. Track migration progress and technical debt in the backlog. This decision prioritizes maintainability, readability, safer refactoring, and IDE/tooling benefits, leverages existing sunk setup effort, and aligns our stack with Vue 3’s direction while minimizing disruption through incremental migration.

The Voice Assistance Platform (VAP) owns VRS determination for explicit utterances via a dedicated VRS Resolver component. Upon classifying an utterance as explicit, the VRS Resolver extracts intent, entities, and context (caller profile, channel metadata, prior turn state) using the platform’s NLU, then maps the result to a specific VRS using a capability registry and routing policy. The VRS capability registry (catalog) is curated by the platform and populated by VRS providers through a governed contract (declared intents, required entities, locales, confidence thresholds, SLAs). Routing policy supports priority ordering, disambiguation, and A/B policies.

Key behaviors:
- For explicit utterances: resolve a single target VRS with confidence ≥ threshold; if multiple candidates match, apply tie-break rules (priority, specialization, tenancy) or request a clarification prompt. If confidence < threshold, fall back to general assistant or a safe default (configurable).
- For implicit utterances: skip VRS resolution and continue passive monitoring; no VRS engaged.
- Errors/timeouts: fail fast with user-friendly fallback and log for triage.
- Multi-turn: maintain resolution state per session; allow handoff or escalation if downstream VRS signals unsupported scope.

Interfaces and contracts:
- Input: utterance text/audio features, metadata, session context.
- Output: VRS identifier, confidence score, rationale code, required slots, and any disambiguation prompt if needed.
- Catalog sync: versioned, backward-compatible schema to onboard/update VRS capabilities without redeploying the VAP.

Governance and observability:
- Telemetry on match rates, confidence distributions, fallbacks, and user clarifications.
- Policy-driven safeguards for jurisdiction/tenant routing and PII minimization.
- Rollout controls (feature flags) for new VRS entries and routing rules.

Rationale: Centralizing VRS determination in the VAP ensures consistent user experience, single enforcement point for policy/compliance, easier observability, and decouples VRS providers from utterance interpretation and routing concerns. VRS services remain focused on fulfilling requests once selected, not on selection logic.

We will replace DynamicServiceLocator and the deprecated dedicated application with a centralized Mapping Orchestration Service that uses a simplified, opinionated configuration model and a single service-location strategy.

Key aspects:
- Configuration model: Convention-over-configuration with only the required fields: source, destination, messageType, mappingSpecRef, version, and optional feature flags. No pluggable locators or redundant indirections.
- Storage and delivery: All configurations are stored centrally (database-backed registry) and managed via an admin UI and a REST API. JSON will be the canonical format; YAML export/import is supported for CI.
- Routing and execution: Routing is determined solely by (SRC, DST, MSG_TYPE[, version]). Mapping execution uses a single standardized pipeline; optional steps (e.g., validation, enrichment) are toggled via feature flags, not via custom XML graphs.
- Backward compatibility: A one-time importer ingests existing filesystem XML (SRC-DST-MSG_TYPE.xml) and deprecated app configs into the new model, preserving identifiers and versions. Runtime fallback to filesystem/XML is removed after migration.
- Extensibility: Extensibility points are limited to mappingSpec implementations and enrichment/validation libraries registered centrally; no custom per-route service locators.
- Governance: Versioning, validation, and approval workflows are enforced in the UI/API. Changes are auditable and rollbacks supported.
- Operations: Zero-downtime rollout via blue/green configuration sets; feature flags allow gradual enablement per route. Access is controlled per tenant/partner.

This decision simplifies the model, aligns with centralized processing, and improves maintainability and UI clarity while providing a structured migration path.
